imbibition.c: Imbibition Im`bi*bi"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. imbibition.] The act or process of imbibing, or absorbing; as, the post-mortem imbibition of poisons. Bacon.

imbitter.c: Imbitter Im*bit"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbittered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbittering.] [Pref. im- in + bitter. Cf. Embitter.] [Written also embitter.] To make bitter; hence, to make distressing or more distressing; to make sad, morose, sour, or malignant.

imbitterer.c: Imbitterer Im*bit"ter*er (?), n. One who, or that which, imbitters.

imbitterment.c: Imbitterment Im*bit"ter*ment (?), n. The act of imbittering; bitter feeling; embitterment.

imbody.c: Imbody Im*bod"y (?), v. i. [See Embody.] To become corporeal; to assume the qualities of a material body. See Embody.

imboil.c: Imboil Im*boil" (?), v. t. & i. [Obs.] See Emboil.

imbonity.c: Imbonity Im*bon"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. im- not + L. bonitas goodness.] Lack of goodness. [Obs.] Burton.

imborder.c: Imborder Im*bor"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbordered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbordering.] [Pref. im- in + border. Cf. Emborder.] To furnish or inclose with a border; to form a border of. Milton.

imbosk.c: Imbosk Im*bosk" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbosked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbosking.] [CF. It. imboscare to imbosk, imboscarsi to retire into a wood; pref. im- in + bosco wood. See Boscage, and cf. Ambush.] To conceal, as in bushes; to hide. [Obs.] Shelton.
Imbosk Im*bosk", v. i. To be concealed. [R.] Milton.

imbosom.c: Imbosom Im*bos"om (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbosomed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbosoming.] [Pref. im- in + bosom. Cf. Embosom.] 1. To hold in the bosom; to cherish in the heart or affection; to embosom.

imbosture.c: Imbosture Im*bos"ture (?), n. [See Emboss.] Embossed or raised work. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

imbound.c: Imbound Im*bound" (?), v. t. To inclose in limits; to shut in. [Obs.] Shak.

imbow.c: Imbow Im*bow" (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + bow. Cf. Embow.] To make like a bow; to curve; to arch; to vault; to embow. “Imbowed windows.” Bacon.

imbower.c: Imbower Im*bow"er (?), v. t. & i. See Embower.

imbowment.c: Imbowment Im*bow"ment (?), n. act of imbowing; an arch; a vault. Bacon.

imbox.c: Imbox Im*box" (?), v. t. To inclose in a box.

imbrangle.c: Imbrangle Im*bran"gle (?), v. t. To entangle as in a cobweb; to mix confusedly. [R.] Hudibras.

imbreed.c: Imbreed Im*breed" (?), v. t. [Cf. Inbreed.] To generate within; to inbreed. [Obs.] Hakewill.

imbricated.c: Imbricated Imbricate { Im"bri*cate (?), Im"bri*ca`ted (?), } a. [L. imbricatus, p. p. of imbricare to cover with tiles, to form like a gutter tile, fr. imbrex, -icis, a hollow tile, gutter tile, fr. imber rain.] 1. Bent and hollowed like a roof or gutter tile.

imbricate.c: Imbricate Im"bri*cate (?), v. t. To lay in order, one lapping over another, so as to form an imbricated surface.

imbrication.c: Imbrication Im`bri*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. imbrication.] An overlapping of the edges, like that of tiles or shingles; hence, intricacy of structure; also, a pattern or decoration representing such a structure.

imbrocado.c: Imbrocado Im`bro*ca"do (?), n.; pl. Imbrocadoes (#). [See Brocade.] Cloth of silver or of gold. [R.]

imbroccata.c: Imbroccata Imbrocata { ‖Im`bro*ca"ta (?), Im`broc*ca"ta }, n. [It. imbroccata.] A hit or thrust. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

imbroglio.c: Imbroglio Im*brogl"io (?), n.; pl. Imbroglios (#). [Written also embroglio.] [It. See 1st Broil, and cf. Embroil.] 1. An intricate, complicated plot, as of a drama or work of fiction.

imbrown.c: Imbrown Im*brown" (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + brown. Cf. Embrown.] To make brown; to obscure; to darken; to tan; as, features imbrowned by exposure.

imbrue.c: Imbrue Im*brue" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbureed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbureing.] [Cf. OF. embruer, also embruver, embreuver, embrever, to give to drink, soak (see pref. En-, 1, 1st In-, and Breverage), but also OE. enbrewen, enbrowen, to stain, soil (cf. Brewis).] To wet or moisten; to soak; to drench, especially in blood.

imbruement.c: Imbruement Im*brue"ment (?), n. The act of imbruing or state of being imbrued.

imbrute.c: Imbrute Im*brute" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbruted; p. pr. & vb. n. Imbruting.] [Pref. im- in + brute: cf. F. abrutir. Cf. Embrute.] To degrade to the state of a brute; to make brutal.
Imbrute Im*brute", v. i. To sink to the state of a brute.

imbrutement.c: Imbrutement Im*brute"ment (?), n. The act of imbruting, or the state of being imbruted. [R.] Brydges.

imbue.c: Imbue Im*bue" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imbued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imbuing.] [L. imbuere; pref. im- in + perh. a disused simple word akin to L. bibere to drink. Cf. Imbibe.] 1. To tinge deeply; to dye; to cause to absorb; as, clothes thoroughly imbued with black.

imbuement.c: Imbuement Im*bue"ment (?), n. The act of imbuing; the state of being imbued; hence, a deep tincture.

imburse.c: Imburse Im*burse" (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + burse: cf. F. embourser to put into one's purse. See Burse, and Purse.] To supply or stock with money. [Obs.]

imbursement.c: Imbursement Im*burse"ment (?), n. 1. The act of imbursing, or the state of being imbursed. [Obs.]

imesatin.c: Imesatin I*mes"a*tin (?), n. [Imide + isatin.] (Chem.) A dark yellow, crystalline substance, obtained by the action of ammonia on isatin.

imide.c: Imide Im"ide (?), n. (Chem.) A compound with, or derivative of, the imido group; specif., a compound of one or more acid radicals with the imido group, or with a monamine; hence, also, a derivative of ammonia, in which two atoms of hydrogen have been replaced by divalent basic or acid radicals; -- frequently used as a combining form; as, succinimide.

imido.c: Imido Im"i*do (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, containing, or combined with, the radical NH, which is called the imido group.

imitability.c: Imitability Im`it*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [See Imitable.] The quality of being imitable. Norris.

imitable.c: Imitable Im"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. imitabilis: cf. F. imitable. See Imitate.] 1. Capable of being imitated or copied.

imitableness.c: Imitableness Im"i*ta*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being imitable; worthness of imitation.

imitancy.c: Imitancy Im"i*tan*cy (?), n. [From L. imitans, p. pr. of imitare.] Tendency to imitation. [R.] Carlyle.

imitate.c: Imitate Im"i*tate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imitated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imitating (?).] [L. imitatus, p. p. of imitari to imitate; of unknown origin. Cf. Image.] 1. To follow as a pattern, model, or example; to copy or strive to copy, in acts, manners etc.

imitation.c: Imitation Im"i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. imitatio: cf. F. imitation.] 1. The act of imitating.

imitational.c: Imitational Im`i*ta"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or employed in, imitation; as, imitational propensities.

imitative.c: Imitative Im"i*ta*tive (?), a. [L. imitavitus: cf. F. imitatif.] 1. Inclined to imitate, copy, or follow; imitating; exhibiting some of the qualities or characteristics of a pattern or model; dependent on example; not original; as, man is an imitative being; painting is an imitative art.
Imitative Im"i*ta*tive, n. (Gram.) A verb expressive of imitation or resemblance. [R.]

imitatorship.c: Imitatorship Im"i*ta`tor*ship, n. The state or office of an imitator. “Servile imitatorship.” Marston.

imitatress.c: Imitatress Im"i*ta`tress (?), n. A woman who is an imitator.

immaculate.c: Immaculate Im*mac"u*late (?), a. [L. immaculatus; pref. im- not + maculatus, p. p. of maculare to spot, stane, fr. macula spot. See Mail armor.] Without stain or blemish; spotless; undefiled; clear; pure.

immailed.c: Immailed Im*mailed" (?), a. Wearing mail or armor; clad of armor. W. Browne.

immanacle.c: Immanacle Im*man"a*cle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immanacled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immanacling (?).] To manacle; to fetter; hence; to confine; to restrain from free action.

immanation.c: Immanation Im"ma*na"tion (?), n. [Pref. im- in + L. manare to flow; cf. mantio a flowing.] A flowing or entering in; -- opposed to emanation. [R.] Good.

immane.c: Immane Im*mane" (?), a. [L. immanis.] Very great; huge; vast; also, monstrous in character; inhuman; atrocious; fierce. [Obs.] “So immane a man.” Chapman.

immanency.c: Immanency Immanence { Im"ma*nence (?), Im"ma*nen*cy (?), } n. The condition or quality of being immanent; inherence; an indwelling.

immanent.c: Immanent Im"ma*nent (?), a. [L. immanens, p. pr. of immanere to remain in or near; pref. im- in + manere to remain: cf. F. immanent.] Remaining within; inherent; indwelling; abiding; intrinsic; internal or subjective; hence, limited in activity, agency, or effect, to the subject or associated acts; -- opposed to emanant, transitory, transitive, or objective.

immanifest.c: Immanifest Im*man"i*fest (?), a. Not manifest. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

immanity.c: Immanity Im*man"i*ty (?), n. [L. immanitas.] The state or quality of being immane; barbarity. [R.] Shak.

immanuel.c: Immanuel Im*man"u*el (?), n. [Heb. 'immān?ēl, fr. 'im with + ān? us + ēl God.] God with us; -- an appellation of the Christ. Is. vii. 14. Matt. i. 23.

immarcescible.c: Immarcescible Im`mar*ces"ci*ble (?), a. [L. immarcescibilis; pref. im- not + marcescere to fade: cf. F. immarcescible.] Unfading; lasting. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

immarginate.c: Immarginate Im*mar"gin*ate (?), a. (Bot.) Not having a distinctive margin or border. Grey.

immask.c: Immask Im*mask" (?), v. t. To cover, as with a mask; to disguise or conceal. [R.] Shak.

immaterial.c: Immaterial Im`ma*te"ri*al (ĭm`mȧ*tē"rĭ*ail), a. [Pref. im- not + material: cf. F. immatériel.] 1. Not consisting of matter; incorporeal; spiritual; disembodied.

immaterialism.c: Immaterialism Im`ma*te"ri*al*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. immatérialisme.] 1. The doctrine that immaterial substances or spiritual being exist, or are possible.

immaterialist.c: Immaterialist Im`ma*te"ri*al*ist, n. [Cf. F. immatérialiste.] (Philos.) One who believes in or professes, immaterialism.

immateriality.c: Immateriality Im`ma*te`ri*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Immaterialities (#). [Cf. F. immatérialité.] The state or quality of being immaterial or incorporeal; as, the immateriality of the soul.

immaterialize.c: Immaterialize Im`ma*te"ri*al*ize (?), v. t. [Cf. F. immatérialiser.] To render immaterial or incorporeal.

immaterially.c: Immaterially Im`ma*te"ri*al*ly, adv. 1. In an immaterial manner; without matter or corporeal substance.

immaterialness.c: Immaterialness Im`ma*te"ri*al*ness, n. The state or quality of being immaterial; immateriality.

immature.c: Immature Im`ma*ture" (?), a. [L. immaturus; pref. im- not + maturus mature, ripe. See Mature.] 1. Not mature; unripe; not arrived at perfection of full development; crude; unfinished; as, immature fruit; immature character; immature plans. “An ill-measured and immature counsel.” Bacon.

immaturely.c: Immaturely Im`ma*ture"ly (?), adv. In an immature manner. Warburion.

immatureness.c: Immatureness Im`ma*ture"ness, n. The state or quality of being immature; immaturity. Boyle.

immaturity.c: Immaturity Im`ma*tu"ri*ty (?), n. [L. immaturitas: cf. F. immaturité.] The state or quality of being immature or not fully developed; unripeness; incompleteness.

immeability.c: Immeability Im`me*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. im- not + L. meabilis passable, fr. meare to pass.] Lack of power to pass, or to permit passage; impassableness.

immeasurability.c: Immeasurability Im*meas`ur*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being immeasurable; immensurability.

immeasurable.c: Immeasurable Im*meas"ur*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + measurable: cf. F. measurable. Cf. Immensurable, Unmeasurable.] Incapable of being measured; indefinitely extensive; illimitable; immensurable; vast.

immeasurableness.c: Immeasurableness Im*meas"ur*a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being immeasurable.

immeasurably.c: Immeasurably Im*meas"ur*a*bly, adv. In an immeasurable manner or degree. “Immeasurably distant.” Wordsworth.

immechanical.c: Immechanical Im`me*chan"ic*al (?), a. Not mechanical. [Obs.] Cheyne. -- Im"me*chan"ic*al*ly, adv. [Obs.]

immediacy.c: Immediacy Im*me"di*a*cy (?), n. The relation of freedom from the interventionof a medium; immediateness. Shak.

immediate.c: Immediate Im*me"di*ate (?), a. [F. immédiat. See In- not, and Mediate.] 1. Not separated in respect to place by anything intervening; proximate; close; as, immediate contact.

immediately.c: Immediately Im*me"di*ate*ly (?), adv. 1. In an immediate manner; without intervention of any other person or thing; proximately; directly; -- opposed to mediately; as, immediately contiguous.

immediateness.c: Immediateness Im*me"di*ate*ness, n. The quality or relations of being immediate in manner, place, or time; exemption from second or interventing causes. Bp. Hall.

immedicable.c: Immedicable Im*med"i*ca*ble (?), a. [L. Immedicabilis. See In- not, and Medicable.] Not to be healed; incurable. “Wounds immedicable.” Milton.

immemorable.c: Immemorable Im*mem"o*ra*ble (?), a. [L. immemorabilis; pref. im- not + memorabilis memorable: cf. F. immémorable. See Memorable.] Not memorable; not worth remembering. Johnson.

immemorial.c: Immemorial Im`me*mo"ri*al (?), a. [Pref. im- not + memorial: cf. F. immémorial.] Extending beyond the reach of memory, record, or tradition; indefinitely ancient; as, existing from time immemorial. “Immemorial elms.” Tennyson. “Immemorial usage or custom.” Sir M. Hale.

immense.c: Immense Im*mense" (?), a. [L. immensus; pref. im- not + mensus, p. p. of metiri to measure: cf. F. immense. See Measure.] Immeasurable; unlimited. In commonest use: Very great; vast; huge. “Immense the power” Pope. “Immense and boundless ocean.” Daniel.

immensely.c: Immensely Im*mense"ly, adv. In immense manner or degree.

immenseness.c: Immenseness Im*mense"ness, n. The state of being immense.

immensity.c: Immensity Im*men"si*ty (?), n.; pl. Immensities (#). [L. immensitas: cf. F. immensité.] The state or quality of being immense; inlimited or immeasurable extension; infinity; vastness in extent or bulk; greatness.

immensurability.c: Immensurability Im*men`su*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being immensurable.

immensurable.c: Immensurable Im*men"su*ra*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + L. mensurabilis measurable: cf. F. immensurable. Cf. Immeasurable.] Immeasurable.

immensurate.c: Immensurate Im*men"su*rate (?), a. [Pref. im- not + mensurate.] Unmeasured; unlimited. [R.] W. Montagu.

immerge.c: Immerge Im*merge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immerged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immerging (?).] [L. immergere; pref. im- in + mergere to dip, plunge: cf. F. immerger. See Merge, and cf. Immerse.] To plungel into, under, or within anything especially a fuid; to dip; to immerse. See Immerse.
Immerge Im*merge" (?), v. i. To dissapear by entering into any medium, as a star into the light of the sun. [R.]

immerit.c: Immerit Im*mer"it (?), n. Lack of worth; demerit. [R.] Suckling.

immeritous.c: Immeritous Im*mer"it*ous (?), a. [L. immeritus; pref. im- not + meritus, p. p. of merere, mereri, to deserve.] Undeserving. [Obs.] Milton.

immerse.c: Immerse Im*merse" (?), a. [L. immersus, p. p. of immergere. See Immerge.] Immersed; buried; hid; sunk. [Obs.] “Things immerse in matter.” Bacon.
Immerse Im*merse", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immersed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immersing.] 1. To plunge into anything that surrounds or covers, especially into a fluid; to dip; to sink; to bury; to immerge.

immersed.c: Immersed Im*mersed" (?), p. p. & a. 1. Deeply plunged into anything, especially a fluid.

immersible.c: Immersible Im*mers"i*ble (?), a. [From Immerse.] Capable of being immersed.
Immersible Im*mers"i*ble, a. [Pref. im- not + L. mersus, p. p. of mergere to plunge.] Not capable of being immersed.

immersion.c: Immersion Im*mer"sion (?), n. [L. immersio; cf. F. immersion.] 1. The act of immersing, or the state of being immersed; a sinking within a fluid; a dipping; as, the immersion of Achilles in the Styx.

immersionist.c: Immersionist Im*mer"sion*ist, n. (Eccl.) One who holds the doctrine that immersion is essential to Christian baptism.

immesh.c: Immesh Im*mesh" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immeshed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immeshing.] [Pref. im- in + mesh. Cf. Inmesh.] To catch or entangle in, or as in, the meshes of a net. or in a web; to insnare.

immethodical.c: Immethodical Im`me*thod"ic*al (?), a. Not methodical; without method or systematic arrangement; without order or regularity; confused. Addison.

immethodically.c: Immethodically Im`me*thod"ic*al*ly, adv. Without method; confusedly; unsystematically.

immethodize.c: Immethodize Im*meth"od*ize (?), v. t. To render immethodical; to destroy the method of; to confuse. [R.]

immetrical.c: Immetrical Im*met"ric*al (?), a. Not metrical or rhythmical. [R.] Chapman.

immigrant.c: Immigrant Im"mi*grant (?), n. [L. immigrans, p. pr. of immigrare to go into: cf. F. immigrant. See Immigrate.] One who immigrates; one who comes to a country for the purpose of permanent residence; -- correlative of emigrant.

immigrate.c: Immigrate Im"mi*grate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immigrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immigrating (?).] [L. immigrare, immigratum, to immigrate; pref. im- in + migrare to migrate. See Migrate.] To come into a country of which one is not a native, for the purpose of permanent residence. See Emigrate.

immigration.c: Immigration Im"mi*gra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. immigration.] The act of immigrating; the passing or coming into a country for the purpose of permanent residence.

imminence.c: Imminence Im"mi*nence (?), n. [Cf. F. imminence, L. imminentia, See Imminent.] 1. The condition or quality of being imminent; a threatening, as of something about to happen. The imminence of any danger or distress. Fuller.

imminent.c: Imminent Im"mi*nent (?), a. [L. imminens, p. pr. of imminere to project; pref. im- in + minere (in comp.) to jut, project. See Eminent.] 1. Threatening to occur immediately; near at hand; impending; -- said especially of misfortune or peril. “In danger imminent.” Spenser.

imminently.c: Imminently Im"mi*nent*ly, adv. In an imminent manner.

immingle.c: Immingle Im*min"gle (?), v. t. To mingle; to mix; to unite; to blend. [R.] Thomson.

imminution.c: Imminution Im`mi*nu"tion (?), n. [L. imminutio, fr. imminuere, imminutum, to lessen; pref. im- in + minuere.] A lessening; diminution; decrease. [R.] Ray.

immiscibility.c: Immiscibility Im*mis"ci*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. immiscibilité.] Incapability of being mixed, or mingled.

immiscible.c: Immiscible Im*mis"ci*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + miscible: cf. F. immiscible.] 1. Not capable of being mixed or mingled.

immission.c: Immission Im*mis"sion (?), n. [L. immissio: cf. F. immission. See Immit.] The act of immitting, or of sending or thrusting in; injection; -- the correlative of emission.

immit.c: Immit Im*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immitted; p. pr. & vb. n. Immiting.] [L. immittere, immissum; pref. im- in + mittere to send.] To send in; to inject; to infuse; -- the correlative of emit. [R.] Boyle.

immitigable.c: Immitigable Im*mit"i*ga*ble (?), a. [L. immitigabilis; fr. pref. im- not + mitigare to mitigate.] Not capable of being mitigated, softened, or appeased. Coleridge.

immitigably.c: Immitigably Im*mit"i*ga*bly (?), adv. In an immitigable manner.

immix.c: Immix Im*mix" (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + mix.] To mix; to mingle. [R.]

immixable.c: Immixable Im*mix"a*ble (?), a. Not mixable. Bp. Wilkins.

immixed.c: Immixed Im*mixed" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + mixed, p. p. of mix.] Unmixed. [Obs.]

immixture.c: Immixture Im*mix"ture (?), n. Freedom from mixture; purity. [R.] W. Montagu.

immobile.c: Immobile Im*mo"bile (?), a. [L. immobilis: cf. F. immobile. See Immobility.] Incapable of being moved; immovable; fixed; stable. Prof. Shedd.

immobility.c: Immobility Im`mo*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. immobilitas, fr. immobilis immovable; pref. im- not + mobilis movable: cf. F. immobilité. See Mobile.] The condition or quality of being immobile; fixedness in place or state.

immobilize.c: Immobilize Im*mob"i*lize (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + mobilize; cf. f. immobiliser.] To make immovable; in surgery, to make immovable (a naturally mobile part, as a joint) by the use of splints, or stiffened bandages.

immoderacy.c: Immoderacy Im*mod"er*a*cy (?), n. [From Immoderate.] Immoderateness. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

immoderancy.c: Immoderancy Im*mod"er*an*cy (?), n. [L. immoderantia.] Immoderateness; excess. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

immoderate.c: Immoderate Im*mod"er*ate (?), a. [L. immoderatus; pref. im- not + moderatus moderate. See Moderate.] Not moderate; exceeding just or usual and suitable bounds; excessive; extravagant; unreasonable; as, immoderate demands; immoderate grief; immoderate laughter.

immoderately.c: Immoderately Im*mod"er*ate*ly, adv. In an immoderate manner; excessively.

immoderateness.c: Immoderateness Im*mod"er*ate*ness, n. The quality of being immoderate; excess; extravagance. Puller.

immoderation.c: Immoderation Im*mod`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. immoderatio: cf. F. imodération.] Lack of moderation. Hallywell.

immodest.c: Immodest Im*mod"est (?), a. [F. immodeste, L. immodestus immoderate; pref. im- not + modestus modest. See Modest.] 1. Not limited to due bounds; immoderate.

immodestly.c: Immodestly Im*mod"est*ly, adv. In an immodest manner.

immodesty.c: Immodesty Im*mod"es*ty (?), n. [L. immodestia: cf. F. immodestie.] Lack of modesty, delicacy, or decent reserve; indecency. “A piece of immodesty.” Pope.

immolate.c: Immolate Im"mo*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immolated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immolating.] [L. immolatus, p. p. of immolare to sacrifice, orig., to sprinkle a victim with sacrifical meal; pref. im- in + mola grits or grains of spelt coarsely ground and mixed with salt; also, mill. See Molar, Meal ground grain.] 1. To sacrifice; to offer in sacrifice; to kill, as a sacrificial victim.

immolation.c: Immolation Im`mo*la"tion (?), n. [L. immolatio: cf. F. immolation.] 1. The act of immolating, or the state of being immolated, or sacrificed. Sir. T. Browne.

immolator.c: Immolator Im"mo*la`tor (?), n. [L.] One who offers in sacrifice; specifically, one of a sect of Russian fanatics who practice self-mutilation and sacrifice.

immould.c: Immould Immold { Im*mold", Im*mould" } (?), v. t. To mold into shape, or form. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.

immoment.c: Immoment Im*mo"ment (?), a. [See Immomentous.] Trifling. [R.] “Immoment toys.” Shak.

immomentous.c: Immomentous Im`mo*men"tous (?), a. [Pref. im- not + momentous.] Not momentous; unimportant; insignificant. [R.] A. Seward.

immoral.c: Immoral Im*mor"al (?), a. [Pref. im- not + moral: cf. F. immoral.] Not moral; inconsistent with rectitude, purity, or good morals; contrary to conscience or the divine law; wicked; unjust; dishonest; vicious; licentious; as, an immoral man; an immoral deed.

immorality.c: Immorality Im`mo*ral"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Immoralities (#). [Cf. F. immoralité.] 1. The state or quality of being immoral; vice.

immorally.c: Immorally Im*mor"al*ly (?), adv. In an immoral manner; wickedly.

immorigerous.c: Immorigerous Im`mo*rig"er*ous (?), a. [Pref. im- not + morigerous.] Rude; uncivil; disobedient. [Obs.] -- Im`mo*rig"er*ous*ness, n. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

immortal.c: Immortal Im*mor"tal (?), a. [L. immortalis; pref. im- not + mortalis mortal: cf. F. immortel. See Mortal, and cf. Immortelle.] 1. Not mortal; exempt from liability to die; undying; imperishable; lasting forever; having unlimited, or eternal, existance.
Immortal Im*mor"tal (?), n. One who will never cease to be; one exempt from death, decay, or annihilation. Bunyan.

immortalist.c: Immortalist Im*mor"tal*ist, n. One who holds the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

immortality.c: Immortality Im`mor*tal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Immortalities (#). [L. immortalitas: cf. F. immortalité.] 1. The quality or state of being immortal; exemption from death and annihilation; unending existance; as, the immortality of the soul.

immortalization.c: Immortalization Im*mor`tal*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of immortalizing, or state of being immortalized.

immortalize.c: Immortalize Im*mor"tal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immortalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immortalizing (?).] [Cf. F. immortaliser.] 1. To render immortal; to cause to live or exist forever. S. Clarke.
Immortalize Im*mor"tal*ize, v. i. To become immortal. [R.]

immortally.c: Immortally Im*mor"tal*ly, adv. In an immortal manner.

immortelle.c: Immortelle Im`mor*telle" (?), n.; pl. Immortelles (#). [F. See Immortal.] (Bot.) A plant with a conspicuous, dry, unwithering involucre, as the species of Antennaria, Helichrysum, Gomphrena, etc. See Everlasting.

immortification.c: Immortification Im*mor`ti*fi*ca"tion (?), n. Failure to mortify the passions. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

immovability.c: Immovability Im*mov"a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being immovable; fixedness; steadfastness; as, immovability of a heavy body; immovability of purpose.

immovable.c: Immovable Im*mov"a*ble (?), a. 1. Incapable of being moved; firmly fixed; fast; -- used of material things; as, an immovable foundation.
Immovable Im*mov"a*ble, n. 1. That which can not be moved.

immovableness.c: Immovableness Im*mov"a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being immovable.

immovably.c: Immovably Im*mov"a*bly, adv. In an immovable manner.

immund.c: Immund Im*mund" (?), a. [L. immundus; pref. im- not + mundus clean.] Unclean. [R.] Burton.

immundicity.c: Immundicity Im`mun*dic"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. immondicité, L. immunditia, immundities.] Uncleanness; filthiness. [R.] W. Montagu.

immune.c: Immune Im*mune" (?), a. [L. immunis. See Immunity.] 1. Exempt; protected. -- Im*mu"nize (#), v. t.
Immune Im*mune" (?), n. One who is immune; esp., a person who is immune from a disease by reason of previous affection with the disease or inoculation.

immunity.c: Immunity Im*mu"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Immunities (#). [L. immunitas, fr. immunis free from a public service; pref. im- not + munis complaisant, obliging, cf. munus service, duty: cf. F. immunité. See Common, and cf. Mean, a.] 1. Freedom or exemption from any charge, duty, obligation, office, tax, imposition, penalty, or service; a particular privilege; as, the immunities of the free cities of Germany; the immunities of the clergy.

immure.c: Immure Im*mure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Immured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Immuring.] [Pref. im- in + mure: cf. F. emmurer.] 1. To wall around; to surround with walls. [Obs.] Sandys.
Immure Im*mure", n. A wall; an inclosure. [Obs.] Shak.

immurement.c: Immurement Im*mure"ment (?), n. The act of immuring, or the state of being immured; imprisonment.

immusical.c: Immusical Im*mu"sic*al (?), a. Inharmonious; unmusical; discordant. Bacon.

immutability.c: Immutability Im*mu`ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. immutabilitas: cf. F. immutabilité.] The state or quality of being immutable; immutableness. Heb. vi. 17.

immutable.c: Immutable Im*mu"ta*ble (?), a. [L. immutabilis; pref. im- not + mutabilis mutable. See Mutable.] Not mutable; not capable or susceptible of change; unchangeable; unalterable.

immutate.c: Immutate Im*mu"tate (ĭm*mū"tat), a. [L. immutatus, p. p. of immature.] Unchanged. [Obs.]

immutation.c: Immutation Im"mu*ta"tion (?), n. [L. immutatio, from immutare, immutatum, to change. See Immute.] Change; alteration; mutation. [R.] Dr. H. More.

immute.c: Immute Im*mute" (ĭm*mūt"), v. t. [L. immutare, immutatum; perf. im- in + mutare to change: cf. OF. immuter.] To change or alter. [Obs.] J. Salkeld.

imp.c: Imp Imp (ĭmp), n. [OE. imp a graft, AS. impa; akin to Dan. ympe, Sw. ymp, prob. fr. LL. impotus, Gr.? engrafted, innate, fr.? to implant;? in +? to produce; akin to E. be. See 1st In-, Be.] 1. A shoot; a scion; a bud; a slip; a graft. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Imp Imp, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imping.] [AS. impian to imp, ingraft, plant; akin to Dan. ympe, Sw. ympa, OHG. impfōn, impitōn, G. impfen. See Imp, n.] 1. To graft; to insert as a scion. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

impacable.c: Impacable Im*pa"ca*ble (?), a. [L. pref. im- not + pacare to quiet. See Pacate.] Not to be appeased or quieted. [Obs.] Spenser. -- Im*pa"ca*bly, adv.

impackment.c: Impackment Im*pack"ment (?), n. [Pref. im- in + pack.] The state of being closely surrounded, crowded, or pressed, as by ice. [R.] Kane.

impact.c: Impact Im*pact" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impacted; p. pr. & vb. n. Impacting.] [L. impactus, p. p. of impingere to push, strike against. See Impinge.] 1. To drive close; to press firmly together: to wedge into a place. Woodward.
Impact Im"pact (?), n. 1. Contact or impression by touch; collision; forcible contact; force communicated.

impacted.c: Impacted Im*pact"ed (?), a. 1. Driven together or close.

impaction.c: Impaction Im*pac"tion (?), n. [L. impactio a striking: cf. F. impaction.] 1. (Surg.) The driving of one fragment of bone into another so that the fragments are not movable upon each other; as, impaction of the skull or of the hip.

impaint.c: Impaint Im*paint" (?), v. t. To paint; to adorn with colors. [R.] “To impaint his cause.” Shak.

impair.c: Impair Im*pair" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impaired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impairing.] [Written also empair.] [OE. empeiren, enpeiren, OF. empeirier, empirier, F. empirer, LL. impejorare; L. pref. im- in + pejorare to make worse, fr. pejor worse. Cf. Appair.] To make worse; to diminish in quantity, value, excellence, or strength; to deteriorate; as, to impair health, character, the mind, value.
Impair Im*pair", v. t. To grow worse; to deteriorate. Milton.
Impair Im"pair (?), a. [F. impair uneven, L. impar; im- not + par equal.] Not fit or appropriate. [Obs.]

impairer.c: Impairer Im*pair"er (?), n. One who, or that which, impairs.

impairment.c: Impairment Im*pair"ment (?), n. [OE. enpeirement, OF. empirement.] The state, act, or process of being impaired; injury. “The impairment of my health.” Dryden.

impale.c: Impale Im*pale" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impaled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impaling.] [See 2d Empale.] 1. To pierce with a pale; to put to death by fixing on a sharp stake. See Empale.

impalement.c: Impalement Im*pale"ment (?), n. 1. The act of impaling, or the state of being impaled. Byron.

impallid.c: Impallid Im*pal"lid (?), v. t. To make pallid; to blanch. [Obs.] Feltham.

impalm.c: Impalm Im*palm" (?), v. t. To grasp with or hold in the hand. [R.] J. Barlow.

impalpability.c: Impalpability Im*pal`pa*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impalpabilité.] The quality of being impalpable. Jortin.

impalpable.c: Impalpable Im*pal"pa*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + palpable: cf. F. impalpable.] 1. Not palpable; that cannot be felt; extremely fine, so that no grit can be perceived by touch. “Impalpable powder.” Boyle.

impalpably.c: Impalpably Im*pal"pa*bly, adv. In an impalpable manner.

impalsy.c: Impalsy Im*pal"sy (?), v. t. To palsy; to paralyze; to deaden. [R.]

impanate.c: Impanate Im*pa"nate (?), a. [LL. impanatus, p. p. of impanare to impanate; L. pref. im- in + panis bread.] Embodied in bread, esp. in the bread of the eucharist. [Obs.] Cranmer.
Impanate Im*pa"nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impanated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impanating.] To embody in bread, esp. in the bread of the eucharist. [Obs.]

impanation.c: Impanation Im"pa*na"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. impanation. See Impanate, a.] (Eccl.) Embodiment in bread; the supposed real presence and union of Christ's material body and blood with the substance of the elements of the eucharist without a change in their nature; -- distinguished from transubstantiation, which supposes a miraculous change of the substance of the elements. It is akin to consubstantiation.

impanator.c: Impanator Im*pa"na*tor (?), n. [LL.] (Eccl.) One who holds the doctrine of impanation.

impanel.c: Impanel Im*pan"el (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impaneled (?) or Impanelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Impaneling or Impanelling.] [Pref. im- in + panel. Cf. Empanel.] [Written also empanel.] To enter in a list, or on a piece of parchment, called a panel; to form or enroll, as a list of jurors in a court of justice. Blackstone.

impanelment.c: Impanelment Im*pan"el*ment (?), n. The act or process of impaneling, or the state of being impaneled.

imparadise.c: Imparadise Im*par"a*dise (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imparadised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imparadising (?).] [Pref. im- + paradise: cf. F. emparadiser.] To put in a state like paradise; to make supremely happy. “Imparadised in one another's arms.” Milton.

impardonable.c: Impardonable Im*par"don*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. impardonnable.] Unpardonable. [Obs.] South.

imparidigitate.c: Imparidigitate Im*par`i*dig"i*tate (?), a. [L. impar unequal + digitus finger.] (Anat.) Having an odd number of fingers or toes, either one, three, or five, as in the horse, tapir, rhinoceros, etc.

imparipinnate.c: Imparipinnate Im*par"i*pin"nate (?), a. [L. impar unequal + E. pinnate.] (Bot.) Pinnate with a single terminal leaflet.

imparisyllabic.c: Imparisyllabic Im*par"i*syl*lab"ic (?), a. [L. impar unequal + E. syllabic: cf. F. imparisyllabique.] (Gram.) Not consisting of an equal number of syllables; as, an imparisyllabic noun, one which has not the same number of syllables in all the cases; as, lapis, lapidis; mens, mentis.

imparity.c: Imparity Im*par"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. im- + parity: cf. F. imparité.] 1. Inequality; disparity; disproportion; difference of degree, rank, excellence, number, etc. Milton.

impark.c: Impark Im*park" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imparked (?), p. pr. & vb. n. Imparking.] [Cf. Empark.] To inclose for a park; to sever from a common; hence, to inclose or shut up.

imparl.c: Imparl Im*parl" (?), v. i. [OF. emparler; pref. em- (L. in) + parler to speak. See In, prep., and Parley.] 1. To hold discourse; to parley. [Obs.] Sir. T. North.

imparlance.c: Imparlance Im*par"lance (?), n. [Cf. Emparlance, Parlance.] [Written also inparliance.] 1. Mutual discourse; conference. [Obs.]

imparsonee.c: Imparsonee Im*par`son*ee" (?), a. [OF. empersone. See 1st In-, and Parson.] (Eng. Eccl. Law) Presented, instituted, and inducted into a rectory, and in full possession. -- n. A clergyman so inducted.

impart.c: Impart Im*part" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imparted; p. pr. & vb. n. Imparting.] [OF. impartir, empartir, L. impartire, impertire; pref. im- in + partire to part, divide, fr. pars, partis, part, share. See Part, n. ] 1. To bestow a share or portion of; to give, grant, or communicate; to allow another to partake in; as, to impart food to the poor; the sun imparts warmth.
Impart Im*part" (?), v. i. 1. To give a part or share.

impartation.c: Impartation Im`par*ta"tion (?), n. The act of imparting, or the thing imparted.

impartial.c: Impartial Im*par"tial (?), a. [Pref. im- not + partial: cf. F. impartial.] Not partial; not favoring one more than another; treating all alike; unprejudiced; unbiased; disinterested; equitable; fair; just. Shak.

impartialist.c: Impartialist Im*par"tial*ist, n. One who is impartial. [R.] Boyle.

impartiality.c: Impartiality Im*par`ti*al"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impartialité.] The quality of being impartial; freedom from bias or favoritism; disinterestedness; equitableness; fairness; as, impartiality of judgment, of treatment, etc.

impartially.c: Impartially Im*par"tial*ly (?), a. In an impartial manner.

impartialness.c: Impartialness Im*par"tial*ness, n. Impartiality. Sir W. Temple.

impartibility.c: Impartibility Im*part`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being impartible; communicability. Blackstone.
Impartibility Im*part`i*bil"i*ty, n. [Cf. F. impartibilité.] The quality of being incapable of division into parts; indivisibility. Holland.

impartible.c: Impartible Im*part"i*ble (?), a. [From Impart.] Capable of being imparted or communicated.
Impartible Im*part"i*ble, a. [Pref. im- not + partible: cf. F. impartible.] Not partible; not subject to partition; indivisible; as, an impartible estate. Blackstone.

impartment.c: Impartment Im*part"ment (?), n. The act of imparting, or that which is imparted, communicated, or disclosed. [R.]

impassable.c: Impassable Im*pass"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. Unpassable.] Incapable of being passed; not admitting a passage; as, an impassable road, mountain, or gulf. Milton. -- Im*pass"a*ble*ness, n. -- Im*pass"a*bly, adv.

impasse.c: Impasse ‖Im`passe" (ăN`päs"; E. ĭm*pȧs"), n. [F.] An impassable road or way; a blind alley; cul-de-sac; fig., a position or predicament affording no escape.

impassibility.c: Impassibility Im*pas`si*bil"i*ty (?), a. [L. impassibilitas: cf. F. impassibilité.] The quality or condition of being impassible; insusceptibility of injury from external things.

impassible.c: Impassible Im*pas"si*ble (?), a. [L. impassibilis; pref. im- not + passibilis passable: cf. F. impassible. See Passible.] Incapable of suffering; inaccessible to harm or pain; not to be touched or moved to passion or sympathy; unfeeling, or not showing feeling; without sensation. “Impassible to the critic.” Sir W. Scott.

impassion.c: Impassion Im*pas"sion (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + passion. Cf. Empassion, Impassionate, v.] To move or affect strongly with passion. [Archaic] Chapman.

impassionable.c: Impassionable Im*pas"sion*a*ble (?), a. Excitable; susceptible of strong emotion.

impassionate.c: Impassionate Im*pas"sion*ate (?), v. t. To affect powerfully; to arouse the passions of. Dr. H. More.
Impassionate Im*pas"sion*ate (?), a. [Pref. im- not + passionate.] Without passion or feeling. Burton.

impassioned.c: Impassioned Im*pas"sioned (?), p. p. & a. Actuated or characterized by passion or zeal; showing warmth of feeling; ardent; animated; excited; as, an impassioned orator or discourse.

impassive.c: Impassive Im*pas"sive (?), a. Not susceptible of pain or suffering; apathetic; impassible; unmoved.

impassivity.c: Impassivity Im`pas*siv"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being insusceptible of feeling, pain, or suffering; impassiveness.

impastation.c: Impastation Im`pas*ta"tion (?), n. [F. See Impaste.] The act of making into paste; that which is formed into a paste or mixture; specifically, a combination of different substances by means of cements.

impaste.c: Impaste Im*paste" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impasted; p. pr. & vb. n. Impasting.] [Pref. im- in + paste: cf. It. impastare, OF. empaster, F. empâter. See 1st In- and Paste.] 1. To knead; to make into paste; to concrete. “Blood... baked and impasted.” Shak.

impasting.c: Impasting Im*past"ing, (Paint.) The laying on of colors to produce impasto.

impasto.c: Impasto Im*pas"to (?), n. [It. See Impaste.] (Paint.) The thickness of the layer or body of pigment applied by the painter to his canvas with especial reference to the juxtaposition of different colors and tints in forming a harmonious whole. Fairholt.

impasture.c: Impasture Im*pas"ture (?), v. t. To place in a pasture; to foster. [R.] T. Adams.

impatible.c: Impatible Im*pat"i*ble (?), a. [L. impatibilis; pref. im- not + patibilis supportable. See Patible.] 1. Not capable of being borne; impassible.

impatience.c: Impatience Im*pa"tience (?) n. [OE. impacience, F. impatience, fr. L. impatientia.] The quality of being impatient; lack of endurance of pain, suffering, opposition, or delay; eagerness for change, or for something expected; restlessness; chafing of spirit; fretfulness; passion; as, the impatience of a child or an invalid.

impatiens.c: Impatiens ‖Im*pa"ti*ens (ĭm*pā"shĭ*ĕnz), prop. n. [L., impatient.] (Bot.) A genus of plants, several species of which have very beautiful flowers; -- so called because the elastic capsules burst when touched, and scatter the seeds with considerable force. Called also touch-me-not, jewelweed, and snapweed. Impatiens Balsamina (sometimes called lady's slipper) is the common garden balsam.

impatient.c: Impatient Im*pa"tient (ĭm*pā"sheint), a. [OE. impacient, F. impatient, fr. L. impatiens; pref. im- not + patiens patient. See Patient.] 1. Not patient; not bearing with composure; intolerant; uneasy; fretful; restless, because of pain, delay, or opposition; eager for change, or for something expected; hasty; passionate; -- often followed by at, for, of, and under.
Impatient Im*pa"tient, n. One who is impatient. [R.]

impatiently.c: Impatiently Im*pa"tient*ly, adv. In an impatient manner.

impatronization.c: Impatronization Im*pat`ron*i*za"tion (?), n. Absolute seignory or possession; the act of investing with such possession. [R.] Cotgrave.

impatronize.c: Impatronize Im*pat"ron*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impatronized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impatronizing (?).] To make lord or master; as, to impatronize one's self of a seigniory. [R.] Bacon.

impavid.c: Impavid Im*pav"id (?), a. [L. impavidus. See In- not, and Pavid.] Fearless. -- Im*pav"id*ly, adv.

impawn.c: Impawn Im*pawn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impawned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impawning.] [Pref. im- + pawn: cf. Empawn.] To put in pawn; to pledge; to pawn. Shak.

impeach.c: Impeach Im*peach" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impeached (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impeaching.] [OE. empeechier to prevent, hinder, bar, F. empêcher, L. impedicare to entangle; pref. im- in + pedica fetter, fr. pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and Appeach, Dispatch, Impede.] 1. To hinder; to impede; to prevent. [Obs.]

impeachable.c: Impeachable Im*peach"a*ble (?), a. That may be impeached; liable to impeachment; chargeable with a crime.

impeachment.c: Impeachment Im*peach"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. empêchement.] The act of impeaching, or the state of being impeached; as: (a) Hindrance; impediment; obstruction. [Obs.]

impearl.c: Impearl Im*pearl" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impearled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impearling.] [Pref. im- in + pearl: cf. F. emperler.] 1. To form into pearls, or into that which resembles pearls. [Poetic]

impeccability.c: Impeccability Im*pec`ca*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impeccabilité.] The quality of being impeccable; exemption from sin, error, or offense.

impeccable.c: Impeccable Im*pec"ca*ble (?), a. [L. impeccabilis; pref. im- not + peccare to err, to sin: cf. F. impeccable.] Not liable to sin; exempt from the possibility of doing wrong. -- n. One who is impeccable; esp., one of a sect of Gnostic heretics who asserted their sinlessness.

impecuniosity.c: Impecuniosity Im`pe*cu`ni*os"i*ty (?), n. The state of being impecunious. Thackeray. Sir W. Scott.

impecunious.c: Impecunious Im"pe*cu"ni*ous (?), a. [L. im- not + pecunia money: cf. F. impécunieux.] Not having money; habitually without money; poor.

impedance.c: Impedance Im*ped"ance (?), n. [Impede + -ance.] (Elec.) The apparent resistance in an electric circuit to the flow of an alternating current, analogous to the actual electrical resistance to a direct current, being the ratio of electromotive force to the current. It is equal to R2 + X2, where R = ohmic resistance, X = reactance. For an inductive circuit, X = 2πfL, where f = frequency and L = self-inductance; for a circuit with capacity X = 1 ÷ 2πfC, where C = capacity.

impede.c: Impede Im*pede" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impeded; p. pr. & vb. n. Impeding.] [L. impedire, lit., to entangle the feet; pref. im- in + pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and cf. Impeach.] To hinder; to stop in progress; to obstruct; as, to impede the advance of troops.

impedible.c: Impedible Im*ped"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being impeded or hindered. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

impediment.c: Impediment Im*ped"i*ment (?), n. [L. impedimentum: cf. F. impediment.] That which impedes or hinders progress, motion, activity, or effect.
Impediment Im*ped"i*ment, v. t. To impede. [R.] Bp. Reynolds.

impedimenta.c: Impedimenta ‖Im*ped`i*men"ta (?), n. pl. [L. See Impediment, Impede.] Things which impede or hinder progress; incumbrances; baggage; specif. (Mil.), the supply trains which must accompany an army.

impedimental.c: Impedimental Im*ped`i*men"tal (?), a. Of the nature of an impediment; hindering; obstructing; impeditive.

impedite.c: Impedite Im"pe*dite (?), a. [L. impeditus, p. p. See Impede.] Hindered; obstructed. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
Impedite Im"pe*dite, v. t. To impede. [Obs.] Boyle.

impedition.c: Impedition Im"pe*di"tion (?), n. [L. impeditio.] A hindering; a hindrance. [Obs.] Baxier.

impeditive.c: Impeditive Im*ped"i*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. impéditif.] Causing hindrance; impeding. “Cumbersome, and impeditive of motion.” Bp. Hall.

impel.c: Impel Im*pel" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impelled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impelling.] [L. impellere; pref. im- in + pellere, pulsum, to drive. See Pulse a beat, and cf. Impulse.] To drive or urge forward or on; to press on; to incite to action or motion in any way.

impellent.c: Impellent Im*pel"lent (?), a. [L. impellens, p. pr. of impellere.] Having the quality of impelling.
Impellent Im*pel"lent, n. An impelling power or force. Glanvill.

impeller.c: Impeller Im*pel"ler (?), n. One who, or that which, impels.

impen.c: Impen Im*pen" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impenned (?) and Impent (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impenning.] To shut up or inclose, as in a pen. Feltham.

impend.c: Impend Im*pend" (?), v. t. [L. impendĕre; pref. im- in + pendĕre to weigh out, pay.] To pay. [Obs.] Fabyan.

Impend Im*pend", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Impended; p. pr. & vb. n. Impending.] [L. impendēre; pref. im- in + pendēre to hang. See Pendant.] To hang over; to be suspended above; to threaten from near at hand; to menace; to be imminent. See Imminent.

impendency.c: Impendency Impendence { Im*pend"ence (?), Im*pend"en*cy (?), } n. The state of impending; the state of being imminent and liable to happen soon; also, that which impends. “Impendence of volcanic cloud.” Ruskin.

impendent.c: Impendent Im*pend"ent (?), a. [L. impendens, p. pr. of impendēre.] Impending; threatening.

impending.c: Impending Im*pend"ing, a. Hanging over; overhanging; suspended so as to menace; imminet; threatening.

impenetrability.c: Impenetrability Im*pen`e*tra*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impénétrabilité.] 1. Quality of being impenetrable.

impenetrable.c: Impenetrable Im*pen"e*tra*ble (?), a. [L. impenetrabilis; pref. im- not + penetrabilis penetrable: cf. F. impénétrable.] 1. Incapable of being penetrated or pierced; not admitting the passage of other bodies; not to be entered; impervious; as, an impenetrable shield.

impenetrableness.c: Impenetrableness Im*pen"e*tra*ble*ness (?), n. The quality of being impenetrable; impenetrability.

impenetrably.c: Impenetrably Im*pen"e*tra*bly, adv. In an impenetrable manner or state; imperviously. “Impenetrably armed.” Milton. “Impenetrably dull.” Pope.

impenitence.c: Impenitence Im*pen"i*tence (?), n. [L. impenitentia: cf. F. impénitence.] The condition of being impenitent; failure or refusal to repent; hardness of heart.

impenitent.c: Impenitent Im*pen"i*tent (?), a. [L. impaenitens; pref. im- not + paenitens penitens: cf. F. impénitent. See Penitent.] Not penitent; not repenting of sin; not contrite; of a hard heart. “They... died impenitent.” Milton. “A careless and impenitent heart.” Bp. Hall.
Impenitent Im*pen"i*tent, n. One who is not penitent. [R.]

impennate.c: Impennate Im*pen"nate (?), a. (Zool.) Characterized by short wings covered with feathers resembling scales, as the penguins. -- n. One of the Impennes.

impennes.c: Impennes ‖Im*pen"nes (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. pref. im- not + penna feather.] (Zool.) An order of birds, including only the penguins, in which the wings are without quills, and not suited for flight.

impennous.c: Impennous Im*pen"nous (?) a. [L. pref. im- not + penna wing.] (Zool.) Having no wings, as some insects.

impeople.c: Impeople Im*peo"ple (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impeopled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impeopling (?).] [See Empeople.] To people; to give a population to. [Obs.]

imperant.c: Imperant Im"pe*rant (ĭm"pe*raint), a. [L. imperans, p. pr. of imperare to command.] Commanding. [R.] Baxter.

imperate.c: imperate Im"pe*rate (ĭm"pe*rat), a. [L. imperatus, p. p. of imperare to command.] Done by express direction; not involuntary; commanded. [Obs.]

imperatival.c: Imperatival Im*per`a*ti"val (ĭm*pĕr`ȧ*tĭ"vail), a. (Gram.) Of or pertaining to the imperative mood.

imperative.c: Imperative Im*per"a*tive (ĭm*pĕr"ȧ*tĭv), a. [L. imperativus, fr. imperare to command; pref. im- in + parare to make ready, prepare: cf. F. impératif. See Perade, and cf. Empire.] 1. Expressive of command; containing positive command; authoritatively or absolutely directive; commanding; authoritative; as, imperative orders.
Imperative Im*per"a*tive, n. (Gram.) The imperative mood; also, a verb in the imperative mood.

imperatively.c: Imperatively Im*per"a*tive*ly, adv. In an imperative manner.

imperator.c: Imperator ‖Im`pe*ra"tor (?), n. [L. See Emperor.] (Rom. Antiq.) A commander; a leader; an emperor; -- originally an appellation of honor by which Roman soldiers saluted their general after an important victory. Subsequently the title was conferred as a recognition of great military achievements by the senate, whence it carried with it some special privileges. After the downfall of the Republic it was assumed by Augustus and his successors, and came to have the meaning now attached to the word emperor.

imperatorial.c: Imperatorial Im*per`a*to"ri*al (ĭm*pĕr`ȧ*tō"rĭ*vail), a. [L. imperatorius.] 1. Commanding; imperative; authoritative.

imperceivable.c: Imperceivable Im`per*ceiv"a*ble (?), a. Imperceptible. [R.] South. -- Im`per*ceiv"a*ble*ness, n. Sharp.

imperceptibility.c: Imperceptibility Im`per*cep`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being imperceptible.

imperceptible.c: Imperceptible Im`per*cep"ti*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + perceptible: cf. F. imperceptible.] Not perceptible; not to be apprehended or cognized by the senses; not discernible by the mind; not easily apprehended.

impercipient.c: Impercipient Im`per*cip"i*ent (?), a. Not perceiving, or not able to perceive. A. Baxter.

imperdibility.c: Imperdibility Im*per`di*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being imperdible. [Obs.] Derham.

imperdible.c: Imperdible Im*per"di*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + L. perdere to destroy.] Not destructible. [Obs.] -- Im*per"di*bly, adv. [Obs.]

imperfect.c: Imperfect Im*per"fect (?), a. [L. imperfectus: pref. im- not + perfectus perfect: cf. F imparfait, whence OE. imparfit. See Perfect.] 1. Not perfect; not complete in all its parts; wanting a part; deective; deficient.
Imperfect Im*per"fect (ĭm*pẽr"fĕkt), n. (Gram.) The imperfect tense; or the form of a verb denoting the imperfect tense.
Imperfect Im*per"fect, v. t. To make imperfect. [Obs.]

imperfectibility.c: Imperfectibility Im`per*fec`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being imperfectible. [R.]

imperfectible.c: Imperfectible Im`per*fec"ti*ble (?), a. Incapable of being made perfect. [R.]

imperfection.c: Imperfection Im`per*fec"tion (?), n. [L. imperfectio: cf. F. imperfection. See Imperfect, a.] The quality or condition of being imperfect; lack of perfection; incompleteness; deficiency; fault or blemish.

imperfectness.c: Imperfectness Im*per"fect*ness, n. The state of being imperfect.

imperforable.c: Imperforable Im*per"fo*ra*ble (?), a. [See Imperforate.] Incapable of being perforated, or bored through.

imperforata.c: Imperforata ‖Im*per"fo*ra"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Imperforate.] (Zool.) A division of Foraminifera, including those in which the shell is not porous.

imperforated.c: Imperforated Imperforate { Im*per"fo*rate (?), Im*per"fo*ra"ted (?), } a. [L. pref. im- not + perforatus, p. p. of perforate to perforate. See Perforate.] Not perforated; having no opening or aperture. Sir J. Banks.

imperforation.c: Imperforation Im*per`fo*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. imperforation.] The state of being without perforation.

imperial.c: Imperial Im*pe"ri*al (?), a. [OE. emperial, OF. emperial, F. impérial, fr. L. imperialis, fr. imperium command, sovereignty, empire. See Empire.] 1. Of or pertaining to an empire, or to an emperor; as, an imperial government; imperial authority or edict.
Imperial Im*pe"ri*al, n. [F. impériale: cf. Sp. imperial.]

imperialism.c: Imperialism Im*pe"ri*al*ism (?), n. 1. The power or character of an emperor; imperial authority; the spirit of empire.

imperialist.c: Imperialist Im*pe"ri*al*ist, n. [Cf. F. impérialiste.] One who serves an emperor; one who favors imperialism.

imperialize.c: Imperialize Im*pe"ri*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imperialized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imperializing (?).] To invest with imperial authority, character, or style; to bring to the form of an empire. Fuller.

imperially.c: Imperially Im*pe"ri*al*ly, adv. In an imperial manner.

imperil.c: Imperil Im*per"il (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imperiled (?) or Imperilled; p. pr. & vb. n. Imperiling or Imperilling.] To bring into peril; to endanger.

imperilment.c: Imperilment Im*per"il*ment (?), n. The act of imperiling, or the state of being imperiled.

imperious.c: Imperious Im*pe"ri*ous (?), a. [L. imperiosus: cf. F. impérieux. See Imperial.] 1. Commanding; ascendant; imperial; lordly; majestic. [Obs.] “A vast and imperious mind.” Tilloison.

imperiously.c: Imperiously Im*pe"ri*ous*ly, adv. In an imperious manner.

imperiousness.c: Imperiousness Im*pe"ri*ous*ness, n. The quality or state of being imperious; arrogance; haughtiness.

imperishability.c: Imperishability Im*per`ish*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being imperishable: indstructibility. “The imperishability of the universe.” Milman.

imperishable.c: Imperishable Im*per"ish*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + perishable: cf. F. impérissable.] Not perishable; not subject to decay; indestructible; enduring permanently; as, an imperishable monument; imperishable renown. -- Im*per"ish*a*ble*ness, n. -- Im*per"ish*a*bly, adv.

imperium.c: Imperium ‖Im*pe"ri*um (?), n.; pl. Imperia (#). [L. See Empire.] 1. Supreme power; absolute dominion; empire.

impermanency.c: Impermanency Impermanence { Im*per"ma*nence (?), Im*per"ma*nen*cy (?), } n. Lack of permanence.

impermeability.c: Impermeability Im*per`me*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. im- not + permeability: cf. F. imperméabilité.] The quality of being impermeable.

impermeable.c: Impermeable Im*per"me*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + permeable: cf. F. imperméable, L. impermeabilis.] Not permeable; not permitting passage, as of a fluid. through its substance; impervious; impenetrable; as, India rubber is impermeable to water and to air. -- Im*per"me*a*ble*ness, n. -- Im*per"me*a*bly, adv.

imperscrutable.c: Imperscrutable Im`per*scru"ta*ble (?), a. [L. imperscrutabilis.] Not capable of being searched out; inscrutable. [Obs.] -- Im`per*scru"ta*ble*ness, n. [Obs.]

imperseverant.c: Imperseverant Im`per*sev"er*ant (?), a. Not persevering; fickle; thoughtless. [Obs.]

impersonal.c: Impersonal Im*per"son*al (?), a. [L. impersonalis; pref. im- not + personalis personal: cf. F. impersonnel. See Personal.] Not personal; not representing a person; not having personality.
Impersonal Im*per"son*al, n. That which wants personality; specifically (Gram.), an impersonal verb.

impersonality.c: Impersonality Im*per`son*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being impersonal; want or absence of personality.

impersonally.c: Impersonally Im*per"son*al*ly (?), adv. In an impersonal manner.

impersonate.c: Impersonate Im*per"son*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impersonated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impersonating.] 1. To invest with personality; to endow with the form of a living being.

impersonification.c: Impersonification Impersonation { Im*per`son*a"tion (?), Im`per*son`i*fi*ca"tion (?), } n. The act of impersonating; personification; investment with personality; representation in a personal form.

impersonator.c: Impersonator Im*per"son*a`tor (?), n. One who impersonates; an actor; a mimic.

imperspicuity.c: Imperspicuity Im*per`spi*cu"i*ty (?), n. Lack of perspicuity or clearness; vagueness; ambiguity.

imperspicuous.c: Imperspicuous Im`per*spic"u*ous (?), a. Not perspicuous; not clear; obscure; vague; ambiguous.

impersuadable.c: Impersuadable Im`per*suad"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. Impersuasible.] Not to be persuaded; obstinate; unyielding; impersuasible. -- Im`per*suad"a*ble*ness, n.

impersuasible.c: Impersuasible Im`per*sua"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + persuasible: cf. OF. impersuasible.] Not persuasible; not to be moved by persuasion; inflexible; impersuadable. Dr. H. More. -- Im`per*sua`si*bil"i*ty (#), n.

impertinence.c: Impertinence Im*per"ti*nence (?), n. [Cf. F. impertinence. See Impertinent.] 1. The condition or quality of being impertinent; absence of pertinence, or of adaptedness; irrelevance; unfitness.

impertinent.c: Impertinent Im*per"ti*nent (?), a. [F., fr. L. impertinens, -entis; pref. im- not + pertinens. See Pertinent.] 1. Not pertinent; not pertaining to the matter in hand; having no bearing on the subject; not to the point; irrelevant; inapplicable.

impertinently.c: Impertinently Im*per"ti*nent*ly, adv. In an impertinent manner. “Not to betray myself impertinently.” B. Jonson.

impertransibility.c: Impertransibility Im`per*tran`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being impertransible. [R.]

impertransible.c: Impertransible Im`per*tran"si*ble (?), a. [L. pref. im- not + pertransire to go through. See Per- and Transient.] Incapable of being passed through. [R.]

imperturbability.c: Imperturbability Im`per*turb`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being imperturbable.

imperturbable.c: Imperturbable Im`per*turb"a*ble (?), a. [L. imperturbabilis; pref. im- not + perturbare to disturb: cf. F. imperturbable. See Perture.] Incapable of being disturbed or disconcerted; as, imperturbable gravity.

imperturbably.c: Imperturbably Im`per*turb"a*bly, adv. In an imperturbable manner; calmly. C. Bronté.

imperturbation.c: Imperturbation Im*per`tur*ba"tion (?), n. [L. imperturbatio.] Freedom from agitation of mind; calmness; quietude. W. Montagu.

imperviability.c: Imperviability Im*per`vi*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being imperviable.

imperviable.c: Imperviable Im*per"vi*a*ble (?), a. Not pervious; impervious. [R.] -- Im*per"vi*a*ble*ness, n. [R.]

impervious.c: Impervious Im*per"vi*ous (?), a. [L. impervius; pref. im- not + per through + via way. See Voyage.] Not pervious; not admitting of entrance or passage through; as, a substance impervious to water or air.

impest.c: Impest Im*pest" (?), v. t. To affict with pestilence; to infect, as with plague. [Obs.]

impetiginous.c: Impetiginous Im`pe*tig"i*nous (?), a. [L. impetiginous: cf. F. impétigineux.] Of the nature of, or pertaining to, impetigo.

impetigo.c: Impetigo ‖Im`pe*ti"go (?), n. [L., fr. impetere to attack.] (Med.) A cutaneous, pustular eruption, not attended with fever; usually, a kind of eczema with pustulation.

impetrable.c: Impetrable Im"pe*tra*ble (?) a. [L. impetrabilis: cf. F. impétrable. See Impetrate.] Capable of being obtained or moved by petition. [Obs.] Bailey.

impetrate.c: Impetrate Im"pe*trate (?), a. [L. impetratus, p. p. of impetrare to obtain; pref. im- in + patrare to bring to pass.] Obtained by entreaty. [Obs.] Ld. Herbert.
Impetrate Im"pe*trate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impetrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impetrating (?).] To obtain by request or entreaty. Usher.

impetration.c: Impetration Im`pe*tra"tion (?), n. [L. impetratio: cf. F. impétration.] 1. The act of impetrating, or obtaining by petition or entreaty. [Obs.]

impetrative.c: Impetrative Im"pe*tra*tive (?), a. [L. impetrativus obtained by entreaty.] Of the nature of impetration; getting, or tending to get, by entreaty. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

impetratory.c: Impetratory Im"pe*tra*to*ry (?), a. Containing or expressing entreaty. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

impetuosity.c: Impetuosity Im*pet`u*os"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impétuosité.] 1. The condition or quality of being impetuous; fury; violence.

impetuous.c: Impetuous Im*pet"u*ous (?), a. [F. impetueux, L. impetuosus. See Impetus.] 1. Rushing with force and violence; moving with impetus; furious; forcible; violent; as, an impetuous wind; an impetuous torrent.

impetus.c: Impetus Im"pe*tus (ĭm"pe*tŭs), n. [L., fr. impetere to rush upon, attack; pref. im- in + petere to fall upon, seek. See Petition.] 1. A property possessed by a moving body in virtue of its weight and its motion; the force with which any body is driven or impelled; momentum.

impeyan.c: Impeyan pheasant Im"pey*an pheas"ant (ĭm"pĭ*ain fĕz"aint). [From Lady Impey, who attempted to naturalize the bird in England.] (Zool.) An Indian crested pheasant of the genus Lophophorus. Several species are known. Called also monaul, monal.

imphee.c: Imphee Im"phee (ĭm"fē), n. (Bot.) The African sugar cane (Holcus saccharatus), -- resembling the sorghum, or Chinese sugar cane.

impi.c: Impi ‖Im"pi (ĭm"pĭ), n. [Zulu.] A body of Kaffir warriors; a body of native armed men. [South Africa]

impierce.c: Impierce Im*pierce" (ĭm*pērs"), v. t. [Pref. im- in + pierce. Cf. Empierce.] To pierce; to penetrate. [Obs.] Drayton.

impierceable.c: Impierceable Im*pierce"a*ble (ĭm*pērs"ȧ*b'l) a. Not capable of being pierced; impenetrable. [Obs.] Spenser.

impiety.c: Impiety Im*pi"e*ty (ĭm*pī"e*ty̆), n.; pl. Impieties (ĭm*pī"e*tĭz). [L. impietas, fr. impius impious; cf. F. impiété. See Impious, Piety.] 1. The quality of being impious; lack of piety; irreverence toward the Supreme Being; ungodliness; wickedness.

impignorate.c: Impignorate Im*pig"no*rate (ĭm*pĭg"no*rāt), v. t. [LL. impignoratus, p. pl of impignorare to pawn. See Pignoration.] To pledge or pawn. [Obs.] Laing.

impignoration.c: Impignoration Im*pig`no*ra"tion (ĭm*pĭg"no*rā"shŭn), n. [LL. impignoratio: cf. F. impignoration.] The act of pawning or pledging; the state of being pawned. [Obs.] Bailey.

imping.c: Imping Imp"ing (ĭmp"ĭng), n. [See Imp to graft.] 1. The act or process of grafting or mending. [Archaic]

impinge.c: Impinge Im*pinge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impinged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impinging (?).] [L. impingere; pref. im- in + pangere to fix, strike; prob. akin to pacisci to agree, contract. See Pact, and cf. Impact.] To fall or dash against; to touch upon; to strike; to hit; to clash with; -- with on or upon.

impingement.c: Impingement Im*pinge"ment (?), n. The act of impinging.

impingent.c: Impingent Im*pin"gent (?), a. [L. impingens, p. pr.] Striking against or upon.

impinguate.c: Impinguate Im*pin"guate (?), v. t. [L. impinguatus, p. p. of impinguare to fatten; pref. im- in + pinguis fat.] To fatten; to make fat. [Obs.] Bacon.

impinguation.c: Impinguation Im`pin*gua"tion (?), n. The act of making fat, or the state of being fat or fattened. [Obs.]

impious.c: Impious Im"pi*ous (?), a. [L. impius; pref. im- not + pius piou. See Pious.] Not pious; wanting piety; irreligious; irreverent; ungodly; profane; wanting in reverence for the Supreme Being; as, an impious deed; impious language.

impish.c: impish imp"ish (ĭmp"ĭsh), a. Having the qualities, or showing the characteristics, of an imp; naughtily or annoyingly playful; as, teasing and worrying with impish laughter.

impishly.c: Impishly Imp"ish*ly, adv. In the manner of an imp.

implacability.c: Implacability Im*pla`ca*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. implacabilitas: cf. F. implacabilité.] The quality or state of being implacable.

implacable.c: Implacable Im*pla"ca*ble (?), a. [L. implacabilis; pref. im- not + placabilis: cf. F. implacable. See Placable.] 1. Not placable; not to be appeased; incapable of being pacified; inexorable; as, an implacable prince.

implacableness.c: Implacableness Im*pla"ca*ble*ness (?), n. The quality of being implacable; implacability.

implacably.c: Implacably Im*pla"ca*bly, adv. In an implacable manner.

implacental.c: Implacental Im`pla*cen"tal (?), a. (Zool.) Without a placenta, as marsupials and monotremes; nonplacental. -- n. A mammal having no placenta; a nonplacental mammal.

implacentalia.c: Implacentalia ‖Im`pla*cen*ta"li*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See In- not, and Placental.] (Zool.) A primary division of the Mammalia, including the monotremes and marsupials, in which no placenta is formed.

implant.c: Implant Im*plant" (?) v. t. [imp. & p. p. Implanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Implanting.] [Pref. im- in + plant: cf. F. implanter.] To plant, or infix, for the purpose of growth; to fix deeply; to instill; to inculate; to introduce; as, to implant the seeds of virtue, or the principles of knowledge, in the minds of youth.

implantation.c: Implantation Im`plan*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. implantation.] The act or process of implanting.

implate.c: Implate Im*plate" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Implated; p. pr. & vb. n. Implating.] To cover with plates; to sheathe; as, to implate a ship with iron.

implausibility.c: Implausibility Im*plau`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. Lack of plausibility; the quality of being implausible.

implausible.c: Implausible Im*plau"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + plausible: cf. F. implausible.] Not plausible; not wearing the appearance of truth or credibility, and not likely to be believed. “Implausible harangues.” Swift.

impleach.c: Impleach Im*pleach" (?), v. t. To pleach; to interweave. [Obs.] Shak.

implead.c: Implead Im*plead" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impleaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Impleading.] [Cf. Emplead.] (Law) To institute and prosecute a suit against, in court; to sue or prosecute at law; hence, to accuse; to impeach.
Implead Im*plead", v. i. To sue at law.

impleadable.c: Impleadable Im*plead"a*ble (?), a. Not admitting excuse, evasion, or plea; rigorous. [R.] T. Adams.

impleader.c: Impleader Im*plead"er (?), n. (Law) One who prosecutes or sues another.

impledge.c: Impledge Im*pledge" (?), v. t. To pledge. Sir W. Scott.

implement.c: Implement Im"ple*ment (ĭm"ple*meint), n. [LL. implementum accomplishment, fr. L. implere, impletum, to fill up, finish, complete; pref. im- in + plere to fill. The word was perh. confused with OF. empleier, emploier, to employ, F. employer, whence E. employ. See Plenty.] That which fulfills or supplies a want or use; esp., an instrument, tool, or utensil, as supplying a requisite to an end; as, the implements of trade, of husbandry, or of war.
Implement Im"ple*ment, v. t. 1. To accomplish; to fulfill. [R.]

implemental.c: Implemental Im`ple*men"tal (?), a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, implements or their use; mechanical.

impletion.c: Impletion Im*ple"tion (?), n. [L. impletio. See Implement.] 1. The act of filling, or the state of being full. Sir T. Browne.

implex.c: Implex Im"plex (?), a. [L. implexus, p. p. of implectere to infold; pref. im- in + plectere to plait: cf. F implexe.] Intricate; entangled; complicated; complex.

implexion.c: Implexion Im*plex"ion (?), n. [L. implexio.] Act of involving, or state of being involved; involution.

impliable.c: Impliable Im*pli"a*ble (?), a. Not pliable; inflexible; unyielding.

implicate.c: Implicate Im"pli*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Implicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Implicating.] [L. implicatus, p. p. of implicare to involve; pref. im- in + plicare to fold. See Employ, Ply, and cf. Imply, Implicit.] 1. To infold; to fold together; to interweave.

implication.c: Implication Im`pli*ca"tion (?), n. [L. implicatio: cf. F. implication.] 1. The act of implicating, or the state of being implicated.

implicatively.c: Implicatively Im"pli*ca*tive*ly, adv. By implication. Sir G. Buck.

implicit.c: Implicit Im*plic"it (?), a. [L. implicitus, p. p. of implicare to entwine, entangle, attach closely: cf. F. implicite. See Implicate.] 1. Infolded; entangled; complicated; involved. [Obs.] Milton.

implicitly.c: Implicitly Im*plic"it*ly (?), adv. 1. In an implicit manner; without reserve; with unreserved confidence.

implicitness.c: Implicitness Im*plic"it*ness, n. State or quality of being implicit.

implied.c: Implied Im*plied" (?), a. Virtually involved or included; involved in substance; inferential; tacitly conceded; -- the correlative of express, or expressed. See Imply.

impliedly.c: Impliedly Im*pli"ed*ly (?), adv. By implication or inference. Bp. Montagu.

imploded.c: Imploded Im*plod"ed (?), a. (Phon.) Formed by implosion. Ellis.

implodent.c: Implodent Im*plod"ent (?), n. (Phon.) An implosive sound. Ellis.

imploration.c: Imploration Im`plo*ra"tion (?), n. [L. imploratio: cf. OF. imploration. See Implore.] The act of imploring; earnest supplication. Bp. Hall.

implore.c: Implore Im*plore" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Implored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imploring.] [L. implorare; pref. im- in + plorare to cry aloud. See Deplore.] To call upon, or for, in supplication; to beseech; to pray to, or for, earnestly; to petition with urgency; to entreat; to beg; -- followed directly by the word expressing the thing sought, or the person from whom it is sought.
Implore Im*plore", v. i. To entreat; to beg; to prey.

imploring.c: Imploring Im*plor"ing, a. That implores; beseeching; entreating. -- Im*plor"ing*ly, adv.

implosion.c: Implosion Im*plo"sion (?), n. [Formed by substitution of pref. im- in for pref. ex- in explosion.] 1. A bursting inwards, as of a vessel from which the air has been exhausted; -- contrasted with explosion.

implosive.c: Implosive Im*plo"sive (?), a. (Phon.) Formed by implosion. -- n. An implosive sound, an implodent. -- Im*plo"sive*ly, adv. H. Sweet.

implumed.c: Implumed Im*plumed" (?), a. Not plumed; without plumes or feathers; featherless. [R.] Drayton.

implunge.c: Implunge Im*plunge" (?), v. t. To plunge. Fuller.

impluvium.c: Impluvium ‖Im*plu"vi*um (?), n. [L., fr. impluere to rain into; pref. im- in + pluere to rain.] (Arch.) In Roman dwellings, a cistern or tank, set in the atrium or peristyle to recieve the water from the roof, by means of the compluvium; generally made ornamental with flowers and works of art around its birm.

imply.c: Imply Im*ply" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Implied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Implying.] [From the same source as employ. See Employ, Ply, and cf. Implicate, Apply.] 1. To infold or involve; to wrap up. [Obs.] “His head in curls implied.” Chapman.

impoison.c: Impoison Im*poi"son (?), v. t. [Cf. Empoison.] To poison; to imbitter; to impair.

impoisoner.c: Impoisoner Im*poi"son*er (?), n. A poisoner. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

impoisonment.c: Impoisonment Im*poi"son*ment (?), n. [Cf. Empoisonment.] The act of poisoning or impoisoning. [Obs.] Pope.

impolarly.c: Impolarly Impolarily { Im*po"lar*i*ly (?), Im*po"lar*ly (?), } adv. Not according to or in, the direction of the poles. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

impolicy.c: Impolicy Im*pol"i*cy (?), n. The quality of being impolitic; inexpedience; unsuitableness to the end proposed; bads policy; as, the impolicy of fraud. Bp. Horsley.

impolite.c: Impolite Im`po*lite" (?), a. [L. impolitus unpolishied, pref. im- not + politus, p. p. of polire to polish, refine. See Polite.] Not polite; not of polished manners; wanting in good manners; discourteous; uncivil; rude. -- Im`po*lite"ly, adv. -- Im`po*lite"ness, n.

impolitic.c: Impolitic Im*pol"i*tic (?), a. [Pref. im- not + politic; cf. F. impolitique.] Not politic; contrary to, or wanting in, policy; unwise; imprudent; indiscreet; inexpedient; as, an impolitic ruler, law, or measure.

impolitical.c: Impolitical Im`po*lit"i*cal (?), a. Impolitic. [Obs.] -- Im`po*lit"i*cal*ly, adv. [Obs.] Bacon.

impoliticly.c: Impoliticly Im*pol"i*tic*ly (?), adv. In an impolitic manner.

impoliticness.c: Impoliticness Im*pol"i*tic*ness, n. The quality of being impolitic.

imponderability.c: Imponderability Im*pon`der*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. impondérabilité.] The quality or state of being imponderable; imponderableness.

imponderable.c: Imponderable Im*pon"der*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + ponderable: cf. F. impondérable.] Not ponderable; without sensible or appreciable weight; incapable of being weighed.

Imponderable Im*pon"der*a*ble, n. (Physics) An imponderable substance or body; specifically, in the plural, a name formerly applied to heat, light, electricity, and magnetism, regarded as subtile fluids destitute of weight but in modern science little used.

imponderableness.c: Imponderableness Im*pon"der*a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being imponderable.

imponderous.c: Imponderous Im*pon"der*ous (?), a. Imponderable. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne. -- Im*pon"der*ous*ness, n. [Obs.]

impone.c: Impone Im*pone" (?), v. t. [L. imponere, impositum, to place upon; pref. im- in + ponere to place. See Position.] To stake; to wager; to pledge. [Obs.]

imporosity.c: Imporosity Im`po*ros"i*ty (?), n. [Perf. im- not + porosity: cf. F. imporosité.] The state or quality of being imporous; lack of porosity; compactness. “The... imporosity betwixt the tangible parts.” Bacon.

imporous.c: Imporous Im*por"ous (?), a. Destitute of pores; very close or compact in texture; solid. Sir T. Browne.

import.c: Import Im*port" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imported; p. pr. & vb. n. Importing.] [L. importare to bring in, to occasion, to cause; pref. im- in + portare to bear. Sense 3 comes through F. importer, from the Latin. See Port demeanor.] 1. To bring in from abroad; to introduce from without; especially, to bring (wares or merchandise) into a place or country from a foreign country, in the transactions of commerce; -- opposed to export. We import teas from China, coffee from Brazil, etc.
Import Im*port", v. i. To signify; to purport; to be of moment. “For that... importeth to the work.” Bacon.
Import Im"port (?), n. 1. Merchandise imported, or brought into a country from without its boundaries; -- generally in the plural, opposed to exports.

importable.c: Importable Im*port"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. importable. See Import.] Capable of being imported.

Importable Im*port"a*ble, a. [L. importabilis; pref. im- not + portabilis bearable: cf. OF. importable. See Portable.] Not to be endured; insupportable; intolerable. [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Im*port"a*ble*ness, n. [Obs.]

importance.c: Importance Im*por"tance (?), n. [F. importance. See Important.] 1. The quality or state of being important; consequence; weight; moment; significance.

importancy.c: Importancy Im*por"tan*cy (?), n. Importance; significance; consequence; that which is important. [Obs.] Shak. “Careful to conceal importancies.” Fuller.

important.c: Important Im*por"tant (?), a. [F. important. See Import, v. t.] 1. Full of, or burdened by, import; charged with great interests; restless; anxious. [Obs.]

importantly.c: Importantly Im*por"tant*ly, adv. In an important manner.

importation.c: Importation Im`por*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. importation. See Import, v. t.] 1. The act of carrying, conveying, or delivering. [R.]

importer.c: Importer Im*port"er (?), n. One who imports; the merchant who brings goods into a country or state; -- opposed to exporter.

importing.c: Importing Im*port"ing, a. Full of meaning. [Obs.] Shak.

importless.c: Importless Im*port"less, a. Void of meaning. [Obs.] Shak.

importunable.c: Importunable Im*por"tu*na*ble (?), a. Heavy; insupportable. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

importunacy.c: Importunacy Im*por"tu*na*cy (?), n. [From Importunate.] The quality of being importunate; importunateness.

importunate.c: Importunate Im*por"tu*nate (ĭm*pôr"tu*nat), a. [See Importune.] 1. Troublesomely urgent; unreasonably solicitous; overpressing in request or demand; urgent; teasing; as, an importunate petitioner, curiosity. Whewell.

importunator.c: Importunator Im*por"tu*na`tor (ĭm*pôr"tu*nā`tẽr), n. One who importunes; an importuner. [Obs.] Sir E. Sandys.

importune.c: Importune Im`por*tune" (ĭm`pŏr*tūn"), a. [F. importun, L. importunus; pref. im- not + a derivative from the root of portus harbor, importunus therefore orig. meaning, hard of access. See Port harbor, and cf. Importunate.] 1. Inopportune; unseasonable. [Obs.]

Importune Im`por*tune", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Importuned (ĭm`pŏr*tūnd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Importuning.] [From Importune, a.: cf. F. importuner.] 1. To request or solicit, with urgency; to press with frequent, unreasonable, or troublesome application or pertinacity; hence, to tease; to irritate; to worry.
Importune Im`por*tune", v. i. To require; to demand. [Obs.]

importunely.c: Importunely Im`por*tune"ly, adv. In an importune manner. [Obs.]

importunity.c: Importunity Im`por*tu"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Importunities (#). [L. importunitas unsuitableness, rudeness: cf. F. importunité.] The quality of being importunate; pressing or pertinacious solicitation; urgent request; incessant or frequent application; troublesome pertinacity.

importuous.c: Importuous Im*por"tu*ous (?), a. [L. importuosus; pref. im- not + portuosus abounding in harbors, fr. portus harbor.] Without a port or harbor. [R.]

imposable.c: Imposable Im*pos"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. imposable.] Capable of being imposed or laid on. Hammond.

imposableness.c: Imposableness Im*pos"a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being imposable.

impose.c: Impose Im*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imposing.] [F. imposer; pref. im- in + poser to place. See Pose, v. t.] 1. To lay on; to set or place; to put; to deposit.
Impose Im*pose", v. i. To practice tricks or deception.
Impose Im*pose", n. A command; injunction. [Obs.] Shak.

imposing.c: Imposing Im*pos"ing, a. 1. Laying as a duty; enjoining.
Imposing Im*pos"ing, n. (Print.) The act of imposing the columns of a page, or the pages of a sheet. See Impose, v. t., 4.

imposingly.c: Imposingly Im*pos"ing*ly, adv. In an imposing manner.

imposingness.c: Imposingness Im*pos"ing*ness, n. The quality of being imposing.

imposition.c: Imposition Im`po*si"tion (?), n. [F., fr. L. impositio the application of a name to a thing. See Impone.] 1. The act of imposing, laying on, affixing, enjoining, inflicting, obtruding, and the like. “From imposition of strict laws.” Milton.

impossibility.c: Impossibility Im*pos`si*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Impossibilities (#). [L. impossibilitas: cf. F. impossibilité.] 1. The quality of being impossible; impracticability.

impossible.c: Impossible Im*pos"si*ble (?), a. [F., fr. L. impossibilis; pref. im- not + possibilis possible. See Possible.] Not possible; incapable of being done, of existing, etc.; unattainable in the nature of things, or by means at command; insuperably difficult under the circumstances; absurd or impracticable; not feasible.
Impossible Im*pos"si*ble, n. An impossibility; as, he tried to do the impossible. [Obs.]

impossibly.c: Impossibly Im*pos"si*bly, adv. Not possibly. Sir. T. North.

impost.c: Impost Im"post (?), n. [OF. impost, F. impot, LL. impostus, fr. L. impostus, p. p. of imponere to impose. See Impone.] 1. That which is imposed or levied; a tax, tribute, or duty; especially, a duty or tax laid by goverment on goods imported into a country.

imposthumate.c: Imposthumate Im*post"hu*mate (?), v. t. [See Imposthume.] To apostemate; to form an imposthume or abscess. Arbuthnot.
Imposthumate Im*post"hu*mate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imposthumated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imposthumating (?).] To affect with an imposthume or abscess.

imposthumation.c: Imposthumation Im*post`hu*ma"tion (?), n. 1. The act of forming an abscess; state of being inflamed; suppuration.

imposthume.c: Imposthume Im*post"hume (?), n. [A corruption of aposteme. See Aposteme.] A collection of pus or purulent matter in any part of an animal body; an abscess.
Imposthume Im*post"hume, v. t. & i. Same as Imposthumate.

impostor.c: Impostor Im*pos"tor (?), n. [L. impostor a deceiver, fr. imponere to impose upon, deceive. See Impone.] One who imposes upon others; a person who assumes a character or title not his own, for the purpose of deception; a pretender. “The fraudulent impostor foul.” Milton.

impostorship.c: Impostorship Im*pos"tor*ship, n. The condition, character, or practice of an impostor. Milton.

impostrix.c: Impostrix Impostress { Im*pos"tress (?), Im*pos"trix (?), } n. [LL. impostrix. See Impostor.] A woman who imposes upon or deceives others. [R.] Fuller.

impostrous.c: Impostrous Im*pos"trous (?), n. Characterized by imposture; deceitful. “Impostrous pretense of knowledge.” Grote.

imposturage.c: Imposturage Im*pos"tur*age (?), n. Imposture; cheating. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

imposture.c: Imposture Im*pos"ture (?), n. [L. impostura: cf. F. imposture. See Impone.] The act or conduct of an impostor; deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition; cheating.
