impotency.c: Impotency Impotence { Im"po*tence (?), Im"po*ten*cy (?), } n. [L. impotenia inability, poverty, lack of moderation. See Impotent.] 1. The quality or condition of being impotent; lack of strength or power, animal, intellectual, or moral; weakness; feebleness; inability; imbecility.

impotent.c: Impotent Im"po*tent (?), a. [F. impotent, L. impotens, -entis; pref. im- not + potens potent, powerful. See Potent.] 1. Not potent; wanting power, strength. or vigor. whether physical, intellectual, or moral; deficient in capacity; destitute of force; weak; feeble; infirm.
Impotent Im"po*tent, n. One who is impotent. [R.] Shak.

impotently.c: Impotently Im"po*tent*ly, adv. In an impotent manner.

impound.c: Impound Im*pound" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impounded; p. pr. & vb. n. Impounding.] To shut up or place in an inclosure called a pound; hence, to hold in the custody of some authority such as police or a court; as, to impound stray cattle; to impound an illegally parked car; to impound a document for safe keeping.

impoundage.c: Impoundage Im*pound"age (ĭm*pound"aj), n. 1. The act of impounding, or the state of being impounded.

impoverish.c: Impoverish Im*pov"er*ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impoverished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impoverishing.] [OF. empovrir; pref. em- (L. in) + povre poor, F. pauvre; cf. OF. apovrir, F. appauvrir, where the prefix is a-, L. ad. Cf. Empoverish, and see Poor, and -ish.] 1. To make poor; to reduce to poverty or indigence; as, misfortune and disease impoverish families.

impoverisher.c: Impoverisher Im*pov"er*ish*er (?), n. One who, or that which, impoverishes.

impoverishment.c: Impoverishment Im*pov"er*ish*ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. empoverissement, and F. appauvrissement.] The act of impoverishing, or the state of being impoverished; reduction to poverty. Sir W. Scott.

imppole.c: Imp-pole Imp"-pole` (?), n. (Building) A pole for supporting a scaffold.

impracticability.c: Impracticability Im*prac`ti*ca*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Impracticabilities (?). 1. The state or quality of being impracticable; infeasibility. Goldsmith.

impracticable.c: Impracticable Im*prac"ti*ca*ble (?), a. 1. Not practicable; incapable of being performed, or accomplished by the means employed, or at command; impossible; as, an impracticable undertaking.

impracticableness.c: Impracticableness Im*prac"ti*ca*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being impracticable; impracticability.

impracticably.c: Impracticably Im*prac"ti*ca*bly, adv. In an impracticable manner.

imprecate.c: Imprecate Im"pre*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imprecated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imprecating (?).] [L. imprecatus, p. p. of imprecari to imprecate; pref. im- in, on + precari to pray. See Pray.] 1. To call down by prayer, as something hurtful or calamitous.

imprecation.c: Imprecation Im`pre*ca"tion (?), n. [L. imprecatio: cf. F. imprécation.] The act of imprecating, or invoking evil upon any one; a prayer that a curse or calamity may fall on any one; a curse.

imprecatory.c: Imprecatory Im"pre*ca*to*ry (?), a. Of the nature of, or containing, imprecation; invoking evil; as, the imprecatory psalms.

impregn.c: Impregn Im*pregn" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. impregner. See Impregnate.] To impregnate; to make fruitful. [Obs.]

impregnability.c: Impregnability Im*preg`na*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being impregnable; invincibility.

impregnable.c: Impregnable Im*preg"na*ble (?), a. [F. imprenable; pref. im- not + prenable pregnable, fr. prendre to take, L. prehendere. See Comprehend, Get to obtain.] Not to be stormed, or taken by assault; incapable of being subdued; able to resist attack; unconquerable; as, an impregnable fortress; impregnable virtue.
Impregnable Im*preg"na*ble (?), a. [See Impregnate.] (Biol.) Capable of being impregnated, as the egg of an animal, or the ovule of a plant.

impregnant.c: Impregnant Im*preg"nant (?), n. [See Impregnate.] That which impregnates. [R.] Glanvill.
Impregnant Im*preg"nant, a. [Pref. im- not + pregnant.] Not pregnant; unfertilized or infertile. [R.]

impregnate.c: Impregnate Im*preg"nate (ĭm*prĕg"nāt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impregnated (-na*tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Impregnating (-na*tĭng).] [LL. impraegnatus, p. p. of impraegnare to impregnate, fr. L. pref. im- in + praegnans pregnant. See Pregnant.] 1. To make pregnant; to cause to conceive; to render prolific; to get with child or young.
Impregnate Im*preg"nate (ĭm*prĕg"nāt), v. i. To become pregnant. Addison.
Impregnate Im*preg"nate (-nat), a. [LL. impraegnatus, p. p.] Impregnated; made prolific.

impregnation.c: Impregnation Im`preg*na"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. imprégnation, LL. impraegnatio.] 1. The act of impregnating or the state of being impregnated; fecundation.

imprejudicate.c: Imprejudicate Im`pre*ju"di*cate (?), a. Not prejudged; unprejudiced; impartial. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

impreparation.c: Impreparation Im*prep`a*ra"tion (?), n. Lack of preparation. [Obs.] Hooker.

impresa.c: Impresa ‖Im*pre"sa (em*prā"sȧ), n. [It. See Emprise, and cf. Impress, n., 4.] (Her.) A device on a shield or seal, or used as a bookplate or the like. [Written also imprese and impress.]

impresario.c: Impresario ‖Im`pre*sa"ri*o (?), n.; pl. Impresarios (#). [It., from impresa enterprise.] 1. The projector, manager, or conductor, of an opera or concert company.

imprescriptibility.c: Imprescriptibility Im`pre*scrip`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. imprescriptibilité.] The quality of being imprescriptible.

imprescriptible.c: Imprescriptible Im`pre*scrip"ti*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + prescriptible: cf. F. imprescriptible.] 1. Not capable of being lost or impaired by neglect, by disuse, or by the claims of another founded on prescription; -- of rights.

imprescriptibly.c: Imprescriptibly Im`pre*scrip"ti*bly, adv. In an imprescriptible manner; obviously.

imprese.c: Imprese Im*prese" (?), n. A device. See Impresa.

impress.c: Impress Im*press" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impressed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impressing.] [L. impressus, p. p. of imprimere to impress; pref. im- in, on + premere to press. See Press to squeeze, and cf. Imprint.] 1. To press, stamp, or print something in or upon; to mark by pressure, or as by pressure; to imprint (that which bears the impression).
Impress Im*press", v. i. To be impressed; to rest. [Obs.]
Impress Im"press (?), n.; pl. Impresses (?). 1. The act of impressing or making.

impressibility.c: Impressibility Im*press`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being impressible; susceptibility.

impressible.c: Impressible Im*press"i*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. impressible.] Capable of being impressed; susceptible; sensitive. -- Im*press"i*ble*ness, n. -- Im*press"i*bly, adv.

impression.c: Impression Im*pres"sion (?), n. [F. impression, L. impressio.] 1. The act of impressing, or the state of being impressed; the communication of a stamp, mold, style, or character, by external force or by influence.

impressionability.c: Impressionability Im*pres`sion*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being impressionable.

impressionable.c: Impressionable Im*pres"sion*a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. impressionnable.] Liable or subject to impression; capable of being molded; susceptible; impressible; as, a bad influence on impressionable youths.

impressionableness.c: Impressionableness Im*pres"sion*a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being impressionable.

impressionism.c: Impressionism Im*pres"sion*ism (?), n. [F. impressionnisme.] (Fine Arts) The theory or method of suggesting an effect or impression without elaboration of the details; -- a disignation of a recent fashion in painting and etching.

impressionist.c: Impressionist Im*pres"sion*ist, n. [F. impressionniste.] (Fine Arts) One who adheres to the theory or method of impressionism in art; especially, a painter who paints in the impressionistic style; as, the skyrocketing prices of paintings by the French impressionists.

impressionistic.c: Impressionistic Impressionist Im*pres"sion*ist, Im*pres`sion*is"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, impressionism.

impressionless.c: Impressionless Im*pres"sion*less, a. Having the quality of not being impressed or affected; not susceptible.

impressive.c: Impressive Im*press"ive (ĭm*prĕs"ĭv), a. [Cf. F. impressif.] 1. Making, or tending to make, an impression; having power to impress; adapted to excite attention and feeling, to touch the sensibilities, or affect the conscience; as, an impressive discourse; an impressive scene.

impressment.c: Impressment Im*press"ment (ĭm*prĕs"meint), n. The act of seizing for public use, or of impressing into public service; compulsion to serve; as, the impressment of provisions or of sailors.

impressor.c: Impressor Im*press"or (ĭm*prĕs"ẽr), n. [LL., a printer.] One who, or that which, impresses. Boyle.

impressure.c: Impressure Im*pres"sure (ĭm*prĕsh"ụr; 135), n. [Cf. OF. impressure, LL. impressura.] Dent; impression. [Obs.] Shak.

imprest.c: Imprest Im*prest" (ĭm*prĕst"), v. t. [ imp. & p. p. Imprested; p. pr. & vb. n. Impresting.] [Pref. im- + prest: cf. It. imprestare. See Prest, n.] To advance on loan. Burke.

Imprest Im"prest (ĭm"prĕst), n. [Cf. It. impresto, imprestito, LL. impraestitum. See Imprest, v. t., and Impress compulsion to serve.] A kind of earnest money; loan; -- specifically, money advanced for some public service, as in enlistment. Burke.

imprevalency.c: Imprevalency Imprevalence { Im*prev"a*lence (?), Im*prev"a*len*cy (?), } n. Lack of prevalence. [Obs.]

impreventability.c: Impreventability Im`pre*vent`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being impreventable; inevitability. [R.]

imprimatur.c: Imprimatur ‖Im`pri*ma"tur (?), n. [L., let it be printed.] 1. (Law) A license to print or publish a book, paper, etc.; also, in countries subjected to the censorship of the press, approval of that which is published.

imprimery.c: Imprimery Im*prim"er*y (?), n. [F. imprimerie, fr. imprimer to imprint.] [Obs.] (a) A print; impression. (b) A printing establishment. (c) The art of printing.

impriming.c: Impriming Im*prim"ing (?), n. A beginning. [Obs.] “Their springings and imprimings.” Sir H. Wotton.

imprimis.c: Imprimis ‖Im*pri"mis (?), adv. [L., for in primis among the first, chiefly; in in + primus first.] In the first place; first in order.

imprint.c: Imprint Im*print" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imptrinted; p. pr. & vb. n. Imprinting.] [OE. emprenten, F. empreint, p. p. of empreindre to imprint, fr. L. imprimere to impres, imprint. See 1st In-, Print, and cf. Impress.] 1. To impress; to mark by pressure; to indent; to stamp.

Imprint Im"print (?), n. [Cf. F. empreinte impress, stamp. See Imprint, v. t.] Whatever is impressed or imprinted; the impress or mark left by something; specifically, the name of the printer or publisher (usually) with the time and place of issue, in the title-page of a book, or on any printed sheet. “That imprint of their hands.” Buckle.

imprison.c: Imprison Im*pris"on (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imprisoned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Imprisoning.] [OE. enprisonen, OF. enprisoner, F. emprisonner; pref. en- (L. in) + F. & OF. prison. See Prison.] 1. To put in prison or jail; To arrest and detain in custody; to confine.
Imprison ment Im*pris"on ment (?), n. [OE. enprisonment; F. emprisonnement.] The act of imprisoning, or the state of being imprisoned; confinement; restraint.

improbability.c: Improbability Im*prob`a*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Improbabilities (#). [Cf. F. improbabilité.] The quality or state of being improbable; unlikelihood; also, that which is improbable; an improbable event or result.

improbable.c: Improbable Im*prob"a*ble (?), a. [L. improbabilis; pref. im- not + probabilis probable: cf. F. improbable. See Probable.] Not probable; unlikely to be true; not to be expected under the circumstances or in the usual course of events; as, an improbable story or event.

improbate.c: Improbate Im"pro*bate (?), v. t. [L. improbatus, p. p. of improbare to disapprove; pref. im- not + probare to approve.] To disapprove of; to disallow. [Obs.]

improbation.c: Improbation Im`pro*ba"tion (?), n. [L. improbatio.] 1. The act of disapproving; disapprobation.

improbatory.c: Improbatory Improbative { Im"pro*ba*tive (?), Im"pro*ba`to*ry (?) }, a. Implying, or tending to, improbation.

improbity.c: Improbity Im*prob"i*ty (?), n. [L. improbitas; pref. im- not + probitas probity: cf. F. improbité.] Lack of probity; lack of integrity or rectitude; dishonesty.

improficiency.c: Improficiency Improficience { Im`pro*fi"cience (?), Im`pro*fi"cien*cy, } n. Lack of proficiency. [R.] Bacon.

improfitable.c: Improfitable Im*prof"it*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- not + profitable: cf. F. improfitable.] Unprofitable. [Obs.]

improgressive.c: Improgressive Im`pro*gress"ive (?), a. Not progressive. De Quincey. -- Im"pro*gress"ive*ly, adv.

improlific.c: Improlific Im`pro*lif"ic (?), a. [Pref. im- not + prolific: cf. F. improlifique.] Not prolific. [Obs.] E. Waterhouse.

improlificate.c: Improlificate Im`pro*lif"ic*ate (?), v. t. [Pref. im- in + prolificate.] To impregnate. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

impromptu.c: Impromptu Im*promp"tu (?), adv. or a. [F. impromptu, fr. L. in promptu in readiness, at hand; in in + promptus visibility, readiness, from promptus visible, ready. See Prompt.] Offhand; without previous study; extemporaneous; extempore; as, an impromptu verse.
Impromptu Im*promp"tu, n. 1. Something made or done offhand, at the moment, or without previous study; an extemporaneous composition, address, or remark.

improper.c: Improper Im*prop"er (?), a. [F. impropre, L. improprius; pref. im- not + proprius proper. See Proper.] 1. Not proper; not suitable; not fitted to the circumstances, design, or end; unfit; not becoming; incongruous; inappropriate; indecent; as, an improper medicine; improper thought, behavior, language, dress.
Improper Im*prop"er, v. t. To appropriate; to limit. [Obs.]

improperation.c: Improperation Im*prop`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. improperare, improperatum, to taunt.] The act of upbraiding or taunting; a reproach; a taunt. [Obs.]

improperia.c: Improperia ‖Im`pro*pe"ri*a (?), n. pl. [L., reproaches.] (Mus.) A series of antiphons and responses, expressing the sorrowful remonstrance of our Lord with his people; -- sung on the morning of the Good Friday in place of the usual daily Mass of the Roman ritual. Grove.

improperly.c: Improperly Im*prop"er*ly (?), adv. In an improper manner; not properly; unsuitably; unbecomingly.

impropitious.c: Impropitious Im`pro*pi"tious (?), a. Unpropitious; unfavorable. [Obs.] “Dreams were impropitious.” Sir H. Wotton.

improportionable.c: Improportionable Im`pro*por"tion*a*ble (?), a. Not proportionable. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

impropriate.c: Impropriate Im*pro"pri*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impropriated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impropriating (?).] [Pref. im- in + L. propriatus, p. p. of propriare to appropriate. See Appropriate.] 1. To appropriate to one's self; to assume. [Obs.]
Impropriate Im*pro"pri*ate, v. i. To become an impropriator. [R.]
Impropriate Im*pro"pri*ate (?), a. (Eng. Eccl. Law) Put into the hands of a layman; impropriated.

impropriation.c: Impropriation Im*pro`pri*a"tion (?), n. 1. The act of impropriating; as, the impropriation of property or tithes; also, that which is impropriated.

impropriator.c: Impropriator Im*pro"pri*a`tor (?), n. One who impropriates; specifically, a layman in possession of church property.

impropriatrix.c: Impropriatrix Im*pro`pri*a"trix (?), n.; pl. E. -trixes, L. -trices (?). A female impropriator.

impropriety.c: Impropriety Im`pro*pri"e*ty (?), n.; pl. Improprieties (#). [L. improprietas; cf. F. impropriété. See Improper.] 1. The quality of being improper; unfitness or unsuitableness to character, time place, or circumstances; as, impropriety of behavior or manners.

improsperity.c: Improsperity Im`pros*per"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. improspérité.] Lack of prosperity. [Obs.]

improsperous.c: Improsperous Im*pros"per*ous (?), a. [Pref. im- not + prosperous: cf. F. improspère, L. improsper.] Not prosperous. [Obs.] Dryden. -- Im*pros"per*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Im*pros"per*ous*ness, n. [Obs.]

improvability.c: Improvability Im*prov`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being improvable; improvableness.

improvable.c: Improvable Im*prov"a*ble (?), a. [From Improve.] 1. Capable of being improved; susceptible of improvement; admitting of being made better; capable of cultivation, or of being advanced in good qualities.

improve.c: Improve Im*prove" (?), v. t. [Pref. im- not + prove: cf. L. improbare, F. improuver.] 1. To disprove or make void; to refute. [Obs.]

Improve Im*prove", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Improved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Improving.] [Pref. in- in + prove, in approve. See Approve, Prove.] 1. To make better; to increase the value or good qualities of; to ameliorate by care or cultivation; as, to improve land. Donne.
Improve Im*prove", v. i. 1. To grow better; to advance or make progress in what is desirable; to make or show improvement; as, to improve in health.

improvement.c: Improvement Im*prove"ment (?), n. 1. The act of improving; advancement or growth; promotion in desirable qualities; progress toward what is better; melioration; as, the improvement of the mind, of land, roads, etc.

improver.c: Improver Im*prov"er (?), n. One who, or that which, improves.

improvided.c: Improvided Im`pro*vid"ed (?), a. Unforeseen; unexpected; not provided against; unprepared. [Obs.]

improvidence.c: Improvidence Im*prov"i*dence (?), n. [L. improvidentia; OF. improvidence. Cf. Imprudence.] The quality of being improvident; lack of foresight or thrift.

improvident.c: Improvident Im*prov"i*dent (?), a. [Pref. im- not + provident: cf. L. improvidus. See Provident, and cf. Imprudent.] Not provident; wanting foresight or forethought; not foreseeing or providing for the future; negligent; thoughtless; as, an improvident man.

improvidently.c: Improvidently Im*prov"i*dent*ly (?), adv. In a improvident manner. “Improvidently rash.” Drayton.

improving.c: Improving Im*prov"ing (?), a. Tending to improve, beneficial; growing better. -- Im*prov"ing*ly, adv.

improvisate.c: Improvisate Im*prov"i*sate (?), a. [See Improvise.] Unpremeditated; impromptu; extempore. [R.]
Improvisate Im*prov"i*sate (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Improvisated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Improvisating (?).] To improvise; to extemporize.

improvisation.c: Improvisation Im*prov`i*sa"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. improvisation.] 1. The act or art of composing and rendering music, poetry, and the like, extemporaneously; as, improvisation on the organ.

improvisatize.c: Improvisatize Im`pro*vis"a*tize (?), v. t. & i. Same as Improvisate.

improvisator.c: Improvisator Im*prov"i*sa`tor (?), n. An improviser, or improvvisatore.

improvisatory.c: Improvisatory Improvisatorial { Im*prov`i*sa*to"ri*al (?), Im*prov"i*sa*to*ry (?), } a. Of or pertaining to improvisation or extemporaneous composition.

improvise.c: Improvise Im`pro*vise" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Improvised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Improvising.] [F. improviser, it. improvvisare, fr. improvviso unprovided, sudden, extempore, L. improvisus; pref. im- not + provisus foreseen, provided. See Proviso.] 1. To compose, recite, or sing extemporaneously, especially in verse; to extemporize; also, to play upon an instrument, or to act, extemporaneously.
Improvise Im`pro*vise", v. i. To produce or render extemporaneous compositions, especially in verse or in music, without previous preparation; hence, to do anything offhand.

improvision.c: Improvision Im`pro*vi"sion (?), n. [Pref. im- not + provision.] Improvidence. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

improviso.c: Improviso Im`pro*vi"so (?), a. [L. improvisus unforeseen; cf. It. improvviso.] Not prepared or mediated beforehand; extemporaneous. [Obs.] Jonhson.

improvvisatore.c: Improvvisatore ‖Im`prov*vi`sa*to"re (?), n.; pl. Improvvisatori (#). [It. See Improvise.] One who composes and sings or recites rhymes and short poems extemporaneously. [Written also improvisatore.]

improvvisatrice.c: Improvvisatrice ‖Im`prov*vi`sa*tri"ce (?), n.; pl. Improvvisatrici (#). [It. See Improvise.] A female improvvisatore. [Written also improvisatrice.]

imprudence.c: Imprudence Im*pru"dence (?), n. [L. imprudentia: cf. F. imprudence. Cf. Improvidence.] The quality or state of being imprudent; want to caution, circumspection, or a due regard to consequences; indiscretion; inconsideration; rashness; also, an imprudent act; as, he was guilty of an imprudence.

imprudent.c: Imprudent Im*pru"dent (?), a. [L. imprudens; pref. im- not + prudens prudent: cf. F. imprudent. See Prudent, and cf. Improvident.] Not prudent; wanting in prudence or discretion; indiscreet; injudicious; not attentive to consequence; improper. -- Im*pru"dent*ly, adv.

impuberal.c: Impuberal Im*pu"ber*al (ĭm*pū"bẽr*ail), a. Not having arrived at puberty; immature.

impuberty.c: Impuberty Im*pu"ber*ty (-ty̆), n. The condition of not having reached puberty, or the age of ability to reproduce one's species; lack of age at which the marriage contract can be legally entered into.

impudence.c: Impudence Im"pu*dence (ĭm"pu*deins), n. [L. impudentia: cf. F. impudence. See Impudent.] The quality of being impudent; assurance, accompanied with a disregard of the presence or opinions of others; shamelessness; forwardness; lack of modesty.

impudent.c: Impudent Im"pu*dent (ĭm"pu*deint), a. [L. impudens, -entis; pref. im- not + pudens ashamed, modest, p. pr. of pudere to feel shame: cf. F. impudent.] 1. Behaving boldly, with contempt or disregard for propriety in behavior toward others; unblushingly forward; impertinent; saucy.

impudently.c: Impudently Im"pu*dent*ly, adv. In an impudent manner; with unbecoming assurance; shamelessly.

impudicity.c: Impudicity Im`pu*dic"i*ty (?), n. [L. impudicus immodest; im- not + pudicus shamefaced, modest: cf. F. impudicité, L. impudicitia.] Immodesty. Sheldon.

impugn.c: Impugn Im*pugn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impugned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impugning.] [OE. impugnen, F. impugner, fr. L. impugnare; in on, against + pugnare to flight. See Pugnacious.] To attack by words or arguments; to contradict; to assail; to call in question; to make insinuations against; to gainsay; to oppose; as, to impugn a person's integrity.

impugnable.c: Impugnable Im*pugn"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being impugned; that may be gainsaid.

impugnation.c: Impugnation Im`pug*na"tion (?), n. [L. impugnatio: cf. OF. impugnation.] Act of impugning; opposition; attack. [Obs.]

impugnment.c: Impugnment Im*pugn"ment (?), n. The act of impugning, or the state of being impugned. Ed. Rev.

impuissance.c: Impuissance Im*pu"is*sance (?), n. [Cf. F. impuissance.] Lack of power; inability. Bacon.

impuissant.c: Impuissant Im*pu"is*sant (?), a. [F., fr. pref. im- not + puissant. See Puissant.] Weak; impotent; feeble.

impulse.c: Impulse Im"pulse (?), n. [L. impulsus, fr. impellere. See Impel.]
Impulse Im*pulse" (?), v. t. [See Impel.] To impel; to incite. [Obs.] Pope.

impulsion.c: Impulsion Im*pul"sion (?), n. [L. impulsio: cf. F. impulsion. See Impel.]

impulsive.c: Impulsive Im*pul"sive (?), n. That which impels or gives an impulse; an impelling agent. Sir W. Wotton.

impulsively.c: Impulsively Im*pul"sive*ly, adv. In an impulsive manner.

impulsiveness.c: Impulsiveness Im*pul"sive*ness, n. The quality of being impulsive.

impulsor.c: Impulsor Im*pul"sor (?), n. [L.] One who, or that which, impels; an inciter. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

impunctate.c: Impunctate Im*punc"tate (?), a. Not punctate or dotted.

impunctual.c: Impunctual Im*punc"tu*al (?), a. [Pref. im- not + punctual: cf. F. imponctuel.] Not punctual. [R.]

impunctuality.c: Impunctuality Im*punc`tu*al"i*ty (?), n. Neglect of, or failure in, punctuality. [R.] A. Hamilton.

impunibly.c: Impunibly Im*pu"ni*bly (?), adv. Without punishment; with impunity. [Obs.] J. Ellis.

impunity.c: Impunity Im*pu"ni*ty (?), n. [L. impunitas, fr. impunis without punishment; pref. im- not + poena punishment: cf. F. impunité. See Pain.] Exemption or freedom from punishment, harm, or loss.

impuration.c: Impuration Im`pu*ra"tion (?), n. Defilement; obscuration. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

impure.c: Impure Im*pure" (?), a. [L. impurus; pref. im- not + purus pure: cf. F. impur. See Pure.]
Impure Im*pure", v. t. To defile; to pollute. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

impurely.c: Impurely Im*pure"ly, adv. In an impure manner.

impureness.c: Impureness Im*pure"ness, n. The quality or condition of being impure; impurity. Milton.

impurity.c: Impurity Im*pu"ri*ty (?), n.; pl. Impurities (#). [L. impuritas: cf. F. impureté.]

impurple.c: Impurple Im*pur"ple (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Impurpled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Impurpling (?).] [Pref. im- in + purple. Cf. Empurple.] To color or tinge with purple; to make red or reddish; to purple; as, a field impurpled with blood.

imputability.c: Imputability Im*put`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being imputable; imputableness.

imputableness.c: Imputableness Im*put"a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being imputable.

imputation.c: Imputation Im`pu*ta"tion (?), [L. imputatio an account, a charge: cf. F. imputation.]

imputative.c: Imputative Im*put"a*tive (?), a. [L. imputativus: cf. F. imputatif.] Transferred by imputation; that may be imputed. -- Im*put"a*tive*ly, adv.

impute.c: Impute Im*pute" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Imputed; p. pr. & vb. n. Imputing.] [F. imputer, L. imputare to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute; pref. im- in + putare to reckon, think. See Putative.]

imputrescible.c: Imputrescible Im`pu*tres"ci*ble (?), a. [Pref. im- + putrescible: cf. F. imputrescible.] Not putrescible.

imrigh.c: Imrigh Im"righ (?), n. [Scot.; Gael. eun-bhrigh chicken soup.] A peculiar strong soup or broth, made in Scotland. [Written also imrich.]

in.c: In- In- (ĭn-). [See In, prep. Cf. Em-, En-.] A prefix from Eng. prep. in, also from Lat. prep. in, meaning in, into, on, among; as, inbred, inborn, inroad; incline, inject, intrude. In words from the Latin, in- regularly becomes il- before l, ir- before r, and im- before a labial; as, illusion, irruption, imblue, immigrate, impart. In- is sometimes used with an simple intensive force.

In- In- (ĭn-). [L. in-; akin to E. un-. See Un-.] An inseparable prefix, or particle, meaning not, non-, un- as, inactive, incapable, inapt. In- regularly becomes il- before l, ir- before r, and im- before a labial.
-in -in. A suffix. See the Note under -ine.

In In, prep. [AS. in; akin to D. & G. in, Icel. ī, Sw. & Dan. i, OIr. & L. in, Gr. 'en. √197. Cf. 1st In-, Inn.] The specific signification of in is situation or place with respect to surrounding, environment, encompassment, etc. It is used with verbs signifying being, resting, or moving within limits, or within circumstances or conditions of any kind conceived of as limiting, confining, or investing, either wholly or in part. In its different applications, it approaches some of the meanings of, and sometimes is interchangeable with, within, into, on, at, of, and among. It is used: --

In In, adv. 1. Not out; within; inside. In, the preposition, becomes an adverb by omission of its object, leaving it as the representative of an adverbial phrase, the context indicating what the omitted object is; as, he takes in the situation (i. e., he comprehends it in his mind); the Republicans were in (i. e., in office); in at one ear and out at the other (i. e., in or into the head); his side was in (i. e., in the turn at the bat); he came in (i. e., into the house).
In In, n. 1. One who is in office; -- the opposite of out.
In In (ĭn), v. t. To inclose; to take in; to harvest. [Obs.]
In and in In and in, a. & adv. Applied to breeding from a male and female of the same parentage. See under Breeding.
In antis ‖In an"tis (?). [L.] (Arch.) Between antæ; -- said of a portico in classical style, where columns are set between two antæ, forming the angles of the building. See Anta.
In commendam ‖In com*men"dam (?). [See Commendam.] (Law) See Commendam, and Partnership in Commendam, under Partnership.
In esse ‖In` es"se (?). [L.] In being; actually existing; -- distinguished from in posse, or in potentia, which denote that a thing is not, but may be.
In loco ‖In lo"co (?). [L.] In the place; in the proper or natural place.
In posse ‖In` pos"se (?). [L.] In possibility; possible, although not yet in existence or come to pass; -- contradistinguished from in esse.
In rem ‖In rem (?). [L.] (Law) Lit., in or against a (or the) thing; --

In situ ‖In si"tu (?) adv. & adj. [L.] 1. In its natural or original position or place; in position; -- said specif., in geology, of a rock, soil, or fossil, when in the situation in which it was originally formed or deposited.
In transitu ‖In` tran"si*tu (?). [L.] (Law) In transit; during passage; as, goods in transitu.
In vacuo ‖In` vac"u*o (?). [L.] (Physics) In a vacuum; in empty space; as, experiments in vacuo.

-in Tetrazine { Tet*raz"ine (?), n. Also -in }. [Tetrazo- + -ine.] (Chem.) A hypothetical compound, C2H2N4 which may be regarded as benzene with four CH groups replaced by nitrogen atoms; also, any of various derivatives of the same. There are three isomeric varieties.

inability.c: Inability In`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + ability: cf. F. inhabileté. See Able, and cf. Unable.] The quality or state of being unable; lack of ability; lack of sufficient power, strength, resources, or capacity.

inabstinence.c: Inabstinence In*ab"sti*nence (?), n. [Pref. in- not + abstinence: cf. F. inabstinence.] Lack of abstinence; indulgence. [Obs.] “The inabstinence of Eve.” Milton.

inaccessibility.c: Inaccessibility In`ac*cess`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inaccessibilité.] The quality or state of being inaccessible; inaccessibleness. “The inaccessibility of the precipice.” Bp. Butler.

inaccessible.c: Inaccessible In`ac*cess"i*ble (?), a. [L. inaccessibilis: cf. F. inaccessible. See In- not, and Accessible.] Not accessible; not to be reached, obtained, or approached; as, an inaccessible rock, fortress, document, prince, etc. -- In`ac*cess"i*ble*ness, n. -- In`ac*cess"i*bly, adv.

inaccurate.c: Inaccurate In*ac"cu*rate (?), a. Not accurate; not according to truth; inexact; not quite correct; incorrect; erroneous; as, in inaccurate man, narration, copy, judgment, calculation, etc.

inaccurately.c: Inaccurately In*ac"cu*rate*ly, adv. In an inaccurate manner; incorrectly; inexactly.

inacquaintance.c: Inacquaintance In`ac*quaint"ance (?), a. Lack of acquaintance. Good.

inacquiescent.c: Inacquiescent In*ac`qui*es"cent (?), a. Not acquiescent or acquiescing.

inaction.c: Inaction In*ac"tion (?), n. [Pref. in. not + action: cf. inaction.] Lack of action or activity; forbearance from labor; idleness; rest; inertness. Berkeley.

inactive.c: Inactive In*ac"tive (?), a. [Pref. in- not + active: cf. F. inactif.]

inactively.c: Inactively In*ac"tive*ly, adv. In an inactive manner. Locke.

inactose.c: Inactose In*ac"tose (?), n. (Chem.) A variety of sugar, found in certain plants. It is optically inactive.

inactuate.c: Inactuate In*ac"tu*ate (?), v. t. To put in action. [Obs.]

inadaptation.c: Inadaptation In*ad`ap*ta"tion (?), n. Lack of adaptation; unsuitableness.

inadequacy.c: Inadequacy In*ad"e*qua*cy (?), n. [From Inadequate.] The quality or state of being inadequate or insufficient; defectiveness; insufficiency; inadequateness.

inadequate.c: Inadequate In*ad"e*quate (?), a. [Pref. in- not + adequate: cf. F. inadéquat.] Not adequate; unequal to the purpose; insufficient; deficient; as, inadequate resources, power, conceptions, representations, etc. Dryden.

inadequation.c: Inadequation In*ad`e*qua"tion (?), n. Lack of exact correspondence. [Obs.] Puller.

inadmissibility.c: Inadmissibility In`ad*mis`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inadmissibilité.] The state or quality of being inadmissible, or not to be received.

inadmissible.c: Inadmissible In`ad*mis"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + admissible: cf. F. inadmissible.] Not admissible; not proper to be admitted, allowed, or received; as, inadmissible testimony; an inadmissible proposition, or explanation. -- In`ad*mis"si*bly, adv.

inadvertency.c: Inadvertency Inadvertence { In`ad*vert"ence (?); pl. -ces (?), In`ad*vert"en*cy (?); pl. -cies (?), } n. [Cf. F. inadvertance.]

inadvertent.c: Inadvertent In`ad*vert"ent (?), a. [Cf. F. inadvertant. See 2d In-, and Advert.] Not turning the mind to a matter; heedless; careless; negligent; inattentive.

inadvisable.c: Inadvisable In`ad*vis"a*ble (?), a. Not advisable. -- In`ad*vis"a*ble*ness, n.

inaffability.c: Inaffability In*af`fa*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inaffabilité.] Lack of affability or sociability; reticence.

inaffable.c: Inaffable In*af"fa*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + affable.] Not affable; reserved in social intercourse.

inaffectation.c: Inaffectation In*af`fec*ta"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + affectation: cf. F. inaffectation.] Freedom from affectation; naturalness. [R.]

inaidable.c: Inaidable In*aid"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being assisted; helpless. [R.] Shak.

inalienability.c: Inalienability In*al`ien*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being inalienable.

inalienable.c: Inalienable In*al"ien*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + alienable: cf. F. inaliénable.] Incapable of being alienated, surrendered, or transferred to another; not alienable; as, in inalienable birthright.

inalienableness.c: Inalienableness In*al"ien*a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inalienable; inalienability.

inalienably.c: Inalienably In*al"ien*a*bly, adv. In a manner that forbids alienation; as, rights inalienably vested.

inalimental.c: Inalimental In*al`i*men"tal (?), a. Affording no aliment or nourishment. [Obs.] Bacon.

inalterability.c: Inalterability In*al`ter*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inaltérabilité.] The quality of being unalterable or unchangeable; permanence.

inalterable.c: Inalterable In*al"ter*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + alterable: cf. F. inaltérable.] Not alterable; incapable of being altered or changed; unalterable. -- In*al"ter*a*ble*ness, n. -- In*al"ter*a*bly, adv.

inamissible.c: Inamissible In`a*mis"si*ble (?), a. [L. inamissibilis: cf. F. inamissible.] Incapable of being lost. [R.] Hammond. -- In`a*mis"si*ble*ness, n. [R.]

inamorata.c: Inamorata In*a`mo*ra"ta (?), n. [It. innamorata, fem., innamorato, masc., p. p. of innamorare to inspire with love. See Enamor.] A woman in love; a mistress. “The fair inamorata.” Sherburne.

inamorate.c: Inamorate In*am"o*rate (?), a. Enamored. Chapman. -- In*am"o*rate*ly, adv. [R.]

inamorato.c: Inamorato ‖In*a`mo*ra"to (?), n.; pl. Inamoratos (#). [See Inamorata.] A male lover.

inamovable.c: Inamovable In`a*mov"a*ble (?), a. Not amovable or removable. [R.] Palgrave.

inandin.c: In-and-in In"-and-in" (?), n. An old game played with four dice. In signified a doublet, or two dice alike; in-and-in, either two doubles, or the four dice alike.

inane.c: Inane In*ane" (?), a. [L. inanis.] Without contents; empty; void of sense or intelligence; purposeless; pointless; characterless; useless. “Vague and inane instincts.” I. Taylor. -- In*ane"ly, adv.
Inane In*ane", n. That which is void or empty. [R.]

inaniloquous.c: Inaniloquous Inaniloquent { In`a*nil"o*quent (?), In`a*nil"o*quous (?), } a. [L. inanis empty + loqui to speak.] Given to talking inanely; loquacious; garrulous. [R.]

inanimate.c: Inanimate In*an"i*mate (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in (or intensively) + animate.] To animate. [Obs.] Donne.

Inanimate In*an"i*mate (?), a. [L. inanimatus; pref. in- not + animatus animate.] Not animate; destitute of life or spirit; lifeless; dead; inactive; dull; as, stones and earth are inanimate substances.

inanimated.c: Inanimated In*an"i*ma`ted (?), a. Destitute of life; lacking animation; unanimated. Pope.

inanimateness.c: Inanimateness In*an"i*mate*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being inanimate.

inanimation.c: Inanimation In*an`i*ma"tion (?), n. [See 2d Inanimate.] Lack of animation; lifeless; dullness.
Inanimation In*an`i*ma"tion, n. [See 1st Inanimate.] Infusion of life or vigor; animation; inspiration. [Obs.]

inanitiate.c: Inanitiate In`a*ni"ti*ate (?), v. t. To produce inanition in; to exhaust for lack of nourishment. [R.]

inanition.c: Inanition In`a*ni"tion (?), n. [F. inanition, L. inanitio emptiness, fr. inanire to empty, fr. inanis empty. Cf. Inane.] The condition of being inane; emptiness; lack of fullness, as in the vessels of the body; hence, specifically, exhaustion from lack of food, either from partial or complete starvation, or from a disorder of the digestive apparatus, producing the same result.

inanity.c: Inanity In*an"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Inanities (#). [L. inanitas, fr. inanis empty: cf. F. inanité. See Inane.]

inantherate.c: Inantherate In*an"ther*ate (?), a. (Bot.) Not bearing anthers; -- said of sterile stamens.

inapathy.c: Inapathy In*ap"a*thy (?), n. Sensibility; feeling; -- opposed to apathy. [R.]

inappealable.c: Inappealable In`ap*peal"a*ble (?), a. Not admitting of appeal; not appealable. Coleridge.

inappeasable.c: Inappeasable In`ap*peas"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being appeased or satisfied; unappeasable.

inappellability.c: Inappellability In`ap*pel`la*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being inappellable; finality.

inappetency.c: Inappetency Inappetence { In*ap"pe*tence (?), In*ap"pe*ten*cy (?), } n. [Pref. in- not + appetence: cf. F. inappétence.] Lack of appetency; lack of desire.

inapplicability.c: Inapplicability In*ap`pli*ca*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inapplicabilité.] The quality of being inapplicable; unfitness; inapplicableness.

inapplicable.c: Inapplicable In*ap"pli*ca*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + applicable.] Not applicable; incapable of being applied; not adapted; not suitable; as, the argument is inapplicable to the case. J. S. Mill.

inapplication.c: Inapplication In*ap`pli*ca"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + application: cf. F. inapplication.] Lack of application, attention, or diligence; negligence; indolence.

inapposite.c: Inapposite In*ap"po*site (?), a. Not apposite; not fit or suitable; not pertinent. -- In*ap"po*site*ly, adv.

inappreciable.c: Inappreciable In`ap*pre"ci*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + appreciable: cf. F. inappréciable.] Not appreciable; too small to be perceived; incapable of being duly valued or estimated. Hallam.

inapprehensible.c: Inapprehensible In*ap`pre*hen"si*ble (?), a. [L. inapprehensibilis: cf. F. inappréhensible.] Not apprehensible; unintelligible; inconceivable. Milton.

inapprehensive.c: Inapprehensive In*ap`pre*hen"sive (?), a. Not apprehensive; regardless; unconcerned. Jer. Taylor.

inapproachable.c: Inapproachable In`ap*proach"a*ble (?), a. Not approachable; unapproachable; inaccessible; unequaled. -- In`ap*proach"a*bly, adv.

inappropriate.c: Inappropriate In`ap*pro"pri*ate (?), a. Not instrument (to); not appropriate; unbecoming; unsuitable; not specially fitted; -- followed by to or for. -- In`ap*pro"pri*ate*ly, adv. -- In`ap*pro"pri*ate*ness, n.

inapt.c: Inapt In*apt" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + apt: cf. F. inapte. Cf. Inept.] Unapt; not apt; unsuitable; inept. -- In*apt"ly, adv. -- In*apt"ness, n.

inaptitude.c: Inaptitude In*apt"i*tude (?), n. [In- + aptitude: cf. F. inaptitude. Cf. Ineptitude.] Lack of aptitude.

inaquate.c: Inaquate In*a"quate (?), a. [L. inaquatus, p. p. of inaquare to make into water; pref. in- in + aqua water.] Embodied in, or changed into, water. [Obs.] Cranmer.

inaquation.c: Inaquation In`a*qua"tion (?), n. The state of being inaquate. [Obs.] Bp. Gardiner.

inarch.c: Inarch In*arch" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inarched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inarching.] To graft by uniting, as a scion, to a stock, without separating either from its root before the union is complete; -- also called to graft by approach. P. Miler.

inarching.c: Inarching In*arch"ing, n. A method of ingrafting. See Inarch.

inarticulate.c: Inarticulate In`ar*tic"u*late (?), a. [L. inarticulatus; pref. in- not + articulatus articulate.]

inarticulated.c: Inarticulated In`ar*tic"u*la`ted (?), a. Not articulated; not jointed or connected by a joint.

inarticulately.c: Inarticulately In`ar*tic"u*late*ly (?), adv. In an inarticulate manner. Hammond.

inarticulateness.c: Inarticulateness In`ar*tic"u*late*ness, n. The state or quality of being inarticulate.

inarticulation.c: Inarticulation In`ar*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inarticulation.] Inarticulateness. Chesterfield.

inartificial.c: Inartificial In*ar`ti*fi"cial (?), a. [Pref. in- not + artificial: cf. F. inartificiel.] Not artificial; not made or elaborated by art; natural; simple; artless; as, an inartificial argument; an inartificial character. -- In*ar`ti*fi"cial*ly, adv. -- In*ar`ti*fi"cial*ness, n.

inasmuch.c: Inasmuch In`as*much" (?), adv. [In + as + much.] In like degree; in like manner; seeing that; considering that; since; -- followed by as. See In as much as, under In, prep.

inattention.c: Inattention In`at*ten"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + attention: cf. F. inattention.] Lack of attention, or failure to pay attention; disregard; heedlessness; neglect.

inattentive.c: Inattentive In`at*ten"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. inattentif.] Not attentive; not fixing the mind on an object; heedless; careless; negligent; regardless; as, an inattentive spectator or hearer; an inattentive habit. I. Watts.

inaudibility.c: Inaudibility In*au`di*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being inaudible; inaudibleness.

inaudible.c: Inaudible In*au"di*ble (?), a. [L. inaudibilis; pref. in- not + audire to hear: cf. F. unaudible. See In- not, and Audible.] Not audible; incapable of being heard; silent. -- In*au"di*ble*ness, n. -- In*au"di*bly, adv.

inaugur.c: Inaugur In*au"gur (?), v. t. [Cf. F. inaugurer. See Inaugurate.] To inaugurate. [Obs.] Latimer.

inaugural.c: Inaugural In*au"gu*ral (?), a. [Cf. F. inaugural.] Pertaining to, or performed or pronounced at, an inauguration; as, an inaugural address; the inaugural exercises.

inaugurate.c: Inaugurate In*au"gu*rate (?), a. [L. inauguratus, p. p. of inaugurare to take omens from the flight of birds (before entering upon any important undertaking); hence, to consecrate, inaugurate, or install, with such divination; pref. in- in + augurare, augurari, to augur. See Augur.] Invested with office; inaugurated. Drayton.
Inaugurate In*au"gu*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inaugurated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inaugurating (?).]

inauguration.c: Inauguration In*au`gu*ra"tion (?), n. [L. inauguratio a beginning: cf. F. inauguration.]

Inauguration Day In*au`gu*ra"tion Day. The day on which the President of the United States is inaugurated, the 20th of January in every year next after a year divisible by four. Prior to the adoption of the twentieth amendment to the Constitution of the United States (ratified February 6, 1933) the date was the 4th of March.

inauguratory.c: Inauguratory In*au"gu*ra*to*ry (?), a. Suitable for, or pertaining to, inauguration. Johnson.

inaurate.c: Inaurate In*au"rate (?), a. [L. inauratus, p. p. inaurare to gild; pref. in- in + aurum gold.] Covered with gold; gilded.
Inaurate In*au"rate (?), v. t. To cover with gold; to gild.

inauration.c: Inauration In`au*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inauration.] The act or process of gilding or covering with gold.

inauspicate.c: Inauspicate In*aus"pi*cate (?), a. [L. inauspicatus; pref. in- not + auspicatus, p. p. auspicari. See Auspicate.] Inauspicious. [Obs.] Sir G. Buck.

inauspicious.c: Inauspicious In`aus*pi"cious (?), a. Not auspicious; ill-omened; unfortunate; unlucky; unfavorable. “Inauspicious stars.” Shak. “Inauspicious love.” Dryden.

inauthoritative.c: Inauthoritative In`au*thor"i*ta*tive (?), a. Without authority; not authoritative.

inbarge.c: Inbarge In"barge (?), v. t. & i. To embark; to go or put into a barge. [Obs.] Drayton.

inbeing.c: Inbeing In"be`ing (?), n. Inherence; inherent existence. I. Watts.

inbind.c: Inbind In*bind" (?), v. t. To inclose. [Obs.] Fairfax.

inblown.c: Inblown In"blown` (?), a. Blown in or into. [Obs.]

inboard.c: Inboard In"board` (?), a. & adv. 1. (Naut.) Inside the line of a vessel's bulwarks or hull; the opposite of outboard; as, an inboard engine; an inboard cargo; haul the boom inboard.

inborn.c: Inborn In"born` (?), a. Born in or with; implanted by nature; innate; congenital; as, inborn passions. Cowper.

inbreaking.c: Inbreaking Inbreak { In"break` (?), In"break`ing, } n. A breaking in; inroad; invasion.

inbreathe.c: Inbreathe In*breathe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inbreathed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inbreathing.] To infuse by breathing; to inspire. Coleridge.

inbred.c: Inbred In"bred` (?), a. Bred within; innate; as, inbred worth. “Inbred sentiments.” Burke.

inbreed.c: Inbreed In*breed" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inbred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inbreeding.] [Cf. Imbreed.]

inburst.c: Inburst In"burst` (?), n. A bursting in or into.

inc.c: Inc Inc (?), n. A Japanese measure of length equal to about two and one twelfth yards. [Written also ink.]

inca.c: Inca In"ca (?), n. (a) An emperor or monarch of Peru before, or at the time of, the Spanish conquest; any member of this royal dynasty, reputed to have been descendants of the sun. (b) pl. The people governed by the Incas, now represented by the Quichua tribe.

incage.c: Incage In*cage" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incaged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incaging (?).] [Cf. Encage.] To confine in, or as in, a cage; to coop up. [Written also encage.] “Incaged birds.” Shak.

incagement.c: Incagement In*cage"ment (?), n. Confinement in, or as in, cage. [Obs.] Shelton.

incalculability.c: Incalculability In*cal`cu*la*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being incalculable.

incalculable.c: Incalculable In*cal"cu*la*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + calculable: cf. F. incalculable.] Not capable of being calculated; beyond calculation; very great; as, his action did incalculable harm. -- In*cal"cu*la*ble*ness, n. -- In*cal"cu*la*bly, adv.

incalescence.c: Incalescence In`ca*les"cence (?), n. The state of being incalescent, or of growing warm. Sir T. Browne.

incalescent.c: Incalescent In`ca*les"cent (?), a. [L. incalescens, -entis, p. pr. of incalescere to grow hot. See 1st In-, and Calescence.] Growing warm; increasing in heat.

incameration.c: Incameration In*cam`er*a"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- in + L. camera chamber, LL., also, jurisdiction: cf. F. incamération, It. incamerazione.] (R. C. Ch.) The act or process of uniting lands, rights, or revenues, to the ecclesiastical chamber, i. e., to the pope's domain.

incan.c: Incan In"can (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Incas.

incandescence.c: Incandescence In`can*des"cence (?), n. [Cf. F. incandescence.] A white heat, or the glowing or luminous whiteness of a body caused by intense heat.

incandescent.c: Incandescent In`can*des"cent (?), a. [L. incandecens, -entis, p. pr. of incandescere to become warm or hot; pref. in- in + candescere to become of a glittering whiteness, to become red hot, incho. fr. candere to be of a glittering whiteness: cf. F. incandescent. See Candle.] White, glowing, or luminous, with intense heat; as, incandescent carbon or platinum; hence, clear; shining; brilliant.

incanescent.c: Incanescent In`ca*nes"cent (?), a. [L. incanescens, p. pr. incanescere to become gray.] Becoming hoary or gray; canescent.

incanous.c: Incanous In*ca"nous (?), a. [L. incanus; pref. in- in + canus hoary.] (Bot.) Hoary with white pubescence.

incantation.c: Incantation In`can*ta"tion (?), n. [L. incantatio, fr. incantare to chant a magic formula over one: cf. F. incantation. See Enchant.]

incantatory.c: Incantatory In*cant"a*to*ry (?), a. Dealing by enchantment; magical. Sir T. Browne.

incanting.c: Incanting In*cant"ing, a. Enchanting. [Obs.] Sir T. Herbert.

incanton.c: Incanton In*can"ton (?), v. t. To unite to, or form into, a canton or separate community. Addison.

incapability.c: Incapability In*ca`pa*bil"i*ty (?), n. 1. The quality of being incapable; incapacity. Suckling.

incapable.c: Incapable In*ca"pa*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + capable: cf. F. incapable, L. incapabilis incomprehensible.]
Incapable In*ca"pa*ble, n. One who is morally or mentally weak or inefficient; an imbecile; a simpleton.

incapableness.c: Incapableness In*ca"pa*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being incapable; incapability.

incapably.c: Incapably In*ca"pa*bly, adv. In an incapable manner.

incapacious.c: Incapacious In`ca*pa"cious (?), a. [Pref. in- not + capacious: cf. L. incapax incapable.] Not capacious; narrow; small; weak or foolish; as, an incapacious soul. Bp. Burnet. -- In`ca*pa"cious*ness, n.

incapacitate.c: Incapacitate In`ca*pac"i*tate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incapacitated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incapacitating (?).] [Pref. in- not + capacitate.]

incapacitation.c: Incapacitation In`ca*pac`i*ta"tion (?), n. The act of incapacitating or state of being incapacitated; incapacity; disqualification. Burke.

incapacity.c: Incapacity In`ca*pac"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Incapacities (?). [Cf. F. incapacité.]

incapsulate.c: Incapsulate In*cap"su*late (?), v. t. (Physiol.) To inclose completely, as in a membrane.

incapsulation.c: Incapsulation In*cap`su*la"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The process of becoming, or the state or condition of being, incapsulated; as, incapsulation of the ovum in the uterus.

incarcerate.c: Incarcerate In*car"cer*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incarcerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incarcerating (?).] [Pref. in- in + L. carceratus, p. p. of carcerare to imprison, fr. carcer prison.]

incarcerated.c: incarcerated incarcerate in*car"cer*ate, in*car"cer*at*ed (?), a. Imprisoned. Dr. H. More.

incarn.c: Incarn In*carn" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. incarner. See Incarnate.] To cover or invest with flesh. [R.] Wiseman.
Incarn In*carn", v. i. To develop flesh. [R.] Wiseman.

incarnadine.c: Incarnadine In*car"na*dine (?), a. [F. incarnadin, It. incarnatino; L. pref. in- in + caro, carnis, flesh. Cf. Carnation, Incarnate.] Flesh-colored; of a carnation or pale red color. [Obs.] Lovelace.
Incarnadine In*car"na*dine, v. t. To dye red or crimson.

incarnate.c: Incarnate In*car"nate (?), a. [Pref. in- not + carnate.] Not in the flesh; spiritual. [Obs.]
Incarnate In*car"nate, a. [L. incarnatus, p. p. of incarnare to incarnate, pref. in- in + caro, carnis, flesh. See Carnal.]

Incarnate In*car"nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incarnated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incarnating (?).] To clothe with flesh; to embody in flesh; to invest, as spirits, ideals, etc., with a human from or nature.
Incarnate In*car"nate, v. i. To form flesh; to granulate, as a wound. [R.]

incarnative.c: Incarnative In*car"na*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. incarnatif.] Causing new flesh to grow; healing; regenerative. -- n. An incarnative medicine.

incarnification.c: Incarnification In*car`ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [See Incarnation, and -fy.] The act of assuming, or state of being clothed with, flesh; incarnation.

incase.c: Incase In*case" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incased (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incasing.] [F. encaisser; pref. en- (L. in) + caisse case. See Case a box, and cf. Encase, Enchase.] To inclose in a case; to inclose; to cover or surround with something solid.

incask.c: Incask In*cask" (?), v. t. To cover with a casque or as with a casque. Sherwood.

incastellated.c: Incastellated In*cas"tel*la`ted (?), a. Confined or inclosed in a castle.

incatenation.c: Incatenation In*cat`e*na"tion (?), n. [LL. incatenatio; L. pref. in- in + catena chain. See Enchain.] The act of linking together; enchaining. [R.] Goldsmith.

incaution.c: Incaution In*cau"tion (?), n. Lack of caution. Pope.

incautious.c: Incautious In*cau"tious (?), a. [Pref. in- not + cautious: cf. L. incautus.] Not cautious; not circumspect; not attending to the circumstances on which safety and interest depend; heedless; careless; as, an incautious step; an incautious remark.

incavated.c: Incavated In"ca*va`ted (ĭn"kȧ*vā`tĕd), a. [L. incavatus, p. p. of incavare to make hollow: pref in- in + cavare to hollow out, fr. cavus hollow.] Made hollow; bent round or in.

incavation.c: Incavation In`ca*va"tion (ĭn`kȧ*vā"shŭn), n. Act of making hollow; also, a hollow; an excavation; a depression.

incaved.c: Incaved In*caved" (ĭn*kāvd"), a. [Pref. in- in + cave. Cf. Encave, Incavated.] Inclosed in a cave.

incaverned.c: Incaverned In*cav"erned (ĭn*kăv"ẽrnd), a. Inclosed or shut up as in a cavern. Drayton.

incedingly.c: Incedingly In*ced"ing*ly (ĭn*sēd"ĭng*ly̆), adv. [L. incedere to walk majestically.] Majestically. [R.] C. Bronté.

incelebrity.c: Incelebrity In`ce*leb"ri*ty (?), n. Lack of celebrity or distinction; obscurity. [R.] Coleridge.

incend.c: Incend In*cend" (?), v. t. [L. incendere, incensum, to kindle, burn. See Incense to inflame.] To inflame; to excite. [Obs.] Marston.

incendiarism.c: Incendiarism In*cen"di*a*rism (?), n. [From Incendiary.] The act or practice of maliciously setting fires; arson.

incendiary.c: Incendiary In*cen"di*a*ry (?; 277), n.; pl. Incendiaries (#). [L. incendiarius: cf. F. incendiaire. See Incense to inflame.]
Incendiary In*cen"di*a*ry, a. [L. incendiarius, fr. incendium a fire, conflagration: cf. F. incendiaire. See Incense to inflame.]

incendious.c: Incendious In*cen"di*ous (?), a. [L. incendiosus burning, hot.] Promoting faction or contention; seditious; inflammatory. [Obs.] Bacon. -- In*cen"di*ous*ly, adv. [Obs.]

incensant.c: Incensant In*cen"sant (?), a. [See Incense to anger.] (Her.) A modern term applied to animals (as a boar) when borne as raging, or with furious aspect.

incensation.c: Incensation In`cen*sa"tion (?), n. (R. C. Ch.) The offering of incense. [R.] Encyc. Brit.

incense.c: Incense In*cense" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incensed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incensing.] [L. incensus, p. p. of incendere; pref. in- in + root of candere to glow. See Candle.]
Incense In"cense (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incensed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incensing.] [LL. incensare: cf. F. encenser. See Incense, n.]
Incense In"cense (?), n. [OE. encens, F. encens, L. incensum, fr. incensus, p. p. of incendere to burn. See Incense to inflame.]

incensebreathing.c: Incense-breathing In"cense-breath`ing (?), a. Breathing or exhaling incense. “Incense-breathing morn.” Gray.

incensement.c: Incensement In*cense"ment (?), n. Fury; rage; heat; exasperation; as, implacable incensement. Shak.

incenser.c: Incenser In*cen"ser (?), n. One who instigates or incites.

incension.c: Incension In*cen"sion (?), n. [L. incensio. See Incense to inflame.] The act of kindling, or the state of being kindled or on fire. Bacon.

incensive.c: Incensive In*cen"sive (?), a. Tending to excite or provoke; inflammatory. Barrow.

incensor.c: Incensor In*cen"sor (?), n. [L.] A kindler of anger or enmity; an inciter.

incensory.c: Incensory In*cen"so*ry (?; 277), n.; pl. Incensories (#). [LL. incensorium: cf. F. encensoir. See 2d Incense, and cf. Censer.] The vessel in which incense is burned and offered; a censer; a thurible. [R.] Evelyn.

incensurable.c: Incensurable In*cen"sur*a*ble (?; 135), a. [Pref. in- not + censurable: cf. F. incensurable.] Not censurable. Dr. T. Dwight. -- In*cen"sur*a*bly, adv.

incenter.c: Incenter In*cen"ter (?), n. (Geom.) The center of the circle inscribed in a triangle.

incentive.c: Incentive In*cen"tive (?), a. [L. incentivus, from incinere to strike up or set the tune; pref. in- + canere to sing. See Enchant, Chant.]

Incentive In*cen"tive, n. [L. incentivum.] That which moves or influences the mind, or operates on the passions; that which incites, or has a tendency to incite, to determination or action; that which prompts to good or ill; motive; spur; as, the love of money, and the desire of promotion, are two powerful incentives to action.

inception.c: Inception In*cep"tion (?), n. [L. inceptio, fr. incipere to begin; pref. in- in + capere to take. See Capable.]

inceptive.c: Inceptive In*cep"tive (?), a. Beginning; expressing or indicating beginning; as, an inceptive proposition; an inceptive verb, which expresses the beginning of action; -- called also inchoative. -- In*cep"tive*ly, adv.
Inceptive In*cep"tive, n. An inceptive word, phrase, or clause.

inceptor.c: Inceptor In*cep"tor (?), n. [L.] 1. A beginner; one in the rudiments. Johnson.

inceration.c: Inceration In`cer*a"tion (?), n. [L. incerare to smear with wax; pref. in- in + cerare to wax, fr. cera wax: cf. F. incération.] The act of smearing or covering with wax. B. Jonson.

incerative.c: Incerative In*cer"a*tive (?), a. Cleaving or sticking like wax. Cotgrave.

incertain.c: Incertain In*cer"tain (?), n. [Pref. in- not + certain: cf. F. incertain, L. incertus. See Certain.] Uncertain; doubtful; unsteady. -- In*cer"tain*ly, adv.

incertitude.c: Incertitude In*cer"ti*tude (?), n. [Cf. F. incertitude, LL. incertitudo, fr. L. incertus. See Incertain.] Uncertainty; doubtfulness; doubt.

incertum.c: Incertum ‖In*cer"tum (?), a. Doubtful; not of definite form.

incessable.c: Incessable In*ces"sa*ble (?), a. [L. incessabilis; pref. in- not + cessare to cease.] Unceasing; continual. [Obs.] Shelton. -- In*ces"sa*bly, adv. [Obs.]

incessancy.c: Incessancy In*ces"san*cy (?), n. [From Incessant.] The quality of being incessant; unintermitted continuance; unceasingness. Dr. T. Dwight.

incessant.c: Incessant In*ces"sant (?), a. [L. incessans, -antis; pref. in- not + cessare to cease: cf. F. incessant. See Cease.] Continuing or following without interruption; unceasing; unitermitted; uninterrupted; continual; as, incessant clamors; incessant pain, etc.

incession.c: Incession In*ces"sion (?), n. [L. incedere, incessum, to walk.] Motion on foot; progress in walking. [Obs.]

incest.c: Incest In"cest (?), n. [F. inceste, L. incestum unchastity, incest, fr. incestus unchaste; pref. in- not + castus chaste. See Chaste.] The crime of cohabitation or sexual intercourse between persons related within the degrees wherein marriage is prohibited by law; broadly, sexual relations between closely related persons, usually taken as first cousins or closer. Shak.

incesttuous.c: Incesttuous In*cest"tu*ous (?; 135), a. [L. incestuosus: cf. F. incestueux.] 1. Guilty of incest; involving, or pertaining to, incest; as, an incestuous person or connection. Shak.

inch.c: Inch Inch (ĭnch), n. [Gael. inis.] An island; -- often used in the names of small islands off the coast of Scotland, as in Inchcolm, Inchkeith, etc. [Scot.]
Inch Inch, n. [OE. inche, unche, AS. ynce, L. uncia the twelfth part, inch, ounce. See Ounce a weight.]
Inch Inch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inching.]
Inch Inch, v. i. To advance or retire by inches or small degrees; to move slowly; as, to inch forward.
Inch Inch, a. Measuring an inch in any dimension, whether length, breadth, or thickness; -- used in composition; as, a two-inch cable; a four-inch plank.

inchamber.c: Inchamber In*cham"ber (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inchambered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inchambering.] [Pref. in- in + chamber: cf. OF. enchambrer.] To lodge in a chamber. [R.] Sherwood.

incharitable.c: Incharitable In*char"i*ta*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. incharitable.] Uncharitable; unfeeling. [Obs.] Shak.

incharity.c: Incharity In*char"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incharité.] Lack of charity. [Obs.] Evelyn.

inchastity.c: Inchastity In*chas"ti*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + chastity: cf. F. inchasteté.] Unchastity. [Obs.] Milton.

inched.c: Inched Inched (?), a. Having or measuring (so many) inches; as, a four-inched bridge. Shak.

inchest.c: Inchest In*chest" (?), v. t. To put into a chest.

inchmeal.c: Inchmeal Inch"meal` (?), n. [See Meal a part, and cf. Piecemeal.] A piece an inch long.
Inchmeal Inch"meal`, adv. Little by little; gradually.

inchoate.c: Inchoate In"cho*ate (?), a. [L. inchoatus, better incohatus, p. p. of incohare to begin.] Recently, or just, begun; beginning; partially but not fully in existence or operation; existing in its elements; incomplete. -- In"cho*ate*ly, adv.
Inchoate In"cho*ate (?), v. t. To begin. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

inchoation.c: Inchoation In`cho*a"tion (?), n. [L. inchoatio, incohatio.] Act of beginning; commencement; inception.

inchoative.c: Inchoative In*cho"a*tive (?; 277), a. [L. inchoativus, incohativus: cf. F. inchoatif.] Expressing or pertaining to a beginning; inceptive; as, an inchoative verb. “Some inchoative or imperfect rays.” W. Montagu. -- n. An inchoative verb. See Inceptive.

inchpin.c: Inchpin Inch"pin (?), n. [Written also inchipin, inche-pinne, inne-pinne.] [Cf. Gael. inne, innidh, bowel, entrail.] The sweetbread of a deer. Cotgrave.

inchworm.c: Inchworm Inch"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) The larva of any geometrid moth. It progresses forward by first bringing the rear end of the body forward, forming a loop, then moving the front part of the body; called also measuring worm, measuringworm, spanner, and looper. See Geometrid.

incicurable.c: Incicurable In*cic"u*ra*ble (?), a. [L. incicur not tame; pref. in- not + cicur name.] Untamable. [R.]

incide.c: Incide In*cide" (?), v. t. [L. incidere; pref. in- in + caedere to cut. See Concise, and cf. Incise.] To cut; to separate and remove; to resolve or break up, as by medicines. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.

incident.c: Incident In"ci*dent (?), a. [L. incidens, -entis, p. pr. & of incidere to fall into or upon; pref. in- in, on + cadere to fall: cf. F. incident. See Cadence.]
Incident In"ci*dent, n. [Cf. F. incident.] 1. That which falls out or takes place; an event; casualty; occurrence.

incidental.c: Incidental In`ci*den"tal (?), a. Happening, as an occasional event, without regularity; coming without design; casual; accidental; hence, not of prime concern; subordinate; collateral; as, an incidental conversation; an incidental occurrence; incidental expenses.

Incidental In`ci*den"tal, n. An incident; that which is incidental; esp., in the plural, an aggregate of subordinate or incidental items not particularized; as, the expense of tuition and incidentals. Pope.

incinerable.c: Incinerable In*cin"er*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being incinerated or reduced to ashes. Sir T. Browne.

incinerate.c: Incinerate In*cin"er*ate (?), [LL. incineratus, p. p. of incinerare to incinerate; L. pref. in- in + cinis, cineris, ashes.] Reduced to ashes by burning; thoroughly consumed by fire. [Obs.] Bacon.
Incinerate In*cin"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incinerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incinerating (?).] To burn to ashes; to consume by fire; to burn. Bacon.

incineration.c: Incineration In*cin`er*a"tion (?), n. [LL. incineratio: cf. F. incinération.] The act of incinerating, or the state of being incinerated; cremation.

incipiency.c: Incipiency Incipience { In*cip"i*ence (?), In*cip"i*en*cy (?), } n. [L. incipientia.] Beginning; commencement; incipient state.

incipient.c: Incipient In*cip"i*ent (?), a. [L. incipiens, p. pr. of incipere to begin. See Inception.] Beginning to be, or to show itself; commencing; initial; as, the incipient stage of a fever; incipient light of day. -- In*cip"i*ent*ly, adv.

incirclet.c: Incirclet In*cir"clet (?), n. [Cf. Encirclet.] A small circle. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

incircumscriptible.c: Incircumscriptible In*cir`cum*scrip"ti*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + circumscriptible: cf. LL. incircumscriptibilis.] Incapable of being circumscribed or limited. Cranmer.

incircumscription.c: Incircumscription In*cir`cum*scrip"tion (?), n. Condition or quality of being incircumscriptible or limitless. Jer. Taylor.

incircumspect.c: Incircumspect In*cir"cum*spect (?), a. [Pref. in- not + circumspect.] Not circumspect; heedless; careless; reckless; impolitic. Tyndale.

incircumspection.c: Incircumspection In*cir`cum*spec"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. incirconspection.] Lack of circumspection. Sir T. Browne.

incise.c: Incise In*cise" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incising.] [L. incisus, p. p. of incidere to incise: cf. F. inciser. See Incide.]

incised.c: Incised In*cised" (?), a. 1. Cut in; carved; engraved.

incisely.c: Incisely In*cise"ly (?), adv. In an incised manner.

incision.c: Incision In*ci"sion (?), n. [L. incisio: cf. F. incision. See Incise.]

incisor.c: Incisor In*ci"sor (?; 277), n. [NL.] (Anat.) One of the teeth in front of the canines in either jaw; an incisive tooth. See Tooth.
Incisor In*ci"sor, a. Adapted for cutting; of or pertaining to the incisors; incisive; as, the incisor nerve; an incisor foramen; an incisor tooth.

incisory.c: Incisory In*ci"so*ry (?), a. Having the quality of cutting; incisor; incisive.

incisure.c: Incisure In*cis"ure (?; 277), n. [L. incisura: cf. F. incisure.] A cut; an incision; a gash. Derham.

incitant.c: Incitant In*cit"ant (?), a. [L. incitans, -antis, p. pr. of incitare. See Incite.] Inciting; stimulating.
Incitant In*cit"ant, n. That which incites; an inciting agent or cause; a stimulant. E. Darwin.

incitation.c: Incitation In`ci*ta"tion (?), n. [L. incitatio: cf. F. incitation.]

incitative.c: Incitative In*cit"a*tive (?), n. A provocative; an incitant; a stimulant. [R.] Jervas.

incite.c: Incite In*cite" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incited (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inciting.] [L. incitare; pref. in- in + citare to rouse, stir up: cf. F. inciter. See Cite.] To move to action; to stir up; to rouse; to spur or urge on.

inciter.c: Inciter In*cit"er (?), n. One who, or that which, incites.

incitingly.c: Incitingly In*cit"ing*ly, adv. So as to incite or stimulate.

incitomotor.c: Incito-motor In*ci`to-mo"tor (?), a. [L. incitus incited + E. motor.] (Physiol.) Inciting to motion; -- applied to that action which, in the case of muscular motion, commences in the nerve centers, and excites the muscles to contraction. Opposed to excito-motor.

incivil.c: Incivil In*civ"il (?), a. [L. incivilis; pref. in- not + civilis civil: cf. F. incivil.] Uncivil; rude. [Obs.] Shak.

incivility.c: Incivility In`ci*vil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Incivilities (#). [L. incivilitas: cf. F. incivilité.]

incivilization.c: Incivilization In*civ`i*li*za"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + civilization.] The state of being uncivilized; lack of civilization; barbarism.

incivism.c: Incivism In*civ"ism (?), n. [Pref. in- not + civism: cf. F. incivisme.] Lack of civism; lack of patriotism or love to one's country; unfriendliness to one's state or government. [R.] Macaulay.

inclamation.c: Inclamation In`cla*ma"tion (?), n. [L. inclamatio. See 1st In-, and Claim.] Exclamation. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

inclasp.c: Inclasp In*clasp" (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + clasp. Cf. Enclasp.] To clasp within; to hold fast to; to embrace or encircle. [Written also enclasp.]

inclaudent.c: Inclaudent In*clau"dent (?), a. Not closing or shutting.

inclavated.c: Inclavated In"cla*va`ted (?), a. [LL. inclavatus; L. pref. in- in + clavare to fasten with nails, fr. clavus nail.] Set; fast; fixed. Dr. John Smith.

inclave.c: Inclave In*clave" (?), a. [See Inclavated.] (Her.) Resembling a series of dovetails; -- said of a line of division, such as the border of an ordinary.

inclemency.c: Inclemency In*clem"en*cy (?), n.; pl. Inclemencies (#). [L. inclementia: cf. F. inclémence.]

inclement.c: Inclement In*clem"ent (?), a. [L. inclemens; pref. in- not + clemens mild: cf. F. inclément. See Clement.]

inclemently.c: Inclemently In*clem"ent*ly, adv. In an inclement manner.

inclinableness.c: Inclinableness In*clin"a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being inclinable; inclination.

inclination.c: Inclination In`cli*na"tion (?), n. [L. inclinatio: cf. F. inclination.]

inclinatory.c: Inclinatory In*clin"a*to*ry (?; 277), a. Having the quality of leaning or inclining; as, the inclinatory needle. -- In*clin"a*to*ri*ly (#), adv. Sir T. Browne.

incline.c: Incline In*cline" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inclined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inclining.] [OE. inclinen, enclinen, OF. encliner, incliner, F. incliner, L. inclinare; pref. in- in + clinare to bend, incline; akin to E. lean. See Lean to incline.]
Incline In*cline", v. t. 1. To cause to deviate from a line, position, or direction; to give a leaning, bend, or slope to; as, incline the column or post to the east; incline your head to the right.
Incline In*cline", n. An inclined plane; an ascent or descent; a grade or gradient; a slope.

inclined.c: Inclined In*clined" (?), p. p. & a. 1. Having a leaning or tendency towards, or away from, a thing; disposed or moved by wish, desire, or judgment; as, a man inclined to virtue. “Each pensively inclined.” Cowper.

incliner.c: Incliner In*clin"er (?), n. One who, or that which, inclines; specifically, an inclined dial.

inclinnometer.c: Inclinnometer In`clin*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Incline + -meter.] (Magnetism) An apparatus to determine the inclination of the earth's magnetic force to the plane of the horizon; -- called also inclination compass, and dip circle.

inclip.c: Inclip In*clip" (?), v. t. To clasp; to inclose.

incloister.c: Incloister In*clois"ter (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + cloister: cf. F. encloîtrer. Cf. Encloister.] To confine as in a cloister; to cloister. Lovelace.

inclose.c: Inclose In*close" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inclosed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inclosing.] [See Enclose, and cf. Include.] [Written also enclose.]

incloser.c: Incloser In*clos"er (?), n. One who, or that which, incloses; one who fences off land from common grounds.

inclosure.c: Inclosure In*clo"sure (?; 135), n. [See Inclose, Enclosure.] [Written also enclosure.]

incloud.c: Incloud In*cloud" (?), v. t. To envelop as in clouds; to darken; to obscure. Milton.

include.c: Include In*clude" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Included; p. pr. & vb. n. Including.] [L. includere, inclusum; pref. in- in + claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Enclose.]

includible.c: Includible In*clud"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being included.

inclusa.c: Inclusa ‖In*clu"sa (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. inclusus, p. p. of includere to shut in.] (Zool.) A tribe of bivalve mollusks, characterized by the closed state of the mantle which envelops the body. The ship borer (Teredo navalis) is an example.

inclusion.c: Inclusion In*clu"sion (?), n. [L. inclusio: cf. F. inclusion. See Include.]

inclusively.c: Inclusively In*clu"sive*ly, adv. In an inclusive manner.

incoach.c: Incoach In*coach" (?), v. t. To put a coach.

incoacted.c: Incoacted Incoact { In`co*act" (?), In`co*act"ed (?), } a. [L. incoactus; pref. in- not + coactus forced. See Coact.] Not compelled; unconstrained. [Obs.] Coles.

incoalescence.c: Incoalescence In`co*a*les"cence (?), n. The state of not coalescing.

incocted.c: Incocted In*coct"ed (?), a. [Cf. Concoct.] Raw; indigestible. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

incoercible.c: Incoercible In`co*er"ci*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + coercible: cf. F. incoercible.]

incoexistence.c: Incoexistence In`co*ex*ist"ence (?), n. The state of not coexisting. [Obs.] Locke.

incogitable.c: Incogitable In*cog"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. incogitabilis; pref. in- not + cogitabilis cogitable.] Not cogitable; inconceivable. Sir T. More.

incogitancy.c: Incogitancy Incogitance { In*cog"i*tance (?), In*cog"i*tan*cy (?), } n. [L. incogitantia.] Lack of thought, or of the power of thinking; thoughtlessness; unreasonableness.

incogitant.c: Incogitant In*cog"i*tant (?), a. [L. incogitans; pref. in- not + cogitans, p. pr. of cogitare to think. See Cogitate.] Thoughtless; inconsiderate. [R.] Milton.

incogitantly.c: Incogitantly In*cog"i*tant*ly, adv. In an incogitant manner.

incogitative.c: Incogitative In*cog"i*ta*tive (?), a. Not cogitative; not thinking; lacking the power of thought; as, a vegetable is an incogitative being. Locke.

incogitativity.c: Incogitativity In*cog`i*ta*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being incogitative; lack of thought or of the power of thinking. Wollaston.

incognito.c: Incognito In*cog"ni*to (?), a. or adv. [It. incognito, masc., incognita, fem., L. incognitus unknown; pref. in- not + cognitus known, p. p. of cognoscere: cf. F. incognito, fr. It. See Cognition.] Without being known; in disguise; in an assumed character, or under an assumed title; -- said esp. of great personages who sometimes adopt a disguise or an assumed character in order to avoid notice.
Incognito In*cog"ni*to, n.; pl. Incognitos (#). [See Incognito, a.]

incognizable.c: Incognizable In*cog"ni*za*ble (?), a. Not cognizable; incapable of being recognized, known, or distinguished. H. Spenser.

incognizance.c: Incognizance In*cog"ni*zance (?), n. Failure to cognize, apprehended, or notice.

incognizant.c: Incognizant In*cog"ni*zant (?), a. Not cognizant; failing to apprehended or notice.

incoherency.c: Incoherency Incoherence { In`co*her"ence (?), In`co*her"en*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. incohérence.]

incoherent.c: Incoherent In`co*her"ent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + coherent: cf. F. incohérent.]

incoherentific.c: Incoherentific In`co*her`en*tif"ic (?), a. [E. incoherent + L. facere to make.] Causing incoherence. [R.]

incoherently.c: Incoherently In`co*her"ent*ly (?), adv. In an incoherent manner; without due connection of parts.

incoincidence.c: Incoincidence In`co*in"ci*dence (?), n. The quality of being incoincident; lack of coincidence. [R.]

incoincident.c: Incoincident In`co*in"ci*dent (?), a. Not coincident; not agreeing in time, in place, or principle.

incolumity.c: Incolumity In`co*lu"mi*ty (?), n. [L. incolumitas, fr. incolumis uninjured, safe; perh. fr. in intens. + (doubtful) columis safe.] Safety; security. [Obs.] Howell.

incombine.c: Incombine In`com*bine" (?), v. i. To be incapable of combining; to disagree; to differ. [Obs.] Milton.

incombustibility.c: Incombustibility In`com*bus`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incombustilité.] The quality of being incombustible.

incombustible.c: Incombustible In`com*bus"ti*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + combustible: cf. F. incombustible.] Not combustible; not capable of being burned, decomposed, or consumed by fire; uninflammable; as, asbestus is an incombustible substance; carbon dioxide is an incombustible gas.

income.c: Income In"come (?), n. 1. A coming in; entrance; admittance; ingress; infusion. [Obs.] Shak.

incomer.c: Incomer In"com`er (?), n. 1. One who comes in.

incoming.c: Incoming In"com`ing, n. 1. The act of coming in; arrival.

incomity.c: Incomity In*com"i*ty (?), n. Lack of comity; incivility; rudeness. [R.]

incommensurability.c: Incommensurability In`com*men`su*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incommensurabilité.] The quality or state of being incommensurable. Reid.

incommensurable.c: Incommensurable In`com*men"su*ra*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + commensurable: cf. F. incommensurable.] Not commensurable; having no common measure or standard of comparison; as, quantities are incommensurable when no third quantity can be found that is an aliquot part of both; the side and diagonal of a square are incommensurable with each other; the diameter and circumference of a circle are incommensurable.
Incommensurable In`com*men"su*ra*ble (?), n. One of two or more quantities which have no common measure.

incommensurate.c: Incommensurate In`com*men"su*rate (?), a. 1. Not commensurate; not admitting of a common measure; incommensurable.

incommiscible.c: Incommiscible In`com*mis"ci*ble (?), a. [L. incommiscibilis; pref. in- not + commiscibilis that can be mingled.] Not commiscible; not mixable.

incommixture.c: Incommixture In`com*mix"ture (?; 135), n. A state of being unmixed; separateness. Sir T. Browne.

incommodate.c: Incommodate In*com"mo*date (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incommodated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incommodating (?).] [L. incommodare. See Incommode.] To incommode. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

incommodation.c: Incommodation In*com`mo*da"tion (?), n. The state of being incommoded; inconvenience. [Obs.]

incommode.c: Incommode In`com*mode" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incommoded; p. pr. & vb. n. Incommoding.] [F. incommoder, L. incommodare inconvenient; pref. in- not + commodus convenient. See Commodious.] To give inconvenience or trouble to; to disturb or molest; to discommode; to worry; to put out; as, we are incommoded by lack of room.

incommodement.c: Incommodement In`com*mode"ment (?), n. The act of incommoded. [Obs.] Cheyne.

incommodious.c: Incommodious In`com*mo"di*ous (?), a. [Pref. in- not + commodious: cf. LL. incommodious, L. incommodus, F. incommode.] Tending to incommode; not commodious; not affording ease or advantage; unsuitable; giving trouble; inconvenient; annoying; as, an incommodious seat; an incommodious arrangement. -- In`com*mo"di*ous*ly, adv. -- In`com*mo"di*ous*ness, n.

incommodity.c: Incommodity In`com*mo"di*ty (?), n.; pl. Incommodities (#). [L. incommoditas: cf. F. incommodité. See Incommodious.] Inconvenience; trouble; annoyance; disadvantage; encumbrance. [Archaic] Bunyan.

incommunicability.c: Incommunicability In`com*mu`ni*ca*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incommunicabilité.] The quality or state of being incommunicable, or incapable of being imparted.

incommunicable.c: Incommunicable In`com*mu"ni*ca*ble (?), a. [L. incommunicabilis: cf. F. incommunicable. See In- not, and Communicable.] Not communicable; incapable of being communicated, shared, told, or imparted, to others.

incommunicated.c: Incommunicated In`com*mu"ni*ca`ted (?), a. Not communicated or imparted. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

incommunicating.c: Incommunicating In`com*mu"ni*ca`ting, a. Having no communion or intercourse with each other. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

incommunicative.c: Incommunicative In`com*mu"ni*ca*tive (?), a. Not communicative; not free or apt to impart to others in conversation; reserved; silent; as, the messenger was incommunicative; hence, not disposed to hold fellowship or intercourse with others; exclusive.

incommutability.c: Incommutability In`com*mu`ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. incommutabilitas: cf. F. incommutabilité.] The quality or state of being incommutable.

incommutable.c: Incommutable In`com*mut"a*ble (?), a. [L. incommutabilis: cf. F. incommutable. See In- not, and Commutable.] Not commutable; not capable of being exchanged with, or substituted for, another. Cudworth. -- In`com*mut"a*ble*ness, n. -- In`com*mut"a*bly, adv.

incompacted.c: Incompacted Incompact { In`com*pact" (?), In`com*pact"ed, } a. Not compact; not having the parts firmly united; not solid; incoherent; loose; discrete. Boyle.

incomparable.c: Incomparable In*com"pa*ra*ble (?), a. [L. incomparabilis: cf. F. incomparable. See In- not, and Comparable.] Not comparable; admitting of no comparison with others; unapproachably eminent; without a peer or equal; matchless; peerless; transcendent.

incompassion.c: Incompassion In`com*pas"sion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + compassion: cf. F. incompassion.] Lack of compassion or pity. [Obs.] Bp. Sanderson.

incompassionate.c: Incompassionate In`com*pas"sion*ate (?), a. Not compassionate; void of pity or of tenderness; remorseless. -- In`com*pas"sion*ate*ly, adv. -- In`com*pas"sion*ate*ness, n.

incompatibility.c: Incompatibility In`com*pat`i*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. -ties (?). [Cf. F. incompatibilité.] The quality or state of being incompatible; inconsistency; irreconcilableness.

incompatible.c: Incompatible In`com*pat"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + compatible: cf. F. incompatible.] [It was formerly sometimes written incompetible.]

Incompatible In`com*pat"i*ble (?), n. (Med. & Chem.) An incompatible substance; esp., in pl., things which can not be placed or used together because of a change of chemical composition or of opposing medicinal qualities; as, the incompatibles of iron.

incompatibleness.c: Incompatibleness In`com*pat"i*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being incompatible; incompatibility.

incompatibly.c: Incompatibly In`com*pat"i*bly, adv. In an incompatible manner; inconsistently; incongruously.

incompetency.c: Incompetency Incompetence { In*com"pe*tence (?), In*com"pe*tency (?), } n. [Cf. F. incompétence.]

incompetent.c: Incompetent In*com"pe*tent (?), a. [L. incompetens: cf. F. incompétent. See In- not, and Competent.]

incompetently.c: Incompetently In*com"pe*tent*ly, adv. In an competent manner; inadequately; unsuitably.

incomplete.c: Incomplete In`com*plete" (?), a. [L. incompletus: cf. F. incomplet. See In- not, and Complete.]

incompletely.c: Incompletely In`com*plete"ly, adv. In an incomplete manner.

incompleteness.c: Incompleteness In`com*plete"ness, n. The state of being incomplete; imperfectness; defectiveness. Boyle.
