incompletion.c: Incompletion In`com*ple"tion (?), n. Lack of completion; incompleteness. Smart.

incomplex.c: Incomplex In`com*plex" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + complex: cf. F. incomplexe.] Not complex; uncompounded; simple. Barrow.

incompliable.c: Incompliable In`com*pli"a*ble (?), a. Not compliable; not conformable.

incompliance.c: Incompliance In`com*pli"ance (?), n. 1. The quality or state of being incompliant; unyielding temper; obstinacy.

incompliant.c: Incompliant In`com*pli"ant (?), a. Not compliant; unyielding to request, solicitation, or command; stubborn. -- In`com*pli"ant*ly, adv.

incomposed.c: Incomposed In`com*posed" (?), a. Disordered; disturbed. [Obs.] Milton. -- In`com*po"sed*ly (#), adv. [Obs.] -- In`com*pos"ed*ness, n. [Obs.]

incomposite.c: Incomposite In`com*pos"ite (?), a. [L. incompositus. See Composite.] Not composite; uncompounded; simple.

incompossible.c: Incompossible In`com*pos"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + compossible: cf. F. incompossible.] Not capable of joint existence; incompatible; inconsistent. [Obs.]

incomprehense.c: Incomprehense In*com`pre*hense" (?), a. [L. incomprehensus.] Incomprehensible. [Obs.] “Incomprehense in virtue.” Marston.

incomprehensibility.c: Incomprehensibility In*com`pre*hen`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incompréhensibilité.] The quality of being incomprehensible, or beyond the reach of human intellect; incomprehensibleness; inconceivability; inexplicability.

incomprehensible.c: Incomprehensible In*com`pre*hen"si*ble (?), a. [L. incomprehensibilis: cf. F. incompréhensible. See In- not, and Comprehensible.]

incomprehension.c: Incomprehension In*com`pre*hen"sion (?), n. Lack of comprehension or understanding. “These mazes and incomprehensions.” Bacon.

incomprehensive.c: Incomprehensive In*com`pre*hen"sive (?), a. Not comprehensive; not capable of including or of understanding; not extensive; limited. -- In*com`pre*hen"sive*ly, a. Sir W. Hamilton. -- In*com`pre*hen"sive*ness, n. T. Warton.

incompressibility.c: Incompressibility In`com*press`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incompressibilité.] The quality of being incompressible, or incapable of reduction in volume by pressure; -- formerly supposed to be a property of liquids.

incompressible.c: Incompressible In`com*press"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + compressible: cf. F. incompressible.] Not compressible; incapable of being reduced by force or pressure into a smaller compass or volume; resisting compression; as, many liquids and solids appear to be almost incompressible. -- In`com*press"i*ble*ness, n.

inconcealable.c: Inconcealable In`con*ceal"a*ble (?), a. Not concealable. “Inconcealable imperfections.” Sir T. Browne.

inconceivability.c: Inconceivability In`con*ceiv`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being inconceivable; inconceivableness.

inconceivable.c: Inconceivable In`con*ceiv"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + conceivable: cf. F. inconcevable.] Not conceivable; incapable of being conceived by the mind; not explicable by the human intellect, or by any known principles or agencies; incomprehensible; as, it is inconceivable to us how the will acts in producing muscular motion.

inconceptible.c: Inconceptible In`con*cep"ti*ble (?), a. Inconceivable. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

inconcerning.c: Inconcerning In`con*cern"ing (?), a. Unimportant; trifling. [Obs.] “Trifling and inconcerning matters.” Fuller.

inconcinne.c: Inconcinne In`con*cinne" (?), a. [See Inconcinnous.] Dissimilar; incongruous; unsuitable. [Obs.] Cudworth.

inconcinnity.c: Inconcinnity In`con*cin"ni*ty (?), n. [L. inconcinnitas.] Lack of concinnity or congruousness; unsuitableness.

inconcinnous.c: Inconcinnous In`con*cin"nous (?), a. [L. inconcinnus. See In- not, and Concinnity.] Not concinnous; unsuitable; discordant. [Obs.] Cudworth.

inconcludent.c: Inconcludent In`con*clud"ent (?), a. Not inferring a conclusion or consequence; not conclusive. [Obs.]

inconclusive.c: Inconclusive In`con*clu"sive (?), a. Not conclusive; leading to no conclusion; not closing or settling a point in debate, or a doubtful question; as, evidence is inconclusive when it does not exhibit the truth of a disputed case in such a manner as to satisfy the mind, and put an end to debate or doubt.

inconcoct.c: Inconcoct In`con*coct" (?), a. [L. pref. in- not + concoctus, p. p. of concoquere. See Concoct.] Inconcocted. [Obs.]

inconcocted.c: Inconcocted In`con*coct"ed, a. [Pref. in- not + concocted.] Imperfectly digested, matured, or ripened. [Obs.] Bacon.

inconcoction.c: Inconcoction In`con*coc"tion (?), n. The state of being undigested; unripeness; immaturity. [Obs.] Bacon.

inconcrete.c: Inconcrete In*con"crete (?), a. [L. inconcretus incorporeal.] Not concrete. [R.] L. Andrews.

inconcurring.c: Inconcurring In`con*cur"ring, a. Not concurring; disagreeing. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

inconcussible.c: Inconcussible In`con*cus"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + L. concussibilis that can be shaken. See Concussion.] Not concussible; that cannot be shaken.

incondensibility.c: Incondensibility Incondensability { In`con*den`sa*bil"i*ty (?), In`con*den`si*bil"i*ty (?), } n. The quality or state of being incondensable.

incondensible.c: Incondensible Incondensable { In`con*den"sa*ble (?), In`con*den"si*ble, } a. Not condensable; incapable of being made more dense or compact, or reduced to liquid form.

incondite.c: Incondite In"con*dite (?; 277), a. [L. inconditus; pref. in- not + conditus, p. p. of condere to put or join together. See Condition.] Badly put together; inartificial; rude; unpolished; irregular. “Carol incondite rhymes.” J. Philips.

inconditional.c: Inconditional In`con*di"tion*al (?), a. [Pref. in- not + conditional: cf. F. inconditionnel.] Unconditional. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

inconditionate.c: Inconditionate In`con*di"tion*ate (?), a. [Pref. in- not + conditionate: cf. F. inconditionné.] Not conditioned; not limited; absolute. [Obs.] Boyle.

inconform.c: Inconform In`con*form" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + conform.] Unconformable. [Obs.] Gauden.

inconformity.c: Inconformity In`con*form"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inconformité.] Lack of conformity; nonconformity. [Obs.]

inconfusion.c: Inconfusion In`con*fu"sion (?) n. Freedom from confusion; distinctness. [Obs.] Bacon.

inconfutable.c: Inconfutable In`con*fut"a*ble (?), a. Not confutable. -- In`con*fut"a*bly, adv. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

incongealable.c: Incongealable In`con*geal"a*ble (?), a. [L. incongelabilis. See Congeal.] Not congealable; incapable of being congealed. -- In`con*geal"a*ble*ness, n.

incongenial.c: Incongenial In`con*gen"ial (?), a. Not congenial; uncongenial. [R.] -- In`con*ge`ni*al"i*ty (#), n.. [R.]

incongruence.c: Incongruence In*con"gru*ence (?), n. [L. incongruentia.] Lack of congruence; incongruity. Boyle.

incongruent.c: Incongruent In*con"gru*ent (?), a. [L. incongruens. See In- not, and Congruent.] Incongruous. Sir T. Elyot.

incongruity.c: Incongruity In`con*gru"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Incongruities (#). [Pref. in- not + congruity: cf. F. incongruité.]

incongruous.c: Incongruous In*con"gru*ous (?), a. [L. incongruus. See In- not, and Congruous.] Not congruous; reciprocally disagreeing; not capable of harmonizing or readily assimilating; inharmonious; inappropriate; unsuitable; not fitting; inconsistent; improper; as, an incongruous remark; incongruous behavior, action, dress, etc. “Incongruous mixtures of opinions.” I. Taylor. “Made up of incongruous parts.” Macaulay.

inconnected.c: Inconnected In`con*nect"ed (?), a. Not connected; disconnected. [R.] Bp. Warburton.

inconnexedly.c: Inconnexedly In`con*nex"ed*ly (?), adv. [Pref. in- not + connexed (p. p. of connex) + -ly.] Not connectedly; without connection. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

inconsecutiveness.c: Inconsecutiveness In`con*sec"u*tive*ness (?), n. The state or quality of not being consecutive. J. H. Newman.

inconsequence.c: Inconsequence In*con"se*quence (?), n. [L. inconsequentia: cf. F. inconséquence.] The quality or state of being inconsequent; lack of just or logical inference or argument; inconclusiveness. Bp. Stillingfleet.

inconsequent.c: Inconsequent In*con"se*quent (?), a. [L. inconsequens: cf. F. inconséquent. See In- not, and Consequent.] Not following from the premises; not regularly inferred; invalid; not characterized by logical method; illogical; arbitrary; inconsistent; of no consequence.

inconsequential.c: Inconsequential In*con`se*quen"tial (?), a. Not regularly following from the premises; hence, irrelevant; unimportant; of no consequence. Chesterfield. -- In*con`se*quen"tial*ly (#), adv.

inconsequentiality.c: Inconsequentiality In*con`se*quen`ti*al"i*ty (?), n. The state of being inconsequential.

inconsiderable.c: Inconsiderable In`con*sid"er*a*ble (?), a. Not considerable; unworthy of consideration or notice; unimportant; small; trivial; as, an inconsiderable distance; an inconsiderable quantity, degree, value, or sum. “The baser scum and inconsiderable dregs of Rome.” Stepney. -- In`con*sid"er*a*ble*ness, n. -- In`con*sid"er*a*bly, adv.

inconsiderate.c: Inconsiderate In`con*sid"er*ate (?), a. [L. inconsideratus. See In- not, and Considerate.]

inconsiderately.c: Inconsiderately In`con*sid"er*ate*ly, adv. In an inconsiderate manner.

inconsiderateness.c: Inconsiderateness In`con*sid"er*ate*ness, n. The quality or state of being inconsiderate. Tillotson.

inconsideration.c: Inconsideration In`con*sid`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. inconsideratio: cf. F. inconsidération.] Lack of due consideration; inattention to consequences; inconsiderateness.

inconsistency.c: Inconsistency In`con*sist"en*cy (?), n.; pl. Inconsistencies (#). [Cf. F. inconsistance.]

inconsistent.c: Inconsistent In`con*sist"ent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + consistent: cf. F. inconsistant.]

inconsistently.c: Inconsistently In`con*sist"ent*ly (?), adv. In an inconsistent manner.

inconsolable.c: Inconsolable In`con*sol"a*ble (?), a. [L. inconsolabilis: cf. F. inconsolable. See In- not, and Console.] Not consolable; incapable of being consoled; grieved beyond susceptibility of comfort; disconsolate. Dryden.

inconsonancy.c: Inconsonancy Inconsonance { In*con"so*nance (?), In*con"so*nan*cy (?), } n. Lack of consonance or harmony of sound, action, or thought; disagreement.

inconsonant.c: Inconsonant In*con"so*nant (?), a. [L. inconsonans. See In- not, and Consonant.] Not consonant or agreeing; inconsistent; discordant. -- In*con"so*nant*ly, adv.

inconspicuous.c: Inconspicuous In`con*spic"u*ous (?), a. [L. inconspicuus. See In- not, and Conspicuous.] Not conspicuous or noticeable; hardly discernible. -- In`con*spic"u*ous*ly, adv. -- In`con*spic"u*ous*ness, n. Boyle.

inconstance.c: Inconstance In*con"stance (?), n. [F. See Inconstancy.] Inconstancy. Chaucer.

inconstancy.c: Inconstancy In*con"stan*cy (?), n. [L. inconstantia.] The quality or state of being inconstant; lack of constancy; mutability; fickleness; variableness.

inconstant.c: Inconstant In*con"stant (?), a. [L. inconstans: cf. F. inconstant. See In- not, and Constant.] Not constant; not stable or uniform; subject to change of character, appearance, opinion, inclination, or purpose, etc.; not firm; unsteady; fickle; changeable; variable; -- said of persons or things; as, inconstant in love or friendship. “The inconstant moon.” Shak.

inconstantly.c: Inconstantly In*con"stant*ly, adv. In an inconstant manner.

inconsumable.c: Inconsumable In`con*sum"a*ble (?), a. Not consumable; incapable of being consumed, wasted, or spent. Paley. -- In`con*sum"a*bly, adv.

inconsummate.c: Inconsummate In`con*sum"mate (?), a. [L. inconsummatus. See In- not, and Consummate.] Not consummated; not finished; incomplete. Sir M. Hale. -- In`con*sum"mate*ness, n.

inconsumptible.c: Inconsumptible In`con*sump"ti*ble (?), a. [L. inconsumptibilis.] Inconsumable. [Obs.] Sir K. Digby.

incontaminate.c: Incontaminate In`con*tam"i*nate (?), a. [L. incontaminatus. See In- not, and not, and Contaminate.] Not contaminated; pure. Moore. -- In`con*tam"i*nate*ness, n.

incontentation.c: Incontentation In*con`ten*ta"tion (?), n. [See In- not, and Content.] Discontent. [Obs.] Goodwin.

incontestability.c: Incontestability In`con*test`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being incontestable.

incontestable.c: Incontestable In`con*test"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + contestable: cf. F. incontestable.] Not contestable; not to be disputed; that cannot be called in question or controverted; incontrovertible; indisputable; as, incontestable evidence, truth, or facts. Locke.

incontiguous.c: Incontiguous In`con*tig"u*ous (?), a. [L. incontiguus that can not be touched. See In- not, and Contiguous.] Not contiguous; not adjoining or in contact; separate. Boyle. -- In`con*tig"u*ous*ly, adv.

incontinency.c: Incontinency Incontinence { In*con"ti*nence (?), In*con"ti*nen*cy (?), } n. [L. incontinentia: cf. F. incontinence.]

incontinent.c: Incontinent In*con"ti*nent (?), a. [L. incontinens: cf. F. incontinent. See In- not, and Continent.]
Incontinent In*con"ti*nent, n. One who is unchaste. B. Jonson.
Incontinent In*con"ti*nent, adv. [Cf. F. incontinent.] Incontinently; instantly; immediately. [Obs.]

incontinently.c: Incontinently In*con"ti*nent*ly, adv. 1. In an incontinent manner; without restraint, or without due restraint; -- used esp. of the passions or appetites.

incontrollable.c: Incontrollable In`con*trol"la*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + controllable: cf. F. incontrôlable.] Not controllable; uncontrollable. -- In`con*trol"la*bly, adv. South.

incontrovertibility.c: Incontrovertibility In*con`tro*ver`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or condition of being incontrovertible.

incontrovertible.c: Incontrovertible In*con`tro*ver"ti*ble (?), a. Not controvertible; too clear or certain to admit of dispute; indisputable. Sir T. Browne. -- In*con`tro*ver"ti*ble*ness, n. -- In*con`tro*ver"ti*bly, adv.

inconvenience.c: Inconvenience In`con*ven"ience (?), n. [L. inconvenientia inconsistency: cf. OF. inconvenience.]
Inconvenience In`con*ven"ience, v. t. To put to inconvenience; to incommode; as, to inconvenience a neighbor.

inconvenient.c: Inconvenient In`con*ven"ient (?), a. [L. inconveniens unbefitting: cf. F. inconvénient. See In- not, and Convenient.]

inconveniently.c: Inconveniently In`con*ven"ient*ly, adv. In an inconvenient manner; incommodiously; unsuitably; unseasonably.

inconversant.c: Inconversant In*con"ver*sant (?), a. Not conversant; not acquainted; not versed; unfamiliar.

inconverted.c: Inconverted In`con*vert"ed (?), a. Not turned or changed about. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

inconvertibility.c: Inconvertibility In`con*vert`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. inconvertibilitas.] The quality or state of being inconvertible; not capable of being exchanged for, or converted into, something else; as, the inconvertibility of an irredeemable currency, or of lead, into gold.

inconvertible.c: Inconvertible In`con*vert"i*ble (?), a. [L. inconvertibilis: cf. F. inconvertible. See In- not, and Convertible.] Not convertible; not capable of being transmuted, changed into, or exchanged for, something else; as, one metal is inconvertible into another; bank notes are sometimes inconvertible into specie. Walsh.

inconvertibly.c: Inconvertibly In`con*vert"i*bly, adv. In an inconvertible manner.

inconvincible.c: Inconvincible In`con*vin"ci*ble (?), a. [L. inconvincibilis. See In- not, and Convince.] Not convincible; incapable of being convinced.

inconvincibly.c: Inconvincibly In`con*vin"ci*bly, adv. In a manner not admitting of being convinced.

incony.c: Incony In*co"ny (?), a. [Cf. Conny, Canny.] Unlearned; artless; pretty; delicate. [Obs.]

incoordination.c: Incoordination In`co*ör`di*na"tion (?), n. Lack of coördination; lack of harmonious adjustment or action.

incoronate.c: Incoronate In*cor"o*nate (?), a. [Pref. in- in + coronate.] Crowned. [R.] Longfellow.

incorporal.c: Incorporal In*cor"po*ral (?), a. [L. incorporalis. See In- not, and Corporal, and cf. Incorporeal.] Immaterial; incorporeal; spiritual. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

incorporality.c: Incorporality In*cor`po*ral"i*ty (?), n. [L. incorporalitas: cf. F. incorporalité.] Incorporeality. [Obs.] Bailey.

incorporate.c: Incorporate In*cor"po*rate (?), a. [L. incorporatus. See In- not, and Corporate.]

Incorporate In*cor"po*rate, a. [L. incorporatus, p. p. of incorporare to incorporate; pref. in- in + corporare to make into a body. See Corporate.] Corporate; incorporated; made one body, or united in one body; associated; mixed together; combined; embodied.
Incorporate In*cor"po*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incorporated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incorporating (?).]
Incorporate In*cor"po*rate (?), v. i. To unite in one body so as to make a part of it; to be mixed or blended; -- usually followed by with.

incorporated.c: Incorporated In*cor"po*ra`ted (?), a. 1. United or combined together to form in one body.

incorporation.c: Incorporation In*cor`po*ra"tion (?), n. [L. incorporatio: cf. F. incorporation.]

incorporative.c: Incorporative In*cor"po*ra*tive (?), a. Incorporating or tending to incorporate; as, the incorporative languages (as of the Basques, North American Indians, etc.) which run a whole phrase into one word.

incorporator.c: Incorporator In*cor"po*ra`tor (?), n. One of a number of persons who gets a company incorporated; one of the original members of a corporation.

incorporeal.c: Incorporeal In`cor*po"re*al (?), a. [Pref. in- not + corporeal: cf. L. incorporeus. Cf. Incorporal.]

incorporealism.c: Incorporealism In`cor*po"re*al*ism (?), n. Existence without a body or material form; immateriality. Cudworth.

incorporealist.c: Incorporealist In`cor*po"re*al*ist, n. One who believes in incorporealism. Cudworth.

incorporeality.c: Incorporeality In`cor*po`re*al"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being incorporeal or bodiless; immateriality; incorporealism. G. Eliot.

incorporeally.c: Incorporeally In`cor*po"re*al*ly (?), adv. In an incorporeal manner. Bacon.

incorporeity.c: Incorporeity In*cor`po*re"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + corporeity: cf. F. incorporéite.] The quality of being incorporeal; immateriality. Berkeley.

incorpse.c: Incorpse In*corpse" (?), v. t. To incorporate. [R.] Shak.

incorrect.c: Incorrect In`cor*rect" (?), a. [L. incorrectus: cf. F. incorrect. See In- not, and Correct.]

incorrection.c: Incorrection In`cor*rec"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + correction: cf. F. incorrection.] Lack of correction, restraint, or discipline. [Obs.] Arnway.

incorrectly.c: Incorrectly In`cor*rect"ly (?), adv. Not correctly; inaccurately; not exactly; as, a writing incorrectly copied; testimony incorrectly stated.

incorrectness.c: Incorrectness In`cor*rect"ness, n. The quality of being incorrect; lack of conformity to truth or to a standard; inaccuracy; inexactness; as, incorrectness may consist in defect or in redundance.

incorrespondency.c: Incorrespondency Incorrespondence { In*cor`re*spond"ence (?), In*cor`re*spond"en*cy (?), } n. Lack of correspondence; disagreement; disproportion. [R.]

incorresponding.c: Incorresponding In*cor`re*spond"ing, a. Not corresponding; disagreeing. [R.] Coleridge.

incorrigibility.c: Incorrigibility In*cor`ri*gi*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incorrigibilité.] The state or quality of being incorrigible.

incorrigible.c: Incorrigible In*cor"ri*gi*ble (?), a. [L. incorrigibilis: cf. F. incorrigible. See In- not, and Corrigible.] Not corrigible; incapable of being corrected or amended; bad beyond correction; irreclaimable; as, incorrigible error. “Incorrigible fools.” Dryden.

Incorrigible In*cor"ri*gi*ble (?), n. One who is incorrigible; a person whose persistent bad behavior cannot be changed; especially, a hardened criminal; as, the perpetual imprisonment of incorrigibles; incorrigible and disruptive children need to be placed in a separate classroom.

incorrigibleness.c: Incorrigibleness In*cor"ri*gi*ble*ness (?), n. Incorrigibility. Dr. H. More.

incorrigibly.c: Incorrigibly In*cor"ri*gi*bly, adv. In an incorrigible manner.

incorrodible.c: Incorrodible In`cor*rod"i*ble (?), a. Incapable of being corroded, consumed, or eaten away.

incorrupt.c: Incorrupt In`cor*rupt" (?), a. [L. incorruptus. See In- not, and Corrupt.]

incorruptibility.c: Incorruptibility In`cor*rupt`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. incorruptibilitas: cf. F. incorruptibilité.] The quality of being incorruptible; incapability of corruption. Holland.

incorruptible.c: Incorruptible In`cor*rupt"i*ble (?), a. [L. incorruptibilis: cf. F. incorruptible. See In- not, and Corrupt.]

Incorruptible In`cor*rupt"i*ble, n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a religious sect which arose in Alexandria, in the reign of the Emperor Justinian, and which believed that the body of Christ was incorruptible, and that he suffered hunger, thirst, pain, only in appearance.

incorruptibleness.c: Incorruptibleness In`cor*rupt"i*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being incorruptible. Boyle.

incorruptibly.c: Incorruptibly In`cor*rupt"i*bly, adv. In an incorruptible manner.

incorruption.c: Incorruption In`cor*rup"tion (?), n. [L. incorruptio: cf. F. incorruption. See In- not, and Corruption.] The condition or quality of being incorrupt or incorruptible; absence of, or exemption from, corruption.

incorruptive.c: Incorruptive In`cor*rupt"ive (?), a. [L. incorruptivus.] Incorruptible; not liable to decay. Akenside.

incorruptness.c: Incorruptness In`cor*rupt"ness, n. 1. Freedom or exemption from decay or corruption.

incrassate.c: Incrassate In*cras"sate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incrassated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incrassating.] [L. incrassatus, p. p. of incrassare; pref. in- in + crassus thick.] To make thick or thicker; to thicken; especially, in pharmacy, to thicken (a liquid) by the mixture of another substance, or by evaporating the thinner parts.
Incrassate In*cras"sate, v. i. To become thick or thicker.

incrassated.c: Incrassated Incrassate { In*cras"sate (?), In*cras"sa*ted (?), } a. [L. incrassatus, p. p.]

incrassative.c: Incrassative In*cras"sa*tive (?), a. Having the quality of thickening; tending to thicken. Harvey.
Incrassative In*cras"sa*tive, n. A substance which has the power to thicken; formerly, a medicine supposed to thicken the humors. Harvey.

increasable.c: Increasable In*creas"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being increased. Sherwood. -- In*creas"a*ble*ness, n.

increase.c: Increase In*crease" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Increased (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Increasing.] [OE. incresen, encresen, enrescen, OF. encreistre, fr. L. increscere; pref. in- in + crescere to grow. See Crescent, and cf. Decrease.]

Increase In*crease" (?), v. t. To augment or make greater in bulk, quantity, extent, value, or amount, etc.; to add to; to extend; to lengthen; to enhance; to aggravate; as, to increase one's possessions, influence.
Increase In"crease (?; 277), n. [OE. encres, encresse. See Increase, v. i.]

increaseful.c: Increaseful In*crease"ful (?), a. Full of increase; abundant in produce. “Increaseful crops.” [R.] Shak.

increaser.c: Increaser In*creas"er (?), n. One who, or that, increases.

increate.c: Increate In`cre*ate" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Increated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Increating.] [Pref. in- in + create.] To create within. [R.]

increated.c: Increated Increate { In"cre*ate (?), In"cre*a`ted (?), } a. [L. increatus. See In- not, and Create.] Uncreated; self-existent. [R.]

incredibility.c: Incredibility In*cred`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. incredibilitas: cf. F. incrédibilité.]

incredible.c: Incredible In*cred"i*ble (?), a. [L. incredibilis: cf. OF. incredible. See In- not, and Credible.] Not credible; surpassing belief; too extraordinary and improbable to admit of belief; unlikely; marvelous; fabulous.

incredibly.c: Incredibly In*cred"i*bly, adv. In an incredible manner.

incredulity.c: Incredulity In`cre*du"li*ty (?), n. [L. incredulitas: cf. F. incrédulité.] The state or quality of being incredulous; a withholding or refusal of belief; skepticism; unbelief; disbelief.

incredulous.c: Incredulous In*cred"u*lous (?; 135), a. [L. incredulus. See In- not, and Credulous.]

incredulously.c: Incredulously In*cred"u*lous*ly, adv. In an incredulous manner; with incredulity.

incremable.c: Incremable In*crem"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + L. cremabilis combustible, fr. cremare to burn.] Incapable of being burnt; incombustibe. Sir T. Browne.

incremate.c: Incremate In"cre*mate (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + cremate.] To consume or reduce to ashes by burning, as a dead body; to cremate.

incremation.c: Incremation In`cre*ma"tion (?), n. Burning; esp., the act of burning a dead body; cremation.

increment.c: Increment In"cre*ment (?), n. [L. incrementum: cf. F. incrément. See Increase.]

incremental.c: Incremental In`cre*men"tal (?), a. (Biol.) Pertaining to, or resulting from, the process of growth; as, the incremental lines in the dentine of teeth.

increpate.c: Increpate In"cre*pate (?), v. t. [L. increpatus, p. p. of increpare to upbraid; pref. in- in, against + crepare to talk noisily.] To chide; to rebuke; to reprove. [Obs.]

increpation.c: Increpation In`cre*pa"tion (?), n. [L. increpatio.] A chiding; rebuke; reproof. [Obs.] Hammond.

increscent.c: Increscent In*cres"cent (?), a. [L. increscens, -entis, p. pr. of increscere. See Increase.]

increst.c: Increst In*crest" (?), v. t. To adorn with a crest. [R.] Drummond.

incriminate.c: Incriminate In*crim"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incriminated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incriminating.] [LL. incriminatus, p. p. of incriminare; in- in + criminare, criminari, to accuse one of a crime. See Criminate.] To accuse; to charge with a crime or fault; to criminate.

incrimination.c: Incrimination In*crim`i*na"tion (?), n. The act of incriminating; crimination.

incriminatory.c: Incriminatory In*crim"i*na*to*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to crimination; tending to incriminate; criminatory.

incroyable.c: Incroyable ‖In`croy`a"ble (?), n. [F., lit., incredible.] A French fop or dandy of the time of the Directory; hence, any fop.

incruental.c: Incruental In`cru*en"tal (?), a. [L. incruentus. See In- not, and Cruentous.] Unbloody; not attended with blood; as, an incruental sacrifice. [Obs.] Brevint.

incrust.c: Incrust In*crust" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incrusted; p. pr. & vb. n. Incrusting.] [L. incrustare; pref. in- in + crustare to cover with a crust: cf. F. incruster. See Crust.] [Written also encrust.]

incrustate.c: Incrustate In*crus"tate (?), a. [L. incrustatus, p. p. See Incrust.] Incrusted. Bacon.
Incrustate In*crus"tate (?), v. t. To incrust. [R.] Cheyne.

incrustation.c: Incrustation In`crus*ta"tion (?), n. [L. incrustatio: cf. F. incrustation. See Incrust.]

incrystallizable.c: Incrystallizable In*crys"tal*li`za*ble (?), a. Not crystallizable; incapable of being formed into crystals.

incubate.c: Incubate In"cu*bate (?), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Incubated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incubating (?).] [L. incubatus, p. p. incubare to lie on; pref. in- in, on + cubare to lie down. Cf. Cubit, Incumbent.] 1. To sit, as on eggs for hatching; to brood; to brood upon, or keep warm, as eggs, for the purpose of hatching.

incubation.c: Incubation In`cu*ba"tion (?), n. [L. incubatio: cf. F. incubation.]

incubative.c: Incubative In"cu*ba*tive (?), a. Of or pertaining to incubation, or to the period of incubation.

incubator.c: Incubator In"cu*ba`tor (?), n. 1. That which incubates, especially, an apparatus by means of which eggs are hatched by artificial heat.

incube.c: Incube In*cube" (?), v. t. To fix firmly, as in cube; to secure or place firmly. [Obs.] Milton.

incubiture.c: Incubiture In*cu"bi*ture (?; 135), n. [Cf. L. incubitus.] Incubation. [Obs.] J. Ellis.

incubous.c: Incubous In"cu*bous (?), a. [From L. incubare to lie on.] (Bot.) Having the leaves so placed that the upper part of each one covers the base of the leaf next above it, as in hepatic mosses of the genus Frullania. See Succubous.

incubus.c: Incubus In"cu*bus (?), n.; pl. E. Incubuses (#), L. Incubi (#). [L., the nightmare. Cf. Incubate.]

inculcate.c: Inculcate In*cul"cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inculcated; p. pr. & vb. n. Inculcating (?).] [L. inculcatus, p. p. of inculcare to tread on; pref. in- in, on + calcare to tread, fr. calx the heel; perh. akin to E. heel. Cf. 2d Calk, Heel.] To teach and impress by frequent repetitions or admonitions; to urge on the mind; as, Christ inculcates on his followers humility.

inculcation.c: Inculcation In`cul*ca"tion (?), n. [L. inculcatio: cf. F. inculcation.] A teaching and impressing by frequent repetitions. Bp. Hall.

inculcator.c: Inculcator In*cul"ca*tor (?), n. [L.] One who inculcates. Boyle.

inculk.c: Inculk In*culk" (?). v. t. [Cf. F. inculquer. See Inculcate.] To inculcate. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

inculp.c: Inculp In*culp" (?), v. t. [Cf. inculper. See Inculpate.] To inculpate. [Obs.] Shelton.

inculpable.c: Inculpable In*cul"pa*ble (?), a. [L. inculpabilis: cf. F. incupable.] Faultless; blameless; innocent. South.

inculpate.c: Inculpate In*cul"pate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inculpated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inculpating (?).] [LL. inculpatus, p. p. of inculpare to blame; pref. in- in + culpa fault. See Culpable.] To blame; to impute guilt to; to accuse; to involve or implicate in guilt. Contrasted with exculpate.

inculpation.c: Inculpation In`cul*pa"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inculpation.] Blame; censure; crimination. Jefferson.

inculpatory.c: Inculpatory In*cul"pa*to*ry (?), a. Imputing blame; causing blame to be imputed to; criminatory; compromising; implicating. Opposite of exculpatory.

incult.c: Incult In*cult" (?), a. [L. incultus; pref. in- not + cultus, p. p. of colere to cultivate: cf. F. inculte.] Untilled; uncultivated; crude; rude; uncivilized.

incultivated.c: Incultivated In*cul"ti*va`ted (?), a. Uncultivated. [Obs.] Sir T. Herbert.

incultivation.c: Incultivation In*cul`ti*va"tion (?), n. Lack of cultivation. [Obs.] Berington.

inculture.c: Inculture In*cul"ture (?; 135), n. [Pref. in- not + culture: cf. F. inculture.] Want or neglect of cultivation or culture. [Obs.] Feltham.

incumbent.c: Incumbent In*cum"bent (?), a. [L. incumbens, -entis, p. pr. of incumbere to lie down upon, press upon; pref. in- in, on + cumbere (in comp.); akin to cubare to lie down. See Incubate.]
Incumbent In*cum"bent, n. A person who is in present possession of a benefice or of any office.

incumbently.c: Incumbently In*cum"bent*ly, adv. In an incumbent manner; so as to be incumbent.

incumber.c: Incumber In*cum"ber (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incumbered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incumbering.] See Encumber.

incumbrancer.c: Incumbrancer In*cum"bran*cer (?), n. (Law) One who holds an incumbrance, or some legal claim, lien, or charge on an estate. Kent.

incumbrous.c: Incumbrous In*cum"brous (?), a. [Cf. OF. encombros.] Cumbersome; troublesome. [Written also encombrous.] [Obs.] Chaucer.

incunabulum.c: Incunabulum ‖In`cu*nab"u*lum (?), n.; pl. Incunabula (#). [L. incunabula cradle, birthplace, origin. See 1st In-, and Cunabula.] A work of art or of human industry, of an early epoch; especially, a book printed before a. d. 1500.

incur.c: Incur In*cur" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incurred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incurring (?).] [L. incurrere to run into or toward; pref. in- in + currere to run. See Current.]
Incur In*cur", v. i. To pass; to enter. [Obs.]

incurability.c: Incurability In*cur`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. incurabilité incurability, LL. incurabilitas negligence.] The state of being incurable; irremediableness. Harvey.

incurable.c: Incurable In*cur"a*ble (?), a. [F. incurable, L. incurabilis. See In- not, and Curable.]
Incurable In*cur"a*ble, n. A person diseased beyond cure.

incurableness.c: Incurableness In*cur"a*ble*ness, n. The state of being incurable; incurability. Boyle.

incurably.c: Incurably In*cur"a*bly, adv. In a manner that renders cure impracticable or impossible; irremediably. “Incurably diseased.” Bp. Hall. “Incurably wicked.” Blair.

incuriosity.c: Incuriosity In*cu`ri*os"i*ty (?), n. [L. incuriositas: cf. F. incurosité.] Lack of curiosity or interest; inattentiveness; indifference. Sir H. Wotton.

incurious.c: Incurious In*cu"ri*ous (?), a. [L. incuriosus: cf. F. incurieux. See In- not, and Curious.] Not curious or inquisitive; without care for or interest in; inattentive; careless; negligent; heedless.

incuriously.c: Incuriously In*cu"ri*ous*ly, adv. In an curious manner.

incurrence.c: Incurrence In*cur"rence (?), n. [See Incur.] The act of incurring, bringing on, or subjecting one's self to (something troublesome or burdensome); as, the incurrence of guilt, debt, responsibility, etc.

incurrent.c: Incurrent In*cur"rent (?), a. [L. incurrens, p. pr. incurere, incursum, to run in; in- + currere to run.] (Zool.) Characterized by a current which flows inward; as, the incurrent orifice of lamellibranch Mollusca.

incursion.c: Incursion In*cur"sion (?), n. [L. incursio: cf. F. incursion. See Incur.]

incursive.c: Incursive In*cur"sive (?), a. Making an incursion; invasive; aggressive; hostile.

incurvate.c: Incurvate In*cur"vate (?), a. [L. incurvatus, p. p. of incurvare to crook; pref. in- in + curvus bent. See Curve, and cf. Incurve.] Curved; bent; crooked. Derham.
Incurvate In*cur"vate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incurvated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Incurvating.] To turn from a straight line or course; to bend; to crook. Cheyne.

incurvation.c: Incurvation In`cur*va"tion (?), n. [L. incurvatio: cf. F. incurvation.]

incurve.c: Incurve In*curve" (ĭn*kûv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Incurved (ĭn*kûvd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Incurving.] [See Incurvate.] To bend; to curve; to make crooked.

incurved.c: Incurved In*curved" (ĭn*kûvd"), a. [Pref. in- in + curved.] (Bot.) Bending gradually toward the axis or center, as branches or petals.

incurvity.c: Incurvity In*cur"vi*ty (ĭn*kû"vĭ*ty̆), n. [From L. incurvus bent. See Incurvate.] A state of being bent or curved; incurvation; a bending inwards. Sir T. Browne.

incuse.c: Incuse In*cuse" (?), a. [See Incuse, v. t.] (Numismatics) Cut or stamped in, or hollowed out by engraving. “Irregular incuse square.” Dr. W. Smith.

incuss.c: Incuss Incuse { In*cuse" (?), In*cuss" (?), } v. t. [L. incussus, p. p. of incutere to strike. See 1st In-, and Concuss.] To form, or mold, by striking or stamping, as a coin or medal.

incute.c: Incute In*cute" (?), v. t. [See Incuse.] To strike or stamp in. [Obs.] Becon.

ind.c: Ind Ind (ĭnd), prop. n. India. [Poetical] Shak. Milton.

indagate.c: Indagate In"da*gate (?), v. t. [L. indagatus, p. p. of indagare to seek.] To seek or search out. [Obs.]

indagation.c: Indagation In`da*ga"tion (?), n. [L. indagatio: cf. F. indagation.] Search; inquiry; investigation. [Obs.]

indagative.c: Indagative In"da*ga*tive (?), a. Searching; exploring; investigating. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

indagator.c: Indagator In"da*ga`tor (?), n. [L.] A searcher; an explorer; an investigator. [Obs.]

indart.c: Indart In*dart" (?), v. t. To pierce, as with a dart.

indazole.c: Indazole In"da*zole (?), n. [Indol + azote.] (Chem.) A bicyclic nitrogenous compound, C7H6N2, analogous to indole, having a benzene ring fused to a pyrazole ring; called also indazol and benzopyrazole. It can be produced from a diazo derivative of cinnamic acid.

inde.c: Inde Inde (?), a. Azure-colored; of a bright blue color. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

indebt.c: Indebt In*debt" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indebted; p. pr. & vb. n. Indebting.] [OE. endetten, F. endetter; pref. en- (L. in) + F. dette debt. See Debt.] To bring into debt; to place under obligation; -- chiefly used in the participle indebted.

indebted.c: Indebted In*debt"ed, a. 1. Brought into debt; being under obligation; held to payment or requital; beholden.

indebtedness.c: Indebtedness In*debt"ed*ness, n. 1. The state of being indebted.

indebtment.c: Indebtment In*debt"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. endettement.] Indebtedness. [R.] Bp. Hall.

indecence.c: Indecence In*de"cence (?), n. See Indecency. [Obs.] “An indecence of barbarity.” Bp. Burnet.

indecency.c: Indecency In*de"cen*cy (?), n.; pl. Indecencies (#). [L. indecentia unseemliness: cf. F. indécence.]

indecent.c: Indecent In*de"cent (?), a. [L. indecens unseemly, unbecoming: cf. F. indécent. See In- not, and Decent.] Not decent; unfit to be seen or heard; offensive to modesty and delicacy; as, indecent language. Cowper.

indecently.c: Indecently In*de"cent*ly, adv. In an indecent manner.

indeciduous.c: Indeciduous In`de*cid"u*ous (?), a. Not deciduous or falling, as the leaves of trees in autumn; lasting; evergreen; persistent; permanent; perennial. Opposite of deciduous.

indecimable.c: Indecimable In*dec"i*ma*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + LL. decimare to tithe: cf. F. indécimable. See Decimate.] Not decimable, or liable to be decimated; not liable to the payment of tithes. Cowell.

indecipherable.c: Indecipherable In`de*ci"pher*a*ble (?), a. Not decipherable; incapable of being deciphered, explained, or solved. -- In`de*ci"pher*a*bly, adv.

indecision.c: Indecision In`de*ci"sion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + decision: cf. F. indécision.] Lack of decision; lack of settled purpose, or of firmness; indetermination; wavering of mind; irresolution; vacillation; hesitation.

indecisiveness.c: Indecisiveness In`de*ci"sive*ness, n. The state of being indecisive; unsettled state.

indeclinable.c: Indeclinable In`de*clin"a*ble (?), a. [L. indeclinabilis: cf. F. indéclinable. See In- not, and Decline.] (Gram.) Not declinable; not varied by inflective terminations; as, nihil (nothing), in Latin, is an indeclinable noun. -- n. An indeclinable word.

indecomposable.c: Indecomposable In*de`com*pos"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + decomposable: cf. F. indécomposable.] Not decomposable; incapable or difficult of decomposition; not resolvable into its constituents or elements.

indecomposableness.c: Indecomposableness In*de`com*pos"a*ble*ness, n. Incapableness of decomposition; stability; permanence; durability.

indecorous.c: Indecorous In`de*co"rous (?; 277), a. [L. indecorous. See In- not, and Decorous.] Not decorous; violating good manners; contrary to good breeding or etiquette; unbecoming; improper; out of place; as, indecorous conduct.

indecorously.c: Indecorously In`de*co"rous*ly, adv. In an indecorous manner.

indecorousness.c: Indecorousness In`de*co"rous*ness, n. The quality of being indecorous; lack of decorum.

indecorum.c: Indecorum In`de*co"rum (?), n. [Pref. in- not + decorum: cf. L. indecorous unbecoming.]

indeed.c: Indeed In*deed" (?), adv. [Prep. in + deed.] In reality; in truth; in fact; verily; truly; -- used in a variety of senses. Esp.: (a) Denoting emphasis; as, indeed it is so. (b) Denoting concession or admission; as, indeed, you are right. (c) Denoting surprise; as, indeed, is it you? Its meaning is not intrinsic or fixed, but depends largely on the form of expression which it accompanies.

indefatigability.c: Indefatigability In`de*fat`i*ga*bil"i*ty (ĭn`de*făt`ĭ*gȧ*bĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. The state of being indefatigable.

indefatigable.c: Indefatigable In`de*fat"i*ga*ble (ĭn`de*făt"ĭ*gȧ*b'l), a. [L. indefatigabilis: cf. OF. indefatigable. See In- not, and Defatigable, and cf. Infatigable.] Incapable of being fatigued; not readily exhausted; unremitting in labor or effort; untiring; unwearying; not yielding to fatigue; as, indefatigable exertions, perseverance, application. “A constant, indefatigable attendance.” South.

indefatigableness.c: Indefatigableness In`de*fat"i*ga*ble*ness, n. Indefatigable quality; unweariedness; persistency. Parnell.

indefatigably.c: Indefatigably In`de*fat"i*ga*bly, adv. Without weariness; without yielding to fatigue; persistently. Dryden.

indefatigation.c: Indefatigation In`de*fat`i*ga"tion (?), n. Indefatigableness; unweariedness. [Obs.] J. Gregory.

indefeasibility.c: Indefeasibility In`de*fea`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being indefeasible.

indefeasible.c: Indefeasible In`de*fea`si*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + defeasible: cf. OF. indefaisable.] Not to be defeated; not defeasible; incapable of being annulled or made void; as, an indefeasible or title.

indefectibility.c: Indefectibility In`de*fect`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. indéfectibilité.] The quality of being indefectible. Barrow.

indefectible.c: Indefectible In`de*fect"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + defectible: cf. F. indéfectible.] Not defectible; unfailing; not liable to defect, failure, or decay.

indefective.c: Indefective In`de*fect"ive (?), a. Not defective; perfect; complete. “Absolute, indefective obedience.” South.

indefensibility.c: Indefensibility In`de*fen`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of not being defensible. Walsh.

indefensible.c: Indefensible In`de*fen"si*ble (?), [Pref. in- not + defensible: cf. OF. indefensible, indefensable.] Not defensible; not capable of being defended, maintained, vindicated, or justified; unjustifiable; untenable; as, an indefensible fortress, position, cause, statement, etc.

indefensibly.c: Indefensibly In`de*fen"si*bly, adv. In an indefensible manner.

indeficiency.c: Indeficiency In`de*fi"cien*cy, n. The state or quality of not being deficient. [Obs.] Strype.

indeficient.c: Indeficient In`de*fi"cient (?), a. [L. indeficiens. See In- not, and Deficient.] Not deficient; full. [Obs.]

indefinable.c: Indefinable In`de*fin"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being defined or described; inexplicable. Bp. Reynolds.

indefinably.c: Indefinably In`de*fin"a*bly, adv. In an indefinable manner.

indefinite.c: Indefinite In*def"i*nite (?), a. [L. indefinitus. See In- not, and Definite.]

indefinitely.c: Indefinitely In*def"i*nite*ly, adv. In an indefinite manner or degree; without any settled limitation; vaguely; not with certainty or exactness; as, to use a word indefinitely.

indefiniteness.c: Indefiniteness In*def"i*nite*ness, n. The quality of being indefinite.

indefinitude.c: Indefinitude In`de*fin"i*tude (?), n. Indefiniteness; vagueness; also, number or quantity not limited by our understanding, though yet finite. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

indehiscence.c: Indehiscence In`de*his"cence (?), n. [Cf. F. indéhiscence.] (Bot.) The property or state of being indehiscent.

indehiscent.c: Indehiscent In`de*his"cent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + dehiscent: cf. F. indéhiscent.] (Bot.) Remaining closed at maturity, or not opening along regular lines, as the acorn, or a cocoanut.

indelectable.c: Indelectable In`de*lec"ta*ble (?), a. Not delectable; unpleasant; disagreeable. [R.] Richardson.

indeliberate.c: Indeliberate In`de*lib"er*ate (?), a. [L. indeliberatus. See In- not, and Deliberate.] Done without deliberation; unpremeditated. [Obs.] -- In`de*lib"er*ate*ly, adv. [Obs.]

indelibility.c: Indelibility In*del`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. indélébilité.] The quality of being indelible. Bp. Horsley.

indelible.c: Indelible In*del"i*ble (?), a. [L. indelebilis; pref. in- not + delebilis capable of being destroyed: cf. F. indélébile. See In- not, and Deleble.] [Formerly written also indeleble, which accords with the etymology of the word.]

indelicacy.c: Indelicacy In*del"i*ca*cy (?), n.; pl. Indelicacies (#). [From Indelicate.] The quality of being indelicate; lack of delicacy, or of a nice sense of, or regard for, purity, propriety, or refinement in manners, language, etc.; rudeness; coarseness; also, that which is offensive to refined taste or purity of mind.

indelicate.c: Indelicate In*del"i*cate (?), a. [Pref. in- not + delicate: cf. F. indélicat.] Not delicate; wanting delicacy; offensive to good manners, or to purity of mind; coarse; rude; as, an indelicate word or suggestion; indelicate behavior. Macaulay. -- In*del"i*cate*ly, adv.

indemnification.c: Indemnification In*dem`ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. 1. The act or process of indemnifying, preserving, or securing against loss, damage, or penalty; reimbursement of loss, damage, or penalty; the state of being indemnified.

indemnify.c: Indemnify In*dem"ni*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indemnified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indemnifying (?).] [L. indemnis unhurt (in- not + damnum hurt, damage) + -fy. Cf. Damn, Damnify.]

indemnity.c: Indemnity In*dem"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Indemnities (#). [L. indemnitas, fr. indemnis uninjured: cf. F. indemnité. See Indemnify.]

indemonstrability.c: Indemonstrability In`de*mon`stra*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being indemonstrable.

indemonstrable.c: Indemonstrable In`de*mon"stra*ble (?), a. [L. indemonstrabilis. See In- not, and Demonstrable.] Incapable of being demonstrated. -- In`de*mon"stra*ble*ness, n.

indenization.c: Indenization In*den`i*za"tion (?), n. The act of naturalizing; endenization. [R.] Evelyn.

indenizen.c: Indenizen In*den"i*zen (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indenizened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indenizening.] To invest with the privileges of a denizen; to naturalize. [R.]

indent.c: Indent In*dent" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indented; p. pr. & vb. n. Indenting.] [OE. endenten to notch, fit in, OF. endenter, LL. indentare, fr. L. in + dens, dentis, tooth. See Tooth, and cf. Indenture.]
Indent In*dent", v. i. 1. To be cut, notched, or dented.
Indent In*dent" (?), n. 1. A cut or notch in the margin of anything, or a recess like a notch. Shak.

indentation.c: Indentation In`den*ta"tion (?), n. 1. The act of indenting or state of being indented.

indented.c: Indented In*dent"ed (?), a. 1. Cut in the edge into points or inequalities, like teeth; jagged; notched; stamped in; dented on the surface.

indenting.c: Indenting In*dent"ing (?), n. Indentation; an impression like that made by a tooth.

indenture.c: Indenture In*den"ture (?; 135), n. [OE. endenture, OF. endenture, LL. indentura a deed in duplicate, with indented edges. See the Note below. See Indent.]
Indenture In*den"ture, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indentured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indenturing.]
Indenture In*den"ture, v. i. To run or wind in and out; to be cut or notched; to indent. Heywood.

independence.c: Independence Day In`de*pend"ence Day. In the United States, a holiday, the 4th of July, commemorating the adoption of the Declaration of Independence on that day in 1776.

independent.c: Independent In`de*pend"ent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + dependent: cf. F. indépendant.]
Independent In`de*pend"ent (?), n. 1. (Eccl.) One who believes that an organized Christian church is complete in itself, competent to self-government, and independent of all ecclesiastical authority.

independentism.c: Independentism In`de*pend"ent*ism (?), n. Independency; the church system of Independents. Bp. Gauden.

independently.c: Independently In`de*pend"ent*ly, adv. In an independent manner; without control.

indeposable.c: Indeposable In`de*pos"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being deposed. [R.]

indepravate.c: Indepravate In*dep"ra*vate (?), a. [L. indepravatus.] Undepraved. [R.] Davies (Holy Roode).

indeprecable.c: Indeprecable In*dep"re*ca*ble (?), a. [L. indeprecabilis. See In- not, and Deprecate.] Incapable or undeserving of being deprecated. Cockeram.

indeprehensible.c: Indeprehensible In*dep`re*hen"si*ble (?), a. [L. indeprehensibilis. See In- not, and Deprehensible.] Incapable of being found out. Bp. Morton.

indeprivable.c: Indeprivable In`de*priv"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being deprived, or of being taken away.

indescribable.c: Indescribable In`de*scrib"a*ble, a. Incapable of being described.

indesinent.c: Indesinent In*des"i*nent (?), a. [L. indesinens. See In- not, and Desinent.] Not ceasing; perpetual. [Obs.] Baxter. -- In*des"i*nent*ly, adv. [Obs.] Ray.

indestructibility.c: Indestructibility In`de*struc`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. indestructibilité.] The quality of being indestructible.

indestructible.c: Indestructible In`de*struc"ti*ble, a. [Pref. in- not + destructible: cf. F. indestructible.] Not destructible; incapable of decomposition or of being destroyed; as, the Russian harvesters had primitive electronics, but they were built so sturdily they were almost indestructible. -- In`de*struc"ti*ble*ness, n. -- In`de*struc"ti*bly, adv.

indeterminable.c: Indeterminable In`de*ter"mi*na*ble (?), a. [L. indeterminabilis: cf. F. indéterminable. See In- not, and Determine.] Not determinable; impossible to be determined; not to be definitely known, ascertained, defined, or limited. -- In`de*ter"mi*na*bly, adv.
Indeterminable In`de*ter"mi*na*ble, n. An indeterminable thing or quantity. Sir T. Browne.

indeterminate.c: Indeterminate In`de*ter"mi*nate (?), a. [L. indeterminatus.] Not determinate; not certain or fixed; indefinite; not precise; as, an indeterminate number of years. Paley.

indetermination.c: Indetermination In`de*ter`mi*na"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + determination: cf. indétermination.]

indevirginate.c: Indevirginate In`de*vir"gin*ate (?), a. [See In- not, Devirginate.] Not devirginate. [Obs.] Chapman.

indevote.c: Indevote In*de*vote" (?), a. [L. indevotus: cf. F. indévot. Cf. Indevout.] Not devoted. [Obs.] Bentley. Clarendon.

indevotion.c: Indevotion In`de*vo"tion (?), n. [L. indevotio: cf. F. indévotion.] Lack of devotion; impiety; irreligion. “An age of indevotion.” Jer. Taylor.

indevout.c: Indevout In*de*vout" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + devout. Cf. Indevote.] Not devout. -- In*de*vout"ly, adv.

indew.c: Indew In*dew" (?), v. t. To indue. [Obs.] Spenser.

index.c: Index In"dex (?), n.; pl. E. Indexes (#), L. Indices (#)(?). [L.: cf. F. index. See Indicate, Diction.]
Index In"dex (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indexed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indexing.] 1. To provide with an index or table of references; to put into an index; as, to index a book, or its contents.

indexer.c: Indexer In"dex*er (?), n. One who makes an index.

indexical.c: Indexical In*dex"ic*al (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or like, an index; having the form of an index.

indexically.c: Indexically In*dex"ic*al*ly, adv. In the manner of an index.

indexterity.c: Indexterity In`dex*ter"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + dexterity: cf. F. indextérité.] Lack of dexterity or readiness, especially in the use of the hands; clumsiness; awkwardness. Harvey.

india.c: India In"di*a (?), n. [See Indian.] A country in Southern Asia; the two peninsulas of Hither and Farther India; in a restricted sense, Hither India, or Hindostan.
India steel In"di*a steel. Same as Wootz.

indiadem.c: Indiadem In*di"a*dem, v. t. To place or set in a diadem, as a gem or gems.

indiaman.c: Indiaman In"di*a*man (?), n.; pl. Indiamen (?). A large vessel in the India trade. Macaulay.

indian.c: Indian In"di*an (?; 277), a. [From India, and this fr. Indus, the name of a river in Asia, L. Indus, Gr.?, OPers. Hindu, name of the land on the Indus, Skr. sindhu river, the Indus. Cf. Hindu.]
Indian In"di*an (?; 277), n. 1. A native or inhabitant of India.

Indian corn Indian corn (Bot.), A cereal plant of the genus Zea (Zea Mays), also simply called corn, used widely as a food; the maize, a native plant of America; more specifically: a primitive variety of Zea Mays having variegated kernels on each cob, in distinction from the more commonly used yellow corn; it is often used as decoration at Thanksgiving time. See Corn, and Maize.

indical.c: Indical In"dic*al (?), a. [From L. index, indicis, an index.] Indexical. [R.] Fuller.

indicant.c: Indicant In"di*cant (?), a. [L. indicans, p. pr. indicare. See Indicate.] Serving to point out, as a remedy; indicating.
Indicant In"di*cant, n. That which indicates or points out; as, an indicant of the remedy for a disease.

indicate.c: Indicate In"di*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indicating (?).] [L. indicatus, p. p. of indicare to indicate; pref. in- in + dicare to proclaim; akin to dicere to say. See Diction, and cf. Indict, Indite.]

indicated.c: Indicated In"di*ca`ted (?), a. Shown; denoted; registered; measured.

indication.c: Indication In`di*ca"tion (?), n. [L. indicatio: cf. F. indication.]

indicative.c: Indicative In*dic"a*tive (?), a. [L. indicativus: cf. F. indicatif.]

indicatively.c: Indicatively In*dic"a*tive*ly, adv. In an indicative manner; in a way to show or signify.

indicatory.c: Indicatory In"di*ca*to*ry (?; 277), a. Serving to show or make known; showing; indicative; signifying; implying.

indicatrix.c: Indicatrix In`di*ca"trix (?), n. [NL.] (Geom. of Three Dimensions) A certain conic section supposed to be drawn in the tangent plane to any surface, and used to determine the accidents of curvature of the surface at the point of contact. The curve is similar to the intersection of the surface with a parallel to the tangent plane and indefinitely near it. It is an ellipse when the curvature is synclastic, and an hyperbola when the curvature is anticlastic.

indicavit.c: Indicavit ‖In`di*ca"vit (?), n. [L., he has indicated.] (Eng. Law) A writ of prohibition against proceeding in the spiritual court in certain cases, when the suit belongs to the common-law courts. Wharton (Law Dict.).

indice.c: Indice In"dice (?), n. [F. indice indication, index. See Index.] Index; indication. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

indicia.c: Indicia ‖In*di"ci*a (?), n. pl. [L., pl. of indicium, fr. index an index.] (Law) Discriminating marks; signs; tokens; indications; appearances. Burrill.

indicolite.c: Indicolite In*dic"o*lite (?), n. [L. indicum indigo + -lite: cf. F. indicolithe.] (Min.) A variety of tourmaline of an indigo-blue color.

indict.c: Indict In*dict" (ĭn*dīt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indicted (ĭn*dīt"ĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Indicting.] [OE. enditen. See Indite.]

indictable.c: Indictable In*dict"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being, or liable to be, indicted; subject to indictment; as, an indictable offender or offense.

indiction.c: Indiction In*dic"tion (?), n. [L. indictio: cf. F. indiction. See Indict, Indite.]

indictive.c: Indictive In*dic"tive (?), a. [L. indictivus. See Indict.] Proclaimed; declared; public. Kennet.

indictor.c: Indictor In*dict"or (?), n. (Law) One who indicts. Bacon.

indies.c: Indies In"dies (?), n. pl. A name designating the East Indies, also the West Indies.

indifference.c: Indifference In*dif"fer*ence (?), n. [L. indifferentia similarity, lack of difference: cf. F. indifférence.]

indifferency.c: Indifferency In*dif"fer*en*cy (?), n. Absence of interest in, or influence from, anything; unconcernedness; equilibrium; indifferentism; indifference. Gladstone.

indifferent.c: Indifferent In*dif"fer*ent (?), a. [F. indifférent, L. indifferens. See In- not, and Different.]
Indifferent In*dif"fer*ent, adv. To a moderate degree; passably; tolerably. [Obs.] “News indifferent good.” Shak.

indifferentist.c: Indifferentist In*dif"fer*ent*ist, n. One governed by indifferentism.

indifferently.c: Indifferently In*dif"fer*ent*ly, adv. In an indifferent manner; without distinction or preference; impartially; without concern, wish, affection, or aversion; tolerably; passably.

indifulvin.c: Indifulvin In`di*ful"vin (?), n. [Indican + L. fulvus reddish yellow.] (Chem.) A reddish resinous substance, obtained from indican.

indifuscin.c: Indifuscin In`di*fus"cin (?), n. [Indican + L. fuscus dusky.] (Chem.) A brown amorphous powder, obtained from indican.

indigeen.c: Indigeen In"di*geen (?), n. Same as Indigene. Darwin.

indigence.c: Indigence In"di*gence (?), n. [L. indigentia: cf. F. indigence. See Indigent.] The condition of being indigent; lack of estate, or means of comfortable subsistence; penury; poverty; as, helpless indigence. Cowper.

indigene.c: Indigene In"di*gene (?), n. [L. indigena: cf. F. indigène. See Indigenous.] One born in a country; an aboriginal animal or plant; an autochthon. Evelyn. Tylor.

indigenous.c: Indigenous In*dig"e*nous (?), a. [L. indigenus, indigena, fr. OL. indu (fr. in in) + the root of L. gignere to beget, bear. See In, and Gender.]

indigent.c: Indigent In"di*gent (?), a. [L. indigent, L. indigens, p. p. of indigere to stand in need of, fr. OL. indu (fr. in- in) + L. egere to be needy, to need.]

indigently.c: Indigently In"di*gent*ly, adv. In an indigent manner.

indigest.c: Indigest In`di*gest" (?), a. [L. indigestus unarranged. See Indigested.] Crude; unformed; unorganized; undigested. [Obs.] “A chaos rude and indigest.” W. Browne. “Monsters and things indigest.” Shak.

indigestedness.c: Indigestedness In`di*gest"ed*ness, n. The state or quality of being undigested; crudeness. Bp. Burnet.

indigestibility.c: Indigestibility In*di*gest`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being indigestible; indigestibleness.

indigestible.c: Indigestible In`di*gest"i*ble (?), a. [L. indigestibilis: cf. F. indigestible. See In- not, and Digest.]

indigestion.c: Indigestion In`di*ges"tion (?; 106), n. [L. indigestio: cf. F. indigestion. See In- not, and Digest.] Discomfort due to a lack of proper digestive action; a failure of the normal changes which food should undergo in the alimentary canal; dyspepsia; incomplete or difficult digestion.

indigitate.c: Indigitate In*dig"i*tate (?), v. i. [Pref. in- in + L. digitus finger.] To communicate ideas by the fingers; to show or compute by the fingers. [Obs.]
Indigitate In*dig"i*tate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indigitated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indigitating (?).] To point out with the finger; to indicate. [Obs.]

indigitation.c: Indigitation In*dig`i*ta"tion (?), n. The act of pointing out as with the finger; indication. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

indiglucin.c: Indiglucin In`di*glu"cin (?), n. [Indican + glucin.] (Chem.) The variety of sugar (glucose) obtained from the glucoside indican. It is unfermentable, but reduces Fehling's solution.

indign.c: Indign In*dign" (?), a. [L. indignus; pref. in- not + dignus worthy: cf. F. indigne. See Dignity.] Unworthy; undeserving; disgraceful; degrading. Chaucer.

indignancy.c: Indignancy Indignance { In*dig"nance (?), In*dig"nan*cy (?), } n. Indignation. [Obs.] Spenser.

indignant.c: Indignant In*dig"nant (?), a. [L. indignans, -antis, p. pr. of indignari to be indignant, disdain. See Indign.] Affected with indignation; wrathful; passionate; irate; feeling wrath, as when a person is exasperated by unworthy or unjust treatment, by a mean action, or by a degrading accusation.

indignantly.c: Indignantly In*dig"nant*ly, adv. In an indignant manner.

indignation.c: Indignation In`dig*na"tion (?), n. [F. indignation, L. indignatio. See Indign.]

indignify.c: Indignify In*dig"ni*fy (?), v. t. [L. indignus unworthy + -fy.] To treat disdainfully or with indignity; to contemn. [Obs.] Spenser.

indignity.c: Indignity In*dig"ni*ty (?), n.; pl. Indignities (#). [L. indignitas: cf. F. indignité. See Indign.] Any action toward another which manifests contempt for him; an offense against personal dignity; unmerited contemptuous treatment; contumely; incivility or injury, accompanied with insult.

indigo.c: Indigo In"di*go (?), n.; pl. Indigoes (#). [F. indigo, Sp. indigo, indico, L. indicum indigo, fr. Indicus Indian. See Indian.]
Indigo In"di*go (?), a. Having the color of, pertaining to, or derived from, indigo.

indigofera.c: Indigofera ‖In`di*gof"e*ra (?), n. [NL., from E. indigo + L. ferre to bear.] (Bot.) A genus of leguminous plants (family Leguminosae) having many species, mostly in tropical countries, several of them yielding indigo, esp. Indigofera tinctoria, Indigofera suffroticosa, and Indigofera Anil.

indigometer.c: Indigometer In`di*gom"e*ter (?), n. [Indigo + -meter.] An instrument for ascertaining the strength of an indigo solution, as in volumetric analysis. Ure.

indigometry.c: Indigometry In`di*gom"e*try (?), n. The art or method of determining the coloring power of indigo.

indigotic.c: Indigotic In`di*got"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. indigotique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, indigo; as, indigotic acid, which is also called anilic or nitrosalicylic acid.

indigotin.c: Indigotin In"di*go*tin (?), n. (Chem.) See Indigo blue, under Indigo.

indigrubin.c: Indigrubin In`dig*ru"bin (?), n. [Indigo + L. ruber red.] (Physiol. Chem.) Same as Urrhodin.

indihumin.c: Indihumin In`di*hu"min (?), n. [Indican + humin.] (Chem.) A brown amorphous substance resembling humin, and obtained from indican.

indiligence.c: Indiligence In*dil"i*gence (?), n. [L. indiligentia: cf. F. indiligence.] Lack of diligence. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

indiligent.c: Indiligent In*dil"i*gent (?), a. [L. indiligens: cf. F. indiligent. See Diligent.] Not diligent; idle; slothful. [Obs.] Feltham. -- In*dil"i*gent*ly, adv. [Obs.]

indiminishable.c: Indiminishable In`di*min"ish*a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being diminished. [R.] Milton.

indin.c: Indin In"din (?), n. [From Indigo.] (Chem.) A dark red crystalline substance, isomeric with and resembling indigo blue, and obtained from isatide and dioxindol.

indirect.c: Indirect In`di*rect" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + direct: cf. F. indirect.]

indirection.c: Indirection In`di*rec"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. indirection.] Oblique course or means; dishonest practices; indirectness. “By indirections find directions out.” Shak.

indirectly.c: Indirectly In`di*rect"ly (?), adv. In an direct manner; not in a straight line or course; not in express terms; obliquely; not by direct means; hence, unfairly; wrongly.

indirectness.c: Indirectness In`di*rect"ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being indirect; obliquity; deviousness; crookedness.

indiretin.c: Indiretin In`di*re"tin (?), n. [Indian + Gr.? resin.] (Chem.) A dark brown resinous substance obtained from indican.

indirubin.c: Indirubin In`di*ru"bin (?), n. [Indigo + L. ruber red.] (Chem.) A substance isomeric with, and resembling, indigo blue, and accompanying it as a side product, in its artificial production.

indiscernible.c: Indiscernible In`dis*cern"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + discernible: cf. F. indiscernable.] Not to be discerned; imperceptible; not discoverable or visible.

indiscerptibility.c: Indiscerptibility Indiscerpibility { In`dis*cerp`i*bil"i*ty (?), In`dis*cerp`ti*bil"i*ty (?) }, n. The state or quality of being indiscerpible. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

indiscerptible.c: Indiscerptible Indiscerpible { In`dis*cerp"i*ble (?), In`dis*cerp"ti*ble (?) }, a. Not discerpible; inseparable. [Obs.] Bp. Butler. -- In`dis*cerp"i*ble*ness, n., In`dis*cerp"ti*ble*ness, n. [Obs.] -- In`dis*cerp"ti*bly, adv. [Obs.]

indisciplinable.c: Indisciplinable In*dis"ci*plin*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + disciplinable: cf. F. indisciplinable.] Not disciplinable; undisciplinable. [R.]

indiscipline.c: Indiscipline In*dis"ci*pline (?), n. [L. indisplina: cf. F. indiscipline. See In- not, and Discipline.] Lack of discipline or instruction. [R.]

indiscoverable.c: Indiscoverable In`dis*cov"er*a*ble (?), a. Not discoverable; undiscoverable. J. Conybeare.

indiscreet.c: Indiscreet In`dis*creet" (?), a. [OE. indiscret, F. indiscret, fr. L. indiscretus unseparated, indiscreet. See In- not, and Discreet, and cf. Indiscrete.] Not discreet; wanting in discretion.

indiscrete.c: Indiscrete In`dis*crete" (?), a. [L. indiscretus unseparated. See Indiscreet.]

indiscretion.c: Indiscretion In`dis*cre"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + discretion: cf. F. indiscrétion.]

indiscriminate.c: Indiscriminate In`dis*crim"i*nate (?), a. Not discriminate; wanting discrimination; undistinguishing; not making any distinction; confused; promiscuous. “Blind or indiscriminate forgiveness.” I. Taylor.

indiscriminating.c: Indiscriminating In`dis*crim"i*na`ting (?), a. Not discriminating. -- In`dis*crim"i*na`ting*ly, adv.

indiscrimination.c: Indiscrimination In`dis*crim`i*na"tion (?), n. Lack of discrimination or distinction; impartiality. Jefferson.

indiscriminative.c: Indiscriminative In`dis*crim"i*na*tive (?), a. Making no distinction; not discriminating.

indiscussed.c: Indiscussed In`dis*cussed" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + discuss: cf. L. indiscussus.] Not discussed. [Obs.] Donne.

indispensable.c: Indispensable In`dis*pen"sa*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + dispensable: cf. F. indispensable.]

indispensableness.c: Indispensableness In`dis*pen"sa*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being indispensable, or absolutely necessary. S. Clarke.

indispensably.c: Indispensably In`dis*pen"sa*bly, adv. In an indispensable manner. “Indispensably necessary.” Bp. Warburton.

indispose.c: Indispose In`dis*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indisposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indisposing.] [OE. indispos indisposed, feeble, or F. indisposé indisposed. See In- not, and Dispose.]

indisposedness.c: Indisposedness In`dis*pos"ed*ness (?), n. The condition or quality of being indisposed. [R.] Bp. Hall.

indisputable.c: Indisputable In*dis"pu*ta*ble (?; 277), a. [Pref. in- not + disputable: cf. F. indisputable.] Not disputable; incontrovertible; too evident to admit of dispute.

indissipable.c: Indissipable In*dis"si*pa*ble (?), a. Incapable o? being dissipated.

indissolubility.c: Indissolubility In*dis`so*lu*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. indissolubilité.] The quality or state of being indissoluble.

indissoluble.c: Indissoluble In*dis"so*lu*ble (?), a. [L. indissolubilis: cf. F. indissoluble. See In- not, and Dissoluble, and cf. Indissolvable.]

indissolubleness.c: Indissolubleness In*dis"so*lu*ble*ness, n. Indissolubility. Sir M. Hale.

indissolubly.c: Indissolubly In*dis"so*lu*bly, adv. In an indissoluble manner.

indissolvable.c: Indissolvable In`dis*solv"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + dissolvable. Cf. Indissoluble.] Not dissolvable; incapable of being dissolved or separated; incapable of separation; perpetually firm and binding; indissoluble; as, an indissolvable bond of union. Bp. Warburton.

indistancy.c: Indistancy In*dis"tan*cy (?), n. Lack of distance or separation; nearness. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

indistinct.c: Indistinct In`dis*tinct" (ĭn`dĭs*tĭṉkt"), a. [L. indistinctus: cf. F. indistinct. See In- not, and Distinct.]

indistinction.c: Indistinction In`dis*tinc"tion (ĭn`dĭs*tĭṉk"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. indistinction.] Lack of distinction or distinguishableness; confusion; uncertainty; indiscrimination.

indistinctive.c: Indistinctive In`dis*tinc"tive (ĭn`dĭs*tĭṉk"tĭv), a. Having nothing distinctive; common. -- In`dis*tinc"tive*ness, n.

indistinctly.c: Indistinctly In`dis*tinct"ly (ĭn`dĭs*tĭṉkt"ly̆), adv. In an indistinct manner; not clearly; confusedly; dimly; as, certain ideas are indistinctly comprehended.

indistinctness.c: Indistinctness In`dis*tinct"ness, n. The quality or condition of being indistinct; lack of definiteness; dimness; confusion; as, the indistinctness of a picture, or of comprehension; indistinctness of vision.

indistinguishable.c: Indistinguishable In`dis*tin"guish*a*ble (ĭn`dĭs*tĭṉ"gwĭsh*ȧ*b'l), a. Not distinguishable; not capable of being perceived, known, or discriminated as separate and distinct; hence, not capable of being perceived or known; as, in the distance the flagship was indisguishable; the two copies were indisguishable in form or color; the difference between them was indisguishable.

indistinguishably.c: Indistinguishably In`dis*tin"guish*a*bly, adv. In a indistinguishable manner. Sir W. Scott.

indistinguished.c: Indistinguished In`dis*tin"guished (?), a. Indistinct. [R.] “That indistinguished mass.” Sir T. Browne.

indistinguishing.c: Indistinguishing In`dis*tin"guish*ing (?), a. Making no difference; indiscriminative; impartial; as, indistinguishing liberalities. [Obs.] Johnson.

indisturbance.c: Indisturbance In`dis*turb"ance (?), n. Freedom from disturbance; calmness; repose; apathy; indifference.

inditch.c: Inditch In*ditch" (?), v. t. To bury in, or cast into, a ditch. Bp. Hall.

indite.c: Indite In*dite" (ĭn*dīt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indited; p. pr. & vb. n. Inditing.] [OE. enditen to indite, indict, OF. enditer to indicate, show, dictate, write, inform, and endicter to accuse; both fr. LL. indictare to show, to accuse, fr. L. indicere to proclaim, announce; pref. in- in + dicere to say. The word was influenced also by L. indicare to indicate, and by dictare to dictate. See Diction, and cf. Indict, Indicate, Dictate.]
Indite In*dite", v. i. To compose; to write, as a poem.

inditement.c: Inditement In*dite"ment (?), n. [Cf. Indictment.] The act of inditing. Craig.

inditer.c: Inditer In*dit"er (?), n. One who indites. Smart.

indium.c: Indium In"di*um (?), n. [NL. See Indigo.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element, of atomic number 49, discovered in certain ores of zinc, by means of its characteristic spectrum of two indigo blue lines; hence, its name. In appearance it resembles zinc, being white or lead gray, soft, malleable and easily fusible, but in its chemical relation it resembles aluminium or gallium (valence +3). Symbol In. Atomic weight, 114.82.

indivertible.c: Indivertible In`di*vert"i*ble (ĭn`dĭ*vẽrt"ĭ*b'l), a. Not to be diverted or turned aside. [R.] Lamb.

individual.c: Individual In`di*vid"u*al (?; 135), a. [L. individuus indivisible; pref. in- not + dividuus divisible, fr. dividere to divide: cf. F. individuel. See Divide.]

Individual In`di*vid"u*al, n. 1. A single person, animal, or thing of any kind; a thing or being incapable of separation or division, without losing its identity; especially, a human being; a person. Cowper.

individualistic.c: Individualistic In`di*vid`u*al*is"tic (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to the individual or individualism. London Athenæum.

individuality.c: Individuality In`di*vid`u*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Individualities (#). [Cf. F. individualité.]

individualization.c: Individualization In`di*vid`u*al*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. individualization.] The act of individualizing; the state of being individualized; individuation.

individualize.c: Individualize In`di*vid"u*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Individualized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Individualizing (?).] [Cf. F. individualiser.] To mark as an individual, or to distinguish from others by peculiar properties; to invest with individuality; to give distinctive character to; to make distinctive; to enable differentiation from others of similar type; -- of properties of things.

individually.c: Individually In`di*vid"u*al*ly, adv. 1. In an individual manner or relation; as individuals; separately; each by itself; as, every person must apply individually for admission. “Individually or collectively.” Burke.

individuate.c: Individuate In`di*vid"u*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Individuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Individuating.] To distinguish from others of the species; to endow with individuality; to divide into individuals; to discriminate.

individuation.c: Individuation In`di*vid`u*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. individuation.] The act of individuating or state of being individuated; individualization. H. Spencer.

individuator.c: Individuator In`di*vid"u*a`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, individuates. Sir K. Digby.

individuity.c: Individuity In`di*vi*du"i*ty (?), n. [L. individuitas.] Separate existence; individuality; oneness. Fuller.

indivinity.c: Indivinity In`di*vin"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + divinity: cf. F. indivinité.] Lack or absence of divine power or of divinity. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

indivisibility.c: Indivisibility In`di*vis`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. indivisibilité.] The state or property of being indivisible or inseparable; inseparability. Locke.

indivisible.c: Indivisible In`di*vis"i*ble (?), a. [L. indivisibilis: cf. F. indivisible. See In- not, and Divisible.]
Indivisible In`di*vis"i*ble, n. 1. That which is indivisible.

indivisibleness.c: Indivisibleness In`di*vis"i*ble*ness (?), n. The state of being indivisible; indivisibility. W. Montagu.

indivisibly.c: Indivisibly In`di*vis"i*bly, adv. In an indivisible manner.

indivision.c: Indivision In`di*vi"sion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + division: cf. F. indivision, LL. indivisio.] A state of being not divided; oneness. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

indo.c: Indo- In"do- (?). [From L. Indus East Indian.] A prefix signifying Indian (i. e., East Indian); of or pertaining of India.

indoaniline.c: Indoaniline In`do*an"i*line (?), n. [Indigo + aniline.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of artificial blue dyes, in appearance resembling indigo, for which they are often used as substitutes.

indoaryan.c: Indo-Aryan In`do-Ar"yan, a. Pertaining to the Indo-Aryans, or designating, or of, the Aryan languages of India.

Indo-Aryan In`do-Ar"yan, n. A member of one of the native races of India of Aryan speech and blood, characterized by tall stature, dolichocephaly, fair complexion with dark hair and eyes, plentiful beard, and narrow and prominent nose.

indobriton.c: Indo-Briton In`do-Brit"on (?), n. [Indo- + Briton.] A person born in India, of mixed Indian and British blood; a half-caste. Malcom.

indochinese.c: Indo-Chinese Indochinese In`do*chi*nese", In`do-Chi*nese" (?), prop. a. [Indo- + Chinese.] 1. Of or pertaining to Indo-China (i. e., Farther India, or India beyond the Ganges).

indodochinese.c: Indo-do-Chinese languages In`do-do-Chinese languages. A family of languages, mostly of the isolating type, although some are agglutinative, spoken in the great area extending from northern India in the west to Formosa in the east and from Central Asia in the north to the Malay Peninsula in the south.

indocibility.c: Indocibility In*doc`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state of being indocible; indocibleness; indocility.

indocible.c: Indocible In*doc"i*ble (?), a. [L. indocibilis. See In- not, and Docible.] Incapable of being taught, or not easily instructed; dull in intellect; intractable; unteachable; indocile. Bp. Hall. -- In*doc"i*ble*ness, n.

indocile.c: Indocile In*doc"ile (?), a. [L. indocilis: cf. F. indocile. See In- not, and Docile.] Not teachable; indisposed to be taught, trained, or disciplined; not easily instructed or governed; dull; intractable.

indocility.c: Indocility In`do*cil"i*ty (?), n. [L. indocilitas: cf. F. indocilité.] The quality or state of being indocile; dullness of intellect; unteachableness; intractableness.

indoctrinate.c: Indoctrinate In*doc"tri*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indoctrinated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indoctrinating.] [Pref. in- in + L. doctrina doctrine: cf. F. endoctriner.] 1. To instruct in the rudiments or principles of learning, or of a branch of learning; to imbue with learning; to teach; -- often followed by in.

indoctrination.c: Indoctrination In*doc`tri*na"tion (?), n. The act of indoctrinating, or the condition of being indoctrinated; instruction in the rudiments and principles of any science or system of belief; information. Sir T. Browne.

indoenglish.c: Indo-English In`do-Eng"lish (?), a. [Indo- + English.] Of or relating to the English who are born or reside in India; Anglo-Indian.

indoeuropean.c: Indo-European In`do-Eu`ro*pe"an (?), a. Aryan; -- applied to the languages of India and Europe which are derived from the prehistoric Aryan language; also, pertaining to the people or nations who speak these languages; as, the Indo-European or Aryan family.
Indo-European In`do-Eu`ro*pe"an. A member of one of the Caucasian races of Europe or India speaking an Indo-European language.

indogen.c: Indogen In"do*gen (?), n. [Indigo + -gen.] (Chem.) A complex, nitrogenous radical, C8H5NO, regarded as the essential nucleus of indigo.

indogenide.c: Indogenide In"do*gen*ide (?), n. (Chem.) Any one of the derivatives of indogen, which contain that group as a nucleus.

indoin.c: Indoin In"do*in (?), n. (Chem.) A substance resembling indigo blue, obtained artificially from certain isatogen compounds.

indol.c: Indol Indole In"dole, In"dol (ĭn"dōl), n. [Indigo + -ol of phenol.] (Chem., Physiol. Chem.) A white, crystalline substance, C8H7N, obtained from blue indigo, and almost all indigo derivatives, by a process of reduction; chemically, it is 2,3-benzopyrrole, a bicyclic heterocyclic compound, having a benzene ring fused to a pyrrole ring. It is also formed from proteinaceous matter, together with skatol, by putrefaction, and by fusion with caustic potash, and is present in human excrement, as well as in the intestinal canal of some herbivora. It is produced in rich growth media by the intestinal bacterium Escherichia coli.

indolence.c: Indolence In"do*lence (?), n. [L. indolentia freedom from pain: cf. F. indolence.]

indolent.c: Indolent In"do*lent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + L. dolens, -entis, p. pr. of dolere to feel pain: cf. F. indolent. See Dolorous.]

indolently.c: Indolently In"do*lent*ly, adv. In an indolent manner.

indoles.c: Indoles ‖In"do*les (?), n. [L. Cf. Adolescence.] Natural disposition; natural quality or abilities.

indolin.c: Indolin In"do*lin (?), n. [See Indol.] (Chem.) A dark resinous substance, polymeric with indol, and obtained by the reduction of indigo white.

indomable.c: Indomable In*dom"a*ble (?), a. [L. indomabilis; pref. in- not + domabilis tamable.] Indomitable. [Obs.]

indomitable.c: Indomitable In*dom"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. indomitabilis; pref. in- not + domitare, intens. fr. domare to tame. See Tame.] Not to be subdued; untamable; invincible; as, an indomitable will, courage, animal.

indomite.c: Indomite In*dom"ite (?), a. [L. indomitus.] Not tamed; untamed; savage; wild. [Obs.] J. Salkeld.

indomptable.c: Indomptable In*domp"ta*ble (?), a. [F. indomptable, L. indomitabilis.] Indomitable. [Obs.] Tooke.

indonesian.c: Indonesian In`do*ne"sian (?), a. [Indo- + Gr.? island.] Of or pertaining to Indonesia or Indonesians.

Indonesian In`do*ne"sian, n. 1. A member of a race forming the chief pre-Malay population of the Malay Archipelago, and probably sprung from a mixture of Polynesian and Mongoloid immigrants. According to Keane, the autochthonous Negritos were largely expelled by the Caucasian Polynesians, themselves followed by Mongoloid peoples of Indo-Chinese affinities, from mixture with whom sprang the Indonesian race.

indoor.c: Indoor In"door` (?), a. Done or being within doors; within a house or institution; domestic; as, indoor work.

indoors.c: Indoors In"doors` (?), adv. Within the house; -- sometimes separated, in doors.

indophenol.c: Indophenol In`do*phe"nol (?), n. [Indigo + phenol.] (Chem.) Any one of a series of artificial blue dyestuffs, resembling indigo in appearance, and obtained by the action of phenol on certain nitrogenous derivatives of quinone. Simple indophenol proper, the parent compound of the dye series, is a quinonimine derivative with the formula C12H9NO2.

indorsable.c: Indorsable In*dors"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being indorsed; transferable; convertible.

indorse.c: Indorse In*dorse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indorsed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indorsing.] [LL. indorsare. See Endorse.] [Written also endorse.]

indorsee.c: Indorsee In`dor*see" (?), n. The person to whom a note or bill is indorsed, or assigned by indorsement.

indorsement.c: Indorsement In*dorse"ment (?), n. [From Indorse; cf. Endorsement.] [Written also endorsement.]

indorsor.c: Indorsor Indorser { In*dors"er (?), In*dors"or (?), } n. The person who indorses. [Written also endorser.]

indoxyl.c: Indoxyl In*dox"yl (?), n. [Indigo + hydroxyl.] (Chem.) A nitrogenous substance, C8H7NO, isomeric with oxindol, obtained as an oily liquid.

indoxylic.c: Indoxylic In`dox*yl"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to, or producing, indoxyl; as, indoxylic acid.

indraught.c: Indraught In"draught` (?), n. 1. An opening from the sea into the land; an inlet. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

indrench.c: Indrench In*drench" (?), v. t. To overwhelm with water; to drench; to drown. [Obs.] Shak.

indri.c: Indri Indris { In"dris (?), In"dri (?), } n. (Zool.) Any lemurine animal of the genus Indris.

indubious.c: Indubious In*du"bi*ous (?), a. [L. indubius. See In- not, and Dubious.]

indubitable.c: Indubitable In*du"bi*ta*ble (?), a. [L. indubitabilis: cf. F. indubitable. See In- not, and Dubitable.] Not dubitable or doubtful; too evident to admit of doubt; unquestionable; evident; apparently certain; as, an indubitable conclusion. -- n. That which is indubitable.

indubitableness.c: Indubitableness In*du"bi*ta*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being indubitable.

indubitably.c: Indubitably In*du"bi*ta*bly, adv. Undoubtedly; unquestionably; in a manner to remove all doubt.

indubitate.c: Indubitate In*du"bi*tate (?), a. [L. indubitatus; pref. in- not + dubitatus, p. p. of dubitare to doubt.] Not questioned or doubtful; evident; certain. [Obs.] Bacon.
Indubitate In*du"bi*tate (?), v. t. [L. indubitatus, p. p. of indubitare; pref. in- in + dubitare to doubt.] To bring into doubt; to cause to be doubted. [Obs.]
