induce.c: Induce In*duce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Induced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inducing (?).] [L. inducere, inductum; pref. in- in + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Induct.]

induced.c: Induced current In*duced" cur"rent. (Elec.) A current due to variation in the magnetic field surrounding its conductor.

inducer.c: Inducer In*du"cer (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, induces or incites.

inducible.c: Inducible In*du"ci*ble (?), a. 1. Capable of being induced, caused, or made to take place.

induct.c: Induct In*duct" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inducted; p. pr. & vb. n. Inducting.] [L. inductus, p. p. of inducere. See Induce.]

inductance.c: Inductance In*duc"tance (?), n. (Elec.) Capacity for induction; the coefficient of self-induction.
Inductance coil In*duc"tance coil. (Elec.) A choking coil.

inducteous.c: Inducteous In*duc"te*ous (?), a. (Elec.) Rendered electro-polar by induction, or brought into the opposite electrical state by the influence of inductive bodies.

inductile.c: Inductile In*duc"tile (?), a. [Pref. in- not + ductile: cf. F. inductile.] Not ductile; incapable of being drawn into threads, as a metal; inelastic; tough.

inductility.c: Inductility In`duc*til"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being inductile.

induction.c: Induction In*duc"tion (?), n. [L. inductio: cf. F. induction. See Induct.]

Induction generator In*duc"tion gen"er*a`tor. A machine built as an induction motor and driven above synchronous speed, thus acting as an alternating-current generator; -- called also asynchronous generator. Below synchronism the machine takes in electrical energy and acts as an induction motor; at synchronism the power component of current becomes zero and changes sign, so that above synchronism the machine (driven for this purpose by mechanical power) gives out electrical energy as a generator.

Induction motor Induction motor. (Elec.) A type of alternating-current motor comprising two wound members, one stationary, called the stator, and the other rotating, called the rotor, these two members corresponding to a certain extent to the field and armature of a direct-current motor.

inductional.c: Inductional In*duc"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or proceeding by, induction; inductive.

inductive.c: Inductive In*duct"ive (?), a. [LL. inductivus: cf. F. inductif. See Induce.]

inductively.c: Inductively In*duct"ive*ly, adv. By induction or inference.

inductometer.c: Inductometer In`duc*tom"e*ter (?), n. [Induction + -meter.] (Elec.) An instrument for measuring or ascertaining the degree or rate of electrical induction.

inductor.c: Inductor In*duct"or (?), n. [L., one who stirs up or rouses. See Induce.]

inductorium.c: Inductorium In`duc*to"ri*um (?), n.; pl. E. Inductoriums (#), L. Inductoria (#). [NL., fr. E. induction.] (Elec.) An induction coil.

inductrical.c: Inductrical Inductric { In*duc"tric (?), In*duc"tric*al (?), } a. (Elec.) Acting by, or in a state of, induction; relating to electrical induction.

indue.c: Indue In*due" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Induing.] [Written also endue.] [L. induere to put on, clothe, fr. OL. indu (fr. in- in) + a root seen also in L. exuere to put off, divest, exuviae the skin of an animal, slough, induviae clothes. Cf. Endue to invest.]

induement.c: Induement In*due"ment (?), n. [From Indue; cf. Indument, Enduement.] The act of induing, or state of being indued; investment; endowment. W. Montagu.

indulge.c: Indulge In*dulge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indulged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indulging (?).] [L. indulgere to be kind or tender to one; cf. OIr. dilgud, equiv. to L. remissio, OIr. dligeth, equiv. to L. lex, Goth. dulgs debt.]

Indulge In*dulge", v. i. To indulge one's self; to gratify one's tastes or desires; esp., to give one's self up (to); to practice a forbidden or questionable act without restraint; -- followed by in, but formerly, also, by to. “Willing to indulge in easy vices.” Johnson.

indulgence.c: Indulgence In*dul"gence (?), n. [L. indulgentia: cf. F. indulgence.]
Indulgence In*dul"gence (?), v. t. To grant an indulgence to.

indulgent.c: Indulgent In*dul"gent (?), a. [L. indulgens, -entis, p. pr. of indulgere: cf. F. indulgent. See Indulge.] Prone to indulge; yielding to the wishes, humor, or appetites of those under one's care; compliant; not opposing or restraining; tolerant; mild; favorable; not severe; as, an indulgent parent. Shak.

indulgential.c: Indulgential In`dul*gen"tial (?), a. Relating to the indulgences of the Roman Catholic Church. Brevint.

indulgently.c: Indulgently In*dul"gent*ly (?), adv. In an indulgent manner; mildly; favorably. Dryden.

indulger.c: Indulger In*dul"ger, n. One who indulges. W. Montagu.

indulgiate.c: Indulgiate In*dul"gi*ate (?), v. t. To indulge. [R.] Sandys.

induline.c: Induline In"du*line (?), n. [Perh. fr. indigo.] (Chem.) (a) Any one of a large series of aniline dyes, colored blue or violet, and represented by aniline violet. (b) A dark green amorphous dyestuff, produced by the oxidation of aniline in the presence of copper or vanadium salts; -- called also aniline black.

indulto.c: Indulto Indult { In*dult" (?), In*dul"to (?), } n. [L. indultum indulgence, favor, fr. indultus, p. p. of indulgere: cf. It. indulto, F. indult. See Indulge.]

indument.c: Indument In"du*ment (?), n. [L. indumentum a covering. See Indue, and cf. Induement.] 1. (Zool.) Plumage; feathers.

induplicate.c: Induplicate In*du"pli*cate (?), a. (Bot.) (a) Having the edges bent abruptly toward the axis; -- said of the parts of the calyx or corolla in æstivation. (b) Having the edges rolled inward and then arranged about the axis without overlapping; -- said of leaves in vernation.

induplicative.c: Induplicative In*du"pli*ca*tive (?), a. (Bot.) (a) Having induplicate sepals or petals in æstivation. (b) Having induplicate leaves in vernation.

indurate.c: Indurate In"du*rate (?), a. [L. induratus, p. p. of indurare to harden. See Endure.]
Indurate In"du*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Indurated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indurating (?).]
Indurate In"du*rate, v. i. To grow hard; to harden, or become hard; as, clay indurates by drying, and by heat.

indurated.c: Indurated In"du*ra`ted (?), a. Hardened; as, indurated clay; an indurated heart. Goldsmith.

induration.c: Induration In`du*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. induration, L. induratio hardness of heart.]

indusial.c: Indusial In*du"sial (?), a. [See Indusium.] Of, pertaining to, or containing, the petrified cases of the larvæ of certain insects.

indusiated.c: Indusiated Indusiate { In*du"si*ate (?), In*du"si*a`ted (?), } a. (Bot.) Furnished with an indusium.

indusium.c: Indusium ‖In*du"si*um (?), n.; pl. Indusia (-ȧ). [L., an under garment, fr. induere to put on: cf. F. indusie the covering of the seed spots of ferns.] (Bot.) (a) A collection of hairs united so as to form a sort of cup, and inclosing the stigma of a flower. (b) The immediate covering of the fruit dots or sori in many ferns, usually a very thin scale attached by the middle or side to a veinlet. (c) A peculiar covering found in certain fungi.

industrial.c: Industrial In*dus"tri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. industriel, LL. industrialis. See Industry.] Consisting in industry; pertaining to industry, or the arts and products of industry; concerning those employed in labor, especially in manual labor, and their wages, duties, and rights.

industrialism.c: Industrialism In*dus"tri*al*ism (?), n. 1. Devotion to industrial pursuits; labor; industry. J. S. Mill.

industrially.c: Industrially In*dus"tri*al*ly, adv. With reference to industry.

industrious.c: Industrious In*dus"tri*ous (?), a. [L. industrius, industriosus: cf. F. industrieux. See Industry.]

industry.c: Industry In"dus*try (?), n.; pl. Industries (#). [L. industria, cf. industrius diligent; of uncertain origin: cf. F. industrie.]

indutive.c: Indutive In*du"tive (?), a. [L. indutus, p. p. of induere to put on. See Indue.] (Bot.) Covered; -- applied to seeds which have the usual integumentary covering.

induviae.c: Induviae ‖In*du"vi*æ (?), n. pl. [L., clothes, fr. induere to put on. See Indue.] (Bot.) Persistent portions of a calyx or corolla; also, leaves which do not disarticulate from the stem, and hence remain for a long time.

induviate.c: Induviate In*du"vi*ate (?), a. (Bot.) Covered with induviæ, as the upper part of the trunk of a palm tree.

indwell.c: Indwell In"dwell` (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Indwelt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Indwelling.] To dwell in; to abide within; to remain in possession.

indwelling.c: Indwelling In"dwell`ing, n. Residence within, as in the heart.

ine.c: -ine -ine (?; 104). 1. (Chem.) A suffix, indicating that those substances of whose names it is a part are basic, in their nature, i.e. contain a basic nitrogen group.

inearth.c: Inearth In*earth" (?), v. t. To inter. [R.] Southey.

inebriant.c: Inebriant In*e"bri*ant (?), a. [L. inebrians, p. pr. of inebriare. See Inebriate.] Intoxicating.
Inebriant In*e"bri*ant, n. Anything that intoxicates, as opium, alcohol, etc.; an intoxicant. Smart.

inebriate.c: Inebriate In*e"bri*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inebriated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inebriating (?).] [L. inebriatus, p. p. of inebriare; pref. in- in + ebriare to make drunk, fr. ebrius drunk. See Ebriety.]
Inebriate In*e"bri*ate, v. i. To become drunk. [Obs.] Bacon.
Inebriate In*e"bri*ate (?), a. [L. inebriatus, p. p.] Intoxicated; drunk; habitually given to drink; stupefied.
Inebriate In*e"bri*ate, n. One who is drunk or intoxicated; esp., an habitual drunkard; as, an asylum for inebriates.

inebriation.c: Inebriation In*e`bri*a"tion (?), n. [L. inebriatio.] The condition of being inebriated; intoxication; figuratively, deprivation of sense and judgment by anything that exhilarates, as success. Sir T. Browne.

inebriety.c: Inebriety In`e*bri"e*ty (?), n. [See Inebriate, Ebriety.] Drunkenness; inebriation. E. Darwin.

inebrious.c: Inebrious In*e"bri*ous (?), a. Intoxicated, or partially so; intoxicating. [R.] T. Brown.

inedible.c: Inedible In*ed"i*ble (?), a. [LL. inedibilis. See In- not, and Edible.] Not edible; not fit for use as food. -- In*ed`i*bil"i*ty (#), n.

inedited.c: Inedited In*ed"it*ed (?), a. Not edited; unpublished; as, an inedited manuscript. T. Warton.

inee.c: Inee ‖I`née" (?), n. [F.] An arrow poison, made from an apocynaceous plant (Strophanthus hispidus) of the Gaboon country; -- called also onaye.

ineffability.c: Ineffability In*ef`fa*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. ineffabilitas: cf. F. ineffabilité.] The quality or state of being ineffable; ineffableness; unspeakableness.

ineffable.c: Ineffable In*ef"fa*ble (?), a. [L. ineffabilis: cf. F. ineffable. See In- not, and Effable, Fame.] Incapable of being expressed in words; unspeakable; unutterable; indescribable; as, the ineffable joys of heaven.

ineffableness.c: Ineffableness In*ef"fa*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being ineffable or unutterable; unspeakableness.

ineffably.c: Ineffably In*ef"fa*bly, adv. In a manner not to be expressed in words; unspeakably. Milton.

ineffaceable.c: Ineffaceable In`ef*face"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + effaceable: cf. F. ineffaçable.] Incapable of being effaced; indelible; ineradicable.

ineffaceably.c: Ineffaceably In`ef*face"a*bly, adv. So as not to be effaceable.

ineffectible.c: Ineffectible In`ef*fect"i*ble (?), a. Ineffectual; impracticable. [R.] Bp. Hall.

ineffective.c: Ineffective In`ef*fect"ive (?), a. [Pref. in- not + effective: cf. F. ineffectif.] Not effective; not having the desired effect; ineffectual; futile; inefficient; useless; as, an ineffective appeal; an ineffective herbal remedy.

ineffectively.c: Ineffectively In`ef*fect"ive*ly, adv. In an ineffective manner; without effect; inefficiently; ineffectually.

ineffectiveness.c: Ineffectiveness In`ef*fect"ive*ness, n. Quality of being ineffective.

ineffectual.c: Ineffectual In`ef*fec"tu*al (?; 135), a. Not producing the proper effect; without effect; inefficient; weak; useless; futile; unavailing; as, an ineffectual attempt; an ineffectual expedient. Pope.

ineffectually.c: Ineffectually In`ef*fec"tu*al*ly, adv. Without effect; in vain.

ineffectualness.c: Ineffectualness In`ef*fec"tu*al*ness, n. Lack of effect, or of power to produce it; inefficacy.

ineffervescence.c: Ineffervescence In*ef`fer*ves"cence (?), n. Lack of effervescence. Kirwan.

ineffervescent.c: Ineffervescent In*ef`fer*ves"cent (?), a. Not effervescing, or not susceptible of effervescence; quiescent.

ineffervescibility.c: Ineffervescibility In*ef`fer*ves`ci*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being ineffervescible.

ineffervescible.c: Ineffervescible In*ef`fer*ves"ci*ble (?), a. Not capable or susceptible of effervescence.

inefficacious.c: Inefficacious In*ef`fi*ca"cious (?), a. [Pref. in- not + efficacious: cf. F. inefficace, L. inefficax.] Not efficacious; not having power to produce the effect desired; inadequate; incompetent; inefficient; impotent. Boyle.

inefficaciously.c: Inefficaciously In*ef`fi*ca"cious*ly, adv. Without efficacy or effect.

inefficaciousness.c: Inefficaciousness In*ef`fi*ca"cious*ness, n. Lack of effect, or of power to produce the effect; inefficacy.

inefficacy.c: Inefficacy In*ef"fi*ca*cy (?), n. [L. inefficacia. See In- not, and Efficacy.] Lack of power to produce the desired or proper effect; inefficiency; ineffectualness; futility; uselessness; fruitlessness; as, the inefficacy of medicines or means.

inefficiency.c: Inefficiency In`ef*fi"cien*cy (?), n. The quality of being inefficient; lack of power or energy sufficient for the desired effect; inefficacy; incapacity; as, he was discharged from his position for inefficiency.

inefficient.c: Inefficient In`ef*fi"cient (?), a. 1. Not efficient; not producing the effect intended or desired, or achieiving the effect by unnnecessary and excessive expenditure of resources; inefficacious; as, inefficient means or measures; inefficient methods are too expensive.

inefficiently.c: Inefficiently In`ef*fi"cient*ly, adv. In an inefficient manner.

inelaborate.c: Inelaborate In`e*lab"o*rate (?), a. [L. inelaboratus. See In- not, and Elaborate.] Not elaborate; not wrought with care; unpolished; crude; unfinished.

inelegancy.c: Inelegancy Inelegance { In*el"e*gance (?), In*el"e*gan*cy (?), } n.; pl. Inelegances (#), Inelegancies (#). [L. inelegantia: cf. F. inélégance.]

inelegant.c: Inelegant In*el"e*gant (?), a. [L. inelegans: cf. F. inélégant. See In- not, and Elegant.] Not elegant; deficient in beauty, polish, refinement, grave, or ornament; wanting in anything which correct taste requires.

inelegantly.c: Inelegantly In*el"e*gant*ly, adv. In an inelegant manner.

ineligibility.c: Ineligibility In*el`i*gi*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inéligibilité.] The state or quality of being ineligible.

ineligible.c: Ineligible In*el"i*gi*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + eligible: cf. F. inéligible.] Not eligible; not qualified to be chosen (for an office, post, position); not worthy to be chosen or preferred; not expedient or desirable. Burke.

inelligibly.c: Inelligibly In*el"li*gi*bly (?), adv. In an ineligible manner.

ineloquent.c: Ineloquent In*e"lo*quent (?), a. [L. ineloquens: cf. F. inéloquent. See In- not, and Eloquent.] Not eloquent; not fluent, graceful, or moving; not persuasive; as, ineloquent language.

ineluctable.c: Ineluctable In`e*luc"ta*ble (?), a. [L. ineluctabilis; pref. in- not + eluctabilis to be surmounted, fr. eluctari to struggle out of, to surmount: cf. F. inéluctable. See Eluctate.] Not to be overcome by struggling; irresistible; inescapable; inevitable. Bp. Pearson.

ineludible.c: Ineludible In`e*lud"i*ble (?), a. Incapable of being eluded or evaded; unvoidable.

inenarrable.c: Inenarrable In`e*nar"ra*ble (?), a. [L. inenarrabilis; pref. in- not + enarrabilis that may be related; fr. enarrare to relate: cf. F. inénarrable. See Enarration.] Incapable of being narrated; indescribable; ineffable. [Obs.] “Inenarrable goodness.” Bp. Fisher.

inept.c: Inept In*ept" (?), a. [L. ineptus; prefix. in- not + aptus apt, fit: cf. F. inepte. Cf. Inapt.]

inequal.c: Inequal In*e"qual (?), a. [L. inaequalis. See In- not, and Equal.] Unequal; uneven; various. [Obs.] Chaucer.

inequidistant.c: Inequidistant In*e`qui*dis"tant (?), a. Not equally distant; not equidistant.

inequilateral.c: Inequilateral In*e`qui*lat"er*al (?), a. 1. Having unequal sides; unsymmetrical; unequal-sided.

inequilobate.c: Inequilobate In*e`qui*lo"bate (?), a. [Pref. in- not + equi- + lobate.] (Biol.) Unequally lobed; cut into lobes of different shapes or sizes.

inequitable.c: Inequitable In*eq"ui*ta*ble (?), a. Not equitable; not just. Burke.

inequitate.c: Inequitate In*eq"ui*tate (?), v. t. [L. inequitatus, p. p. inequitare to ride over. See 1st In-, and Equitant.] To ride over or through. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

inequity.c: Inequity In*eq"ui*ty (?), n. Lack of equity; injustice; wrong. “Some form of inequity.” H. Spencer.

inequivalvular.c: Inequivalvular Inequivalve { In*e"qui*valve (?), In*e`qui*val"vu*lar (?), } a. (Zool.) Having unequal valves, as the shell of an oyster.

ineradicable.c: Ineradicable In`e*rad"i*ca*ble (?), a. Incapable of being eradicated or rooted out.

ineradicably.c: Ineradicably In`e*rad"i*ca*bly, adv. So as not to be eradicable.

inergetical.c: Inergetical Inergetic { In`er*get"ic (?), In`er*get"ic*al (?), } a. [Pref. in- not + energetic, -ical.] Having no energy; sluggish. [R.] Boyle.

inermous.c: Inermous Inerm { In*erm" (?), In*er"mous (?), } a. (Bot.) Same as Inermis.

inermis.c: Inermis ‖In*er"mis (?), a. [L. inermis, inermus; pref. in- not + arma arms: cf. F. inerme.] (Bot.) Unarmed; destitute of prickles or thorns, as a leaf. Gray.

inerrability.c: Inerrability In*er`ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. Freedom or exemption from error; infallibility. Eikon Basilike.

inerrable.c: Inerrable In*er"ra*ble (?), a. [L. inerrabilis. See In- not, and Err.] Incapable of erring; infallible; unerring. “Inerabble and requisite conditions.” Sir T. Browne. “Not an inerrable text.” Gladstone.

inerrableness.c: Inerrableness In*er"ra*ble*ness (ĭn*ĕr"rȧ*b'l*nĕs), n. Exemption from error; inerrability; infallibility. Hammond.

inerrably.c: Inerrably In*er"ra*bly, adv. With security from error; infallibly; unerringly.

inerratic.c: Inerratic In`er*rat"ic (ĭn`ĕr*răt"ĭk), a. Not erratic or wandering; fixed; settled; established.

inerringly.c: Inerringly In*err"ing*ly (?), adv. Without error, mistake, or deviation; unerringly. Glanvill.

inert.c: Inert In*ert" (?), a. [L. iners, inertis, unskilled, idle; pref. in- + ars art: cf. F. inerte. See Art.]

inertia.c: Inertia In*er"ti*a (?), n. [L., idleness, fr. iners idle. See Inert.]

inertion.c: Inertion In*er"tion (?), n. Lack of activity or exertion; inertness; quietude. [R.]

inertitude.c: Inertitude In*ert"i*tude (?), n. [See Inert.] Inertness; inertia. [R.] Good.

inertly.c: Inertly In*ert"ly, adv. Without activity; sluggishly. Pope.

inertness.c: Inertness In*ert"ness, n. 1. Lack of activity or exertion; habitual indisposition to action or motion; sluggishness; apathy; insensibility. Glanvill.

inerudite.c: Inerudite In*er"u*dite (?), a. [L. ineruditus. See In- not, and Erudite.] Not erudite; unlearned; ignorant.

inescate.c: Inescate In*es"cate (?), v. t. [L. inescatus, p. p. of inescare; in- in + esca bait.] To allure; to lay a bait for. [Obs.]

inescation.c: Inescation In`es*ca"tion (?), n. [L. inescatio.] The act of baiting; allurement. [Obs.] Hallywell.

inescutcheon.c: Inescutcheon In`es*cutch"eon (?), n. (Her.) A small escutcheon borne within a shield.

inessential.c: Inessential In`es*sen"tial (?), a. [Pref. in- not + essential: cf. F. inessentiel.]

inestimable.c: Inestimable In*es"ti*ma*ble (?), a. [L. inaestimabilis: cf. F. inestimable. See In- not, and Estimate.] Incapable of being estimated or computed; especially, too valuable or excellent to be measured or fully appreciated; above all price; as, inestimable rights or privileges.

inestimably.c: Inestimably In*es"ti*ma*bly, adv. In a manner, or to a degree, above estimation; as, things inestimably excellent.

inevasible.c: Inevasible In`e*va"si*ble (?), a. Incapable of being evaded; inevitable; unavoidable.

inevidence.c: Inevidence In*ev"i*dence (?), n. [Cf. F. inévidence.] Lack of evidence; obscurity. [Obs.] Barrow.

inevident.c: Inevident In*ev"i*dent (?), a. [Cf. F. inévident.] Not evident; not clear or obvious; obscure.

inevitability.c: Inevitability In*ev`i*ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inévitabilité.] Impossibility to be avoided or shunned; inevitableness. Shelford.

inevitable.c: Inevitable In*ev"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. inevitabilis: cf. F. inévitable. See In- not, and Evitable.]

inevitableness.c: Inevitableness In*ev"i*ta*ble*ness (?), n. The state of being unavoidable; certainty to happen; inevitability. Prideaux.

inevitably.c: Inevitably In*ev"i*ta*bly, adv. Without possibility of escape or evasion; unavoidably; certainly.

inexact.c: Inexact In`ex*act" (?), a. [Pref. in- not + exact: cf. F. inexact.] Not exact; not precisely correct or true; inaccurate.

inexactitude.c: Inexactitude In`ex*act"i*tude (?), n. 1. Inexactness; uncertainty; as, geographical inexactitude.

inexactly.c: Inexactly In`ex*act"ly, adv. In a manner not exact or precise; inaccurately. R. A. Proctor.

inexactness.c: Inexactness In`ex*act"ness, n. Incorrectness; lack of exactness.

inexcitability.c: Inexcitability In`ex*cit`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being inexcitable; insusceptibility to excitement.

inexcitable.c: Inexcitable In`ex*cit"a*ble (?), a. [L. inexcitabilis from which one cannot be aroused. See In- not, and Excite.] Not susceptible of excitement; dull; lifeless; torpid.

inexcusable.c: Inexcusable In`ex*cus"a*ble (?), a. [L. inexcusabilis: cf. F. inexcusable. See Excuse.] Not excusable; not admitting excuse or justification; as, inexcusable folly.

inexcusableness.c: Inexcusableness In`ex*cus"a*ble*ness, n. The quality of being inexcusable; enormity beyond forgiveness. South.

inexcusably.c: Inexcusably In`ex*cus"a*bly, adv. With a degree of guilt or folly beyond excuse or justification.

inexecrable.c: Inexecrable In*ex"e*cra*ble (?), a. That can not be execrated enough. [R.]

inexecutable.c: Inexecutable In*ex"e*cu`ta*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + executable: cf. F. inexécutable.] Incapable of being executed or performed; impracticable; infeasible.

inexecution.c: Inexecution In*ex`e*cu"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + execution: cf. F. inexécution.] Neglect of execution; nonperformance; as, the inexecution of a treaty. Spence.

inexertion.c: Inexertion In`ex*er"tion (?), n. Lack of exertion; lack of effort; defect of action; indolence; laziness.

inexhalable.c: Inexhalable In`ex*hal"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being exhaled. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

inexhausted.c: Inexhausted In`ex*haust"ed (?), a. [Pref. in- not + exhausted: cf. F. inexhaustus.] Not exhausted; not emptied; not spent; not having lost all strength or resources; unexhausted. Dryden.

inexhaustibility.c: Inexhaustibility In`ex*haust`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being inexhaustible; abundance.

inexhaustible.c: Inexhaustible In`ex*haust"i*ble (?), a. Incapable of being exhausted, emptied, or used up; unfailing; not to be wasted or spent; as, inexhaustible stores of provisions; an inexhaustible stock of elegant words. Dryden.

inexist.c: Inexist In`ex*ist" (?), v. i. [Pref. in- in + exist.] To exist within; to dwell within. [Obs.]

inexistant.c: Inexistant In`ex*ist"ant (?), a. [Cf. F. inexistant. See 1st Inexistent.] Inexistent; nonexistent; not existing. [Obs.] Gudworth.

inexistence.c: Inexistence In`ex*ist"ence (?), n. [Pref. in- in + existence.] [Obs.] (a) Inherence; subsistence. Bp. Hall. (b) That which exists within; a constituent. A. Tucker.
Inexistence In`ex*ist"ence, n. [Pref. in- in + existence: cf. F. inexistence.] Lack of being or existence.

inexistent.c: Inexistent In`ex*ist"ent (?), a. [Pref. in- in + existent: cf. F. inexistant.] Not having being; not existing.
Inexistent In`ex*ist"ent, a. [Pref. in- in + existent.] Inherent; innate; indwelling. Boyle.

inexorability.c: Inexorability In*ex`o*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. inexorabilitas: cf. F. inexorabilité.] The quality of being inexorable, or unyielding to entreaty. Paley.

inexorable.c: Inexorable In*ex"o*ra*ble (?), a. [L. inexorabilis: cf. F. inexorable. See In- not, and Exorable, Adore.] Not to be persuaded or moved by entreaty or prayer; firm; determined; unyielding; unchangeable; inflexible; relentless; -- of people and impersonal forces; as, an inexorable prince or tyrant; an inexorable judge; the inexorable advance of a glacier. “Inexorable equality of laws.” Gibbon. “Death's inexorable doom.” Dryden.

inexorableness.c: Inexorableness In*ex"o*ra*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inexorable. Chillingworth.

inexorably.c: Inexorably In*ex"o*ra*bly, adv. In an inexorable manner; inflexibly. “Inexorably firm.” Thomson.

inexpansible.c: Inexpansible In`ex*pan"si*ble (?), a. Incapable of expansion, enlargement, or extension. Tyndall.

inexpectable.c: Inexpectable In`ex*pect"a*ble (?), a. Not to be expected or anticipated. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

inexpectant.c: Inexpectant In"ex*pect"ant (?), a. Not expectant. C. Bronté.

inexpectation.c: Inexpectation In*ex`pec*ta"tion (?), n. Absence of expectation. Feltham.

inexpected.c: Inexpected In`ex*pect"ed (?), a. [Pref. in- not + expected: cf. L. inexspectatus.] Unexpected. [Obs.]

inexpediency.c: Inexpediency Inexpedience { In`ex*pe"di*ence (?), In`ex*pe"di*en*cy (?), } n. The quality or state of being inexpedient; lack of fitness; unsuitableness to the end or object; impropriety; as, the inexpedience of some measures.

inexpedient.c: Inexpedient In`ex*pe"di*ent (?), a. Not expedient; not tending to promote a purpose; not tending to the end desired; inadvisable; unfit; improper; unsuitable to time and place; as, what is expedient at one time may be inexpedient at another.

inexperience.c: Inexperience In`ex*pe"ri*ence (?), n. [L. inexperientia, cf. F. inexpérience. See In- not, and Experience.] Absence or lack of experience; lack of personal and experimental knowledge; as, the inexperience of youth.

inexperienced.c: Inexperienced In`ex*pe"ri*enced (?), a. Not having experience; unskilled; naive. “Inexperienced youth.” Cowper.

inexpert.c: Inexpert In`ex*pert" (?), a. [L. inexpertus inexperienced: cf. F. inexpert. See In- not, and Expert.]

inexpertness.c: Inexpertness In`ex*pert"ness, n. Lack of expertness or skill.

inexpiable.c: Inexpiable In*ex"pi*a*ble (?), a. [L. inexpiabilis: cf. F. inexpiable. See In- not, and Expiable.]

inexpiableness.c: Inexpiableness In*ex"pi*a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being inexpiable.

inexpiably.c: Inexpiably In*ex"pi*a*bly, adv. In an inexpiable manner of degree; to a degree that admits of no atonement.

inexpiate.c: Inexpiate In*ex"pi*ate (?), a. [L. inexpiatus. See In- not, and Expiate.] Not appeased or placated. [Obs.]

inexplainable.c: Inexplainable In`ex*plain"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + explainable; cf. L. inexplanabilis.] Incapable of being explained; inexplicable.

inexpleably.c: Inexpleably In*ex"ple*a*bly (?), adv. [Cf. L. inexplebilis; pref. in- not + explere to fill up. See Expletion.] Insatiably. [Obs.] Sandys.

inexplicability.c: Inexplicability In*ex`pli*ca*bil"i*ty, n. [Cf. F. inexplicabilité.] The quality or state of being inexplicable. H. Spencer.

inexplicable.c: Inexplicable In*ex"pli*ca*ble (?), a. [L. inexplicabilis: cf. F. inexplicable. See In- not, and Explicable.] Not explicable; not explainable; incapable of being explained, interpreted, or accounted for; as, an inexplicable mystery. “An inexplicable scratching.” Cowper.

inexplicableness.c: Inexplicableness In*ex"pli*ca*ble*ness, n. A state of being inexplicable; inexplicability.

inexplicably.c: Inexplicably In*ex"pli*ca*bly, adv. In an inexplicable manner.

inexplicit.c: Inexplicit In`ex*plic"it (?), a. [L. inexplicitus: cf. F. inexplicite. See In- not, and Explicit.] Not explicit; not clearly stated; indefinite; vague.

inexplorable.c: Inexplorable In`ex*plor"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being explored, searched out, or discovered. Sir G. Buck.

inexposure.c: Inexposure In`ex*po"sure (?; 135), n. A state of not being exposed.

inexpressible.c: Inexpressible In`ex*press"i*ble (?), a. Not capable of expression or utterance in language; ineffable; unspeakable; indescribable; unutterable; as, inexpressible grief or pleasure. “Inexpressible grandeur.” Blair.

inexpressibles.c: Inexpressibles In`ex*press"i*bles (?), n. pl. Breeches; trousers;; underwear generally, especially women's; -- now usually referred to as unmentionables. [Colloq. or Slang] Ld. Lytton.

inexpressibly.c: Inexpressibly In`ex*press"i*bly, adv. In an inexpressible manner or degree; unspeakably; unutterably. Spectator.

inexpressiveness.c: Inexpressiveness In`ex*press"ive*ness, n. The state or quality of being inexpressive.

inexpugnable.c: Inexpugnable In`ex*pug"na*ble (?), a. [L. inexpugnabilis: cf. F. inexpugnable. See In- not, and Expugnable.] Incapable of being subdued by force; impregnable; unconquerable. Burke.

inexpugnably.c: Inexpugnably In`ex*pug"na*bly, adv. So as to be inexpugnable; in an inexpugnable manner. Dr. H. More.

inexsuperable.c: Inexsuperable In`ex*su"per*a*ble (?), a. [L. inexsuperabilis; pref. in- not + exsuperabilis that may be surmounted. See In- not, Ex-, and Superable.] Not capable of being passed over; insuperable; insurmountable.

inextensible.c: Inextensible In`ex*ten"si*ble (?), a. Not capable of being extended; not elastic; as, inextensible fibers.

inextension.c: Inextension In`ex*ten"sion (?), n. Lack of extension; unextended state.

inexterminable.c: Inexterminable In`ex*ter"mi*na*ble (?), a. [L. inexterminabilis. See In- not, and Exterminate.] Incapable of extermination. Rush.

inextinct.c: Inextinct In`ex*tinct" (?), a. [L. inextinctus, inexstinctus. See Extinct.] Not quenched; not extinct.

inextinguible.c: Inextinguible In`ex*tin"gui*ble (?), a. [L. inexstinguibilis: cf. F, inextinguible. See Inextinct.] Inextinguishable. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

inextinguishable.c: Inextinguishable In`ex*tin"guish*a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being extinguished; extinguishable; unquenchable; as, inextinguishable flame, light, thirst, desire, feuds. “Inextinguishable rage.” Milton.

inextinguishably.c: Inextinguishably In`ex*tin"guish*a*bly, adv. So as not to be extinguished; in an inextinguishable manner.

inextirpable.c: Inextirpable In`ex*tir"pa*ble (?), a. [L. inexstirpabilis: cf. F. inextirpable. See In- not, and Extirpate.] Not capable of being extirpated or rooted out; ineradicable.

inextricable.c: Inextricable In*ex"tri*ca*ble (?), a. [L. inextricabilis: cf. F. inextricable. See In- not, and Extricate.]

inextricableness.c: Inextricableness In*ex"tri*ca*ble*ness (?), n. The state of being inextricable.

inextricably.c: Inextricably In*ex"tri*ca*bly, adv. In an inextricable manner.

ineye.c: Ineye In*eye" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ineyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ineyeing.] [Pref. in- in + eye.] To ingraft, as a tree or plant, by the insertion of a bud or eye; to inoculate.

infabricated.c: Infabricated In*fab"ri*ca`ted (?), a. Not fabricated; unwrought; not artificial; natural. [Obs.]

infallibilist.c: Infallibilist In*fal"li*bil*ist (?), n. One who accepts or maintains the dogma of papal infallibility.

infallibility.c: Infallibility In*fal`li*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. infaillibilité.] The quality or state of being infallible, or exempt from error; inerrability.

infallible.c: Infallible In*fal"li*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + fallible: cf. F. infallible.]

infallibleness.c: Infallibleness In*fal"li*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being infallible; infallibility. Bp. Hall.

infallibly.c: Infallibly In*fal"li*bly, adv. In an infallible manner; certainly; unfailingly; unerringly. Blair.

infame.c: Infame In*fame" (?), v. t. [L. infamare, fr. infamis infamous: cf. F. infamer, It. infamare. See Infamous.] To defame; to make infamous. [Obs.] Milton.

infamize.c: Infamize In"fa*mize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infamized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infamizing (?).] To make infamous; to defame. [R.] Coleridge.

infamous.c: Infamous In"fa*mous (?), a. [Pref. in- not + famous: cf. L. infamis. See Infamy.]

infamously.c: Infamously In"fa*mous*ly, adv. In an infamous manner or degree; scandalously; disgracefully; shamefully.

infamousness.c: Infamousness In"fa*mous*ness, n. The state or quality of being infamous; infamy.

infamy.c: Infamy In"fa*my (?), n.; pl. Infamies (#). [L. infamia, fr. infamis infamous; pref. in- not + fama fame: cf. F. infamie. See Fame.]

infancy.c: Infancy In"fan*cy (?), n. [L. infantia: cf. F. enfance. See Infant.]

infandous.c: Infandous In*fan"dous (?), a. [L. infandus; pref. in- not + fari to speak.] Too odious to be expressed or mentioned. [Obs.] Howell.

infangthef.c: Infangthef In*fang"thef (?), n. [AS. in-fangen-þeóf; in in, into + fangen taken (p. p. of fōn to take) + þeóf thief.] (O. Eng. Law) The privilege granted to lords of certain manors to judge thieves taken within the seigniory of such lords. Cowell.

infant.c: Infant In"fant (?), n. [L. infans; pref. in- not + fari to speak: cf. F. enfant, whence OE. enfaunt. See Fame, and cf. Infante, Infanta.] 1. A child in the first period of life, beginning at his birth; a young babe; sometimes, a child several years of age.
Infant In"fant (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to infancy, or the first period of life; tender; not mature; as, infant strength.
Infant In"fant, v. t. [Cf. F. enfanter.] To bear or bring forth, as a child; hence, to produce, in general. [Obs.]

infanta.c: Infanta ‖In*fan"ta (?), n. [Sp. & Pg., fem. of infante. See Infante.] A title borne by every one of the daughters of the kings of Spain and Portugal, except the eldest.

infante.c: Infante ‖In*fan"te (?), n. [Sp. & Pg. See Infant.] A title given to every one of sons of the kings of Spain and Portugal, except the eldest or heir apparent.

infanticidal.c: Infanticidal In*fan"ti*ci`dal (?), a. Of or pertaining to infanticide; engaged in, or guilty of, child murder.

infanticide.c: Infanticide In*fan"ti*cide (?), n. [L. infanticidium child murder; infans, -antis, child + caedere to kill: cf. F. infanticide. See Infant, and Homicide.] The murder of an infant born alive; the murder or killing of a newly born or young child; child murder.
Infanticide In*fan"ti*cide, n. [L. infanticida: cf. F. infanticide.] One who commits the crime of infanticide; one who kills an infant.

infantile.c: Infantile In"fan*tile (?; 277), a. [L. infantilis: cf. F. infantile. See Infant.] Of or pertaining to infancy, or to an infant; similar to, or characteristic of, an infant; childish; as, infantile behavior.

Infantile paralysis In"fan*tile pa*ral"y*sis. (Med.) An acute viral disease, affecting almost exclusively infants and young adults, characterized by inflammation of the anterior horns of the gray substance of the spinal cord. It is attended with febrile symptoms, motor paralysis, and muscular atrophy, often producing permanent deformities. Called also acute anterior poliomyelitis, poliomyelitis and polio. It is caused by any one of three polioviruses, and by the end of the twentieth century had been almost completely eradicated in developed countries by a widespread campaign of immunization.

infantine.c: Infantine In"fan*tine (?; 277), a. [Cf. F. enfantin.] Infantile; childish.

infantlike.c: Infantlike In"fant*like` (?), a. Like an infant. Shak.

infantly.c: Infantly In"fant*ly, a. Like an infant. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

infantry.c: Infantry In"fan*try (?), n. [F. infanterie, It. infanteria, fr. infante infant, child, boy servant, foot soldier, fr. L. infans, -antis, child; foot soldiers being formerly the servants and followers of knights. See Infant.]

infarce.c: Infarce In*farce" (?), v. t. [L. infarcire: pref. in- in + farcire, fartum and farctum, to stuff, cram.] To stuff; to swell. [Obs.]

infarct.c: Infarct In*farct" (?), n. [See Infarce.] 1. (Med.) An obstruction or embolus in one of the blood vessels.

infarction.c: Infarction In*farc"tion (?), n. [See Infarce.] 1. The act of stuffing or filling; Specifically: (Med.) the formation of an infarct; an overloading and obstruction of any organ or vessel of the body; constipation.

infare.c: Infare In"fare` (?), n. [AS. infær entrance.] A house-warming; especially, a reception, party, or entertainment given by a newly married couple, or by the husband upon receiving the wife to his house. [Written also infair.] [Scot., & Local, U. S.]

infatigable.c: Infatigable In*fat"i*ga*ble (?), a. [L. infatigabilis: cf. F. infatigable.] Indefatigable. [Obs.] Daniel.

infatuate.c: Infatuate In*fat"u*ate (?; 135), a. [L. infatuatus, p. p. of infatuare to infatuate; pref. in- in + fatuus foolish. See Fatuous.] Infatuated. Bp. Hall.
Infatuate In*fat"u*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infatuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infatuating.]

infatuated.c: Infatuated In*fat"u*a`ted (?), a. Overcome by some foolish passion or desire; affected by infatuation.

infatuation.c: Infatuation In*fat`u*a"tion (?), n. [LL. infatuatio: cf. F. infatuation.] The act of infatuating; the state of being infatuated; folly; that which infatuates.

infaust.c: Infaust In*faust" (?), a. [L. infaustus; pref. in- not + faustus fortunate, lucky.] Not favorable; unlucky; unpropitious; sinister. [R.] Ld. Lytton.

infausting.c: Infausting In*faust"ing (?), n. The act of making unlucky; misfortune; bad luck. [Obs.] Bacon.

infeasibility.c: Infeasibility In*fea`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state of being infeasible; impracticability.

infeasible.c: Infeasible In*fea"si*ble (?), a. Not capable of being done or accomplished; impracticable. Glanvill.

infeasibleness.c: Infeasibleness In*fea"si*ble*ness, n. The state of quality of being infeasible; infeasibility. W. Montagu.

infect.c: Infect In*fect" (?), a. [L. infectus: cf. F. infect. See Infect, v. t.] Infected. Cf. Enfect. [Obs.] Shak.

Infect In*fect", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infected; p. pr. & vb. n. Infecting.] [L. infectus, p. p. of inficere to put or dip into, to stain, infect; pref. in- in + facere to make; cf. F. infecter. See Fact.]

infecter.c: Infecter In*fect"er (?), n. One who, or that which, infects.

infectible.c: Infectible In*fect"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being infected.

infection.c: Infection In*fec"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. infection, L. infectio a dyeing.]

infectious.c: Infectious disease In*fec"tious dis*ease". (a) Any disease caused by the entrance, growth, and multiplication of microorganisms in the body; a germ disease. It may not be contagious. (b) Sometimes, as distinguished from contagious disease, such a disease communicated by germs carried in the air or water, and thus spread without contact with the patient, as measles.

infectiously.c: Infectiously In*fec"tious*ly, adv. In an infectious manner. Shak.

infectiousness.c: Infectiousness In*fec"tious*ness, n. The quality of being infectious.

infective.c: Infective In*fect"ive (?), a. [L. infectivus pertaining to dyeing.] Infectious. Beau. & Fl.

infecund.c: Infecund In*fec"und (?), a. [L. infecundus: cf. F. infécond. See In- not, and Fecund.] Unfruitful; not producing young; barren; infertile. [Obs.] Evelyn.

infecundity.c: Infecundity In`fe*cun"di*ty (?), n. [L. infecunditas: cf. F. infécondité.] Lack of fecundity or fruitfulness; barrenness; sterility; unproductiveness.

infecundous.c: Infecundous In`fe*cun"dous (?), a. [See Infecund.] Infertile; barren; unprofitable; unproductive. [Obs.] Glanvill.

infelicitous.c: Infelicitous In`fe*lic"i*tous (?), a. Not felicitous; unhappy; unfortunate; not fortunate or appropriate in application; not well said, expressed, or done; as, an infelicitous condition; an infelicitous remark; an infelicitous description; infelicitous words.

infelicity.c: Infelicity In`fe*lic"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Infelicities (#). [L. infelicitas: cf. F. infélicité. See In- not, and Felicity.]

infelonious.c: Infelonious In`fe*lo"ni*ous (?), a. Not felonious, malignant, or criminal. G. Eliot.

infelt.c: Infelt In"felt` (?), a. [Pref. in- in + felt.] Felt inwardly; heartfelt. [R.]

infer.c: Infer In*fer" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inferred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inferring.] [L. inferre to bring into, bring forward, occasion, infer; pref. in- in + ferre to carry, bring: cf. F. inférer. See 1 st Bear.]

inferable.c: Inferable In*fer"a*ble (ĭn*fẽr"ȧ*b'l or ĭn*fĕr"-; 277), a. Capable of being inferred or deduced from premises. [Written also inferrible.] H. Spencer.

inferential.c: Inferential In`fer*en"tial (?), a. Deduced or deducible by inference. “Inferential proofs.” J. S. Mill.

inferentially.c: Inferentially In`fer*en"tial*ly, adv. By way of inference; using inference.

inferiae.c: Inferiae ‖In*fe"ri*æ (?), n. pl. [L., fr. inferus underneath.] (Rom. Antiq.) Sacrifices offered to the souls of deceased heroes or friends.

inferior.c: Inferior In*fe"ri*or (?), a. [L., compar. of inferus that is below, underneath, the lower; akin to E. under: cf. F. inférieur. See Under.]
Inferior In*fe"ri*or, n. A person lower in station, rank, intellect, etc., than another.

inferiority.c: Inferiority In*fe`ri*or"i*ty (?), [Cf. F. infériorité.] The state of being inferior; a lower state or condition; as, inferiority of rank, of talents, of age, of worth.

inferiorly.c: Inferiorly In*fe"ri*or*ly (?), adv. In an inferior manner, or on the inferior part.

infernal.c: Infernal In*fer"nal (?), a. [F. infernal, L. infernalis, fr. infernus that which lies beneath, the lower. See Inferior.]
Infernal In*fer"nal, n. An inhabitant of the infernal regions; also, the place itself. [Obs.] Drayton.

infernally.c: Infernally In*fer"nal*ly, adv. In an infernal manner; diabolically. “Infernally false.” Bp. Hacket.

inferno.c: Inferno In*fer"no (?), n. [It. See Infernal.] 1. The infernal regions; hell.

inferobranchian.c: Inferobranchian In`fe*ro*bran"chi*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Inferobranchiata.

inferobranchiata.c: Inferobranchiata In`fe*ro*bran`chi*a"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Inferobranchiate.] (Zool.) A suborder of marine gastropod mollusks, in which the gills are between the foot and the mantle.

inferobranchiate.c: Inferobranchiate In`fe*ro*bran"chi*ate (?), a. [L. inferus lower + E. branchiate.] (Zool.) Having the gills on the sides of the body, under the margin of the mantle; belonging to the Inferobranchiata.

infertile.c: Infertile In*fer"tile (?), a. [L. infertilis: cf. F. infertile. See In- not, and Fertile.] Not fertile; not productive; barren; sterile; unable to propagate its kind; as, an infertile soil; an infertile hybrid; -- of living things and of soil or land.

infertilely.c: Infertilely In*fer"tile*ly, adv. In an infertile manner.

infertility.c: Infertility In`fer*til"i*ty (?), n. [L. infertilitas: cf. F. infertilité.] The state or quality of being infertile; unproductiveness; barrenness.

infest.c: Infest In*fest" (?), a. [L. infestus. See Infest, v. t.] Mischievous; hurtful; harassing. [Obs.] Spenser.

Infest In*fest", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infested; p. pr. & vb. n. Infesting.] [L. infestare, fr. infestus disturbed, hostile, troublesome; in in, against + the root of defendere: cf. F. infester. See Defend.] To trouble greatly by numbers or by frequency of presence; to disturb; to annoy; to frequent and molest or harass; as, fleas infest dogs and cats; a sea infested with pirates.

infestation.c: Infestation In`fes*ta"tion (?), n. [L. infestatio: cf. F. infestation.] The act of infesting or state of being infested; molestation; vexation; annoyance. Bacon.

infester.c: Infester In*fest"er (?), n. One who, or that which, infests.

infestive.c: Infestive In*fest"ive (?), a. [L. infestivus. See In- not, and Festive.] Having no mirth; not festive or merry; dull; cheerless; gloomy; forlorn. [R.]

infestivity.c: Infestivity In`fes*tiv"i*ty (?), n. Lack of festivity, cheerfulness, or mirth; dullness; cheerlessness. [R.]

infestuous.c: Infestuous In*fes"tu*ous (?; 135), a. [L. infestus. See Infest, a.] Mischievous; harmful; dangerous. [Obs.] “Infestuous as serpents.” Bacon.

infeudation.c: Infeudation In`feu*da"tion (?), n. [LL. infeudatio, fr. infeudare to enfeoff: cf. F. inféodation. See Feud a fief.]

infibulation.c: Infibulation In*fib`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. infibulare, infibulatum, to clasp, buckle, or button together; pref. in- in + fibula clasp, buckle: cf. F. infibulation.]

infidel.c: Infidel In"fi*del (?), a. [L. infidelis; pref. in- not + fidelis faithful, fr. fides faith: cf. F. infidèle. See Fidelity.] Not holding the faith; -- applied by Christians to one who does not believe in the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the supernatural origin of Christianity; used by Muslims to refer to those who do not believe in Islam.
Infidel In"fi*del, n. One who does not believe in the prevailing religious faith; a heathen; a freethinker; -- used especially by Christians and Muslims.

infidelity.c: Infidelity In`fi*del"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Infidelities (?). [L. infidelitas: cf. F. infidélité.]

infield.c: Infield In*field" (?), v. t. To inclose, as a field. [R.]
Infield In"field` (?), n. 1. Arable and manured land kept continually under crop; -- distinguished from outfield. [Scotland] Jamieson.

infile.c: Infile In*file" (?), v. t. To arrange in a file or rank; to place in order. [Obs.] Holland.

infilm.c: Infilm In*film" (?), v. t. To cover with a film; to coat thinly; as, to infilm one metal with another in the process of gilding; to infilm the glass of a mirror. [R.]

infilter.c: Infilter In*fil"ter (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Infiltered; p. pr. & vb. n. Infiltering.] [Cf. Infiltrate.] To filter or sift in.

infiltrate.c: Infiltrate In*fil"trate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Infiltrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infiltrating (?).] [Pref. in- + filtrate: cf. F, s'infiltrer. Cf. Infilter.] 1. To enter by penetrating the pores or interstices of a substance; to filter into or through something.
Infiltrate In*fil"trate, v. t. To penetrate gradually; -- sometimes used reflexively. J. S. Mill.

infiltrative.c: Infiltrative In*fil"tra*tive (?), a. Of or pertaining to infiltration. Kane.

infinite.c: Infinite In"fi*nite (?), a. [L. infinitus: cf. F. infini. See In- not, and Finite.]
Infinite In"fi*nite, n. 1. That which is infinite; boundless space or duration; infinity; boundlessness.

infinitely.c: Infinitely In"fi*nite*ly, adv. 1. Without bounds or limits; beyond or below assignable limits; as, an infinitely large or infinitely small quantity.

infiniteness.c: Infiniteness In"fi*nite*ness, n. The state or quality of being infinite; infinity; greatness; immensity. Jer. Taylor.

infinitesimal.c: Infinitesimal In`fin*i*tes"i*mal (?), a. [Cf. F. infinitésimal, fr. infinitésime infinitely small, fr. L. infinitus. See Infinite, a.] Infinitely or indefinitely small; less than any assignable quantity or value; very small.
Infinitesimal In`fin*i*tes"i*mal, n. (Math.) An infinitely small quantity; that which is less than any assignable quantity.

infinitesimally.c: Infinitesimally In`fin*i*tes"i*mal*ly, adv. By infinitesimals; in infinitely small quantities; in an infinitesimal degree.

infinitival.c: Infinitival In*fin`i*ti"val (?), a. Pertaining to the infinite mood. “Infinitival stems.” Fitzed. Hall.

infinitive.c: Infinitive In*fin"i*tive (?), n. [L. infinitivus: cf. F. infinitif. See Infinite.] Unlimited; not bounded or restricted; undefined.
Infinitive In*fin"i*tive, n. (Gram.) An infinitive form of the verb; a verb in the infinitive mood; the infinitive mood.
Infinitive In*fin"i*tive, adv. (Gram.) In the manner of an infinitive mood.

infinito.c: Infinito ‖In`fi*ni"to (?), a. [It.] (Mus.) Infinite; perpetual, as a canon whose end leads back to the beginning. See Infinite, a., 5.

infinitude.c: Infinitude In*fin"i*tude (?), n. 1. The quality or state of being infinite, or without limits; infiniteness.

infinituple.c: Infinituple In*fin"i*tu`ple (?), a. [Cf. Quadruple.] Multiplied an infinite number of times. [R.] Wollaston.

infinity.c: Infinity In*fin"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Infinities (#). [L. infinitas; pref. in- not + finis boundary, limit, end: cf. F. infinité. See Finite.]

infirm.c: Infirm In*firm" (ĭn*fẽrm"), a. [L. infirmus: cf. F. infirme. See In- not, and Firm, a.] 1. Not firm or sound; weak; feeble; as, an infirm body; an infirm constitution.
Infirm In*firm", v. t. [L. infirmare: cf. F. infirmer.] To weaken; to enfeeble. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

infirmarian.c: Infirmarian In`fir*ma"ri*an (ĭn`fẽr*mā"rĭ*ain), n. A person dwelling in, or having charge of, an infirmary, esp. in a monastic institution.

infirmary.c: Infirmary In*firm"a*ry (ĭn*fẽrm"ȧ*ry̆), n.; pl. Infirmaries (-rĭz). [Cf. OE. fermerie, OF. enfermerie, F. infirmerie, LL. infirmaria. See Infirm.] A hospital, or place where the infirm or sick are lodged and nursed gratuitously, or where out-patients are treated.

infirmative.c: Infirmative In*firm"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. infirmatif.] Weakening; annulling, or tending to make void. [Obs.]

infirmity.c: Infirmity In*firm"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Infirmities (#). [L. infirmitas: cf. F. infirmite. See Infirm, a.] 1. The state of being infirm; feebleness; an imperfection or weakness; esp., an unsound, unhealthy, or debilitated state; a disease; a malady; as, infirmity of body or mind.

infirmly.c: Infirmly In*firm"ly, adv. In an infirm manner.

infix.c: Infix In*fix" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infixed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infixing.] [L. infixus, p. p of infigere to infix; pref. in- in + figere to fix: cf. F. infixer. See Fix.] 1. To set; to fasten or fix by piercing or thrusting in; as, to infix a sting, spear, or dart. Shak.

infix notation in"fix no*ta"tion (?), n. (Computers) A notation for commands or instructions in which the operator is inserted between the terms on which it operates. Contrasted with prefix notation and postfix notation.

inflame.c: Inflame In*flame" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inflamed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inflaming.] [OE. enflamen, OF. enflamer, F. enflammer, L. inflammare, inflammatum; pref. in- in + flammare to flame, fr. flamma flame. See Flame.] 1. To set on fire; to kindle; to cause to burn, flame, or glow.
Inflame In*flame", v. i. To grow morbidly hot, congested, or painful; to become angry or incensed. Wiseman.

inflamed.c: Inflamed In*flamed" (?), p. a. 1. Set on fire; enkindled; heated; congested; provoked; exasperated.

inflamer.c: Inflamer In*flam"er (ĭn*flām"ẽr), n. The person or thing that inflames. Addison.

inflammabillty.c: Inflammabillty In*flam"ma*bil"l*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inflammabilite.] Susceptibility of taking fire readily; the state or quality of being inflammable.

inflammable.c: Inflammable In*flam"ma*ble (?), a. [CF. F. inflammable.] 1. Capable of being easily set fire; easily enkindled; combustible; as, inflammable oils or spirits.

inflammableness.c: Inflammableness In*flam"ma*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inflammable; inflammability. Boyle.

inflammably.c: Inflammably In*flam"ma*bly (ĭn*flăm"mȧ*bly̆), adv. In an inflammable manner.

inflammation.c: Inflammation In*flam*ma"tion (ĭn*flăm*mā"shŭn), n. [L. inflammatio: cf. F. inflammation. See Inflame.] 1. The act of inflaming, kindling, or setting on fire; also, the state of being inflamed. “The inflammation of fat.” Wilkins.

inflammatory.c: Inflammatory In*flam"ma*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. inflammatoire.] 1. Tending to inflame, kindle, or irritate.

inflatable.c: Inflatable In*flat"a*ble (?), a. That may be inflated.

inflate.c: Inflate In*flate" (?), p. a. [L. inflatus, p. p. of inflare to inflate; pref. in- in + flare to blow. See Blow to puff wind.] Blown in; inflated. Chaucer.
Inflate In*flate", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inflated; p. pr. & vb. n. Inflating.] 1. To swell or distend with air or gas; to dilate; to expand; to enlarge; as, to inflate a bladder; to inflate the lungs.
Inflate In*flate", v. i. To expand; to fill; to distend.

inflated.c: Inflated In*flat"ed (?), a. 1. Filled, as with air or gas; blown up; distended; as, a balloon inflated with gas.

inflater.c: Inflater In*flat"er (?), n. One who, or that which, inflates; as, the inflaters of the stock exchange.

inflatingly.c: Inflatingly In*flat"ing*ly, adv. In a manner tending to inflate.

inflation.c: Inflation In*fla"tion (?), n. [L. inflatio: cf. F. inflation.] 1. The act or process of inflating, or the state of being inflated, as with air or gas; distention; expansion; enlargement. Boyle.

inflationist.c: Inflationist In*fla"tion*ist, n. One who favors an increased or very large issue of paper money. [U.S.]

inflatus.c: Inflatus ‖In*fla"tus (?), n. [L. See Inflate, v. t.] A blowing or breathing into; inflation; inspiration.

inflect.c: Inflect In*flect" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inflected; p. pr. & vb. n. Inflecting.] [L. inflectere, inflexum; pref. in- in + flectere to bend. See Flexible, and cf. Inflex.] 1. To turn from a direct line or course; to bend; to incline, to deflect; to curve; to bow.

inflection.c: Inflection In*flec"tion (?), n. [L. inflexio: cf. F. inflexion. See Inflect.] [Written also inflecxion.] 1. The act of inflecting, or the state of being inflected.

inflectional.c: Inflectional In*flec"tion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to inflection; having, or characterized by, inflection. Max Müller.

inflective.c: Inflective In*flect"ive (?), a. 1. Capable of, or pertaining to, inflection; deflecting; as, the inflective quality of the air. Derham.

inflex.c: Inflex In*flex" (?), v. t. [Cf. Flex, Inflect.] To bend; to cause to become curved; to make crooked; to deflect. J. Philips.

inflexibility.c: Inflexibility In*flex"i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inflexibilité.] The quality or state of being inflexible, or not capable of being bent or changed; unyielding stiffness; inflexibleness; rigidity; firmness of will or purpose; unbending pertinacity; steadfastness; resoluteness; unchangeableness; obstinacy.

inflexible.c: Inflexible In*flex"i*ble (?), a. [L. inflexiblis: cf. F. inflexible. See In- not, and Flexible.] 1. Not capable of being bent; stiff; rigid; firm; unyielding.

inflexibleness.c: Inflexibleness In*flex"i*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inflexible; inflexibility; rigidity; firmness.

inflexibly.c: Inflexibly In*flex"i*bly, adv. In an inflexible manner.

inflexure.c: Inflexure In*flex"ure (?), n. An inflection; a bend or fold. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

inflict.c: Inflict In*flict" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inflicted; p. pr. & vb. n. Inflicting.] [L. inflictus, p. p. of infligere to strike on, to inflict; pref. in- in, on + fligere to strike. Cf. Flail.] To give, cause, or produce by striking, or as if by striking; to apply forcibly; to lay or impose; to send; to cause to bear, feel, or suffer; as, to inflict blows; to inflict a wound with a dagger; to inflict severe pain by ingratitude; to inflict punishment on an offender; to inflict the penalty of death on a criminal.

infliction.c: Infliction In*flic"tion (?), n. [L. inflictio: cf. F. infliction.] 1. The act of inflicting or imposing; as, the infliction of torment, or of punishment.

inflictive.c: Inflictive In*flict"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. inflictif.] Causing infliction; acting as an infliction. Whitehead.

inflorescence.c: Inflorescence In`flo*res"cence (?), n. [L. inflorescens, p. pr. of inflorescere to begin to blossom; pref. in- in + florescere to begin to blossom: cf. F. inflorescence. See Florescent.] 1. A flowering; the putting forth and unfolding of blossoms.

inflow.c: Inflow In*flow" (?), v. i. To flow in. Wiseman.

influence.c: Influence In"flu*ence (ĭn"flu*eins), n. [F. influence, fr. L. influens, -entis, p. pr. See Influent, and cf. Influenza.] 1. A flowing in or upon; influx. [Obs.]

Influence In"flu*ence, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Influenced (ĭn"flu*einst); p. pr. & vb. n. Influencing (ĭn"flu*ein*sĭng).] To control or move by power, physical or moral; to affect by gentle action; to exert an influence upon; to modify, bias, or sway; to affect; to move; to persuade; to induce.

influencer.c: Influencer In"flu*en*cer (ĭn"flu*ein*sẽr), n. One who, or that which, influences.

influencive.c: Influencive In"flu*en*cive (ĭn"flu*ein*sĭv), a. Tending to influence; influential.

influent.c: Influent In"flu*ent (ĭn"flu*eint), a. [L. influens, -entis, p. pr. of influere, influxum, to flow in; pref. in- in + fluere to flow. See Fluid.] 1. Flowing in. “With influent tide.” Cowper. “Influent odors.” Mrs. Browning.

influential.c: Influential In`flu*en"tial (ĭn`flu*ĕn"shail), a. [See Influence.] Exerting or possessing influence or power; potent; efficacious; effective; strong; having authority or ascendency; as, an influential man, station, argument, etc.

influentially.c: Influentially In`flu*en"tial*ly, adv. In an influential manner.

influenza.c: Influenza In`flu*en"za (?), n. [It. influenza influence, an epidemic formerly attributed by astrologers to the influence of the heavenly bodies, influenza. See Influence.] (Med.) An epidemic viral infectious disease characterized by acute nasal catarrh, or by inflammation of the throat or the bronchi, and usually accompanied by fever and general weakness; also called grippe. It is caused by several forms of RNA virus which mutate readily and thereby render vaccines prepared against older forms ineffective, often requiring a new form of vaccine for each new outbreak.

influx.c: Influx In"flux` (?), n. [L. influxus, fr. influere, influxum, to flow in: cf. F. influx. See Influent.] 1. The act of flowing in; as, an influx of light.

influxion.c: Influxion In*flux"ion (?), n. [L. influxio: cf. F. influxion.] A flowing in; infusion. [R.] Bacon.

influxive.c: Influxive In*flux"ive (?), a. Having a tendency to flow in; having influence; influential. [R.] Holdsworth.

infold.c: Infold In*fold" (ĭn*fōld"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infolded; p. pr. & vb. n. Infolding.] [Pref. in- in + fold.] [Written also enfold.] 1. To wrap up or cover with folds; to envelop; to inwrap; to inclose; to involve.

infoldment.c: Infoldment In*fold"ment (?), n. The act of infolding; the state of being infolded.

infoliate.c: Infoliate In*fo"li*ate (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + L. folium leaf.] To cover or overspread with, or as with, leaves. [R.] Howell.

inform.c: Inform In*form" (?), a. [L. informis; pref. in- not + forma form, shape: cf. F. informe] Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed. Cotton.

Inform In*form", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Informed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Informing.] [OE. enformen, OF. enformer, F. informer. L. informare; pref. in- in + formare to form, share, fr. forma form. See Form.] 1. To give form or share to; to give vital or organizing power to; to give life to; to imbue and actuate with vitality; to animate; to mold; to figure; to fashion. “The informing Word.” Coleridge.
Inform In*form", v. t. 1. To take form; to become visible or manifest; to appear. [Obs.]

informal.c: Informal In*form"al (?), a. [Pref. in- not + formal.] 1. Not in the regular, usual, or established form; not according to official, conventional, prescribed, or customary forms or rules; irregular; hence, without ceremony; as, an informal writing, proceeding, or visit.

informality.c: Informality In`for*mal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Informalities (?). 1. The state of being informal; lack of regular, prescribed, or customary form; as, the informality of legal proceedings.

informally.c: Informally In*form"al*ly (?), adv. In an informal manner.

informant.c: Informant In*form"ant (?), n. [L. informans, -antis, p. pr. of informare. See Inform, v. t.] 1. One who, or that which, informs, animates, or vivifies. [Obs.] Glanvill.

information.c: Information In`for*ma"tion (?), n. [F., fr. L. informatio representation, conception. See Inform, v. t.] 1. The act of informing, or communicating knowledge or intelligence.

informative.c: Informative In*form"a*tive (?), a. Having power to inform, animate, or vivify. Dr. H. More.

informatory.c: Informatory In*form"a*to*ry (?), a. Full of, or conveying, information; instructive. [R.] London Spectator.

informed.c: Informed In*formed" (ĭn*fôrmd"), a. Unformed or ill-formed; deformed; shapeless. [Obs.] Spenser.

informer.c: Informer In*form"er (ĭn*fôrm"ẽr), n. [From Inform, v.] 1. One who informs, animates, or inspires. [Obs.] Thomson.

informidable.c: Informidable In*for"mi*da*ble (ĭn*fôr"mĭ*dȧ*b'l), a. [L. informidabilis. See In- not, and Formidable.] Not formidable; not to be feared or dreaded. [Obs.] “Foe not informidable.” Milton.

informity.c: Informity In*form"i*ty (ĭn*fôrm"ĭ*ty̆), n. [L. informitas. See Inform, a.] Lack of regular form; shapelessness. [Obs.]

informous.c: Informous In*form"ous (ĭn*fôrm"ŭs), a. [See Inform, a.] Of irregular form; shapeless. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

infortunate.c: Infortunate In*for"tu*nate (ĭn*fôr"tu*nat), a. [L. infortunatus.] Unlucky; unfortunate. [Obs.] Shak. “A most infortunate chance.” Howell.

infortune.c: Infortune In*for"tune (?), n. [L. infortunium. See In- not, and Fortune.] Misfortune. [Obs.] Chaucer.

infound.c: Infound In*found" (?), v. t. [L. infundere to pour in. See Infuse.] To pour in; to infuse. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

infra.c: Infra ‖In*"fra (?), adv. [L. Cf. Inferior.] Below; beneath; under; after; -- often used as a prefix.

infraaxillary.c: Infra-axillary In`fra-ax"il*la*ry (?), a. [Infra + axillary.] (Bot.) Situated below the axil, as a bud.

infrabranchial.c: Infrabranchial In`fra*bran"chi*al (?), a. [Infra + branchial.] (Zool.) Below the gills; -- applied to the ventral portion of the pallial chamber in the lamellibranchs.

infraclavicular.c: Infraclavicular In`fra*cla*vic"u*lar (?), a. [Infra + clavicular.] (Anat.) Below the clavicle; as, the infraclavicular fossa.

infract.c: Infract In*fract" (ĭn*frăkt"), a. [L. infractus; pref. in- not + fractus. p. p. of frangere to break.] Not broken or fractured; unharmed; whole. [Obs.] Chapman.
Infract In*fract", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infracted; p. pr. & vb. n. Infracting.] [L. infractus, p. p. of of infringere. See Infringe.] To break; to infringe. [R.] Thomson.

infractible.c: Infractible In*fract"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being broken.[R.]

infraction.c: Infraction In*frac"tion (?), n. [L. infractio: cf. F. infraction.] The act of infracting or breaking; breach; violation; nonobservance; infringement; as, an infraction of a treaty, compact, rule, or law. I. Watts.

infractor.c: Infractor In*fract"or (?), n. [Cf. F. infracteur.] One who infracts or infringes; a violator; a breaker.

infrahyoid.c: Infrahyoid In`fra*hy"oid (?), a. [Infra + hyoid.] (Anat.) Same as Hyosternal (a).

infralabial.c: Infralabial In`fra*la"bi*al (?), a. (Zool.) Below the lower lip; -- said of certain scales of reptiles and fishes.

infralapsarian.c: Infralapsarian In`fra*lap*sa"ri*an (?), n. [Infra + lapse: cf. F. infralapsaire. See Lapse.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of that class of Calvinists who consider the decree of election as contemplating the apostasy as past and the elect as being at the time of election in a fallen and guilty state; -- opposed to Supralapsarian. The former considered the election of grace as a remedy for an existing evil; the latter regarded the fall as a part of God's original purpose in regard to men.
Infralapsarian In`fra*lap*sa"ri*an, a. (Theol.) Of or pertaining to the Infralapsarians, or to their doctrine.

infralapsarianism.c: Infralapsarianism In`fra*lap*sa"ri*an*ism (?), n. (Theor.) The doctrine, belief, or principles of the Infralapsarians.

inframarginal.c: Inframarginal In`fra*mar"gin*al (?), a. [Infra + marginal.] Below the margin; submarginal; as, an inframarginal convolution of the brain.

inframaxillary.c: Inframaxillary In`fra*max"il*la*ry (?), a. [Infra + maxillary.] (Anat.) (a) Under the lower jaw; submaxillary; as, the inframaxillary nerve. (b) Of or pertaining to the lower iaw.

inframedian.c: Inframedian In`fra*me"di*an (?), a. [Infra + median.] (Zoological Geog.) Of or pertaining to the interval or zone along the sea bottom, at the depth of between fifty and one hundred fathoms. E. Forbes.

inframundane.c: Inframundane In`fra*mun"dane (?), a. [Infra + mundane.] Lying or situated beneath the world.

infrangibility.c: Infrangibility In*fran`gi*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being infrangible; infrangibleness.

infrangible.c: Infrangible In*fran"gi*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + grangible: cf. F. infrangible.] 1. Not capable of being broken or separated into parts; as, infrangible atoms.

infrangibleness.c: Infrangibleness In*fran"gi*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being infrangible; infrangibility.

infraocular.c: Infraocular In`fra*oc"u*lar (?), a. [Infra + ocular.] (Zool.) Situated below the eyes, as the antenna of certain insects.

infraorbital.c: Infraorbital In`fra*or"bit*al (?), a. [Infra + orbital.] (Anat.) Below the orbit; as, the infraorbital foramen; the infraorbital nerve.

infrapose.c: Infrapose In`fra*pose" (?), v. t. [Infra + pose.] To place under or beneath. [R.]

infraposition.c: Infraposition In`fra*po*si"tion (?), n. [Infra + position.] A situation or position beneath. Kane.

infrared.c: Infra-red Infrared In`fra*red", In`fra-red" (?), a. [Infra- + red.] 1. (Physics) Lying outside the visible spectrum at its red end; -- said of rays having a longer wavelength (and thus less refrangible) than the extreme red rays, specifically those electromagnetic waves having a wavelength of between 700 nanometers and 1 millimeter.

infrascapular.c: Infrascapular In`fra*scap"u*lar (?), a. [Infra + scapular.] (Anat.) Beneath the scapula, or shoulder blade; subscapular.

infraspinal.c: Infraspinal In`fra*spi"nal (?), a. [Infra + spinal.] (Anat.) (a) Below the vertebral column, subvertebral. (b) Below the spine; infraspinate; infraspinous.

infraspinous.c: Infraspinous Infraspinate { In`fra*spi"nate (?), In`fra*spi*nous (?), } a. [Infra + spinate, spinous.] (Anat.) Below the spine; infraspinal; esp., below the spine of the scapula; as, the infraspinous fossa; the infraspinate muscle.

infrastapedial.c: Infrastapedial In`fra*sta*pe"di*al (?), a. [Infra + stapedial.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a part of the columella of the ear, which in many animals projects below the connection with the stapes. -- n. The infrastapedial part of the columella.

infrasternal.c: Infrasternal In`fra*ster"nal (?), a. [Infra + sternal.] (Anat.) Below the sternum; as, the infrasternal depression, or pit of the stomach.

infratemporal.c: Infratemporal In`fra*tem"po*ral (?), a. [Infra + temporal.] (Anat.) Below the temple; below the temporal bone.

infraterritorial.c: Infraterritorial In`fra*ter"ri*to"ri*al (?), a. [Infra + territorial.] Within the territory of a state. Story.

infratrochlear.c: Infratrochlear In`fra*troch"le*ar (?), a. [Infra + trochlear.] (Anat.) Below a trochlea, or pulley; -- applied esp. to one of the subdivisions of the trigeminal nerve.

infrequency.c: Infrequency Infrequence { In*fre"quence (?), In*fre"quen*cy (?), } n. [L. infrequentia scantiness: cf. F. infrequence.] 1. The state of rarely occuring; uncommonness; rareness; as, the infrequence of his visits.

infrequent.c: Infrequent In*fre"quent (?), a. [L. infrequens: cf. F. infrequent. See In- not, and Frequent.] Seldom happening or occurring; rare; uncommon; unusual.

infrigidate.c: Infrigidate In*frig"i*date (?), v. t. [L. infrigidatus, p. p. of infrigidare to chill. See 1st In-, and Frigid.] To chill; to make cold; to cool. [Obs.] Boyle.

infrigidation.c: Infrigidation In*frig`i*da"tion (?), n. [L. infrigidatio.] The act of chilling or causing to become cold; a chilling; coldness; congelation. [Obs.] Boyle.

infringe.c: Infringe In*fringe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infringed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infringing (?).] [L. infringere; pref. in- in + frangere to break. See Fraction, and cf. Infract.] 1. To break; to violate; to transgress; to neglect to fulfill or obey; as, to infringe a law, right, or contract.
Infringe In*fringe", v. i. 1. To break, violate, or transgress some contract, rule, or law; to injure; to offend.

infringement.c: Infringement In*fringe"ment (?), n. 1. The act of infringing; breach; violation; nonfulfillment; as, the infringement of a treaty, compact, law, or constitution.

infringer.c: Infringer In*frin"ger (?), n. One who infringes or violates; a violator. Strype.

infructuose.c: Infructuose In*fruc"tu*ose" (?), a. [L. infructuosus. See In- not, and Fruit.] Not producing fruit; unfruitful; unprofitable. [R.] T. Adams.

infrugal.c: Infrugal In*fru"gal (?), a. Not frugal; wasteful; as, an infrugal expense of time. J. Goodman.

infrugiferous.c: Infrugiferous In`fru*gif"er*ous (?), a. Not bearing fruit; not fructiferous.

infucate.c: Infucate In`fu*cate (?), v. t. [L. infucatus painted; pref. in- in + fucare to paint, dye. See Fucate.] To stain; to paint; to daub.

infucation.c: Infucation In`fu*ca"tion (?), n. The act of painting or staining, especially of painting the face.

infula.c: Infula ‖In"fu*la (?), n.; pl. Infule (#). [L.] A sort of fillet worn by dignitaries, priests, and others among the ancient Romans. It was generally white.

infumate.c: Infumate In"fu*mate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infumated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infumating.] [L. infumatus, p. p. of infumare to infumate; pref. in- in + fumare to smoke, fr. fumus smoke.] To dry by exposing to smoke; to expose to smoke.

infumated.c: Infumated In"fu*ma`ted (?), a. (Zool.) Clouded; having a cloudy appearance.

infumation.c: Infumation In`fu*ma"tion (?), n. Act of drying in smoke.

infumed.c: Infumed In*fumed" (?), a. Dried in smoke; smoked.

infundibulate.c: Infundibulate Infundibular { In`fun*dib"u*lar (?), In`fun*dib"u*late (?), } a. [See Infundibulum.] Having the form of a funnel; pertaining to an infundibulum.

infundibuliform.c: Infundibuliform In`fun*dib"u*li*form (?), a. [L. infundibulum funnel + -form: cf. F. infundibuliforme.] 1. Having the form of a funnel or cone; funnel-shaped.

infundibulum.c: Infundibulum ‖In`fun*dib"u*lum (?), n.; pl. L. Infundibula (#), E. Infundibulums (#). [L., a funnel, from infundere to pour in or into. See Infuse.] 1. (Anat.) A funnel-shaped or dilated organ or part; as, the infundibulum of the brain, a hollow, conical process, connecting the floor of the third ventricle with the pituitary body; the infundibula of the lungs, the enlarged terminations of the bronchial tubes.

infuneral.c: Infuneral In*fu"ner*al (?), v. t. To inter with funeral rites; to bury. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.

infurcation.c: Infurcation In`fur*ca"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- in + L. furca fork.] A forked expansion or divergence; a bifurcation; a branching. Craig.

infuriate.c: Infuriate In*fu"ri*ate (?), a. [It. infuriato, p. p. of infuriare. See Infuriate, v. t.] Enraged; raging; furiously angry; infuriated. Milton.

Infuriate In*fu"ri*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infuriated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infuriating] [It. infuriato, p. p. of infuriare; pref. in- (L. in) + furia fury, L. furia. See Fury.] To render furious; to enrage; to exasperate.

infuscate.c: Infuscate In*fus"cate (?), v. t. [L. infuscatus, p. p. of infuscare; pref. in- in + fuscare to make dark, fr. fuscus dark.] To darken; to make black; to obscure.

infuscated.c: Infuscated In*fus"ca*ted (?), a. (Zool.) Darkened with a blackish tinge.

infuscation.c: Infuscation In`fus*ca"tion (?), n. The act of darkening, or state of being dark; darkness; obscurity. Johnson.

infuse.c: Infuse In*fuse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Infused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Infusing.] [L. infusus, p. p. of infundere to pour in or into; pref. in- in + fundere to pour: cf. F. infuser. See Found to cast.] 1. To pour in, as a liquid; to pour (into or upon); to shed.

infuser.c: Infuser In*fus"er (?), n. One who, or that which, infuses.

infusibility.c: Infusibility In*fu`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. [From Infuse.] Capability of being infused, poured in, or instilled.
Infusibility In*fu`si*bil"i*ty, n. [Pref. in- not + fusibility: cf. F. infusibilité.] Incapability or difficulty of being fused, melted, or dissolved; as, the infusibility of carbon.

infusible.c: Infusible In*fu"si*ble (?), a. [From Infuse, v.] Capable of being infused.
Infusible In*fu"si*ble, a. [Pref. in- not + fusible: cf. F. infusible.] Not fusible; incapable or difficult of fusion, or of being dissolved or melted. Sir T. Browne.

infusion.c: Infusion In*fu"sion (?), n. [L. infusio a pouring in: cf. F. infusion. See Infuse, v. t.] 1. The act of infusing, pouring in, or instilling; instillation; as, the infusion of good principles into the mind; the infusion of ardor or zeal.

infusionism.c: Infusionism In*fu"sion*ism (?), n. The doctrine that the soul is preexistent to the body, and is infused into it at conception or birth; -- opposed to traducianism and creationism.

infusive.c: Infusive In*fu"sive (?), a. Having the power of infusion; inspiring; influencing.

infusoria.c: Infusoria ‖In`fu*so"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL.; -- so called because found in infusions which are left exposed to the air for a time. See Infuse.] (Zool.) One of the classes of Protozoa, including a large number of species, all of minute size. Formerly, the term was applied to any microbe found in infusions of decaying organic material, but the term is now applied more specifically to one of the classes of the phylum Ciliophora, of ciliated protozoans.

infusorial.c: Infusorial In`fu*so"ri*al (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Infusoria; composed of, or containing, Infusoria; as, infusorial earth.

infusorian.c: Infusorian In`fu*so"ri*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Infusoria.

infusory.c: Infusory In*fu"so*ry (?), n.; pl. Infusories (?). (Zool.) One of the Infusoria; -- usually in the pl.

ing.c: -ing -ing (?). 1. [For OE. -and, -end, -ind, AS. -ende; akin to Goth. -and-, L. -ant-, -ent-, Gr.?.] A suffix used to from present participles; as, singing, playing.
Ing Ing (ĭng), n. [AS. ing.] A pasture or meadow; generally one lying low, near a river. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

ingannation.c: Ingannation In`gan*na"tion (?), n. [LL. ingannare to decieve.] Cheat; deception. [Obs.] Sir T. Brown.

ingathering.c: Ingathering In"gath`er*ing (?), n. The act or business of gathering or collecting anything; especially, the gathering of the fruits of the earth; harvest.

ingeminate.c: Ingeminate In*gem"i*nate (?), a. [L. ingeminatus, p. p.] Redoubled; repeated. Jer. Taylor.

Ingeminate In*gem"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingeminated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ingeminating (?).] [L. ingeminatus, p. p. of ingeminare to double; pref. in- in + geminare. See Geminate.] To redouble or repeat; to reiterate. Clarendon.

ingemination.c: Ingemination In*gem`i*na"tion (?), n. Repetition; reduplication; reiteration. De Quincey.

ingenerabillty.c: Ingenerabillty In*gen`er*a*bil"l*ty (?), n. Incapacity of being engendered or produced. Cudworth.

ingenerable.c: Ingenerable In*gen"er*a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + generable: cf. F. ingenerable.] Incapable of being engendered or produced; original. Holland.

ingenerably.c: Ingenerably In*gen"er*a*bly, adv. In an ingenerable manner.

ingenerate.c: Ingenerate In*gen"er*ate (?), a. [L. ingeneratus, p. p. of ingenerare. See engender] Generated within; inborn; innate; as, ingenerate powers of body. W. Wotton.
Ingenerate In*gen"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingenerat (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ingenerating (?).] To generate or produce within; to beget; to engender; to occasion; to cause. Mede.

ingeniate.c: Ingeniate In*ge"ni*ate (?), v. t. & i. [See Ingenious.] To invent; to contrive. [Obs.] Daniel.

ingeniosity.c: Ingeniosity In*ge`ni*os"i*ty (?), n. [LL. ingeniositas.] Ingenuity; skill; cunning. [Obs.] Cudworth.

ingenious.c: Ingenious In*gen"ious (?), a. [L. ingeniosus, fr. ingenium innate or natural quality, natural capacity, genius: cf. F. ingénieux. See Engine.] 1. Possessed of genius, or the faculty of invention; skillful or promp to invent; having an aptitude to contrive, or to form new combinations; as, an ingenious author, mechanic.

ingeniously.c: Ingeniously In*gen"ious*ly (?), adv. In an ingenious manner; with ingenuity; skillfully; wittily; cleverly.

ingeniousness.c: Ingeniousness In*gen"ious*ness, n. The quality or state of being ingenious; ingenuity.

ingenit.c: Ingenit Ingenite { In*gen"ite, In*gen"it } (?), a. [L. ingenitus, p. p. of ingignere to instill by birth or nature; pref. in- + gignere to beget.] Innate; inborn; inbred; inherent; native; ingenerate. [Obs.]

ingenue.c: Ingenue ‖In`gé`nue" (ăN`zha`nụ"), n.; pl. -nues (#). [F., fem. of ingénu ingenious.] An ingenuous or naïve girl or young woman, or an actress representing such a person.

ingenuity.c: Ingenuity In`ge*nu"i*ty (?), n. [L. ingenuitas ingenuousness: cf. F. ingénuité. See Ingenuous.] 1. The quality or power of ready invention; quickness or acuteness in forming new combinations; ingeniousness; skill in devising or combining.

ingenuous.c: Ingenuous In*gen"u*ous (?), a. [L. ingenuus inborn, innate, freeborn, noble, frank; pref. in- in + the root of gignere to beget. See Genius, and cf. Ingenious.] 1. Of honorable extraction; freeborn; noble; as, ingenuous blood of birth.

ingenuously.c: Ingenuously In*gen"u*ous*ly, adv. In an ingenuous manner; openly; fairly; candidly; artlessly.

ingenuousness.c: Ingenuousness In*gen"u*ous*ness, n. 1. The state or quality of being ingenuous; openness of heart; frankness.

ingeny.c: Ingeny In"ge*ny (?), n. [L. ingenium. See Ingenious.] Natural gift or talent; ability; wit; ingenuity. [Obs.] [Written also ingenie.] Becon.

ingerminate.c: Ingerminate In*ger"mi*nate (?), v. t. To cause to germinate.

ingest.c: Ingest In*gest" (?), v. t. [L. ingenium, p. p. of ingerere to put in; pref. in- in + gerere to bear.] 1. To take into, or as into, the stomach or alimentary canal. Sir T. Browne.

ingesta.c: Ingesta ‖In*ges"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Ingest.] (Physiol.) That which is introduced into the body by the stomach or alimentary canal; -- opposed to egesta.

ingestion.c: Ingestion In*ges"tion (?), n. [L. ingestio: cf. F. ingestion.] (Physiol.) The act of taking or putting into the stomach; as, the ingestion of milk or other food.

inghalla.c: Inghalla ‖In*ghal"la (?), n. (Zool.) The reedbuck of South Africa. [Written also ingali.]

ingirt.c: Ingirt In*girt" (?), v. t. [See Ingirt.] To encircle; to gird; to engirt.

ingle.c: Ingle In"gle (ĭṉ"g'l), n. [Gael. & Ir. aingeali fire; cf. L. igniculusi spark, dim. of ignis fire. Cf. Ignite.] Flame; blaze; a fire; a fireplace. [Obs. or Scot.] Burns.
Ingle In"gle, n. [Written also engle, enghle: cf. Gael. & Ir. aingeal an angel. Cf. Engle.] A paramour; a favourite; a sweetheart; an engle. [Obs.] Toone.
Ingle In"gle (ĭṉ"g'l), v. t. To cajole or coax; to wheedle. See Engle. [Obs.]

inglobate.c: Inglobate In*glo"bate (?), a. In the form of a globe or sphere; -- applied to nebulous matter collected into a sphere by the force of gravitation.

inglobe.c: Inglobe In*globe" (?), v. t. To infix, as in a globe; to fix or secure firmly. [Obs.] Milton.

inglorious.c: Inglorious In*glo"ri*ous (?), a. [L. inglorious; pref. in- not + gloria glory, fame: cf. F. inglorieux. See Glory.]

ingloriously.c: Ingloriously In*glo"ri*ous*ly, adv. In an inglorious manner; dishonorably; with shame; ignominiously; obscurely.

ingloriousness.c: Ingloriousness In*glo"ri*ous*ness, n. The state of being inglorious.

inglut.c: Inglut In*glut" (?), v. t. To glut. [R.] Ascham.

ingluvial.c: Ingluvial In*glu"vi*al (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the ingluvies or crop of birds.

ingluvies.c: Ingluvies ‖In*glu"vi*es (?), n. [L.] (Anat.) The crop, or craw, of birds.

ingoing.c: In-going In"-go`ing (?), n. The act of going in; entrance.
In-going In"-go`ing, a. Going; entering, as upon an office or a possession; as, an in-going tenant.

ingorge.c: Ingorge In*gorge" (?), v. t. & i. See Engorge. Milton.

ingot.c: Ingot In"got (?), n. [Prob. from AS. in in + geótan to pour: cf. F. linglot, LL. lingotus a mass of gold or silver, extended in the manner of a tongue, and G. einguss, LG. & OE. ingot ingot, a mold for casting metals in. See Found to cast, and cf. Linget, Lingot, Nugget.]
