Ingot steel In"got steel. Steel cast in ingots from the Bessemer converter or open-hearth furnace.

ingrace.c: Ingrace In*grace" (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + grace.] To ingratiate. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.

ingracious.c: Ingracious In*gra"cious (?), a. [Pref. in- not + gracious.] Ungracious; unkind. [Obs.] Holland.

ingraft.c: Ingraft In*graft" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingrafted; p. pr. & vb. n. Ingrafting.] [Written also engraft.]

ingrafter.c: Ingrafter In*graft"er (?), n. A person who ingrafts.

ingraftment.c: Ingraftment In*graft"ment (?), n. 1. The act of ingrafting.

ingrain.c: Ingrain In"grain` (?; 277), a. [Pref. in- in + grain kermes. See Engrain, Grain.]
Ingrain In"grain`, n. An ingrain fabric, as a carpet.
Ingrain In"grain` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingrained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ingraining.] [Written also engrain.]

ingrapple.c: Ingrapple In*grap"ple (?), v. t. & i. To seize; to clutch; to grapple. [Obs.] Drayton.

ingrate.c: Ingrate In"grate` (?; 277), a. [L. ingratus. See Ingrateful.] Ingrateful. [Obs. or Poetic] Bacon.
Ingrate In"grate`, n. An ungrateful person. Milton.

ingrateful.c: Ingrateful In"grate`ful (?), a. [L. ingratus ingrateful (pref. in- not + gratus beloved, dear, grateful) + -ful: cf. F. ingrat. See Grateful.]

ingratiate.c: Ingratiate In*gra"ti*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingratiated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ingratiating (?).] [Pref. in- in + L. gratia. See Grace.]
Ingratiate In*gra"ti*ate, v. i. To gain favor. [R.] Sir W. Temple.

ingratitude.c: Ingratitude In*grat"i*tude (?), n. [F. ingratitude, L. ingratitudo. See Ingrate.] Lack of gratitude; insensibility to, forgetfulness of, or ill return for, kindness or favors received; unthankfulness; ungratefulness.

ingrave.c: Ingrave In*grave" (?), v. t. To engrave. [R.] “Whose gleaming rind ingrav'n.” Tennyson.
Ingrave In*grave", v. t. [Pref. in- in + grave. Cf. Engrave.] To bury. [Obs.] Heywood.

ingravidate.c: Ingravidate In*grav"i*date (?), v. t. [L. ingravidatus, p. p. of ingravidare to impregnate. See 1st In-, and Gravidated.] To impregnate. [Obs.] Fuller.

ingravidation.c: Ingravidation In*grav`i*da"tion (?), n. The state of being pregnant or impregnated. [Obs.]

ingreat.c: Ingreat In*great" (?), v. t. To make great; to enlarge; to magnify. [Obs.] Fotherby.

ingredient.c: Ingredient In*gre"di*ent (?), n. [F. ingrédient, L. ingrediens, -entis, entering into, p. pr. of ingredi, p. p. ingressus, to go into, to enter; pref. in- in + gradi to walk, go. See Grade.] That which enters into a compound, or is a component part of any combination, recipe, or mixture; an element; a constituent.
Ingredient In*gre"di*ent, a. Entering as, or forming, an ingredient or component part.

ingress.c: Ingress In"gress (?), n. [L. ingressus, fr. ingredi. See Ingredient.]
Ingress In"gress (?), v. i. To go in; to enter. [R.]

ingression.c: Ingression In*gres"sion (?), n. [L. ingressio: cf. F. ingression.] Act of entering; entrance. Sir K. Digby.

ingrieve.c: Ingrieve In*grieve (?), v. t. To render more grievous; to aggravate. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

ingroove.c: Ingroove In*groove" (?), v. t. To groove in; to join in or with a groove. Tennyson.

ingrowing.c: Ingrowing In"grow`ing (?), a. Growing or appearing to grow into some other substance.

ingrown.c: Ingrown In"grown` (?), a. Having grown or appearing to grow into some other substance, especially a fingernail or toenail growing into the adjacent flesh.

ingrowth.c: Ingrowth In"growth` (?), n. A growth or development inward. J. LeConte.

inguilty.c: Inguilty In*guilt"y (?), a. Not guilty. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

inguinal.c: Inguinal In"gui*nal (?), a. [L. inguinalis, fr. inguen, inguinis, the groin: cf. F. inguinal.] (Astron. & Med.) Of or pertaining to, or in the region of, the inguen or groin; as, an inguinal canal or ligament; inguinal hernia.

ingulf.c: Ingulf In*gulf" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ingulfed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ingulfing.] [Cf. Engulf.] [Written also engulf.] To swallow up or overwhelm in, or as in, a gulf; to cast into a gulf. See Engulf.

ingulfment.c: Ingulfment In*gulf"ment (?), n. The act of ingulfing, or the state of being ingulfed.

ingurgitate.c: Ingurgitate In*gur"gi*tate (?), v. t. [L. ingurgitatus, p. p. of ingurgitare to pour in; pref. in- in + gurges whirlpool, gulf.]
Ingurgitate In*gur"gi*tate, v. i. To guzzle; to swill. Burton.

ingurgitation.c: Ingurgitation In*gur`gi*ta"tion (?), n. [L. ingurgitatio: cf. F. ingurgitation.] The act of swallowing greedily or immoderately; that which is so swallowed. E. Darwin.

ingustable.c: Ingustable In*gust"a*ble (?), a. [L. ingustabilis. See Gustable.] Tasteless; insipid. Sir T. Browne.

inhabile.c: Inhabile In*hab"ile (?), a. [L. inhabilis: cf. F. inhabile. See In- not, and Habile, and cf. Unable.]

inhability.c: Inhability In`ha*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. inhabileté, inhabilité. See Inability.] Unsuitableness; unaptness; unfitness; inability. [Obs.] Barrow.

inhabit.c: Inhabit In*hab"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inhabited; p. pr. & vb. n. Inhabiting.] [OE. enhabiten, OF. enhabiter, L. inhabitare; pref. in- in + habitare to dwell. See Habit.] To live or dwell in; to occupy, as a place of settled residence; as, wild beasts inhabit the forest; men inhabit cities and houses.
Inhabit In*hab"it, v. i. To have residence in a place; to dwell; to live; to abide. [Archaic or Poetic] Shak.

inhabitable.c: Inhabitable In*hab"it*a*ble (?), a. [L. inhabitabilis. See Inhabit.] Capable of being inhabited; habitable.
Inhabitable In*hab"it*a*ble, a. [L. inhabitabilis: cf. F. inhabitable. See In- not, and Habitable.] Not habitable; not suitable to be inhabited. [Obs.]

inhabitancy.c: Inhabitancy Inhabitance { In*hab"it*ance (?), In*hab"it*an*cy (?), } n. 1. The act of inhabiting, or the state of being inhabited; the condition of an inhabitant; residence; occupancy.

inhabitant.c: Inhabitant In*hab"it*ant (?), n. [L. inhabitans, -antis, p. pr. of inhabitare.]

inhabitativeness.c: Inhabitativeness In*hab"it*a*tive*ness (?), n. (Phrenol.) A tendency or propensity to permanent residence in a place or abode; love of home and country.

inhalant.c: Inhalant In*hal"ant (?), a. [Cf. F. inhalant.] Inhaling; used for inhaling.
Inhalant In*hal"ant (?), n. An apparatus also called an inhaler (which see); also, that which is to be inhaled, especially a medicine taken by inhalation.

inhalation.c: Inhalation In`ha*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inhalation.] The act of inhaling; also, that which is inhaled.

inhale.c: Inhale In*hale" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inhaled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inhaling.] [L. inhalare to breathe upon; pref. in- in + halare to breathe: cf. F. inhaler. Cf. Exhale.] To breathe or draw into the lungs; to inspire; as, to inhale air; -- opposed to exhale.

inhalent.c: Inhalent In*hal"ent (?), a. Used for inhaling; as, the inhalent end of a duct. Dana.

inharmonical.c: Inharmonical Inharmonic { In`har*mon"ic (?), In`har*mon"ic*al (?), } a. Not harmonic; inharmonious; discordant; dissonant.

inharmonious.c: Inharmonious In`har*mo"ni*ous (?), a. [Pref. in- not + harmonious: cf. F. inharmonieux.]

inharmoniousness.c: Inharmoniousness In`har*mo"ni*ous*ness, n. The quality of being inharmonious; lack of harmony; discord.

inhauler.c: Inhauler Inhaul { In"haul` (?), In"haul`er (?) }, n. (Naut.) A rope used to draw in the jib boom, or flying jib boom.

inhearse.c: Inhearse In*hearse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inhearsed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inhearsing.] To put in, or as in, a hearse or coffin. Shak.

inhere.c: Inhere In*here" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inhered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inhering.] [L. inhaerere; pref. in- in + haerere to stick, hang. See Hesitate.] To be inherent; to stick (in); to be fixed in or permanently incorporated with something; to cleave (to); to belong, as attributes or qualities.

inherency.c: Inherency Inherence { In*her"ence (?), In*her"en*cy (?), } n. [Cf. F. inhérence.] The state of inhering; permanent existence in something; innateness; inseparable and essential connection. Jer. Taylor.

inherent.c: Inherent In*her"ent (?), a. [L. inhaerens, -entis, p. pr. of inhaerere: cf. F. inhérent. See Inhere.] Permanently existing in something; inseparably attached or connected; naturally pertaining to; innate; inalienable; as, polarity is an inherent quality of the magnet; the inherent right of men to life, liberty, and protection. “A most inherent baseness.” Shak.

inherit.c: Inherit In*her"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inherited; p. pr. & vb. n. Inheriting.] [OE. enheriten to inherit, to give a heritage to, OF. enheriter to appoint as an heir, L. inhereditare; pref. in- in + hereditare to inherit, fr. heres heir. See Heir.]
Inherit In*her"it (?), v. i. To take or hold a possession, property, estate, or rights by inheritance.

inheritability.c: Inheritability In*her`it*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being inheritable or descendible to heirs. Jefferson.

inheritable.c: Inheritable In*her"it*a*ble (?), a. 1. Capable of being inherited; transmissible or descendible; as, an inheritable estate or title. Blackstone.

inheritor.c: Inheritor In*her"it*or (?), n. One who inherits; an heir.

inheritrix.c: Inheritrix In*her"it*rix (?), n. Same as Inheritress. Shak.

inhesion.c: Inhesion In*he"sion (?), n. [L. inhaesio. See Inhere.] The state of existing, of being inherent, in something; inherence. A. Baxter.

inhiation.c: Inhiation In`hi*a"tion (?), n. [L. inhiatio, fr. inhiare to gape; pref. in- + hiare to gape.] A gaping after; eager desire; craving. [R.] Bp. Hall.

inhibit.c: Inhibit In*hib"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inhibited; p. pr. & vb. n. Inhibiting.] [L. inhibitus, p. p. of inhibere; pref. in- in + habere to have, hold. See Habit.]

inhibition.c: Inhibition In`hi*bi"tion (?), n. [L. inhibitio: cf. F. inhibition.]

inhibitor.c: Inhibitor In*hib"i*tor (?), n. [NL.] That which causes inhibitory action; esp., an inhibitory nerve.

inhibitory.c: Inhibitory In*hib"i*to*ry (?), a. [LL. inhibitorius: cf. F. inhibitoire.] Of or pertaining to, or producing, inhibition; consisting in inhibition; tending or serving to inhibit; as, the inhibitory action of the pneumogastric on the respiratory center.

inhibitorymotor.c: Inhibitory-motor In*hib"i*to*ry-mo"tor (?), a. (Physiol.) A term applied to certain nerve centers which govern or restrain subsidiary centers, from which motor impressions issue. McKendrick.

inhive.c: Inhive In*hive" (?), v. t. To place in a hive; to hive.

inhold.c: Inhold In*hold" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inheld (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inholding.] To have inherent; to contain in itself; to possess. [Obs.] Sir W. Raleigh.

inhoop.c: Inhoop In*hoop" (?), v. t. To inclose in a hoop, or as in a hoop. [R.] Shak.

inhospitable.c: Inhospitable In*hos"pi*ta*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + hospitable: cf. L. inhospitalis.]

inhospitality.c: Inhospitality In*hos`pi*tal"i*ty (?), n. [L. inhospitalitas: cf. F. inhospitalité. See In- not, and Hospitality.] The quality or state of being inhospitable; inhospitableness; lack of hospitality. Bp. Hall.

inhuman.c: Inhuman In*hu"man (?), a. [L. inhumanus: cf. F. inhumain. See In- not, and Human.]

inhumanity.c: Inhumanity In`hu*man"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Inhumanities (#). [L. inhumanitas: cf. F. inhumanité.] The quality or state of being inhuman or inhumane; cruelty; barbarity.

inhumanly.c: Inhumanly In*hu"man*ly (?), adv. In an inhuman manner; cruelly; barbarously.

inhumate.c: Inhumate In*hu"mate (?), v. t. [L. inhumatus, p. p. of inhumare to inhume; pref. in- in + humare to cover with earth. See Humation, and cf. Inhume.] To inhume; to bury; to inter. Hedge.

inhume.c: Inhume In*hume" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inhumed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inhuming.] [Cf. F. inhumer. See Inhumate.]

inia.c: Inia ‖In"i*a (?), n. (Zool.) A South American freshwater dolphin (Inia Boliviensis). It is ten or twelve feet long, and has a hairy snout.

inial.c: Inial In"i*al (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to the inion.

inimaginable.c: Inimaginable In`im*ag"i*na*ble (?), a. Unimaginable; inconceivable. [R.] Bp. Pearson.

inimical.c: Inimical In*im"i*cal (?; 277), a. [L. inimicalis, fr. inimicus unfriendly, hostile; pref. in- not + amicus friendly. See Amity.]

inimicality.c: Inimicality In*im`i*cal"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being inimical or hostile; hostility; unfriendliness. [R.]

inimically.c: Inimically In*im"i*cal*ly (?), adv. In an inimical manner.

inimicitious.c: Inimicitious In*im`i*ci"tious (?), a. [L. inimicitia enmity. See Inimical.] Inimical; unfriendly. [R.] Sterne.

inimicous.c: Inimicous In*im"i*cous (?), a. [L. inimicus.] Inimical; hurtful. [Obs.] Evelyn.

inimitability.c: Inimitability In*im`i*ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being inimitable; inimitableness. Norris.

inimitable.c: Inimitable In*im"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. inimitabilis: cf. F. inimitable. See In- not, and Imitable.] Not capable of being imitated, copied, or counterfeited; beyond imitation; surpassingly excellent; matchless; unrivaled; exceptional; unique; as, an inimitable style; inimitable eloquence. “Inimitable force.” Dryden.

inion.c: Inion ‖In"i*on (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'ini`on the back of the head.] (Anat.) The external occipital protuberance of the skull.

iniquitous.c: Iniquitous In*iq"ui*tous (?), a. [From Iniquity.] Characterized by iniquity; unjust; wicked; as, an iniquitous bargain; an iniquitous proceeding.

iniquitously.c: Iniquitously In*iq"ui*tous*ly, adv. In an iniquitous manner; unjustly; wickedly.

iniquity.c: Iniquity In*iq"ui*ty (?), n.; pl. Iniquities (#). [OE. iniquitee, F. iniquité, L. iniquitas, inequality, unfairness, injustice. See Iniquous.]

iniquous.c: Iniquous In*i"quous (?), a. [L. iniquus; pref. in- not + aequus. See Equal.] Iniquitous. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

inirritable.c: Inirritable In*ir"ri*ta*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + irritable: cf. F. inirritable.] Not irritable; esp. (Physiol.), incapable of being stimulated to action, as a muscle. -- In*ir`ri*ta*bil"i*ty (#), n.

inirritative.c: Inirritative In*ir"ri*ta*tive (?), a. Not accompanied with excitement; as, an inirritative fever. E. Darwin.

inisle.c: Inisle In*isle" (?), v. t. [Cf. Enisled.] To form into an island; to surround. [Obs.] Drayton.

initial.c: Initial In*i"tial (?), a. [L. initialis, from initium a going in, entrance, beginning, fr. inire to go into, to enter, begin; pref. in- in + ire to go: cf. F. initial. See Issue, and cf. Commence.]
Initial In*i"tial, n. The first letter of a word or a name.
Initial In*i"tial, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Initialed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Initialing.] To put an initial to; to mark with an initial of initials. [R.]

initially.c: Initially In*i"tial*ly, adv. In an initial or incipient manner or degree; at the beginning. Barrow.

initiate.c: Initiate In*i"ti*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Initiated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Initiating (?).] [L. initiatus, p. p. of initiare to begin, fr. initium beginning. See Initial.]
Initiate In*i"ti*ate, v. i. To do the first act; to perform the first rite; to take the initiative. [R.] Pope.
Initiate In*i"ti*ate, n. One who is, or is to be, initiated.

initiation.c: Initiation In*i`ti*a"tion (?), n. [L. initiatio: cf. F. initiation.]

initiative.c: Initiative In*i"ti*a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. initiatif.] Serving to initiate; inceptive; initiatory; introductory; preliminary.
Initiative In*i"ti*a*tive, n. [Cf. F. initiative.] 1. An introductory step or movement; an act which originates or begins.

initiatory.c: Initiatory In*i"ti*a*to*ry (?), a. 1. Suitable for an introduction or beginning; introductory; prefatory; as, an initiatory step. Bp. Hall.
Initiatory In*i"ti*a*to*ry, n. An introductory act or rite. [R.]

inition.c: Inition In*i"tion (?), n. [Cf. OF. inition. See Initial.] Initiation; beginning. [Obs.] Sir R. Naunton.

inject.c: Inject In*ject" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Injected; p. pr. & vb. n. Injecting.] [L. injectus, p. p. of inicere, injicere, to throw in; pref. in- in + jacere to throw: cf. F. injecter. See Jet a shooting forth.]

injection.c: Injection In*jec"tion (?), n. [L. injectio: cf. F. injection.] 1. The act of injecting or throwing in; -- applied particularly to the forcible insertion of a liquid or gas, by means of a syringe, pump, etc.

injector.c: Injector In*ject"or (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, injects.

injelly.c: Injelly In*jel"ly (?), v. t. To place in jelly. [R.]

injoint.c: Injoint In*joint (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + joint.] To join; to unite. [R.] Shak.
Injoint In*joint, v. t. [Pref. in- in + joint.] To disjoint; to separate. [Obs.] Holland.

injucundity.c: Injucundity In`ju*cun"di*ty (?), n. [L. injucunditas. See In- not, and Jocund.] Unpleasantness; disagreeableness. [Obs.] Cockeram.

injudicable.c: Injudicable In*ju"di*ca*ble (?), a. Not cognizable by a judge. [Obs.] Bailey.

injudicial.c: Injudicial In`ju*di"cial (?), a. Not according to the forms of law; not judicial. [R.]

injudicious.c: Injudicious In`ju*di"cious (?), a. [Pref. in- not + judicious; cf. F. injudicieux.] 1. Not judicious; wanting in sound judgment; undiscerning; indiscreet; unwise; as, an injudicious adviser.

injudiciously.c: Injudiciously In`ju*di"cious*ly, adv. In an injudicious manner.

injudiciousness.c: Injudiciousness In`ju*di"cious*ness, n. The quality of being injudicious; lack of sound judgment; indiscretion. Whitlock.

injunction.c: Injunction In*junc"tion (?), n. [L. injunctio, fr. injungere, injunctum, to join into, to enjoin. See Enjoin.] 1. The act of enjoining; the act of directing, commanding, or prohibiting.

injure.c: Injure In"jure (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Injured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Injuring.] [L. injuriari, fr. injuria injury, perh. through F. injurier to insult, in OF. also, to injure; or perhaps fr. E. injury, or F. injure injury. See Injury.] To do harm to; to impair the excellence and value of; to hurt; to damage; -- used in a variety of senses; as: (a) To hurt or wound, as the person; to impair soundness, as of health. (b) To damage or lessen the value of, as goods or estate. (c) To slander, tarnish, or impair, as reputation or character. (d) To impair or diminish, as happiness or virtue. (e) To give pain to, as the sensibilities or the feelings; to grieve; to annoy. (f) To impair, as the intellect or mind.

injurer.c: Injurer In"jur*er (?), n. One who injures or wrongs.

injuria.c: Injuria ‖In*ju"ri*a (?), n.; pl. Injurie (#). [L.] (Law) Injury; invasion of another's rights.

injurious.c: Injurious In*ju"ri*ous (?), a. [L. injuriousus, injurius; cf. F. injurieux. See Injury.] 1. Not just; wrongful; iniquitous; culpable. [Obs.] Milton.

injuriously.c: Injuriously In*ju"ri*ous*ly, adv. In an injurious or hurtful manner; wrongfully; hurtfully; mischievously.

injuriousness.c: Injuriousness In*ju"ri*ous*ness, n. The quality of being injurious or hurtful; harmfulness; injury.

injury.c: Injury In"ju*ry (?), n.; pl. Injuries (#). [OE. injurie, L. injuria, fr. injurius injurious, wrongful, unjust; pref. in- not + jus, juris, right, law, justice: cf. F. injure. See Just, a.] Any damage or hurt done to a person or thing; detriment to, or violation of, the person, character, feelings, rights, property, or interests of an individual; that which injures, or occasions wrong, loss, damage, or detriment; harm; hurt; loss; mischief; wrong; evil; as, his health was impaired by a severe injury; slander is an injury to the character.

injustice.c: Injustice In*jus"tice (?), n. [F. injustice, L. injustitia. See In- not, and Justice, and cf. Unjust.] 1. Lack of justice and equity; violation of the rights of another or others; iniquity; wrong; unfairness; imposition.

ink.c: Ink Ink (ĭṉk), n. (Mach.) The step, or socket, in which the lower end of a millstone spindle runs.

Ink Ink, n. [OE. enke, inke, OF. enque, F. encre, L. encaustum the purple red ink with which the Roman emperors signed their edicts, Gr.?, fr.? burnt in, encaustic, fr.? to burn in. See Encaustic, Caustic.] 1. A fluid, or a viscous material or preparation of various kinds (commonly black or colored), used in writing or printing.
Ink Ink, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inked (ĭṉkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Inking.] To put ink upon; to supply with ink; to blacken, color, or daub with ink.

inker.c: Inker Ink"er (?), n. One who, or that which, inks; especially, in printing, the pad or roller which inks the type.

inkfish.c: Inkfish Ink"fish` (?), n. A cuttlefish. See Cuttlefish.

inkhorn.c: Inkhorn Ink"horn` (?), n. [Ink + horn; cf. F. cornet à encre, G. dintenhorn.] A small bottle of horn or other material formerly used for holding ink; an inkstand; a portable case for writing materials. “With a writer's inkhorn by his side.” Ezek. ix. 2.
Inkhorn Ink"horn", a. Learned; pedantic; affected. [Obs.] “Inkhorn terms.” Bale.

inkhornism.c: Inkhornism Ink"horn`ism (?), n. Pedantry. Sir T. Wilson.

inkiness.c: Inkiness Ink"i*ness (?), n. [From Inky.] The state or quality of being inky; blackness.

inking.c: Inking Ink"ing, a. Supplying or covering with ink.

inkle.c: Inkle In"kle (?), n. [Prob.the same word as lingle, the first l being mistaken for the definite article in French. See Lingle.] A kind of tape or braid. Shak.
Inkle In"kle, v. t. [OE. inklen to hint; cf. Dan. ymte to whisper.] To guess. [Prov. Eng.] “She inkled what it was.” R. D. Blackmore.

inkling.c: Inkling In"kling (?), n. A hint; an intimation.

inknot.c: Inknot In*knot" (?), v. t. To fasten or bind, as with a knot; to knot together. Fuller.

inkstand.c: Inkstand Ink"stand` (?), n. A small vessel for holding ink, to dip the pen into; also, a device for holding ink and writing materials.

inkstone.c: Inkstone Ink"stone" (?), n. A kind of stone containing native vitriol or sulphate of iron, used in making ink.

inky.c: Inky Ink"y (?), a. Consisting of, or resembling, ink; soiled with ink; black. “Inky blots.” Shak. “Its inky blackness.” Boyle.

inlace.c: Inlace In*lace" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inlaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inlacing (?).] [Pref. in- + lace: cf. OE. enlacen to entangle, involve, OF. enlacier, F. enlacer. See Lace, and cf. Enlace.] To work in, as lace; to embellish with work resembling lace; also, to lace or enlace. P. Fletcher.

inlagation.c: Inlagation In"la*ga"tion (?), n. [Law L. inlagatio, fr. inlagare to restore to law. See In, and Law.] (Old Eng. Law) The restitution of an outlawed person to the protection of the law; inlawing. Bouvier.

inland.c: Inland In"land (?), a. 1. Within the land; more or less remote from the ocean or from open water; interior; as, an inland town. “This wide inland sea.” Spenser.
Inland In"land, n. The interior part of a country. Shak.
Inland In"land, adv. Into, or towards, the interior, away from the coast. Cook.

inlander.c: Inlander In"land*er (?), n. One who lives in the interior of a country, or at a distance from the sea. Sir T. Browne.

inlapidate.c: Inlapidate In*lap"i*date (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + L. lapis, lapidis, stone.] To convert into a stony substance; to petrify. [R.] Bacon.

inlaw.c: Inlaw In*law" (?), v. t. [In + law. Cf. Inlagation.] (Old Eng. Law) To clear of outlawry or attainder; to place under the protection of the law. Burrill.

inlay.c: Inlay In*lay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inlaied (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inlaying.] To lay within; hence, to insert, as pieces of pearl, ivory, mother-of-pearl, choice woods, or the like, in a groundwork of some other material; to form an ornamental surface; to diversify or adorn with insertions.
Inlay In"lay` (?), n. Matter or pieces of wood, ivory, etc., inlaid, or prepared for inlaying; that which is inserted or inlaid for ornament or variety; as, ornamented with ivory inlay.

inlayer.c: Inlayer In*lay"er (?), n. One who inlays, or whose occupation it is to inlay.

inleague.c: Inleague In*league" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inleagued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inleaguing (?).] To ally, or form an alliance with; to unite; to combine.

inleaguer.c: Inleaguer In*lea"guer (?), v. t. To beleaguer. Holland.

inlet.c: Inlet In"let (?), n. 1. A passage by which an inclosed place may be entered; a place of ingress; entrance; especially, a narrow waterway leading into a harbor.

inlive.c: Inlive In*live" (?), v. t. To animate. [R.] B. Jonson.

inlock.c: Inlock In*lock" (?), v. t. To lock in, or inclose.

inly.c: Inly In"ly (?), a. [OE. inlich, AS. inlīc. See In.] Internal; interior; secret.
Inly In"ly, adv. Internally; within; in the heart. “Whereat he inly raged.” Milton.

inmacy.c: Inmacy In"ma*cy (?), n. [From Inmate.] The state of being an inmate. [R.] Craig.

inmate.c: Inmate In"mate` (ĭn"māt`), n. [In + mate an associate.] One who lives in the same house or apartment with another; a fellow lodger; esp., one of the occupants of an asylum, hospital, or prison; by extension, one who occupies or lodges in any place or dwelling.
Inmate In"mate`, a. Admitted as a dweller; resident; internal. [R.] “Inmate guests.” Milton.

inmeats.c: Inmeats In"meats` (?), n. pl. The edible viscera of animals, as the heart, liver, etc.

inmesh.c: Inmesh In*mesh" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inmeshed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inmeshing.] To bring within meshes, as of a net; to enmesh; to entangle.

inmew.c: Inmew In*mew" (?), v. t. [Cf.Emmew, Immew.] To inclose, as in a mew or cage. [R.] “Inmew the town below.” Beau. & Fl.

inmost.c: Inmost In"most` (?), a. [OE. innemest, AS. innemest, a double superlative form fr. inne within, fr. in in. The modern form is due to confusion with most. See In, and cf. Aftermost, Foremost, Innermost.] Deepest within; farthest from the surface or external part; innermost.

inn.c: Inn Inn (ĭn), n. [AS. in, inn, house, chamber, inn, from AS. in in; akin to Icel. inni house. See In.] 1. A place of shelter; hence, dwelling; habitation; residence; abode. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Inn Inn (ĭn), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inned (ĭnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Inning.] To take lodging; to lodge. [R.] Addison.
Inn Inn, v. t. 1. To house; to lodge. [Obs.]

innate.c: Innate In"nate (ĭn"nat or ĭn*nāt"; 277), a. [L. innatus; pref. in- in + natus born, p. p. of nasci to be born. See Native.] 1. Inborn; native; natural; as, innate vigor; innate eloquence.
Innate In*nate" (?), v. t. To cause to exit; to call into being. [Obs.] “The first innating cause.” Marston.

innateness.c: Innateness In"nate*ness, n. The quality of being innate.

innavigable.c: Innavigable In*nav"i*ga*ble (?), a. [L. innavigabilis: cf. F. innavigable. See In- not, and Navigable.] Incapable of being navigated; impassable by ships or vessels. Drygen. -- In*nav"i*ga*bly, adv.

inner.c: Inner In"ner (ĭn"nẽr), a. [AS. innera, a compar. fr. inne within, fr. in in. See In.] 1. Further in; interior; internal; not outward; as, an inner chamber.

innermost.c: Innermost In"ner*most` (ĭn"nẽr*mōst`), a. [A corruption of inmost due to influence of inner. See Inmost.] Farthest inward; most remote from the outward part; inmost; deepest within. Prov. xviii. 8.

innermostly.c: Innermostly In"ner*most`ly, adv. In the innermost place. [R.]

innervate.c: Innervate In*ner"vate (ĭn*nẽr"vāt), v. t. [See Innerve.] (Anat.) To supply with nerves; as, the heart is innervated by pneumogastric and sympathetic branches.

innervation.c: Innervation In`ner*va"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. innervation.] 1. The act of innerving or stimulating.

innerve.c: Innerve In*nerve" (ĭn*nẽrv"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Innerved (ĭn*nẽrvd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Innerving.] [Pref. in- in + nerve.] To give nervous energy or power to; to give increased energy, force, or courage to; to invigorate; to stimulate.

innholder.c: Innholder Inn"hold`er (?), n. One who keeps an inn.

inning.c: Inning In"ning (?), n. [AS. innung, fr. in in, prep. & adv.] 1. Ingathering; harvesting. [Obs.] Holland.

innitency.c: Innitency In*ni"ten*cy (?), n. [L. inniti, p. p. innixus, to lean upon; pref. in- in, on + niti to lean.] A leaning; pressure; weight. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

innixion.c: Innixion In*nix"ion (?), n. [See Innitency.] Act of leaning upon something; incumbency. [Obs.] Derham.

innkeeper.c: Innkeeper Inn"keep`er (?), n. One who keeps an inn; the proprietor or manager of an inn or hotel.

innocence.c: Innocence In"no*cence (?), n. [F. innocence, L. innocentia. See Innocent.] 1. The state or quality of being innocent; freedom from that which is harmful or infurious; harmlessness.

innocent.c: Innocent In"no*cent (?), a. [F. innocent, L. innocens, -entis; pref. in- not + nocens, p. pr. of nocere to harm, hurt. See Noxious.] 1. Not harmful; free from that which can injure; innoxious; innocuous; harmless; as, an innocent medicine or remedy.
Innocent In"no*cent, n. 1. An innocent person; one free from, or unacquainted with, guilt or sin. Shak.

innocently.c: Innocently In"no*cent*ly, adv. In an innocent manner.

innocuous.c: Innocuous In*noc"u*ous (?), a. [L. innocuus; in- not + nocuus hurtful, fr. nocere to hurt. See Innocent.] Harmless; producing no ill effect.

innodate.c: Innodate In"no*date (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Innodated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Innodating (?).] [L. innodatus, p. p. of innodare; pref. in- in + nodus knot.] To bind up, as in a knot; to include. [Obs.] Fuller.

innominable.c: Innominable In*nom"i*na*ble (?), a. [L. innominabilis; pref. in- not + nominare to name: cf. F. innominable.] Not to be named. [R.] Testament of Love.

innominate.c: Innominate In*nom"i*nate (?), a. [L. innominatus; pref. in- not + nominare to name.] 1. Having no name; unnamed; as, an innominate person or place. [R.] Ray.

innovate.c: Innovate In"no*vate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Innovated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Innovating (?).] [L. innovatus, p. p. of innovare to revew; pref. in- in + novare to make new, fr. novus new. See New.] 1. To bring in as new; to introduce as a novelty; as, to innovate a word or an act. [Archaic]
Innovate In"no*vate, v. i. To introduce novelties or changes; -- sometimes with in or on. Bacon.

innovation.c: Innovation In`no*va"tion (?), n. [L. innovatio; cf. F. innovation.] 1. The act of innovating; introduction of something new, in customs, rites, commercial products, etc. Dryden.

innovationist.c: Innovationist In`no*va"tion*ist, n. One who favors innovation.

innovative.c: Innovative In"no*va*tive (?), a. Characterized by, or introducing, innovations. Fitzed. Hall.

innovator.c: Innovator In"no*va`tor (?), n. [Cf. F. innovateur.] One who innovates. Shak.

innoxious.c: Innoxious In*nox"ious (?), a. [L. innoxius. See In- not, and Noxious.] 1. Free from hurtful qualities or effects; harmless; innocuous. “Innoxious flames.” Sir K. Digby.

innubilous.c: Innubilous In*nu"bi*lous (?), a. [L. innubilus. See Nubilous.] Cloudless. [Obs.] Blount.

innuendo.c: Innuendo In`nu*en"do (?), n.; pl. Innuedoes(?). [L., by intimation, by hinting, gerund of innuere, innutum, to give a nod, to intimate; pref. in- in, to + -nuere (in comp.) to nod. See Nutation.] 1. An oblique hint; a remote allusion or reference, usually derogatory to a person or thing not named; an insinuation.

innuent.c: Innuent In"nu*ent (?), a. [L. innuens, p. pr.] Conveying a hint; significant. [Obs.] Burton.

innumerability.c: Innumerability In*nu`mer*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. innumerabilitas.] State of being innumerable. Fotherby.

innumerable.c: Innumerable In*nu`mer*a*ble (?), a. [L. innumerabilis: cf. F. innumefable. See In- not, and Numerable.] Not capable of being counted, enumerated, or numbered, for multitude; countless; numberless; unnumbered, hence, indefinitely numerous; of great number.

innumerous.c: Innumerous In*nu"mer*ous (?), a. [L. innumerosus, innumerus. See Numerous.] Innumerable. [Archaic] Milton.

innutrition.c: Innutrition In`nu*tri"tion (?), n. Lack of nutrition; failure of nourishment. E. Darwin.

innutritious.c: Innutritious In`nu*tri"tious (?), a. Not nutritious; not furnishing nourishment.

innyard.c: Innyard Inn"yard` (?), n. The yard adjoining an inn.

inobedience.c: Inobedience In`o*be"di*ence (?), n. [L. inoboedientia: cf. F. inobedience.] Disobedience. [Obs.] Wyclif. Chaucer.

inobedient.c: Inobedient In`o*be"di*ent (?), a. [L. inoboediens, p. pr. of inoboedire: cf. F. inobedient. See Obedient.] Not obedient; disobedient. [Obs.] Chaucer.

inobservable.c: Inobservable In`ob*serv"a*ble (?), a. [L. inobservabilis: cf. F. inobservable. See In- not, and Observable.] Not observable.

inobservance.c: Inobservance In`ob*serv"ance (?), a. [L. inobservantia: cf. F. inobservance.] Lack or neglect of observance. Bacon.

inobservant.c: Inobservant In`ob*serv"ant (?), a. [L. inobservans. See In- not, and Observant.] Not observant; regardless; heedless. Bp. Hurd.

inobservation.c: Inobservation In*ob`ser*va"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inobservation.] Neglect or lack of observation. [R.]

inocarpin.c: Inocarpin In`o*car"pin (?), n. [Gr. 'i`s, 'ino`s, muscle + karpo`s fruit.] (Chem.) A red, gummy, coloring matter, extracted from the colorless juice of the Otaheite chestnut (Inocarpus edulis).

inoceramus.c: Inoceramus ‖In`o*cer"a*mus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'i`s, 'ino`s, a muscle +? an earthen vessel.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of large, fossil, bivalve shells, allied to the mussels. The genus is characteristic of the Cretaceous period.

inoculability.c: Inoculability In*oc`u*la*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being inoculable.

inoculable.c: Inoculable In*oc"u*la*ble (?), a. [See Inoculate.] Capable of being inoculated; capable of communicating disease, or of being communicated, by inoculation.

inocular.c: Inocular In*oc"u*lar (?), a. (Zool) Inserted in the corner of the eye; -- said of the antennæ of certain insects.

inoculate.c: Inoculate In*oc"u*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inoculated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inoculating (?).] [L. inoculatus, p. p. of inoculare to ingraft; pref. in- in, on + oculare to furnish with eyes, fr. oculus an eye, also, a bud. See Ocular.] 1. To bud; to insert, or graft, as the bud of a tree or plant in another tree or plant.
Inoculate In*oc"u*late, v. i. 1. To graft by inserting buds.

inoculation.c: Inoculation In*oc"u*la"tion (?), n. [L. inoculatio: cf. F. inoculation.] 1. The act or art of inoculating trees or plants.

inoculator.c: Inoculator In*oc"u*la`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. inoculateur.] One who inoculates; one who propagates plants or diseases by inoculation.

inodiate.c: Inodiate In*o"di*ate (ĭn*ō"dĭ*āt), v. t. [Pref. in- in + L. odium hatred.] To make odious or hateful. [Obs.] South.

inodorous.c: Inodorous In*o"dor*ous (?), a. [L. inodorus. See In- not, and Odorous.] Emitting no odor; without smell; scentless; odorless. -- In*o"dor*ous*ness, n.

inoffensive.c: Inoffensive In"of*fen"sive (?), a. [Pref. in- not + offensiue: cf. F. inoffensif.] 1. Giving no offense, or provocation; causing no uneasiness, annoyance, or disturbance; as, an inoffensive man, answer, appearance.

inofficial.c: Inofficial In"of*fi"cial (?), a. Not official; not having official sanction or authority; unofficial; not according to the forms or ceremony of official business; as, inofficial intelligence.

inofficially.c: Inofficially In`of*fi"cial*ly, adv. Without the usual forms, or not in the official character; unofficially.

inofficious.c: Inofficious In`of*fi"cious (?), a. [L. inofficiosus: cf. F. inofficieux. See In- not, and Officious.] 1. Indifferent to obligation or duty. [Obs.]

inogen.c: Inogen In"o*gen (?), n. [Gr. 'i`s, 'ino`s, a muscle + -gen.] (Physiol.) A complex nitrogenous substance, which, by Hermann's hypothesis, is continually decomposed and reproduced in the muscles, during their life.

inoperation.c: Inoperation In*op`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. inoperari to effect; pref. in- in + operari to operate.] Agency; influence; production of effects. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

inoperative.c: Inoperative In*op"er*a*tive (?), a. [Pref. in- not + operative.] Not operative; not active; producing no effects; as, laws renderd inoperative by neglect; inoperative remedies or processes.

inoperculate.c: Inoperculate Inopercular { In`o*per"cu*lar (?), In`o*per"cu*late (?), } a. (Zool.) Having no operculum; -- said of certain gastropod shells.

inopinable.c: Inopinable In`o*pin"a*ble (?), a. [L. inopinabilis. See Inopinate.] Not to be expected; inconceivable. [Obs.] “Inopinable, incredible... sayings.” Latimer.

inopinate.c: Inopinate In*op"i*nate (?), a. [L. inopinatus. See In- not, and Opine.] Not expected or looked for. [Obs.]

inopportune.c: Inopportune In*op`por*tune" (?), a. [L. inopportunus: cf. F. inopportun. See In- not, and Opportune.] Not opportune; inconvenient; unseasonable; as, an inopportune occurrence, remark, etc.

inopportunely.c: Inopportunely In*op`por*tune"ly, adv. Not opportunely; unseasonably; inconveniently.

inopportunity.c: Inopportunity In*op`por*tu"ni*ty (?), n. Lack of opportunity; unseasonableness; inconvenience. [R.]

inoppressive.c: Inoppressive In`op*press"ive (?), a. Not oppressive or burdensome. O. Wolcott.

inopulent.c: Inopulent In*op"u*lent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + opulent: cf. F. inopulent.] Not opulent; not affluent or rich.

inordinacy.c: Inordinacy In*or"di*na*cy (?), n. The state or quality of being inordinate; excessiveness; immoderateness; as, the inordinacy of love or desire. Jer. Taylor.

inordinate.c: Inordinate In*or"di*nate (?), a. [L. inordinatus disordered. See In- not, and Ordinate.] Not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds; irregular; excessive; immoderate; as, an inordinate love of the world. “Inordinate desires.” Milton. “Inordinate vanity.” Burke.

inordination.c: Inordination In*or`di*na"tion (?), n. [L. inordinatio.] Deviation from custom, rule, or right; irregularity; inordinacy. [Obs.] South.

inorganic.c: Inorganic In`or*gan"ic (?), a. [Pref. in- not + organic: cf. F. inorganique.] 1. Not organic; without the organs necessary for life; devoid of an organized structure; unorganized; lifeness; inanimate.

inorganically.c: Inorganically In`or*gan"ic*al*ly, adv. In an inorganic manner.

inorganity.c: Inorganity In`or*gan"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being inorganic. [Obs.] “The inorganity of the soul.” Sir T. Browne.

inorganization.c: Inorganization In*or`gan*i*za"tion (?), n. The state of being without organization.

inorganized.c: Inorganized In*or"gan*ized (?), a. Not having organic structure; devoid of organs; inorganic.

inorthography.c: Inorthography In`or*thog"ra*phy (?), n. Deviation from correct orthography; bad spelling. [Obs.] Feltham.

inosculate.c: Inosculate In*os"cu*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inosculated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inosculating (?).] [Pref. in- in + osculate.] 1. To unite by apposition or contact, as two tubular vessels at their extremities; to anastomose.
Inosculate In*os"cu*late (?), v. t. 1. To unite by apposition or contact, as two vessels in an animal body. Berkeley.

inosculation.c: Inosculation In*os`cu*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. inosculation.] The junction or connection of vessels, channels, or passages, so that their contents pass from one to the other; union by mouths or ducts; anastomosis; intercommunication; as, inosculation of veins, etc. Ray.

inosinic.c: Inosinic In`o*sin"ic (?), a. [From Inosite.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, inosite; as, inosinic acid.

inositol.c: inositol i*no"si*tol (ĭ*nŏs"ĭ*tŏl), n. [Gr. 'i`s, 'ino`s, strength, muscle.] (Physiol. Chem.) A white crystalline substance (C6H12O6) with a sweet taste, widely distributed in certain animal tissues and fluids, particularly in the muscles of the heart and lungs, and also in some plants, as in unripe pease, beans, potato sprouts, etc. Although isomeric with dextrose, it has no carbonyl (aldehyde or ketone) group, and is therefore not a carbohydrate, but a derivative of cyclohexane. Called also inosite, cyclohexitol, cyclohexanehexol, hexahydroxycyclohexane and phaseomannite. There are nine possible steroisomers, not all of which are found naturally. The predominate natural form is cis-1,2,3,5-trans-4,6-cyclohexanehexol, also called myo-inositol. The naturally occurring phytic acid in plants is the hexaphosphate of inositol, from which inositol may be manufactured; phytin is the calcium-magnesium salt of phytic acid. It is also a component of phosphatidylinositol. MI11

inoxidizable.c: Inoxidizable In*ox"idi`za*ble (?), a. (Chem.) Incapable of being oxidized; as, gold and platinum are inoxidizable in the air.

inoxidize.c: Inoxidize In*ox"i*dize (?), v. i. To prevent or hinder oxidation, rust, or decay; as, inoxidizing oils or varnishes.

inpatient.c: Inpatient In"pa`tient (?), n. A patient who receives lodging and food, as well as treatment, in a hospital or an infirmary; -- distinguished from outpatient.

inquest.c: Inquest In"quest (?), n. [OE. enqueste, OF. enqueste, F. enquête, LL. inquesta, for inquisita, fr. L. inquisitus, p. p. of inquirere. See Inquire.] 1. Inquiry; quest; search. [R.] Spenser.

inquiet.c: Inquiet In*qui"et (?), v. t. [L. inquietare: cf. F. inquieter. See Quiet.] To disquiet. [Obs.] Joye.

inquietation.c: Inquietation In*qui`e*ta"tion (?), n. [L. inquietatio: cf. F. inquielation.] Disturbance. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

inquietude.c: Inquietude In*qui"e*tude (?), n. [L. inquietudo: cf. F. inquietude.] Disturbed state; uneasiness either of body or mind; restlessness; disquietude. Sir H. Wotton.

inquiline.c: Inquiline In"qui*line (?), n. [L. inquilinus a tenant, lodger.] (Zool.) A gallfly which deposits its eggs in galls formed by other insects.

inquinate.c: Inquinate In"qui*nate (?), v. t. [L. inquinatus, p. p. of inquinare to defile.] To defile; to pollute; to contaminate; to befoul. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

inquination.c: Inquination In`qui*na"tion (?), n. [L. inquinatio.] A defiling; pollution; stain. [Obs.] Bacon.

inquirable.c: Inquirable In*quir"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. enquerable.] Capable of being inquired into; subject or liable to inquisition or inquest. Bacon.

inquire.c: Inquire In*quire" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inquired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inquiring.] [OE. enqueren, inqueren, OF. enquerre, F. enquérir, L. inquirere, inquisitum; pref. in- in + quarere to seek. See Quest a seeking, and cf. Inquiry.] [Written also enquire.] 1. To ask a question; to seek for truth or information by putting queries.
Inquire In*quire", v. t. 1. To ask about; to seek to know by asking; to make examination or inquiry respecting.

inquirent.c: Inquirent In*quir"ent (?), a. [L. inquirens, p. pr.] Making inquiry; inquiring; questioning. [Obs.] Shenstone.

inquirer.c: Inquirer In*quir"er (?), n. [Written also enquirer.] One who inquires or examines; questioner; investigator. Locke.

inquiring.c: Inquiring In*quir"ing, a. Given to inquiry; disposed to investigate causes; curious; as, an inquiring mind.

inquiringly.c: Inquiringly In*quir"ing*ly, adv. In an inquiring manner.

inquiry.c: Inquiry In*quir"y (?), n.; pl. Inquiries (#). [See Inquire.] [Written also enquiry.] 1. The act of inquiring; a seeking for information by asking questions; interrogation; a question or questioning.

inquisible.c: Inquisible In*quis"i*ble (?), a. Admitting judicial inquiry. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

inquisition.c: Inquisition In`qui*si"tion (?), n. [L. inquisitio: cf. F. inquisition. See Inquire, and cf. Inquest.] 1. The act of inquiring; inquiry; search; examination; inspection; investigation.
Inquisition In`qui*si"tion, v. t. To make inquisition concerning; to inquire into. [Obs.] Milton.

inquisitional.c: Inquisitional In`qui*si"tion*al (?), a. [LL. inquisitionalis.] Relating to inquiry or inquisition; inquisitorial; also, of or pertaining to, or characteristic of, the Inquisition.

inquisitive.c: Inquisitive In*quis"i*tive (?), a. [OE. inquisitif, F. inquisitif.] 1. Disposed to ask questions, especially in matters which do not concern the inquirer.
Inquisitive In*quis"i*tive, n. A person who is inquisitive; one curious in research. Sir W. Temple.

inquisitively.c: Inquisitively In*quis"i*tive*ly, adv. In an inquisitive manner.

inquisitiveness.c: Inquisitiveness In*quis"i*tive*ness, n. The quality or state of being inquisitive; the disposition to seek explanation and information; curiosity to learn what is unknown; esp., uncontrolled and impertinent curiosity.

inquisitor.c: Inquisitor In*quis"i*tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. inquisiteur. See Inquire.] 1. An inquisitive person; one fond of asking questions. [R.] “Inquisitors are tatlers.” Feltham.

inquisitorial.c: Inquisitorial In*quis`i*to"ri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. inquisitorial.] 1. Pertaining to inquisition; making rigorous and unfriendly inquiry; searching; as, inquisitorial power. “Illiberal and inquisitorial abuse.” F. Blackburne.

inquisitorially.c: Inquisitorially In*quis`i*to"ri*al*ly, adv. In an inquisitorial manner.

inquisitorious.c: Inquisitorious In*quis`i*to"ri*ous (?), a. Making strict inquiry; inquisitorial. [Obs.] Milton.

inquisiturient.c: Inquisiturient In*quis`i*tu"ri*ent (?), a. Inquisitorial. [Obs.] “Our inquisiturient bishops.” Milton.

inracinate.c: Inracinate In*rac"i*nate (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + F. racine root: cf. F. enraciner.] To enroot or implant.

inrail.c: Inrail In*rail" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inrailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inrailing.] To rail in; to inclose or surround, as with rails. Hooker.

inregister.c: Inregister In*reg"is*ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inregistered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inregistering.] [Pref. in- in + register: cf. F. enregistrer. Cf. Enregister.] To register; to enter, as in a register. [R.] Walsh.

inro.c: Inro ‖In"ro (?), n. [Jap. inrō; in seal + rō box.] A small closed receptacle or set of receptacles of hard material, as lacquered wood, iron, bronze, or ivory, used by the Japanese to hold medicines, perfumes, and the like, and carried in the girdle. It is usually secured by a silk cord by which the wearer may grasp it, which cord passes through an ornamental button or knob called a netsuke.

inroad.c: Inroad In"road` (ĭn"rōd`), n. The entrance of an enemy into a country with purposes of hostility; a sudden or desultory incursion or invasion; raid; encroachment.
Inroad In*road" (ĭn*rōd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inroaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Inroading.] To make an inroad into; to invade. [Obs.]

inrunning.c: Inrunning In"run`ning (?), n. The act or the place of entrance; an inlet. Tennyson.

inrush.c: Inrush In"rush` (?), n. A rush inwards; as, the inrush of the tide. G. Eliot.
Inrush In*rush" (?), v. i. To rush in. [Obs.] Holland.

insabbatati.c: Insabbatati ‖In*sab`ba*ta"ti (?), n. pl. [LL. Insabatati. See 1st In-, and Sabot.] The Waldenses; -- so called from their peculiarly cut or marked sabots, or shoes.

insalivation.c: Insalivation In*sal`i*va"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The mixing of the food with the saliva and other secretions of the mouth in eating.

insalubrious.c: Insalubrious In`sa*lu"bri*ous (?), a. [Pref. in- not + salubrious: cf. L. insalubris, F. insalubre.] Not salubrious or healthful; unwholesome; as, an insalubrious air or climate.

insalubrity.c: Insalubrity In`sa*lu"bri*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. insalubrite.] Unhealthfulness; unwholesomeness; as, the insalubrity of air, water, or climate. Boyle.

insalutary.c: Insalutary In*sal"u*ta*ry (?), a. [L. insaluteris: cf. F. insalutaire. See In- not, and Salutary.] 1. Not salutary or wholesome; unfavorable to health.

insanability.c: Insanability In*san`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state of being insanable or incurable; insanableness.

insanable.c: Insanable In*san"a*ble (?), a. [L. insanabilis; cf. OF. insanable. See In- not, and Sanable.] Not capable of being healed; incurable; irremediable.

insanableness.c: Insanableness In*san"a*ble*ness, n. The state of being insanable; insanability; incurableness.

insanably.c: Insanably In*san"a*bly, adv. In an incurable manner.

insane.c: Insane In*sane" (?), a. [L. insanus. See In- not, and Sane.] 1. Exhibiting unsoundness or disorder of mind; not sane; mad; deranged in mind; delirious; distracted. See Insanity, 2.

insanely.c: Insanely In*sane"ly, adv. Without reason; madly; foolishly.

insaniate.c: Insaniate In*sa"ni*ate (?), v. t. To render unsound; to make mad. [Obs.] Feltham.

insanitary.c: Insanitary In*san"i*ta*ry (?), a. Not sanitary; unhealthy; unsanitary; as, insanitary conditions of drainage.

insanitation.c: Insanitation In*san`i*ta"tion (?), n. Lack of sanitation; careless or dangerous hygienic conditions.

insanity.c: Insanity In*san"i*ty (?), n. [L. insanitas unsoundness; cf. insania insanity, F. insanite.] 1. The state of being insane; unsoundness or derangement of mind; madness; lunacy.

insapory.c: Insapory In*sa"po*ry (?), a. [Pref. in- not + sapor.] Tasteless; unsavory. [R.] Sir T. Herbert.

insatiability.c: Insatiability In*sa`tia*bil"i*ty (?), n., [L. insatiabilitas; cf. F. insatiabilite.] The state or quality of being insatiable; insatiableness.

insatiable.c: Insatiable In*sa"tia*ble (?), a. [F. insatiable, L. ionsatiabilis. See In- not, and Satiable.] Not satiable; incapable of being satisfied or appeased; very greedy; as, an insatiable appetite, thirst, or desire.

insatiableness.c: Insatiableness In*sa"tia*ble*ness, n. Greediness of appetite that can not be satisfied or appeased; insatiability.

insatiably.c: Insatiably In*sa"tia*bly, adv. In an insatiable manner or degree; unappeasably. “Insatiably covetous.” South.

insatiate.c: Insatiate In*sa"ti*ate (?), a. [L. insatiatus.] Insatiable; as, insatiate thirst.

insatiately.c: Insatiately In*sa"ti*ate*ly, adv. Insatiably. Sir T. Herbert.

insatiateness.c: Insatiateness In*sa"ti*ate*ness, n. The state of being insatiate.

insatiety.c: Insatiety In`sa*ti"e*ty (?), n. [L. insatietas: cf. F. insatiete. See Satiety.] Insatiableness. T. Grander.

insaturable.c: Insaturable In*sat"u*ra*ble (?), a. [L. insaturabilis: cf. F. insaturable. See In- not, and Saturable.] Not capable of being saturated or satisfied.

inscience.c: Inscience In"science (ĭn"sheins), n. [L. inscientia: cf. F. inscience.] Lack of knowledge; ignorance. [Obs.]

inscient.c: Inscient In"scient (ĭn"sheint), a. [L. insciens, -entis, ignorant. See In- not, and Scient, Science.] Having little or no knowledge; ignorant; stupid; silly. [R.] N. Bacon.
Inscient In"scient, a. [Pref. in- in + L. sciens knowing.] Having knowledge or insight; intelligent. [R.]

inscribable.c: Inscribable In*scrib"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being inscribed, -- used specif. (Math.) of solids or plane figures capable of being inscribed in other solids or figures.

inscribableness.c: Inscribableness In*scrib"a*ble*ness, n. Quality of being inscribable.

inscribe.c: Inscribe In*scribe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inscribed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inscribing.] [L. inscribere. See 1st In-, and Scribe.] 1. To write or engrave; to mark down as something to be read; to imprint.

inscriber.c: Inscriber In*scrib"er (?), n. One who inscribes. Pownall.

inscriptible.c: Inscriptible In*scrip"ti*ble (?), a. Capable of being inscribed; inscribable.

inscription.c: Inscription In*scrip"tion (?), n. [L. inscriptio, fr. inscribere, inscriptum, to inscribe: cf. F. inscription. See Inscribe.] 1. The act or process of inscribing.

inscriptive.c: Inscriptive In*scrip"tive (?), a. Bearing inscription; of the character or nature of an inscription.

inscroll.c: Inscroll In*scroll" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inscrolled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inscrolling.] To write on a scroll; to record. [Written also inscrol.] Shak.

inscrutability.c: Inscrutability In*scru`ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being inscrutable; inscrutableness.

inscrutable.c: Inscrutable In*scru"ta*ble (?), a. [L. inscrutabilis: cf. F. inscrutable. See In- not, and Scrutiny.] Unsearchable; incapable of being searched into and understood by inquiry or study; impossible or difficult to be explained or accounted for satisfactorily; obscure; incomprehensible; as, an inscrutable design or event.

inscrutableness.c: Inscrutableness In*scru"ta*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inscrutable; inscrutability.

inscrutably.c: Inscrutably In*scru"ta*bly, adv. In an inscrutable manner.

insculp.c: Insculp In*sculp" (?), v. t. [L. insculpere: cf. F. insculper. See 1st In-, and Sculptor.] To engrave; to carve; to sculpture. [Obs. & R.] Shak.

insculpture.c: Insculpture In*sculp"ture (?), n. An engraving, carving, or inscription. [Obs.]

inseam.c: Inseam In*seam" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inseamed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inseaming.] To impress or mark with a seam or cicatrix. Pope.

insearch.c: Insearch In*search" (?), v. t. To make search after; to investigate or examine; to ensearch. [Obs.]

insecable.c: Insecable In*sec"a*ble (ĭn*sĕk"ȧ*b'l), a. [L. insecabilis; pref. in- not + secabilis that may be cut: cf. F. insecable.] Incapable of being divided by cutting; indivisible.

insect.c: Insect In"sect (ĭn"sĕkt), n. [F. insecte, L. insectum, fr. insectus, p. p. of insecare to cut in. See Section. The name was originally given to certain small animals, whose bodies appear cut in, or almost divided. Cf. Entomology.] 1. (Zool.) One of the Insecta; esp., one of the Hexapoda. See Insecta.
Insect In"sect (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to an insect or insects.

insecta.c: Insecta ‖In*sec"ta (?), n. pl. [NL. See Insect.] 1. (Zool.) One of the classes of Arthropoda, including those that have one pair of antennæ, three pairs of mouth organs, and breathe air by means of tracheæ, opening by spiracles along the sides of the body. In this sense it includes the Hexapoda, or six-legged insects and the Myriapoda, with numerous legs. See Insect, n.

insectary.c: Insectary In"sec*ta*ry (?), n. A place for keeping living insects. -- In`sec*ta"ri*um (#), n. [L.]

insectation.c: Insectation In`sec*ta"tion (?), n. [L. insectatio. See Insectator.] The act of pursuing; pursuit; harassment; persecution. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

insectator.c: Insectator In`sec*ta"tor (?), n. [L., fr. insectari to pursue, freq. fr. insequi. See Ensue.] A pursuer; a persecutor; a censorious critic. [Obs.] Bailey.

insected.c: Insected In"sect*ed (?), a. Pertaining to, having the nature of, or resembling, an insect. Howell.

insecticide.c: Insecticide In*sec"ti*cide (?), n. [Insect + L. caedere to kill.] An agent or preparation for destroying insects; an insect powder or spray. -- In*sec"ti*ci`dal (#), a.

insectile.c: Insectile In*sec"tile (?), a. Pertaining to, or having the nature of, insects. Bacon.

insection.c: Insection In*sec"tion (?), n. [See Insect.] A cutting in; incisure; incision.

insectivora.c: Insectivora ‖In`sec*tiv"o*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., from L. insectum an insect + vorare to devour.] (Zool.) 1. An order of mammals which feed principally upon insects.

insectivore.c: Insectivore In*sec"ti*vore (?), n.; pl. Insectivores (-vōrz). [F.] (Zool.) One of the Insectivora.

insectivorous.c: Insectivorous In`sec*tiv"o*rous (?), a. [See Insectivora.] Feeding or subsisting on insects; carnivorous. The term is applied: (a) to plants which have some special adaptation for catching and digesting insects, as the sundew, Venus's flytrap, Sarracenia, etc. (b) to the Insectivora, and many bats, birds, and reptiles.

insectology.c: Insectology In`sec*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Insect + -logy: cf. F. insectologie.] Entomology. [Obs.]

insecure.c: Insecure In`se*cure" (?), a. 1. Not secure; not confident of safety or permanence; distrustful; suspicious; apprehensive of danger or loss.

insecurely.c: Insecurely In`se*cure"ly, adv. In an insecure manner.

insecurity.c: Insecurity In`se*cu"ri*ty (?), n.; pl. Insecurities (#). [Pref. in- not + security: cf. LL. insecuritas, F. insecurite.] 1. The condition or quality of being insecure; lack of safety; danger; hazard; as, the insecurity of a building liable to fire; insecurity of a debt.

insecution.c: Insecution In`se*cu"tion (?), n. [L. insecutio, fr. insequi p. p. insecutus. See Ensue.] A following after; close pursuit. [Obs.] Chapman.

inseminate.c: Inseminate In*sem"i*nate (?), v. t. [L. inseminatus, p. p. of inseminare to sow. See Seminate.] 1. To sow seed into. [Obs.]

insensate.c: Insensate In*sen"sate (?), a. [L. insensatus. See In- not, and Sensate.] Wanting sensibility; destitute of sense; stupid; foolish.

insense.c: Insense In*sense" (?), v. t. [Pref. in- in + sense.] To make to understand; to instruct. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

insensible.c: Insensible In*sen"si*ble (?), a. [L. insensibilis: cf. F. insensible. See In- not, and Sensible.]

insensibly.c: Insensibly In*sen"si*bly, adv. In a manner not to be felt or perceived; imperceptibly; gradually.

insensitive.c: Insensitive In*sen"si*tive (?), a. Not sensitive; wanting sensation, or wanting acute sensibility. Tillotson. Ruskin.

insensuous.c: Insensuous In*sen"su*ous (?), a. [Pref. in- not + sensuous.] Not sensuous; not pertaining to, affecting, or addressing, the senses.

insentient.c: Insentient In*sen"ti*ent (?), a. Not sentient; not having perception, or the power of perception; devoid of feeling, consciousness and animation; inanimate; as, insentient stone. Opposite of sentient. [wns=1+3]

inseparability.c: Inseparability In*sep`a*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. inseparabilitas: cf. F. inséparabilité.] The quality or state of being inseparable; inseparableness. Locke.

inseparable.c: Inseparable In*sep"a*ra*ble (?), a. [L. inseparabilis: cf. F. inséparable. See In-, and Separable.]

inseparableness.c: Inseparableness In*sep"a*ra*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being inseparable; inseparability. Bp. Burnet.

inseparably.c: Inseparably In*sep"a*ra*bly, adv. In an inseparable manner or condition; so as not to be separable. Bacon.

inseparate.c: Inseparate In*sep"a*rate (?), a. [L. inseparatus. See In- not, and Separate.] Not separate; together; united. Shak.

insert.c: Insert In*sert" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inserted; p. pr. & vb. n. Inserting.] [L. insertus, p. p. of inserere to insert; pref. in- in + serere to join, connect. See Series.] To set within something; to put or thrust in; to introduce; to cause to enter, or be included, or contained; as, to insert a scion in a stock; to insert a letter, word, or passage in a composition; to insert an advertisement in a newspaper.

inserted.c: Inserted In*sert"ed, a. (Bot.) Situated upon, attached to, or growing out of, some part; -- said especially of the parts of the flower; as, the calyx, corolla, and stamens of many flowers are inserted upon the receptacle. Gray.

insertion.c: Insertion In*ser"tion (?), n. [L. insertio: cf. F. insertion. See Insert.]

inserve.c: Inserve In*serve" (?), v. i. [L. inservire; in- in + servire to serve.] To be of use to an end; to serve. [Obs.]

inservient.c: Inservient In*serv"i*ent (?), a. [L. inserviens, p. pr. of inservire.] Conducive; instrumental. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

insession.c: Insession In*ses"sion (?), n. [L. insessio, fr. insidere, insessum, to sit in. See Insidious.]

insessor.c: Insessor ‖In*ses"sor (?), n.; pl. Insessores (#). [See Insessores.] (Zool.) One of the Insessores. The group includes most of the common singing birds.

insessores.c: Insessores ‖In`ses*so"res (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. insessor, lit., one who sits down, fr. incidere. See Insession.] (Zool.) An order of birds, formerly established to include the perching birds, but now generally regarded as an artificial group.

insessorial.c: Insessorial In`ses*so"ri*al (?), a. (Zool.) 1. Pertaining to, or having the character of, perching birds.

inset.c: Inset In*set" (?), v. t. To infix. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Inset In"set (?), n. 1. That which is inserted or set in; an insertion.

inseverable.c: Inseverable In*sev"er*a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being severed; indivisible; inseparable. De Quincey.

inshaded.c: Inshaded In*shad"ed (?), a. Marked with different shades. W. Browne.

inshave.c: Inshave In"shave` (?), n. (Mech.) A plane for shaving or dressing the concave or inside faces of barrel staves.

insheathe.c: Insheathe In*sheathe" (?), v. t. To insert as in a sheath; to sheathe. Hughes.

inshell.c: Inshell In*shell" (?), v. t. To hide in a shell. [Obs.] Shak.

inship.c: Inship In*ship" (?), v. t. To embark. [Obs.] Shak.

inshore.c: Inshore In"shore` (?), a. Being near or moving towards the shore; as, inshore fisheries; inshore currents. -- adv. Towards the shore; as, the boat was headed inshore.

insiccation.c: Insiccation In`sic*ca"tion (?), n. The act or process of drying in.

inside.c: Inside In"side` (?), prep. or adv. Within the sides of; in the interior; contained within; as, inside a house, book, bottle, etc.
Inside In"side`, a. 1. Being within; included or inclosed in anything; contained; interior; internal; as, the inside passengers of a stagecoach; inside decoration.
Inside In"side`, n. 1. The part within; interior or internal portion; content.

insidiate.c: Insidiate In*sid"i*ate (?), v. t. [L. insidiatus, p. p. of insidiare to lie in ambush, fr. insidiae. See Insidious.] To lie in ambush for. [Obs.] Heywood.

insidiator.c: Insidiator In*sid"i*a`tor (?), n. [L.] One who lies in ambush. [Obs.] Barrow.

insidious.c: Insidious In*sid"i*ous (?), a. [L. insidiosus, fr. insidiae an ambush, fr. insidere to sit in; pref. in- + sedere to sit: cf. F. insidieux. See Sit.]

insight.c: Insight In"sight` (?), n. 1. A sight or view of the interior of anything; a deep inspection or view; introspection; -- frequently used with into.

insignia.c: Insignia In*sig"ni*a (?), n. pl. [L. insigne, pl. insignia, fr. insignis distinguished by a mark; pref. in- in + signum a mark, sign. See Ensign, Sign.]

insignificance.c: Insignificance In`sig*nif"i*cance (?), n. 1. The condition or quality of being insignificant; lack of significance, sense, or meaning; as, the insignificance of words or phrases.

insignificant.c: Insignificant In`sig*nif"i*cant (?), a. 1. Not significant; void of signification, sense, or import; meaningless; as, insignificant words.

insignificantly.c: Insignificantly In`sig*nif"i*cant*ly, adv. without significance, importance, or effect; to no purpose. “Anger insignificantly fierce.” Cowper.

insignificative.c: Insignificative In`sig*nif"i*ca*tive (?), a. [L. insignificativus. See In- not, and Significative.] Not expressing meaning; not significant.

insignment.c: Insignment In*sign"ment (?), n. [See Insignia.] A token, mark, or explanation. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

insimulate.c: Insimulate In*sim"u*late (?), v. t. [L. insimulatus, p. p. of insimulare to accuse.] To accuse. [Obs.] Donne.

insincere.c: Insincere In`sin*cere" (?), a. [L. insincerus. See In- not, and Sincere.]

insincerity.c: Insincerity In`sin*cer"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. insincérité.] The quality of being insincere; lack of sincerity, or of being in reality what one appears to be; dissimulation; hypocritical; deceitfulness; hollowness; untrustworthiness; as, the insincerity of a professed friend; the insincerity of professions of regard.

insinew.c: Insinew In*sin"ew (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insinewed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insinewing.] To strengthen, as with sinews; to invigorate. [Obs.]

insinuant.c: Insinuant In*sin"u*ant (?), a. [L. insinuans, p. pr.: cf. F. insinuant.] Insinuating; insinuative. [Obs.]

insinuate.c: Insinuate In*sin"u*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insinuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insinuating.] [L. insinuatus, p. p. of insinuareto insinuate; pref. in- in + sinus the bosom. See Sinuous.]
Insinuate In*sin"u*ate, v. i. 1. To creep, wind, or flow in; to enter gently, slowly, or imperceptibly, as into crevices.

insinuating.c: Insinuating In*sin"u*a`ting (?), a. Winding, creeping, or flowing in, quietly or stealthily; suggesting; winning favor and confidence insensibly. Milton.

insinuation.c: Insinuation In*sin"u*a`tion (?), n. [L. insinuatio: cf. F. insinuation.]

insinuator.c: Insinuator In*sin"u*a`tor (?), n. [L., an introducer.] One who, or that which, insinuates. De Foe.

insipid.c: Insipid In*sip"id (?), a. [L. insipidus; pref. in- not + sapidus savory, fr. sapere to taste: cf. F. insipide. See Savor.]

insipidness.c: Insipidness Insipidity { In`si*pid"i*ty (?), In*sip"id*ness (?), } n. [Cf. F. insipidité.] The quality or state of being insipid; vapidity. “Dryden's lines shine strongly through the insipidity of Tate's.” Pope.

insipidly.c: Insipidly In*sip"id*ly, adv. In an insipid manner; without taste, life, or spirit; flatly. Locke. Sharp.

insipience.c: Insipience In*sip"i*ence (?), n. [L. insipientia: cf. OF. insipience.] Lack of intelligence; stupidity; folly. [R.] Blount.

insipient.c: Insipient In*sip"i*ent (?), a. [L. insipiens; pref. in- not + sapiens wise.] Wanting wisdom; stupid; foolish. [R.] Clarendon. -- n. An insipient person. [R.] Fryth.

insist.c: Insist In*sist" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Insisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Insisting.] [F. insister, L. insistere to set foot upon, follow, persist; pref. in- in + sistere to stand, cause to stand. See Stand.]

insistence.c: Insistence In*sist"ence (?), n. The quality of insisting, or being urgent or pressing; the act of dwelling upon as of special importance; persistence; urgency.

insistent.c: Insistent In*sist"ent (?), a. [L. insistens, -entis, p. pr. of insistere.]

insistently.c: Insistently In*sist"ent*ly, adv. In an insistent manner.

insisture.c: Insisture In*sis"ture (?; 135), n. A dwelling or standing on something; fixedness; persistence. [Obs.] Shak.

insitiency.c: Insitiency In*si"ti*en*cy (?), n. [Pref. in- not + L. sitiens, p. pr. of sitire to be thirsty, fr. sitis thirst.] Freedom from thirst. [Obs.]

insition.c: Insition In*si"tion (?; 277), n. [L. insitio, fr. inserere, insitum, to sow or plant in, to ingraft; pref. in- in + serere, satum, to sow.] The insertion of a scion in a stock; ingraftment. Ray.

insnare.c: Insnare In*snare" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insnared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insnaring.] [Written also ensnare.]

insnarl.c: Insnarl In*snarl" (?), v. t. To make into a snarl or knot; to entangle; to snarl. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

insobriety.c: Insobriety In`so*bri"e*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not +?obriety: cf. F. insobriété.] Lack of sobriety, moderation, or calmness; intemperance; drunkenness.

insociability.c: Insociability In*so`cia*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. insociabilité.] The quality of being insociable; lack of sociability; unsociability. [R.] Bp. Warburton.

insociable.c: Insociable In*so"cia*ble (?), a. [L. insociabilis: cf. F. insociable. See In- not, and Sociable.]

insociate.c: Insociate In*so"ci*ate (?), a. Not associate; without a companion; single; solitary; recluse. [Obs.] “The insociate virgin life.” B. Jonson.

insolate.c: Insolate In"so*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insolated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insolating.] [L. insolatus, p. p. of insolare to expose to the sun; pref. in- in + sol the sun.] To dry in, or to expose to, the sun's rays; to ripen or prepare by such exposure. Johnson.

insolation.c: Insolation In`so*la"tion (?), n. [L. insolatio: cf. F. insolation.]

insole.c: Insole In"sole` (?), n. The inside sole of a boot or shoe; also, a loose, thin strip of leather, felt, etc., placed inside the shoe for warmth or ease.

insolence.c: Insolence In"so*lence (?), n. [F. insolence, L. insolentia. See Insolent.]
Insolence In"so*lence, v. t. To insult. [Obs.] Eikon Basilike.

insolent.c: Insolent In"so*lent (?), a. [F. insolent, L. insolens, -entis, pref. in- not + solens accustomed, p. pr. of solere to be accustomed.]

insolently.c: Insolently In"so*lent*ly, adv. In an insolent manner.

insolidity.c: Insolidity In`so*lid"i*ty (?), n. [Pref. in- not + solidity: cf. F. insolidité.] Lack of solidity; weakness; as, the insolidity of an argument. [R.] Dr. H. More.

insolubility.c: Insolubility In*sol`u*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. insolubilitas: cf. F. insolubilité.]

insoluble.c: Insoluble In*sol"u*ble (?), a. [L. insolubilis indissoluble, that can not be loosed: cf. F. insoluble. See In- not, and Soluble, and cf. Insolvable.]

insolubleness.c: Insolubleness In*sol"u*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being insoluble; insolubility. Boyle.

insolvable.c: Insolvable In*solv"a*ble (?), a. 1. Not solvable; insoluble; admitting no solution or explanation; as, an insolvable problem or difficulty. I. Watts.

insolvency.c: Insolvency In*sol"ven*cy (?), n.; pl. Insolvencies (?). (Law) (a) The condition of being insolvent; the state or condition of a person who is insolvent; the condition of one who is unable to pay his debts as they fall due, or in the usual course of trade and business; as, a merchant's insolvency. (b) Insufficiency to discharge all debts of the owner; as, the insolvency of an estate.

insolvent.c: Insolvent In*sol"vent (?), a. [Pref. in- not + solvent: cf. OF. insolvent.] (Law) (a) Not solvent; not having sufficient estate to pay one's debts; unable to pay one's debts as they fall due, in the ordinary course of trade and business; as, in insolvent debtor. (b) Not sufficient to pay all the debts of the owner; as, an insolvent estate. (c) Relating to persons unable to pay their debts.
Insolvent In*sol"vent, n. (Law) One who is insolvent; as insolvent debtor; -- in England, before 1861, especially applied to persons not traders. Bouvier.

insomnia.c: Insomnia In*som"ni*a (?), n. [L., fr. insomnis sleepless; pref. in- not + somnus sleep.] Lack of sleep; inability to sleep, especially when chronic; wakefulness; sleeplessness.

insomnious.c: Insomnious In*som"ni*ous (?), a. [L. insomniosus, fr. insomnia insomnia.] Restless; sleepless. Blount.

insomuch.c: Insomuch In`so*much" (?), adv. So; to such a degree; in such wise; -- followed by that or as, and formerly sometimes by both. Cf. Inasmuch.

insonorous.c: Insonorous In`so*no"rous (?), a. Not clear or melodious.

insouciant.c: Insouciant ‖In`sou`ciant" (?), a. [F.] Careless; heedless; indifferent; unconcerned. J. S. Mill.

insoul.c: Insoul In*soul" (?), v. t. To set a soul in; reflexively, to fix one's strongest affections on. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

inspan.c: Inspan In*span" (?), v. t. & i. [D. inspannen.] To yoke or harness, as oxen to a vehicle. [South Africa]

inspect.c: Inspect In*spect" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inspected; p. pr. & vb. n. Inspecting.] [L. inspectus, p. p. of inspicere to inspect; pref. in- in + specere to look at, to view: cf. F. inspecter, fr. L. inspectare, freq. fr. inspicere. See Spy.]
Inspect In*spect", n. [L. inspectus. See Inspect, v. t.] Inspection. [Obs.] Thomson.

inspection.c: Inspection In*spec"tion (?), n. [L. inspectio: cf. F. inspection.] 1. The act or process of inspecting or looking at carefully; a strict or prying examination; close or careful scrutiny; investigation. Spenser.

inspective.c: Inspective In*spect"ive (?), a. [L. inspectivus.] Engaged in inspection; inspecting; involving inspection.

inspector.c: Inspector In*spect"or (?), n. [L.: cf. F. inspecteur.] 1. One who inspects, views, or oversees; one to whom the supervision of any work is committed; one who makes an official view or examination, as a military or civil officer; a superintendent; a supervisor; an overseer.

inspectorial.c: Inspectorial In`spec*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to an inspector or to inspection. [R.]

inspectorship.c: Inspectorship In*spect"or*ship (?), n. 1. The office of an inspector.

insperse.c: Insperse In*sperse" (?), v. t. [L. inspersus, p. p. of inspergere to sprinkle upon; pref. in- in, on + spargere to sprinkle.] To sprinkle; to scatter. [Obs.] Bailey.

inspersion.c: Inspersion In*sper"sion (?), n. [L. inspersio.] The act of sprinkling. [Obs.] Chapman.

inspeximus.c: Inspeximus ‖In*spex"i*mus (?), n. [L., we have inspected.] The first word of ancient charters in England, confirming a grant made by a former king; hence, a royal grant.

insphere.c: Insphere In*sphere" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insphered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insphering.] [Cf. Ensphere.] To place in, or as in, an orb a sphere. Cf. Ensphere.

inspirable.c: Inspirable In*spir"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being inspired or drawn into the lungs; inhalable; respirable; admitting inspiration. Harvey.

inspiration.c: Inspiration In`spi*ra"tion (?), n. [F. inspiration, L. inspiratio. See Inspire.]

inspirationist.c: Inspirationist In`spi*ra"tion*ist, n. One who holds to inspiration.

inspirator.c: Inspirator In"spi*ra`tor (?), n. (Mach.) A kind of injector for forcing water by steam. See Injector, n., 2.

inspiratory.c: Inspiratory In*spir"a*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or aiding, inspiration; as, the inspiratory muscles.

inspire.c: Inspire In*spire" (ĭn*spīr"), v. t. [OE. enspiren, OF. enspirer, inspirer, F. inspirer, fr. L. inspirare; pref. in- in + spirare to breathe. See Spirit.]
Inspire In*spire" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Inspired; p. pr. & vb. n. Inspiring.]

inspirer.c: Inspirer In*spir"er (?), n. One who, or that which, inspires. “Inspirer of that holy flame.” Cowper.

inspiring.c: Inspiring In*spir"ing, a. Animating; cheering; moving; exhilarating; as, an inspiring or scene.

inspirit.c: Inspirit In*spir"it (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inspirited; p. pr. & vb. n. Inspiriting.] To infuse new life or spirit into; to animate; to encourage; to invigorate.

inspissate.c: Inspissate In*spis"sate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inspissated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inspissating (?).] [L. inspissatus, p. p. of inspissare to thicken; pref. in- + spissare to thicken, fr. spissus thick.] To thicken or bring to greater consistence, as fluids by evaporation.
Inspissate In*spis"sate (?), a. [L. inspissatus, p. p.] Thick or thickened; inspissated. Greenhill.

inspissation.c: Inspissation In`spis*sa"tion (?), n. The act or the process of inspissating, or thickening a fluid substance, as by evaporation; also, the state of being so thickened.

instability.c: Instability In`sta*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Instabilities (#). [L. instabilitas: cf. F. instabilité.]

instable.c: Instable In*sta"ble (?), a. [L. instabilis: cf. F. instable. See In- not, and Stable, a., and cf. Unstable.] Not stable; not standing fast or firm; unstable; prone to change or recede from a purpose; mutable; inconstant.

install.c: Install In*stall" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Installed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Installing.] [F. installer, LL. installare, fr. pref. in- in + OHG. stal a place, stall, G. stall, akin to E. stall: cf. It. installare. See Stall.] [Written also instal.]

installation.c: Installation In`stal*la"tion (?), n. [F. installation, LL. installatio: cf. It. installazione. See Install.]

instalment.c: instalment installment in*stall"ment, in*stal"ment (?), n. 1. The act of installing; installation.

instance.c: Instance In"stance (?), n. [F. instance, L. instantia, fr. instans. See Instant.]
Instance In"stance (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Instancing (?).] To mention as a case or example; to refer to; to cite; as, to instance a fact. H. Spenser.
Instance In"stance, v. i. To give an example. [Obs.]

instant.c: Instant In"stant (?), a. [L. instans, -antis, p. pr. of instare to stand upon, to press upon; pref. in- in, on + stare to stand: cf. F. instant. See Stand.]
Instant In"stant, n. [F. instant, fr. L. instans standing by, being near, present. See Instant, a.]

instantaneity.c: Instantaneity In*stan`ta*ne"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. instantanéité.] Quality of being instantaneous. Shenstone.

instanter.c: Instanter ‖In*stan"ter (?), adv. [L., vehemently, earnestly. See Instant, n. & a.] Immediately; instantly; at once; as, he left instanter.

instantly.c: Instantly In"stant*ly (?), adv. 1. Without the least delay or interval; at once; immediately. Macaulay.

instar.c: Instar In*star" (?), v. t. To stud as with stars. [R.] “A golden throne instarred with gems.” J. Barlow.

instate.c: Instate In*state" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instated; p. pr. & vb. n. Instating.] To set, place, or establish, as in a rank, office, or condition; to install; to invest; as, to instate a person in greatness or in favor. Shak.

instaurate.c: Instaurate In*stau"rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instaurated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Instaurating (?).] [L. instauratus, p. p. of instaurare to renew. See 1st In-, and Store.] To renew or renovate. [R.]

instauration.c: Instauration In`stau*ra"tion (?), n. [L. instauratio: cf. F. instauration.] Restoration after decay, lapse, or dilapidation; renewal; repair; renovation; renaissance.

instaurator.c: Instaurator In"stau*ra`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. instaurateur.] One who renews or restores to a former condition. [R.] Dr. H. More.

instaure.c: Instaure In*staure" (?), v. t. [See Instaurate.] To renew or renovate; to instaurate. [Obs.] Marston.

insteep.c: Insteep In*steep" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insteeped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insteeping.] To steep or soak; to drench. [R.] “In gore he lay insteeped.” Shak.

instigate.c: Instigate In"sti*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instigated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Instigating (?).] [L. instigatus, p. p. of instigare to instigate; pref. in- in + a root akin to G. stechen to prick, E. stick. See Stick.] To goad or urge forward; to set on; to provoke; to incite; -- used chiefly with reference to evil actions; as, to instigate one to a crime.

instigation.c: Instigation In`sti*ga"tion (?), n. [L. instigatio: cf. F. instigation.] The act of instigating, or the state of being instigated; incitement; esp. to evil or wickedness.

instigator.c: Instigator In"sti*ga`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. instigateur.] One who instigates or incites. Burke.

instill.c: Instill In*still" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instilled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Instilling.] [L. instillare, instillatum; pref. in- in + stillare to drop, fr. stilla a drop: cf. F. instiller. See Distill.] [Written also instil.] 1. To drop in; to pour in drop by drop.

instillation.c: Instillation In`stil*la"tion (?), n. [L. instillatio: cf. F. instillation.] The act of instilling; also, that which is instilled. Johnson.

instiller.c: Instiller In*still"er (?), n. One who instills. Skelton.

instillment.c: Instillment In*still"ment (?), n. The act of instilling; also, that which is instilled. [Written also instilment.]

instimulate.c: Instimulate In*stim"u*late (?), v. t. [Pref. in- not + stimulate.] Not to stimulate; to soothe; to quiet. [Obs.] Cheyne.
Instimulate In*stim"u*late, v. t. [L. instimulatus, p. p. instimulare to stimulate. See 1st In-, and Stimulate.] To stimulate; to excite. [Obs.] Cockeram.

instinct.c: Instinct In*stinct" (?), a. [L. instinctus, p. p. of instinguere to instigate, incite; cf. instigare to instigate. Cf. Instigate, Distinguish.] Urged or stimulated from within; naturally moved or impelled; imbued; animated; alive; quick; as, birds instinct with life.
Instinct In"stinct (ĭn"stĭṉkt), n. [L. instinctus instigation, impulse, fr. instinguere to instigate: cf. F. instinct. See Instinct, a.]
Instinct In*stinct" (ĭn*stĭṉkt"), v. t. To impress, as an animating power, or instinct. [Obs.] Bentley.

instinction.c: Instinction In*stinc"tion (?), n. Instinct; incitement; inspiration. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

instinctive.c: Instinctive In*stinc"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. instinctif.] Of or pertaining to instinct; derived from, or prompted by, instinct; of the nature of instinct; determined by natural impulse or propensity; acting or produced without reasoning, deliberation, instruction, or experience; spontaneous. “Instinctive motion.” Milton. “Instinctive dread.” Cowper.

instinctively.c: Instinctively In*stinc"tive*ly, adv. In an instinctive manner; by force of instinct; by natural impulse.

instinctivity.c: Instinctivity In`stinc*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being instinctive, or prompted by instinct. [R.] Coleridge.

institute.c: Institute In"sti*tute (ĭn"stĭ*tūt), p. a. [L. institutus, p. p. of instituere to place in, to institute, to instruct; pref. in- in + statuere to cause to stand, to set. See Statute.] Established; organized; founded. [Obs.]
Institute In"sti*tute (ĭn"stĭ*tūt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instituted (ĭn"stĭ*tū`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Instituting.]
Institute In"sti*tute, n. [L. institutum: cf. F. institut. See Institute, v. t. & a.]

institution.c: Institution In`sti*tu"tion (?), n. [L. institutio: cf. F. institution.]

institutional.c: Institutional In`sti*tu"tion*al (?), a. 1. Pertaining to, or treating of, an institution or institutions; as, institutional legends.

institutionary.c: Institutionary In`sti*tu"tion*a*ry (?), a. 1. Relating to an institution, or institutions.

institutist.c: Institutist In"sti*tu`tist (?), n. A writer or compiler of, or a commentator on, institutes. [R.] Harvey.
