institutive.c: Institutive In"sti*tu`tive (?), a. 1. Tending or intended to institute; having the power to establish. Barrow.

institutively.c: Institutively In"sti*tu`tive*ly adv. In conformity with an institution. Harrington.

instop.c: Instop In*stop" (?), v. t. To stop; to close; to make fast; as, to instop the seams. [Obs.] Dryden.

instore.c: Instore In*store" (?), v. t. [See Instaurate, Store.] To store up; to inclose; to contain. [Obs.] Wyclif.

instroke.c: Instroke In"stroke` (?), n. An inward stroke; specif., in a steam or other engine, a stroke in which the piston is moving away from the crank shaft; -- opposed to outstroke.

instruct.c: Instruct In*struct" (?), a. [L. instructus, p. p. of instruere to furnish, provide, construct, instruct; pref. in- in, on + struere. See Structure.] 1. Arranged; furnished; provided. [Obs.] “He had neither ship instruct with oars, nor men.” Chapman.
Instruct In*struct" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Instructed; p. pr. & vb. n. Instructing.]

instructible.c: Instructible In*struct"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being instructed; teachable; docible. Bacon.

instruction.c: Instruction In*struc"tion (?), n. [L. instructio: cf. F. instruction.]

instructional.c: Instructional In*struc"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or promoting, instruction; educational.

instructive.c: Instructive In*struct"ive (?), a. [Cf. F. instructif.] Conveying knowledge; serving to instruct or inform; as, experience furnishes very instructive lessons. Addison.

instructor.c: Instructor In*struct"or (?), n. [L., a preparer: cf. F. instructeur.] [Written also instructer.] One who instructs; one who imparts knowledge to another; a teacher.

instructress.c: Instructress In*struct"ress (?), n. A woman who instructs; a preceptress; a governess. Johnson.

instrument.c: Instrument In"stru*ment (?), n. [F. instrument, L. instrumentum. See Instruct.]
Instrument In"stru*ment (?), v. t. 1. To perform upon an instrument; to prepare for an instrument; as, a sonata instrumented for orchestra.

instrumentalism.c: Instrumentalism In`stru*men"tal*ism (?), n. (Philos.) The view that the sanction of truth is its utility, or that truth is genuine only in so far as it is a valuable instrument. -- In`stru*men"tal*ist, n.

instrumentalist.c: Instrumentalist In`stru*men"tal*ist, n. One who plays upon an instrument of music, as distinguished from a vocalist.

instrumentality.c: Instrumentality In`stru*men*tal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Instrumentalities (?). The quality or condition of being instrumental; that which is instrumental; anything used as a means; medium; agency.

instrumentally.c: Instrumentally In`stru*men"tal*ly (?), adv. 1. By means of an instrument or agency; as means to an end. South.

instrumentalness.c: Instrumentalness In`stru*men"tal*ness, n. Usefulness or agency, as means to an end; instrumentality. [R.] Hammond.

instrumentation.c: Instrumentation In`stru*men*ta"tion (?), n. 1. The act of using or adapting as an instrument; a series or combination of instruments; means; agency.

instrumentist.c: Instrumentist In"stru*men`tist (?), n. A performer on a musical instrument; an instrumentalist.

instyle.c: Instyle In*style" (?), v. t. To style. [Obs.] Crashaw.

insuavity.c: Insuavity In*suav"i*ty (?), n. [L. insuavitas: cf. F. insuavité. See In- not, and Suavity.] Lack of suavity; unpleasantness. [Obs.] Burton.

insubjection.c: Insubjection In`sub*jec"tion (?), n. Lack of subjection or obedience; a state of disobedience, as to government.

insubmergible.c: Insubmergible In`sub*mer"gi*ble (?), a. Not capable of being submerged; buoyant. [R.]

insubmission.c: Insubmission In`sub*mis"sion (?), n. Lack of submission; disobedience; noncompliance.

insubordinate.c: Insubordinate In`sub*or"di*nate (?), a. Not submitting to authority; disobedient; rebellious; mutinous.

insubordination.c: Insubordination In`sub*or`di*na"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. insubordination.] The quality of being insubordinate; disobedience to lawful authority.

insubstantial.c: Insubstantial In`sub*stan"tial (?), a. Unsubstantial; not real or strong. “Insubstantial pageant.” [R.] Shak.

insuccation.c: Insuccation In`suc*ca"tion (?), n. [L. insucare, insucatum, to soak in; pref. in- + succus, sucus, sap.] The act of soaking or moistening; maceration; solution in the juice of herbs. [Obs.] Coxe.

insuccess.c: Insuccess In`suc*cess" (?), n. Lack of success. [R.] Feltham.

insue.c: Insue In*sue" (?), v. i. See Ensue, v. i.

insuetude.c: Insuetude In"sue*tude (?), n. [L. insuetudo, from insuetus unaccustomed; pref. in- not + suetus, p. p. of suescere to be accustomed.] The state or quality of being unaccustomed; absence of use or habit.

insufferable.c: Insufferable In*suf"fer*a*ble (?), a. 1. Incapable of being suffered, borne, or endured; insupportable; unendurable; intolerable; as, insufferable heat, cold, or pain; insufferable wrongs. Locke.

insufferably.c: Insufferably In*suf"fer*a*bly, adv. In a manner or to a degree beyond endurance; intolerably; as, a blaze insufferably bright; a person insufferably proud.

insufficiency.c: Insufficiency In`suf*fi"cien*cy (?), n. [L. insufficientia: cf. F. insuffisance, whence OE. insuffisance. See Insufficient.]

insufficient.c: Insufficient In`suf*fi"cient (?), a. [L. insufficiens, -entis. See In- not, and Sufficient.]

insufficiently.c: Insufficiently In`suf*fi"cient*ly, adv. In an insufficient manner or degree; unadequately.

insufflate.c: Insufflate In*suf"flate (?), a. [See Insufflation.] To blow upon; to breath upon or into; to use insufflation upon.

insufflation.c: Insufflation In`suf*fla"tion (?), n. [L. insuffatio: cf. F. insuffation. See In- in, and Sufflation.] The act of breathing on or into anything; especially: (a) (R. C. Ch.) The breathing upon a person in the sacrament of baptism to symbolize the inspiration of a new spiritual life. (b) (Med.) The act of blowing (a gas, powder, or vapor) into any cavity of the body.

insular.c: Insular In"su*lar (?), a. [L. insularis, fr. insula island: cf. F. insulaire. See Isle.]

insularly.c: Insularly In"su*lar*ly (?), adv. In an insular manner.

insulate.c: Insulate In"su*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insulating (?).] [L. insulatus insulated, fr. insula island. See Isle, and cf. Isolate.]

insulated.c: Insulated In"su*la`ted (ĭn"su*lā"tĕd), p. a. 1. Standing by itself; not being contiguous to other bodies; separated; unconnected; isolated; as, an insulated house or column.

insulation.c: Insulation In`su*la"tion (?), n. 1. The act of insulating, or the state of being insulated; detachment from other objects; isolation.

insulator.c: Insulator In"su*la`tor (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, insulates.

insulite.c: Insulite In"su*lite (?), n. (Elec.) An insulating material, usually some variety of compressed cellulose, made of sawdust, paper pulp, cotton waste, etc.

insulous.c: Insulous In"su*lous (?), a. [L. insulosus, fr. insula island.] Abounding in islands. [R.]

insulse.c: Insulse In*sulse" (?), a. [L. insulsus; pref. in- not + salsus salted, fr. salire, salsum, to salt.] Insipid; dull; stupid. [Obs.] Milton.

insulsity.c: Insulsity In*sul"si*ty (?), n. [L. insulsitas.] Insipidity; stupidity; dullness. [Obs.]

insult.c: Insult In"sult (?), n. [L. insultus, fr. insilire to leap upon: cf. F. insulte. See Insult, v. t.]
Insult In*sult" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insulted; p. pr. & vb. n. Insulting.] [F. insulter, L. insultare, freq. fr. insilire to leap into or upon; pref. in- in, on + salire to leap. See Salient.]
Insult In*sult", v. i. 1. To leap or jump.

insultable.c: Insultable In*sult"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being insulted or affronted. [R.] Emerson.

insultation.c: Insultation In`sul*ta"tion (?), n. [L. insultatio, fr. insultare: cf. OF. insultation.]

insulter.c: Insulter In*sult"er (?), n. One who insults. Shak.

insulting.c: Insulting In*sult"ing, a. Containing, or characterized by, insult or abuse; tending to insult or affront; as, insulting language, treatment, etc. -- In*sult"ing*ly, adv.

insultment.c: Insultment In*sult"ment (?), n. Insolent treatment; insult. [Obs.] “My speech of insultment ended.” Shak.

insume.c: Insume In*sume" (?), v. t. [L. insumere; pre. in- in + sumere to take.] To take in; to absorb. [Obs.]

insuperability.c: Insuperability In*su`per*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being insuperable; insuperableness.

insuperable.c: Insuperable In*su"per*a*ble (?), a. [L. insuperabilis: cf. OF. insuperable. See In- not, and Superable.] Incapable of being passed over or surmounted; insurmountable; as, insuperable difficulties.

insupportable.c: Insupportable In`sup*port"a*ble (?), a. [L. insupportabilis: cf. F. insupportable. See In- not, and Support.] Incapable of being supported or borne; unendurable; insufferable; intolerable; as, insupportable burdens; insupportable pain. -- In`sup*port"a*ble*ness, n. -- In`sup*port"a*bly, adv.

insupposable.c: Insupposable In`sup*pos"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being supposed; not supposable; inconceivable.

insuppressible.c: Insuppressible In`sup*press"i*ble (?), a. That can not be suppressed or concealed; irrepressible. Young. -- In`sup*press"i*bly, adv.

insuppressive.c: Insuppressive In`sup*press"ive (?), a. Insuppressible. [Obs.] “The insuppressive mettle of our spirits.” Shak.

insurable.c: Insurable In*sur"a*ble (?), a. [From Insure.] Capable of being insured against loss, damage, death, etc.; proper to be insured.

insurancer.c: Insurancer In*sur"an*cer (?), n. One who effects insurance; an insurer; an underwriter. [Obs.] Dryden.

insurant.c: Insurant In*sur"ant (?), n. The person insured, called also the insured. Champness.

insure.c: Insure In"sure (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Insured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Insuring.] [OE. ensuren, prob. for assuren, by a change of prefix. See 1st In-, and Sure, and cf. Assure, Ensure.] [Written also ensure.]
Insure In*sure", v. i. To underwrite; to make insurance; as, a company insures at three per cent.

insurer.c: Insurer In*sur"er (?), n. One who, or that which, insures; the person or company that contracts to indemnify losses for a premium; an underwriter.

insurgency.c: Insurgency Insurgence { In*sur"gence (?), In*sur"gen*cy (?), } n. A state of insurrection; an uprising; an insurrection.

insurgent.c: Insurgent In*sur"gent (?), a. [L. insurgens, p. pr. of insurgere to rise up; pref. in- in + surgere to rise. See Surge.] Rising in opposition to civil or political authority, or against an established government; insubordinate; rebellious. “The insurgent provinces.” Motley.
Insurgent In*sur"gent, n. [Cf. F. insurgent.] A person who rises in revolt against civil authority or an established government; one who openly and actively resists the execution of laws; a rebel.

insurmountability.c: Insurmountability In`sur*mount`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being insurmountable.

insurmountable.c: Insurmountable In`sur*mount"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + surmountable: cf. F. insurmountable.] Incapable of being passed over, surmounted, or overcome; insuperable; as, insurmountable difficulty or obstacle. Locke.

insurmountableness.c: Insurmountableness In`sur*mount"a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being insurmountable; insurmountability.

insurmountably.c: Insurmountably In`sur*mount"a*bly, adv. In a manner or to a degree not to be overcome.

insurrection.c: Insurrection In`sur*rec"tion (?), n. [L. insurrectio, fr. insurgere, insurrectum: cf. F. insurrection. See Insurgent.]

insurrectional.c: Insurrectional In`sur*rec"tion*al (?), a. [Cf. F. insurrectionnel.] Pertaining to insurrection; consisting in insurrection.

insurrectionary.c: Insurrectionary In`sur*rec"tion*a*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, insurrection; rebellious; seditious.

insurrectionist.c: Insurrectionist In`sur*rec"tion*ist, n. One who favors, or takes part in, insurrection; an insurgent.

insusceptibility.c: Insusceptibility In`sus*cep`ti*bil"i*ty (?), n. Lack of susceptibility, or of capacity to feel or perceive.

insusceptible.c: Insusceptible In`sus*cep`ti*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + susceptible: cf. F. insusceptible.] Not susceptible; not capable of being moved, affected, or impressed; that can not feel, receive, or admit; as, a limb insusceptible of pain; a heart insusceptible of pity; a mind insusceptible to flattery; new strains of bacteria insusceptible to penicillin. -- In`sus*cep`ti*bly adv.

insusceptive.c: Insusceptive In`sus*cep"tive (?), a. Not susceptive or susceptible. [R.] Rambler.

insusurration.c: Insusurration In*su`sur*ra"tion (?), n. [L. insusurratio, fr. insusurrare to whisper into.] The act of whispering into something. [Obs.] Johnson.

inswathe.c: Inswathe In*swathe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Inswathed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Inswating.] To wrap up; to infold; to swathe.

inswept.c: Inswept In"swept` (?), a. Narrowed at the forward end; -- said of an automobile frame when the side members are closer together at the forward end than at the rear.

intact.c: Intact In*tact" (?), a. [L. intactus; pref. in- not + tactus, p. p. of tangere to touch: cf. F. intact. See In- not, and Tact, Tangent.] Untouched, especially by anything that harms, defiles, or the like; uninjured; undefiled; left complete or entire. Buckle.

intactable.c: Intactable Intactible { In*tac"ti*ble (?), In*tac"ta*ble (?) }, a. Not perceptible to the touch.

intagliated.c: Intagliated In*tagl"ia*ted (?), a. [It. intagliato, p. p. of intagliare. See Intaglio.] Engraved in intaglio; as, an intagliated stone. T. Warton.

intaglio.c: Intaglio In*tagl"io (?), n.; pl. E. Intaglius (#), It. Intagli (#). [It., fr. intagliare to engrave, carve; pref. in- in + tagliare to cut, carve. See Detail.] A cutting or engraving; a figure cut into something, as a gem, so as to make a design depressed below the surface of the material; hence, anything so carved or impressed, as a gem, matrix, etc.; -- opposed to cameo. Also used adjectively.

intail.c: Intail In*tail", v. t. See Entail, v. t.

intake.c: Intake In"take` (?), n. 1. The place where water, air, or other substance is taken into a pipe, conduit, or machine; -- opposed to outlet.

intaminated.c: Intaminated In*tam"i*na`ted (?), a. [L. intaminatus. See Contaminate.] Uncontaminated. [Obs.] Wood.

intangibility.c: Intangibility In*tan`gi*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Intangibilities (#). [Cf. F. intangibilité.] The quality or state of being intangible; intangibleness.

intangible.c: Intangible In*tan"gi*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + tangible: cf. F. intangible.] Not tangible; incapable of being touched; not perceptible to the touch; impalpable; imperceptible. Bp. Wilkins.

intastable.c: Intastable In*tast"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being tasted; tasteless; unsavory. [R.] Grew.

integer.c: Integer In"te*ger (?), n. [L. integer untouched, whole, entire. See Entire.] A complete entity; a whole number, in contradistinction to a fraction or a mixed number.

integrability.c: Integrability In`te*gra*bil"i*ty (?), n. (Math.) The quality of being integrable.

integrable.c: Integrable In"te*gra*ble (?), a. (Math.) Capable of being integrated.

integral.c: Integral In"te*gral (?), a. [Cf. F. intégral. See Integer.]
Integral In"te*gral, n. 1. A whole; an entire thing; a whole number; an individual.

integrality.c: Integrality In`te*gral"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. intégralité.] Entireness. [Obs.] Whitaker.

integrally.c: Integrally In"te*gral*ly (?), adv. In an integral manner; wholly; completely; also, by integration.

integrant.c: Integrant In"te*grant (?), a. [L. integrans, -antis, p. pr. of integrare to make whole, renew: cf. F. intégrant. See Integrate.] Making part of a whole; necessary to constitute an entire thing; integral. Boyle.

integrate.c: Integrate In"te*grate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Integrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Integrating (?).] [L. integratus, p. p. of integrare to make whole, renew: cf. F. intégrer. See Integer, Entire.]

integration.c: Integration In`te*gra"tion (ĭn`te*grā"shŭn), n. [L. integratio a renewing, restoring: cf. F. intégration.]

integrator.c: Integrator In"te*gra`tor (?), n. (Math. & Mech.) That which integrates; esp., an instrument by means of which the area of a figure can be measured directly, or its moment of inertia, or statical moment, etc., be determined.

integrity.c: Integrity In*teg"ri*ty (?), n. [L. integritas: cf. F. intégrité. See Integer, and cf. Entirety.]

integropallial.c: Integropallial In`te*gro*pal"li*al (?), a. [L. integer whole + E. pallial.] (Zool.) Having the pallial line entire, or without a sinus, as certain bivalve shells.

integumation.c: Integumation In*teg`u*ma"tion (?), n. [See Integument.] That part of physiology which treats of the integuments of animals and plants.

integument.c: Integument In*teg"u*ment (?), n. [L. integumentum, fr. integere to cover; pref. in- in, on + tegere to cover: cf. F. intégument. See 1st n-, and Tegument.] That which naturally invests or covers another thing, as the testa or the tegmen of a seed; specifically (Anat.), a covering which invests the body, as the skin, or a membrane that invests a particular part.

integumentary.c: Integumentary In*teg`u*men"ta*ry (?), n. Belonging to, or composed of, integuments.

integumentation.c: Integumentation In*teg`u*men*ta"tion (?), n. The act or process of covering with integuments; the state or manner of being thus covered.

intellect.c: Intellect In"tel*lect (?), n. [L. intellectus, fr. intelligere, intellectum, to understand: cf. intellect. See Intelligent.] 1. (Metaph.) The part or faculty of the human mind by which it knows, as distinguished from the power to feel and to will; the power to judge and comprehend; the thinking faculty; the understanding.

intellected.c: Intellected In"tel*lect`ed (?), a. Endowed with intellect; having intellectual powers or capacities. [R.]

intellection.c: Intellection In`tel*lec"tion (?), n. [L. intellectio synecdoche: cf. F. intellection.] A mental act or process; especially: (a) The act of understanding; simple apprehension of ideas; intuition. Bentley. (b) A creation of the mind itself. Hickok.

intellectively.c: Intellectively In`tel*lec"tive*ly, adv. In an intellective manner. [R.] “Not intellectivelly to write.” Warner.

intellectual.c: Intellectual In`tel*lec"tu*al (?; 135), a. [L. intellectualis: cf. F. intellectuel.]
Intellectual In`tel*lec"tu*al, n. 1. The intellect or understanding; mental powers or faculties.

intellectualist.c: Intellectualist In`tel*lec"tu*al*ist (?), n. 1. One who overrates the importance of the understanding. [R.] Bacon.

intellectuality.c: Intellectuality In`tel*lec`tu*al"i*ty (?), n. [L. intellectualitas: cf. F. intellectualité.] Intellectual powers; possession of intellect; quality of being intellectual.

intellectualize.c: Intellectualize In`tel*lec"tu*al*ize (?), v. t. 1. To treat in an intellectual manner; to discuss intellectually; to reduce to intellectual form; to express intellectually; to idealize.

intellectually.c: Intellectually In`tel*lec"tu*al*ly, adv. In an intellectual manner.

intelligence.c: Intelligence In*tel"li*gence (?), n. [F. intelligence, L. intelligentia, intellegentia. See Intelligent.]

intelligencer.c: Intelligencer In*tel"li*gen*cer (?), n. One who, or that which, sends or conveys intelligence or news; a messenger.

intelligencing.c: Intelligencing In*tel"li*gen*cing (?), a. Informing; giving information; talebearing. [Obs.] Shak.

intelligent.c: Intelligent In*tel"li*gent (?), a. [L. intelligens, intellegens, -entis, p. pr. of intelligere, intellegere, to perceive; inter between + legere to gather, collect, choose: cf. F. intelligent. See Legend.]

intelligentiary.c: Intelligentiary In*tel`li*gen"tia*ry (?), n. One who gives information; an intelligencer. [Obs.] Holinshed.

intelligently.c: Intelligently In*tel"li*gent*ly (?), adv. In an intelligent manner; with intelligence.

intelligibility.c: Intelligibility In*tel`li*gi*bil"i*ty (?), [Cf. F. intelligilibilité.] The quality or state of being intelligible; clearness; perspicuity; definiteness.

intelligible.c: Intelligible In*tel"li*gi*ble (?), [L. intellegibilis: cf. F. intelligible. See Intelligent.] Capable of being understood or comprehended; as, an intelligible account or description; intelligible pronunciation, writing, etc.

intelligibleness.c: Intelligibleness In*tel"li*gi*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being intelligible; intelligibility. Locke.

intelligibly.c: Intelligibly In*tel"li*gi*bly, adv. In an intelligible manner; so as to be understood; clearly; plainly; as, to write or speak intelligibly.

intemerated.c: Intemerated Intemerate { In*tem"er*ate (?), In*tem"er*a`ted (?), } a. [L. intemeratus; pref. in- not + temeratus defiled.] Pure; undefiled. [Obs.]

intemerateness.c: Intemerateness In*tem"er*ate*ness (?), n. The state of being unpolluted; purity. [Obs.] Donne.

intemperament.c: Intemperament In*tem"per*a*ment (?), n. A bad state; as, the intemperament of an ulcerated part. [R.] Harvey.

intemperance.c: Intemperance In*tem"per*ance (?), n. [F. intempérance, L. intemperantia. See In- not, and Temperance.]

intemperant.c: Intemperant In*tem"per*ant (?), a. [L. intemperans, -antis. See In- not, and Temperant.] Intemperate. [Obs.]

intemperate.c: Intemperate In*tem`per*ate (?), a. [L. intemperatus. See In- not, and Temperate.] 1. Indulging any appetite or passion to excess; immoderate in enjoyment or exertion.

intemperately.c: Intemperately In*tem`per*ate*ly (?), adv. In an intemperate manner; immoderately; excessively; without restraint.

intemperateness.c: Intemperateness In*tem`per*ate*ness, n. 1. The state of being intemperate; excessive indulgence of any appetite or passion; as, intemperateness in eating or drinking.

intemperature.c: Intemperature In*tem"per*a*ture (?; 135), n. [Cf. OF. intemperature.] Intemperateness. [Obs.] Boyle.

intempestive.c: Intempestive In`tem*pes"tive (?), a. [L. intempestivus: cf. F. intempestif. See In- not, and Tempestive.] Out of season; untimely. [Obs.] Burton.

intempestivity.c: Intempestivity In*tem`pes*tiv"i*ty (?), n. [L. intempestivitas: cf. F. intempestivité.] Unseasonableness; untimeliness. [Obs.] Hales.

intenable.c: Intenable In*ten"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + tenable: cf. F. intenable.] Incapable of being held; untenable; not defensible; as, an intenable opinion; an intenable fortress. [Obs.] Bp. Warburton.

intend.c: Intend In*tend" (ĭn*tĕnd"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intended; p. pr. & vb. n. Intending.] [OE. entenden to be attentive, F. entendre, fr. L. intendre, intentum, and intensum, to intend, attend, stretch out, extend; pref. in- in + tendere to stretch, stretch out. See Tend.]

intendancy.c: Intendancy In*tend"an*cy (?), n.; pl. Intendancies (#). [Cf. F. intendance. See Intendant.]

intendant.c: Intendant In*tend"ant (?), n. [F. intendant, fr. L. intendere to direct (one's thoughts) to a thing. See Intend.] One who has the charge, direction, or management of some public business; a superintendent; as, an intendant of marine; an intendant of finance.

intended.c: Intended In*tend"ed, a. 1. Made tense; stretched out; extended; forcible; violent. [Obs.] Spenser.
Intended In*tend"ed, n. One with whom marriage is designed; one who is betrothed; an affianced lover.

intender.c: Intender In*tend"er (?), n. One who intends. Feltham.

intendiment.c: Intendiment In*tend"i*ment (?), n. [LL. intendimentum. See Intendment.] Attention; consideration; knowledge; understanding. [Obs.] Spenser.

intendment.c: Intendment In*tend"ment (?), n. [OE. entendement understanding, insight, F. entendement, fr. LL. intendimentum. See Intend.]

intenerate.c: Intenerate In*ten"er*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intenerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intenerating.] [Pref. in- in + L. tener soft, tender. See Tender, a.] To make tender or sensitive; to soften.
Intenerate In*ten"er*ate (ĭn*tĕn"ẽr*at), a. Made tender or soft; softened. [Obs.]

inteneration.c: Inteneration In*ten`er*a"tion (ĭn*tĕn`ẽr*ā"shŭn), n. The act or process of intenerating, or the state of being intenerated; softening. [R.] Bacon.

intenible.c: Intenible In*ten"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. in- not + L. tenere to hold: cf. L. intenibilis not to be grasped. Cf. Intenable.] Incapable of holding or containing. [Obs.]

intensate.c: Intensate In*ten"sate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intensated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intensating.] [See Intense.] To intensify. [R.] Emerson.

intensation.c: Intensation In`ten*sa"tion (?), n. The act or process of intensifying; intensification; climax. [R.] Carlyle.

intense.c: Intense In*tense" (?), a. [L. intensus stretched, tight, p. p. of intendere to stretch: cf. F. intense. See Intend, and cf. Intent, and cf. Intent, a.]

intenseness.c: Intenseness In*tense"ness, n. The state or quality of being intense; intensity; as, the intenseness of heat or cold; the intenseness of study or thought.

intensification.c: Intensification In*ten`si*fi*ca"tion (?), n. The act or process of intensifying, or of making more intense.

intensifier.c: Intensifier In*ten"si*fi`er (?), n. One who or that which intensifies or strengthens; in photography, an agent used to intensify the lights or shadows of a picture.

intensify.c: Intensify In*ten"si*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intensified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intensifying (?).] [Intense + -fly.] To render more intense; as, to intensify heat or cold; to intensify colors; to intensify a photographic negative; to intensify animosity. Bacon.
Intensify In*ten"si*fy, v. i. To become intense, or more intense; to act with increasing power or energy.

intension.c: Intension In*ten"sion (?), n. [L. intensio: cf. F. intension. See Intend, and cf. Intention.]

intensitive.c: Intensitive In*ten"si*tive (?), a. Increasing the force or intensity of; intensive; as, the intensitive words of a sentence. H. Sweet.

intensity.c: Intensity In*ten"si*ty (?), n. [LL. intensitas: cf. F. intensité. See Intense.]

intensive.c: Intensive In*ten"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. intensif. See Intense.]
Intensive In*ten"sive, n. That which intensifies or emphasizes; an intensive verb or word.

intensively.c: Intensively In*ten"sive*ly, adv. In an intensive manner; by increase of degree. Abp. Bramhall.

intensiveness.c: Intensiveness In*ten"sive*ness, n. The quality or state of being intensive; intensity. Sir M. Hale.

intent.c: Intent In*tent" (?), a. [L. intentus, p. p. of intendere. See Intend, and cf. Intense.]

Intent In*tent", n. [OE. entent, entente, attention, purpose, OF. entente, F. entente understanding, meaning; a participial noun, fr. F. & OF. entendre. See Intend.] The act of turning the mind toward an object; hence, a design; a purpose; intention; meaning; drift; aim.

intention.c: Intention In*ten"tion (?), n. [F. intention, L. intentio. See Intend, and cf. Intension.]

intentional.c: Intentional In*ten"tion*al (?), a. [Cf. F. intentionnel.] Done by intention or design; intended; designed; as, the act was intentional, not accidental. Opposite of unintentional or unintended.

intentionality.c: Intentionality In*ten`tion*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being intentional; purpose; design. Coleridge.

intentionally.c: Intentionally In*ten"tion*al*ly (?), adv. In an intentional manner; with intention; by design; of purpose.

intentioned.c: Intentioned In*ten"tioned (?), a. Having designs; -- chiefly used in composition; as, well-intentioned, having good designs; ill-intentioned, having ill designs.

intentive.c: Intentive In*ten"tive (?), a. [OE. ententif, OF. ententif, fr. L. intentivus intensive. See Intent, n., and cf. Intensive.] Attentive; intent. [Obs.] Spenser.

intentively.c: Intentively In*ten"tive*ly, adv. Attentively; closely. [Obs.] “Intentively to observe.” Holland.

intentiveness.c: Intentiveness In*ten"tive*ness, n. Closeness of attention or application of mind; attentiveness. [Obs.] W. Montagu.

intently.c: Intently In*tent"ly (?), adv. In an intent manner; as, the eyes intently fixed.

intentness.c: Intentness In*tent"ness, n. The state or quality of being intent; close application; attention.

inter.c: Inter- In"ter- (?). [L. inter, prep., among, between, a compar. form of in in; akin to intra, intro, within, Skr. antar between, in, and E. in. See In, and cf. Entrails, Interior, Enter-, Exterior.] A prefix signifying among, between, amid; as, interact, interarticular, intermit.

Inter In*ter" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interring (?).] [OE. enteren, OF. enterer, enterrer, LL. interrare; L. pref. in- in + terra the earth. See Terrace.] To deposit and cover in the earth; to bury; to inhume; as, to inter a dead body. Shak.

interact.c: Interact In`ter*act" (?), n. [Pref. inter- + act. Cf. Entr'acte.] A short act or piece between others, as in a play; an interlude; hence, intermediate employment or time. Chesterfield.
Interact In`ter*act", v. i. To act upon each other; as, two agents mutually interact. Emerson. Tyndall.

interadditive.c: Interadditive In`ter*ad"di*tive (?), a. Added or placed between the parts of another thing, as a clause inserted parenthetically in a sentence.

interall.c: Interall In"ter*all (?), n. Entrail or inside. [Obs.] G. Fletcher.

interalveolar.c: Interalveolar In`ter*al"ve*o*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between alveoli; as, the interalveolar septa between adjacent air cells in the lungs.

interambulacral.c: Interambulacral In`ter*am`bu*la"cral (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the interambulacra.

interambulacrum.c: Interambulacrum ‖In`ter*am`bu*la"crum (?), n.; pl. L. Interambulacra (?), E. Interambulacrums (?). (Zool.) In echinoderms, one of the areas or zones intervening between two ambulacra. See Illust. of Ambulacrum.

interamnian.c: Interamnian In`ter*am"ni*an (?), a. [Pref. inter- + L. amnis river: cf. L. interamnus.] Situated between rivers. [R.] “An interamnian country.” J. Bryant.

interanimate.c: Interanimate In`ter*an"i*mate (?), v. t. To animate or inspire mutually. [Obs.] Donne.

interarboration.c: Interarboration In`ter*ar`bo*ra"tion (?), n. The interweaving of branches of trees. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

interarticular.c: Interarticular In`ter*ar*tic"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated between joints or articulations; as, interarticular cartilages and ligaments.

interatomic.c: Interatomic In`ter*a*tom"ic (?), a. (Chem. & Physics) Between atoms; situated, or acting, between the atoms of bodies; as, interatomic forces.

interaulic.c: Interaulic In`ter*au"lic (?), a. Existing between royal courts. [R.] “Interaulic politics.” Motley.

interauricular.c: Interauricular In`ter*au*ric"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between the auricles; as, the interauricular partition of the heart.

interaxal.c: Interaxal In`ter*ax"al (?), a. (Arch.) Situated in an interaxis. Gwilt.

interaxillary.c: Interaxillary In`ter*ax"il*la*ry (?), a. (Bot.) Situated within or between the axils of leaves.

interaxis.c: Interaxis In`ter*ax"is (?), n.; pl. Interaxes (?). (Arch.) The space between two axes. See Axis, 6.

interbastation.c: Interbastation In`ter*bas*ta"tion (?), n. [Pref. inter- + baste to sew.] Patchwork. [Obs.] Dr. J. Smith.

interbreed.c: Interbreed In`ter*breed" (?), v. t. & i. To breed by crossing different stocks of animals or plants.

intercalary.c: Intercalary In*ter"ca*la*ry (?; 277), a. [L. intercalaris, intercalarius: cf. F. intercalaire. See Intercalate.]

intercalate.c: Intercalate In*ter"ca*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intercalated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intercalating (?).] [L. intercalatus, p. p. of intercalare to intercalate to intercalate; inter between + calare to call, proclaim. See Calendar.]

intercalation.c: Intercalation In*ter`ca*la"tion (?), n. [L. intercalatio: cf. F. intercalation.]

intercarotid.c: Intercarotid In`ter*ca*rot"id (?), a. (Anat.) Situated between the external and internal carotid arteries; as, an intercarotid ganglion.

intercarpal.c: Intercarpal In`ter*car"pal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the carpal bone; as, intercarpal articulations, ligaments.

intercartilaginous.c: Intercartilaginous In`ter*car`ti*lag"i*nous (?), a. (Anat.) Within cartilage; endochondral; as, intercartilaginous ossification.

intercavernous.c: Intercavernous In`ter*cav"ern*ous (?), a. (Anat.) Between the cavernous sinuses; as, the intercavernous sinuses connecting the cavernous sinuses at the base of the brain.

intercede.c: Intercede In`ter*cede" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Interceded; p. pr. & vb. n. Interceding.] [L. intercedere, intercessum; inter between + cedere to pass: cf. F. intercéder. See Cede.]
Intercede In`ter*cede", v. t. To be, to come, or to pass, between; to separate. [Obs.] Sir I. Newton.

intercedence.c: Intercedence In`ter*ced"ence (?), n. The act of interceding; intercession; intervention. [R.] Bp. Reynolds.

intercedent.c: Intercedent In`ter*ced"ent, a. [L. intercedens, p. pr. of intercedere.] Passing between; mediating; pleading. [R.] -- In`ter*ced"ent*ly, adv.

interceder.c: Interceder In`ter*ced"er (?), n. One who intercedes; an intercessor; a mediator. Johnson.

intercellular.c: Intercellular In`ter*cel"lu*lar (?), a. Lying between cells or cellules; as, intercellular substance, space, or fluids; intercellular blood channels.

intercentrum.c: Intercentrum ‖In`ter*cen"trum (?), n.; pl. Intercentra (?). (Anat.) The median of the three elements composing the centra of the vertebræ in some fossil batrachians.

intercept.c: Intercept In`ter*cept" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intercepted; p. pr. & vb. n. Intercepting.] [L. interceptus, p. p. of intercipere to intercept; inter between + capere to take, seize: cf. F. intercepter. See Capable.]
Intercept In"ter*cept` (?), n. (Math.) A part cut off or intercepted, as a portion of a line included between two points, or cut off two straight lines or curves.

intercepter.c: Intercepter In`ter*cept"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, intercepts. Shak.

interception.c: Interception In`ter*cep"tion (?), n. [L. interceptio a taking away: cf. F. interception.] The act of intercepting; as, interception of a letter; interception of the enemy.

interceptive.c: Interceptive In`ter*cept"ive (?), a. Intercepting or tending to intercept.

intercession.c: Intercession In`ter*ces"sion (?), n. [L. intercessio an intervention, a becoming surety: cf. F. intercession. See Intercede.] The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconcilation; prayer, petition, or entreaty in favor of, or (less often) against, another or others.

intercessional.c: Intercessional In`ter*ces"sion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, of the nature of, or characterized by, intercession or entreaty.

intercessor.c: Intercessor In`ter*ces"sor (?), n. [L., a surety: cf. F. intercesseur.]

intercessory.c: Intercessory In`ter*ces"so*ry (?), a. [LL. intercessorius.] Pertaining to, of the nature of, or characterized by, intercession; interceding; as, intercessory prayer.

interchain.c: Interchain In`ter*chain" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interchained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interchaining.] To link together; to unite closely or firmly, as by a chain.

interchange.c: Interchange In`ter*change" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interchanged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interchanging (?).] [OE. entrechangen, OF. entrechangier. See Inter-, and Change.]
Interchange In`ter*change", v. i. To make an interchange; to alternate. Sir P. Sidney.

interchangeability.c: Interchangeability In`ter*change`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being interchangeable; interchangeableness.

interchangement.c: Interchangement In`ter*change"ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. entrechangement.] Mutual transfer; exchange. [Obs.] Shak.

interchapter.c: Interchapter In`ter*chap"ter (?), n. An intervening or inserted chapter.

intercidence.c: Intercidence In*ter"ci*dence (?), n. [See Intercident.] The act or state of coming or falling between; occurrence; incident. [Obs.] Holland.

intercident.c: Intercident In*ter"ci*dent (?), a. [L. intercidens, -entis, p. pr. of intercidere to fall between; inter between + cadere to fall.] Falling or coming between; happening accidentally. [Obs.] Boyle.

intercipient.c: Intercipient In`ter*cip"i*ent (?), a. [L. intercipiens, -entis, p. pr. of intercipere. See Intercept.] Intercepting; stopping. -- n. One who, or that which, intercepts or stops anything on the passage. Wiseman.

intercision.c: Intercision In`ter*ci"sion (?), n. [L. intercisio a cutting through, fr. intercidere to cut asunder.] A cutting off, through, or asunder; interruption. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

intercitizenship.c: Intercitizenship In`ter*cit"i*zen*ship (?), n. The mutual right to civic privileges, in the different States. Bancroft.

interclavicular.c: Interclavicular In`ter*cla*vic"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Between the clavicles; as, the interclavicular notch of the sternum. (b) Of or pertaining to the interclavicle.

interclose.c: Interclose In`ter*close" (?), v. t. [Pref. inter- + close. See Interclude.] To shut in; to inclose. [Obs.]

intercloud.c: Intercloud In`ter*cloud" (?), v. t. To cloud. [R.] Daniel.

interclude.c: Interclude In`ter*clude" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intercluded; p. pr. & vb. n. Intercluding.] [L. intercludere, interclusum; inter between + claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Interclose.] To shut off or out from a place or course, by something intervening; to intercept; to cut off; to interrupt. Mitford.

interclusion.c: Interclusion In`ter*clu"sion (?), n. [L. interclusio. See Interclude.] Interception; a stopping; obstruction.

intercollegiate.c: Intercollegiate In`ter*col*le"gi*ate (?), a. Existing or carried on between colleges or universities; as, intercollegiate relations, rivalry, games, etc.

intercolline.c: Intercolline In`ter*col"line (?), a. (Geol.) Situated between hills; -- applied especially to valleys lying between volcanic cones.

intercolonial.c: Intercolonial In`ter*co*lo"ni*al (?), a. Between or among colonies; pertaining to the intercourse or mutual relations of colonies; as, intercolonial trade. -- In`ter*co*lo"ni*al*ly, adv.

intercolumnar.c: Intercolumnar In`ter*co*lum"nar (?), a. Between columns or pillars; as, the intercolumnar fibers of Poupart's ligament; an intercolumnar statue.

intercolumniation.c: Intercolumniation In`ter*co*lum`ni*a"tion (?), n. (Arch.) The clear space between two columns, measured at the bottom of their shafts. Gwilt.

intercoming.c: Intercoming In`ter*com"ing (?), n. The act of coming between; intervention; interference. [Obs.]

intercommon.c: Intercommon In`ter*com"mon (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intercommoned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intercommoning.] [OF. entrecommuner. See Inter-, and Common, and cf. Intercommune.]

intercommonage.c: Intercommonage In`ter*com"mon*age (?), n. (O. Eng. Law) The right or privilege of intercommoning.

intercommune.c: Intercommune In`ter*com*mune" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Intercommuned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intercommuning.] [Cf. Intercommon, Intercommunicate, Commune.]

intercommunicable.c: Intercommunicable In`ter*com*mu"ni*ca*ble (?), a. Capable of being mutually communicated.

intercommunicate.c: Intercommunicate In`ter*com*mu"ni*cate (?), v. i. To communicate mutually; to hold mutual communication.
Intercommunicate In`ter*com*mu"ni*cate, v. t. To communicate mutually; to interchange. Holland.

intercommunion.c: Intercommunion In`ter*com*mun"ion (?), n. Mutual communion; as, an intercommunion of deities. Faber.

intercommunity.c: Intercommunity In`ter*com*mu"ni*ty (?), n. Intercommunication; community of possessions, religion, etc.

intercomparison.c: Intercomparison In`ter*com*par"i*son (?), n. Mutual comparison of corresponding parts.

intercondyloid.c: Intercondyloid Intercondylar { In`ter*con"dy*lar (?), In`ter*con"dy*loid (?), } a. (Anat.) Between condyles; as, the intercondylar fossa or notch of the femur.

interconnect.c: Interconnect In`ter*con*nect" (?), v. t. To join together; to connect with one another.

interconnection.c: Interconnection In`ter*con*nec"tion (?), n. Connection between; mutual connection.

intercontinental.c: Intercontinental In`ter*con`ti*nen"tal (?), a. 1. Between or among continents; subsisting or carried on between continents; as, intercontinental relations or commerce.

interconvertible.c: Interconvertible In`ter*con*vert"i*ble (?), a. Convertible the one into the other; as, coin and bank notes are interconvertible.

intercostal.c: Intercostal In`ter*cos"tal (?), a. (Anat. & Physiol.) Between the ribs; pertaining to, or produced by, the parts between the ribs; as, intercostal respiration, in which the chest is alternately enlarged and contracted by the intercostal muscles.

intercourse.c: Intercourse In"ter*course (?), n. [Formerly entercourse, OF. entrecours commerce, exchange, F. entrecours a reciprocal right on neighboring lands, L. intercursus a running between, fr. intercurrere to run between. See Inter-, and Course.] 1. A commingling; intimate connection or dealings between persons or nations, as in common affairs and civilities, in correspondence or trade; communication; commerce; especially, interchange of thought and feeling; association; communion.

intercrop.c: Intercrop In"ter*crop` (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. -cropped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. -cropping.] (Agric.) To cultivate by planting simultaneous crops in alternate rows; as, to intercrop an orchard. Also, to use for catch crops at seasons when the ground is not covered by crops of the regular rotation.
Intercrop In"ter*crop`, n. (Agric.) A crop grown among or between the rows of another crop; a catch crop.

intercross.c: Intercross In`ter*cross" (?; 115), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Intercrossed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intercrossing.]
Intercross In"ter*cross` (?), n. The process or result of cross fertilization between different kinds of animals, or different varieties of plants.

intercrural.c: Intercrural In`ter*cru"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Between crura; -- applied especially to the interneural plates in the vertebral column of many cartilaginous fishes.

intercur.c: Intercur In`ter*cur" (?), v. i. [L. intercurrere. See Intercourse.] To intervene; to come or occur in the meantime. [Obs.] Shelton.

intercurrence.c: Intercurrence In`ter*cur"rence (?), n. [See Intercurrent.] A passing or running between; occurrence. Boyle.

intercurrent.c: Intercurrent In`ter*cur"rent (?), a. [L. intercurrens, p. pr. of intercurrere: cf. F. intercurrent. See Intercur.]

interdash.c: Interdash In`ter*dash" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interdashed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interdashing.] To dash between or among; to intersperse. Cowper.

interdeal.c: Interdeal In`ter*deal", v. i. To intrigue. [Obs.] Daniel.

interdenominational.c: Interdenominational In`ter*de*nom`i*na"tion*al (?), a. Occurring between or among, or common to, different denominations; as, interdenominational fellowship or belief.

interdental.c: Interdental In`ter*den"tal (?), a. 1. Situated between teeth; as, an interdental space, the space between two teeth in a gear wheel.

interdentil.c: Interdentil In`ter*den"til (?), n. (Arch.) The space between two dentils. Gwilt.

interdependence.c: Interdependence In`ter*de*pend"ence (?), n. Mutual dependence. “The interdependence of virtue and knowledge.” M. Arnold.

interdependency.c: Interdependency In`ter*de*pend"en*cy (?), n. Mutual dependence; as, interdependency of interests. De Quincey.

interdict.c: Interdict In`ter*dict" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interdicted; p. pr. & vb. n. Interdicting.] [OE. entrediten to forbid communion, L. interdicere, interdictum. See Interdict, n.]
Interdict In"ter*dict` (?), n. [OE. entredit, enterdit, OF. entredit, F. interdit, fr. L. interdictum, fr. interdicere to interpose, prohibit; inter between + dicere to say. See Diction.]

interdiction.c: Interdiction In`ter*dic"tion (?), n. [L. interdictio: cf. F. interdiction.] The act of interdicting; prohibition; prohibiting decree; curse; interdict.

interdictive.c: Interdictive In`ter*dict"ive (?), a. Having the power to prohibit; as, an interdictive sentence. Milton.

interdictory.c: Interdictory In`ter*dict"o*ry (?), a. [L. interdictorius.] Belonging to an interdiction; prohibitory.

interdigital.c: Interdigital In`ter*dig"i*tal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the fingers or toes; as, interdigital space.

interdigitate.c: Interdigitate In`ter*dig"i*tate, v. i. [Pref. inter- + L. digitus finger.] To interlock, as the fingers of two hands that are joined; to be interwoven; to commingle. Owen.

interdigitation.c: Interdigitation In`ter*dig`i*ta"tion (?), n. (Anat.) The state of interdigitating; interdigital space. Owen.

interdome.c: Interdome In"ter*dome` (?), n. (Arch.) The open space between the inner and outer shells of a dome or cupola of masonry.

interduce.c: Interduce In"ter*duce (?), n. [Cf. F. entre-deux, literally, between two.] (Carp.) An intertie.

interepimeral.c: Interepimeral In"ter*e*pim"er*al (?), a. (Zool.) Between the epimeral plates of insects and crustaceans.

interequinoctial.c: Interequinoctial In`ter*e`qui*noc"tial (?), a. Coming between the equinoxes.

interess.c: Interess In"ter*ess (?), v. t. [See Interest, v. t.] To interest or affect. [Obs.] Hooker.

interest.c: Interest In"ter*est (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interested (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interesting.] [From interess'd, p. p. of the older form interess, fr. F. intéresser, L. interesse. See Interest, n.]

Interest In"ter*est, n. [OF. interest, F. intérêt, fr. L. interest it interests, is of interest, fr. interesse to be between, to be difference, to be importance; inter between + esse to be; cf. LL. interesse usury. See Essence.]

interestedness.c: Interestedness In"ter*est*ed*ness, n. The state or quality of being interested; selfishness. Richardson.

interesting.c: Interesting In"ter*est*ing, a. Engaging the attention; exciting, or adapted to excite, interest, curiosity, or emotion; as, an interesting story; interesting news. Cowper.

interestingly.c: Interestingly In"ter*est*ing*ly, adv. In an interesting manner.

interestingness.c: Interestingness In"ter*est*ing*ness, n. The condition or quality of being interesting. A. Smith.

interfacial.c: Interfacial In`ter*fa"cial (?), a. (Geom.) 1. Included between two plane surfaces or faces; as, an interfacial angle.

interfascicular.c: Interfascicular In`ter*fas*cic"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between fascicles or bundles; as, the interfascicular spaces of connective tissue.

interferant.c: Interferant In`ter*fer"ant (?), n. (Law) One of the contestants in interference before the Patent Office. [U.S.]

interfere.c: Interfere In`ter*fere" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Interfered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interfering.] [OF. entreferir to strike each other; entre between (L. inter) + OF. ferir to strike, F. férir, fr. L. ferire. See Ferula.]

interferingly.c: Interferingly In`ter*fer"ing*ly, adv. By or with interference.

interferometer.c: Interferometer In`ter*fe*rom"e*ter (?), n. [See Interfere and -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring small movements, distances, or displacements by means of the interference of two beams of light; -- formerly also called also refractometer, but that word now has a different meaning.

interflow.c: Interflow In`ter*flow" (?), v. i. To flow in. [R.] Holland.

interfluous.c: Interfluous Interfluent { In*ter"flu*ent (?), In*ter"flu*ous (?), } a. [L. interfluens, p. pr., and interfluus. See Inter-, and Fluent.] Flowing between or among; intervening. Boyle.

interfolded.c: Interfolded In`ter*fold"ed (?), p. a. Intertwined; interlocked; clasped together. Longfellow.

interfoliaceous.c: Interfoliaceous In`ter*fo`li*a"ceous (?), a. [Pref. inter- + foliaceous: cf. F. interfoliacé.] (Bot.) At the same node with opposite or whorled leaves, but occupying a position between their places of attachment.

interfoliate.c: Interfoliate In`ter*fo"li*ate (?), v. t. [Pref. inter- + L. folium leaf.] To interleave. [Obs.] Evelyn.

interfollicular.c: Interfollicular In`ter*fol*lic"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between follicles; as, the interfollicular septa in a lymphatic gland.

interfretted.c: Interfretted In`ter*fret"ted (?), a. (Her.) Interlaced; linked together; -- said of charges or bearings. See Fretted.

interfulgent.c: Interfulgent In`ter*ful"gent (?), a. [L. interfulgens, p. pr. See Inter-, and Fulgent.] Shining between.

interfuse.c: Interfuse In`ter*fuse" (?), v. t. [L. interfusus, p. p. of interfundere to pour between; inter between + fundere to pour. See Fuse to melt.]

interfusion.c: Interfusion In`ter*fu"sion (?), n. [L. interfusio.] The act of interfusing, or the state of being interfused. Coleridge.

interganglionic.c: Interganglionic In`ter*gan`gli*on"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Between and uniting the nervous ganglions; as, interganglionic cords.

interglobular.c: Interglobular In`ter*glob"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between globules; -- applied esp. to certain small spaces, surrounded by minute globules, in dentine.

intergrave.c: Intergrave In`ter*grave" (?), v. t. [imp. Intergraved (?); p. p. Intergraved or Intergraven (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intergraving.] To grave or carve between; to engrave in the alternate sections.

interhaemal.c: Interhaemal Interhemal { In`ter*he"mal, In`ter*hæ"mal } (?), a. (Anat.) Between the hemal arches or hemal spines. -- n. An interhemal spine or cartilage.

interhyal.c: Interhyal In`ter*hy"al (?), a. [Inter- + the Greek letter?.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to a segment sometimes present at the proximal end of the hyoidean arch. -- n. An interhyal ligament or cartilage.

interim.c: Interim In"ter*im (?), n. [L., fr. inter between + im, an old accusative of is he, this, that.]

interior.c: Interior In*te"ri*or (?), a. [L., compar. fr. inter between: cf. F. intérieur. See Inter-, and cf. Intimate.]
Interior In*te"ri*or, n. 1. That which is within; the internal or inner part of a thing; the inside.

interiority.c: Interiority In*te`ri*or"i*ty (?), n. State of being interior.

interjacency.c: Interjacency Interjacence { In`ter*ja"cence (?), In`ter*ja"cen*cy (?), } n. [See Interjacent.] The state of being between; a coming or lying between or among; intervention; also, that which lies between.

interjacent.c: Interjacent In`ter*ja"cent (?), a. [L. interjacens, -entis, p. pr. of interjacere to lie between; inter between + jacēre to lie.] Lying or being between or among; intervening; as, interjacent isles. Sir W. Raleigh.

interjaculate.c: Interjaculate In`ter*jac"u*late (?), v. t. To ejaculate parenthetically. [R.] Thackeray.

interjangle.c: Interjangle In`ter*jan"gle (?), v. i. To make a dissonant, discordant noise one with another; to talk or chatter noisily. [R.] Daniel.

interject.c: Interject In`ter*ject" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interjected; p. pr. & vb. n. Interjecting.] [L. interjectus, p. p. of interjicere to interject; inter between + jacĕre to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.] To throw in between; to insert; to interpose. Sir H. Wotton.
Interject In`ter*ject", v. i. To throw one's self between or among; to come between; to interpose. Sir G. Buck.

interjection.c: Interjection In`ter*jec"tion (?), n. [L. interjectio: cf. F. interjection. See Interject.]

interjectional.c: Interjectional In`ter*jec"tion*al (?), a. 1. Thrown in between other words or phrases; parenthetical; ejaculatory; as, an interjectional remark.

interjectionalize.c: Interjectionalize In`ter*jec"tion*al*ize (?), v. t. To convert into, or to use as, an interjection. Earle.

interjectionally.c: Interjectionally In`ter*jec"tion*al*ly, adv. In an interjectional manner. G. Eliot.

interjoin.c: Interjoin In`ter*join" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interjoined; p. pr. & vb. n. Interjoining.] [Pref. inter + join.] To join mutually; to unite. [R.] Shak.

interjoist.c: Interjoist In"ter*joist` (?), n. (Carp.) 1. The space or interval between two joists. Gwilt.

interjunction.c: Interjunction In`ter*junc"tion (?), n. [L. interjunctus, p. p. of interjungere to join together. See Inter-, and Join, and cf. Interjoin.] A mutual joining. [R.]

interknit.c: Interknit In`ter*knit" (?), v. t. To knit together; to unite closely; to intertwine.

interknow.c: Interknow In`ter*know" (?), v. t. To know mutually. [Obs.]

interknowledge.c: Interknowledge In`ter*knowl"edge (?), n. Mutual knowledge or acquaintance. [Obs.] Bacon.

interlace.c: Interlace In`ter*lace" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Interlaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interlacing (?).] [OE. entrelacen, F. entrelacer. See Inter-, and Lace.] To unite, as by lacing together; to insert or interpose one thing within another; to intertwine; to interweave.

interlacement.c: Interlacement In`ter*lace"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. entrelacement.] The act of interlacing, or the state of being interlaced; also, that which is interlaced.

interlaminar.c: Interlaminar Interlamellar { In`ter*lam"el*lar (?), In`ter*lam"i*nar (?) }, a. (Anat.) Between lammellæ or laminæ; as, interlamellar spaces.

interlaminated.c: Interlaminated In`ter*lam"i*na`ted (?), a. Placed between, or containing, laminæ or plates.

interlamination.c: Interlamination In`ter*lam`i*na"tion (?), n. The state of being interlaminated.

interlapse.c: Interlapse In"ter*lapse` (?), n. [Pref. inter- + lapse: cf. L. interlabi, interlapsus, to fall, slide, or flow, between.] The lapse or interval of time between two events. [R.] Harvey.

interlard.c: Interlard In`ter*lard" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interlarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Interlarding.] [F. entrelarder. See Inter-, and Lard.]

interlay.c: Interlay In`ter*lay" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interlaid (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interlaying.] To lay or place among or between. Daniel.

interleaf.c: Interleaf In"ter*leaf` (?), n.; pl. Interleaves (#). [See Interleave.] A leaf inserted between other leaves; a blank leaf inserted, as in a book.

interleave.c: Interleave In`ter*leave" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interleaved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interleaving.] [Pref. inter- + leaf.] 1. To insert a leaf or leaves in; to bind with blank leaves inserted between the others; as, to interleave a book.

interlibel.c: Interlibel In`ter*li"bel (?), v. t. To libel mutually.

interline.c: Interline In`ter*line" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interlined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interlining.] [Pref. inter- + line: cf. LL. interlineare, F. interlinéer, OF. entreligner.]

interlinear.c: Interlinear Interlineal { In`ter*lin"e*al (?), In`ter*lin"e*ar (?), } a. [Cf. LL. interlinearis, F. interlinéaire.] Contained between lines; written or inserted between lines already written or printed; containing interlineations; as, an interlinear manuscript, translation, etc. -- In`ter*lin"e*ar*ly, adv.

interlineary.c: Interlineary In`ter*lin"e*a*ry (?), a. Interlinear. -- n. A book containing interlineations. [R.]

interlining.c: Interlining In`ter*lin"ing (?), n. Correction or alteration by writing between the lines; interlineation. Bp. Burnet.

interlink.c: Interlink In`ter*link" (?), v. t. To link together; to join, as one chain to another. Dryden.
Interlink In`ter*link" (?), n. An intermediate or connecting link.

interlobar.c: Interlobar In`ter*lo"bar (?), a. (Anat.) Between lobes; as, the interlobar notch of the liver; the interlobar ducts of a gland.

interlobular.c: Interlobular In`ter*lob"u*lar (?), a. [Pref. inter- + lobular: cf. F. interlobulaire.] (Anat.) Between lobules; as, the interlobular branches of the portal vein.

interlocation.c: Interlocation In`ter*lo*ca"tion (?), n. A placing or coming between; interposition.

interlock.c: Interlock In`ter*lock" (?), v. i. To unite, embrace, communicate with, or flow into, one another; to be connected in one system; to lock into one another; to interlace firmly.
Interlock In`ter*lock", v. t. 1. To unite by locking or linking together; to secure in place by mutual fastening.

interlocution.c: Interlocution In`ter*lo*cu"tion (?), n. [L. interlocutio, from interloqui, interlocutus, to speak between; inter between + loqui to speak: cf. F. interlocution. See Loquacious.]

interlocutory.c: Interlocutory In`ter*loc"u*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. LL. interlocutorius, F. interlocutoire.]
Interlocutory In`ter*loc"u*to*ry, n. [Cf. F. interlocutoire.] Interpolated discussion or dialogue.

interlope.c: Interlope In`ter*lope" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Interloped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interloping.] [See Interloper.] To run between parties and intercept without right the advantage that one should gain from the other; to traffic without a proper license; to intrude; to forestall others; to intermeddle.

interloper.c: Interloper In"ter*lo`per (?; 277), n. [Pref. inter- + D. looper a runner, fr. loopen to run; akin to E. leap. See Leap, and cf. Elope.] One who interlopes; one who unlawfully intrudes upon a property, a station, or an office; one who interferes wrongfully or officiously.

interlucate.c: Interlucate In`ter*lu"cate (?), v. t. [L. interlucatus, p. p. of interlucare; inter between + lux, lucis, light.] To let in light upon, as by cutting away branches. [Obs.]

interlucation.c: Interlucation In`ter*lu*ca"tion (?), n. [L. interlucatio.] Act of thinning a wood to let in light. [Obs.] Evelyn.

interlucent.c: Interlucent In`ter*lu"cent (?), a. [L. interlucens, p. pr. See Inter-, and Lucent.] Shining between.

interlude.c: Interlude In`ter*lude (?), n. [OE. enterlude, LL. interludium; LL. inter between + ludus play, fr. ludere to play: cf. F. interlude. See Ludicrous.]

interluded.c: Interluded In"ter*lu`ded (?), a. Inserted in the manner of an interlude; having or containing interludes.

interluder.c: Interluder In"ter*lu`der (?), n. An actor who performs in an interlude. B. Jonson.

interluency.c: Interluency In"ter*lu`en*cy (?), n. [L. interluens, p. pr. of interluere to flow between; inter + luere.] A flowing between; intervening water. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

interlunary.c: Interlunary Interlunar { In`ter*lu"nar (?), In`ter*lu"na*ry (?), } a. [Pref. inter- + lunar: cf. L. interlunis.] Belonging or pertaining to the time when the moon, at or near its conjunction with the sun, is invisible. Milton.

intermandibular.c: Intermandibular In`ter*man*dib"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between the mandibles; interramal; as, the intermandibular space.

intermarriage.c: Intermarriage In`ter*mar"riage (?), n. Connection by marriage; reciprocal marriage; giving and taking in marriage, as between two families, tribes, races, castes, or nations.

intermarry.c: Intermarry In`ter*mar"ry (?), v. i. To become connected by marriage between their members; to give and take mutually in marriage; -- said of families, ranks, races, castes, etc.

intermaxillary.c: Intermaxillary In`ter*max"il*la*ry (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Between the maxillary bones. (b) Of or pertaining to the intermaxillæ. -- n. An intermaxilla.

intermean.c: Intermean In"ter*mean` (?), n. Something done in the meantime; interlude. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

intermeation.c: Intermeation In`ter*me*a"tion (?), n. [L. intermeare, intermeatum; to go between; inter between + meare to go.] A flowing between. [Obs.] Bailey.

intermeddle.c: Intermeddle In`ter*med"dle (?), v. i. [OE. entremedlen, entermellen, to mix together, OF. entremedler, entremeller, entremesler, F. entremêler. Intermeddle In`ter*med"dle (?), v. t. To intermix; to mingle. [Obs.]

intermediacy.c: Intermediacy In`ter*me"di*a*cy (?), n. [From Intermediate.] Interposition; intervention. Derham.

intermediae.c: Intermediae ‖In`ter*me"di*æ (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. intermedius intermedial.] (Zool.) The middle pair of tail feathers, or middle rectrices.

intermedial.c: Intermedial In`ter*me"di*al (?), a. [Pref. inter- + medial: cf. L. intermedius.] Lying between; intervening; intermediate. “Intermedial colors.” Evelyn.

Intermediary In`ter*me"di*a*ry, n.; pl. Intermediaries (?). One who, or that which, is intermediate; an interagent; a go-between; a mediator.

intermediate.c: Intermediate In`ter*me"di*ate (?), a. [Pref. inter- + mediate: cf. F. intermédiat.] 1. Lying or being in the middle place or degree, or between two extremes; coming or done between; intervening; interposed; interjacent; as, an intermediate space or time; intermediate colors.

intermediately.c: Intermediately In`ter*me"di*ate*ly (?), adv. In an intermediate manner; by way of intervention.

intermediation.c: Intermediation In`ter*me`di*a"tion (?), n. The act of coming between; intervention; mediation; interposition. Burke.

intermedium.c: Intermedium In`ter*me"di*um (?), n.; pl. Intermediums (#), L. Intermedia (#). [NL., neut. of L. intermedius intermediate.]

intermembral.c: Intermembral In`ter*mem"bral (?), a. (Anat.) Between members or limbs; as, intermembral homology, the correspondence of the limbs with each other.

intermetacarpal.c: Intermetacarpal In`ter*me`ta*car"pal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the metacarpal bones.

intermetatarsal.c: Intermetatarsal In`ter*me`ta*tar"sal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the metatarsal bones.

intermezzo.c: Intermezzo ‖In`ter*mez"zo (?), n. [It. See Intermede.] (Mus.) An interlude; an intermede. See Intermede.

intermicate.c: Intermicate In`ter*mi"cate (?), v. i. [L. intermicare; inter- between + micare to glitter.] To flash or shine between or among. [R.] Blount.

intermication.c: Intermication In`ter*mi*ca"tion (?), n. A shining between or among. [R.] Smart.

intermigration.c: Intermigration In`ter*mi*gra"tion (?), n. Reciprocal migration; interchange of dwelling place by migration. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

interminable.c: Interminable In*ter"mi*na*ble (?), a. [L. interminabilis: cf. F. interminable. See Terminate.] Without termination; admitting no limit; boundless; endless; wearisomely protracted; as, interminable space or duration; interminable sufferings; an interminable sermon.

interminableness.c: Interminableness In*ter"mi*na*ble*ness, n. The state of being endless.

interminably.c: Interminably In*ter"mi*na*bly, adv. Without end or limit.

interminate.c: Interminate In*ter"mi*nate, a. [L. interminatus; in- not + terminatus, p. p. of terminate.] Endless; as, interminate sleep. Chapman.
Interminate In*ter"mi*nate (?), v. t. [L. interminatus, p. p. of interminari; inter between + minari to threaten.] To menace; to threaten. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

interminated.c: Interminated In*ter"mi*na`ted (?), a. Interminable; interminate; endless; unending. [Obs.] Akenside.

Intermingle In`ter*min"gle, v. i. To be mixed or incorporated.

intermise.c: Intermise In"ter*mise (?), n. [Cf. F. entremise. See Intermission.] Interference; interposition. [Obs.] Bacon.

intermission.c: Intermission In`ter*mis"sion (?), n. [L. intermissio: cf. F. intermission. See Intermit.]

intermissive.c: Intermissive In`ter*mis"sive (?), a. Having temporary cessations; not continual; intermittent. “Intermissive miseries.” Shak. “Intermissive wars.” Howell.

intermit.c: Intermit In`ter*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intermitted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intermitting.] [L. intermittere; inter between + mittere, missum, to send: cf. intermittent.c: Intermittent In`ter*mit"tent (?), a. [L. intermittens, -entis, p. pr. of intermittere: cf. F. intermittent.] Coming and going at intervals; alternating; recurrent; periodic; as, an intermittent fever. Boyle.

intermittently.c: Intermittently In`ter*mit"tent*ly, adv. With intermissions; in an intermittent manner; intermittingly.

intermittingly.c: Intermittingly In`ter*mit"ting*ly (?), adv. With intermissions; at intervals. W. Montagu.

intermix.c: Intermix In`ter*mix" (?), v. t. To mix together; to intermingle.
Intermix In`ter*mix", v. i. To be mixed together; to be intermingled.

intermixedly.c: Intermixedly In`ter*mix"ed*ly (?), adv. In a mixed manner.

intermixture.c: Intermixture In`ter*mix"ture (?; 135), n. 1. A mass formed by mixture; a mass of ingredients mixed. Boyle.

intermobility.c: Intermobility In`ter*mo*bil"i*ty (?), n. Capacity of things to move among each other; as, the intermobility of fluid particles.

intermodillion.c: Intermodillion In`ter*mo*dil"lion (?), n. (Arch.) The space between two modillions.

intermontane.c: Intermontane In`ter*mon"tane (?), a. [Pref. inter- + L. montanus belonging to a mountain, fr. mons, montis, mountain.] Between mountains; as, intermontane soil.

intermundane.c: Intermundane In`ter*mun"dane (?), a. Being, between worlds or orbs. [R.] “Intermundane spaces.” Locke.

intermural.c: Intermural In`ter*mu"ral (?), a. 1. Lying between walls; inclosed by walls.

intermure.c: Intermure In`ter*mure" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Intermured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Intermuring.] [Pref. inter- + L. murus wall.] To wall in; to inclose. [Obs.] Ford.

intermuscular.c: Intermuscular In`ter*mus"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between muscles; as, intermuscular septa.

intermutation.c: Intermutation In`ter*mu*ta"tion (?), n. Interchange; mutual or reciprocal change.

intermutual.c: Intermutual In`ter*mu"tu*al (?; 135), a. Mutual. [Obs.] Daniel. -- In`ter*mu"tu*al*ly, adv. [Obs.]

intern.c: Intern In*tern" (?), a. [L. internus: cf. F. interne. See Internal.] Internal. [Obs.] Howell.

Intern In*tern", v. t. [F. interne. See Intern, a.] 1. To put for safe keeping in the interior of a place or country; to confine to one locality; as, to intern troops which have fled for refuge to a neutral country.

intern in*tern" (?), n. [F.] (F. pron. ăN`târn") 1. (Med.) A resident physician in a hospital, especially one who has recently received the Doctorate and is practising under supervision of experienced physicians, as a continuation of the training process; a house physician; also called houseman in Britain. [Also spelled interne.]

internal.c: Internal In*tern"al (?), a. [L. internus; akin to interior. See Interior.]

internalcombustion.c: Internal-combustion engine Internal-combustion In*ter"nal-com*bus"tion, a. (Mach.) Designating, or pertaining to, any engine (called an Internal-combustion engine) in which the heat or pressure energy necessary to produce motion is developed in the engine cylinder, as by the explosion of a gas, and not in a separate chamber, as in a steam-engine boiler. The gas used may be a fixed gas, or one derived from alcohol, ether, gasoline (petrol), naphtha, oil (petroleum), etc. There are three main classes: (1) gas engines proper, using fixed gases, as coal, blast-furnace, or producer gas; (2) engines using the vapor of a volatile fluid, as the typical gasoline (petrol) engine; (3) oil engines, using either an atomized spray or the vapor (produced by heat) of a comparatively heavy oil, as petroleum or kerosene. In all of these the gas is mixed with a definite amount of air, the charge is composed in the cylinder and is then exploded either by a flame of gas (flame ignition -- now little used), by a hot tube (tube ignition) or the like, by an electric spark (electric ignition, the usual method is gasoline engines, or by the heat of compression, as in the Diesel engine. Gas and oil engines are chiefly of the stationary type. Gasoline engines are largely used for automobile vehicles, boats, etc. Most internal-combustion engines use the Otto (four-stroke) cycle, though many use the two-stroke cycle. They are almost universally trunk engines and single-acting. Because of the intense heat produced by the frequent explosions, the cylinders must be cooled by a water jacket (water-cooled) or by air currents (air cooled) to give the maximum thermodynamic efficiency and to avoid excessive friction or seizing.

internality.c: Internality In`ter*nal"i*ty (?), n. The state of being internal or within; interiority.

internally.c: Internally In*ter"nal*ly (?), adv. 1. Inwardly; within the enveloping surface, or the boundary of a thing; within the body; beneath the surface.

internasal.c: Internasal In`ter*na"sal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the nasal cavities; as, the internasal cartilage.

international.c: International In`ter*na"tion*al (?), a. [Pref. inter- + national: cf. F. international.]

internationalism.c: Internationalism In`ter*na"tion*al*ism (?), n. 1. The state or principles of international interests and intercourse.

internationalist.c: Internationalist In`ter*na"tion*al*ist, n. 1. One who is versed in the principles of international law.

internationalize.c: Internationalize In`ter*na"tion*al*ize (?), v. t. To make international; to cause to affect the mutual relations of two or more nations; as, to internationalize a principle of law, or a philanthropic enterprise.

internationally.c: Internationally In`ter*na"tion*al*ly, adv. In an international manner; from an international point of view.

interne.c: Interne In*terne" (?), n. [See Intern, a.] That which is within; the interior. [Poetic] Mrs. Browning.

internecine.c: Internecine In`ter*ne"cine (?), a. [L. internecinus deadly, murderous, fr. internecare to kill, to slaughter; inter between + necare to kill; akin to Gr.? dead. See Necromancy.] 1. Involving, or accompanied by, mutual slaughter; mutually destructive.

internecion.c: Internecion In`ter*ne"cion (?), n. [L. internecio.] Mutual slaughter or destruction; massacre. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.

internecive.c: Internecive In`ter*ne"cive (?), a. [L. internecivus.] Internecine. [R.] Sydney Smith.

internection.c: Internection In`ter*nec"tion (?), n. [L. internectere to bind together; inter between + nectere to fasten.] Intimate connection. [Obs.] W. Montagu.

interneural.c: Interneural In`ter*neu"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Between the neural arches or neural spines. -- n. An interneural spine or cartilage.

internity.c: Internity In*ter"ni*ty (?), n. State of being within; interiority. [R.] H. Brooke.

internment.c: Internment In*tern"ment (?), n. [F. internement. See Intern.] 1. Confinement within narrow limits, -- as of foreign troops, to the interior of a country.

internodal.c: Internodal In`ter*no"dal (?), a. Of or pertaining to internodes; intervening between nodes or joints.

internode.c: Internode In"ter*node` (?), n. [L. internodium; inter between + nodus knot.]

internuncio.c: Internuncio In`ter*nun"ci*o (?), n.; pl. Internuncios (#). [L. internuntius; inter between + nuntius, nuncius, messenger: cf. It. internunzio. See Nuncio.]

internuncioship.c: Internuncioship In`ter*nun"ci*o*ship, n. The office or function of an internuncio. Richardson.

interoceanic.c: Interoceanic In`ter*o`ce*an"ic (?), a. Between oceans; connecting oceans; as, interoceanic communication; an interoceanic canal.

interocular.c: Interocular In`ter*oc"u*lar (?), a. Between, or within, the eyes; as, the interocular distance; situated between the eyes, as the antennæ of some insects.

interopercular.c: Interopercular In`ter*o*per"cu*lar (?), a. Of or pertaining to the interoperculum. -- n. The interopercular bone.

interoperculum.c: Interoperculum ‖In`ter*o*per"cu*lum (?), n.; pl. -la (-lȧ). (Anat.) The postero-inferior opercular bone, in fishes.

interorbital.c: Interorbital In`ter*or"bit*al (?), a. (Anat.) Between the orbits; as, the interorbital septum.

interosculant.c: Interosculant In`ter*os"cu*lant (?), a. 1. Mutually touching or intersecting; as, interosculant circles.

interosculate.c: Interosculate In`ter*os"cu*late (?), v. i. & t. 1. To kiss together to touch. See Osculate.

interosseous.c: Interosseous Interosseal { In`ter*os"se*al (?), In`ter*os"se*ous (?), } a. [Pref. inter- + osseous: cf. F. interosseux.] (Anat.) Situated between bones; as, an interosseous ligament.

interpale.c: Interpale In`ter*pale" (?), v. t. 1. To place pales between or among; to separate by pales.

interparietal.c: Interparietal In`ter*pa*ri"e*tal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the parietal bones or cartilages; as, the interparietal suture. -- n. The interparietal bone or cartilage.

interpedencular.c: Interpedencular In`ter*pe*den"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Between peduncles; esp., between the peduncles, or crura, of the cerebrum.

interpel.c: Interpel In`ter*pel" (?), v. t. [L. interpellare, interpellatum; inter between + pellare (in comp.), akin to pellere to drive: cf. F. interpeller. Cf. Interpellate.] To interrupt, break in upon, or intercede with. [Obs.]

interpellant.c: Interpellant In`ter*pel"lant (?), a. [L. interpellans, p. pr. See Interpel.] Interpelling; interrupting. -- n. One who, or that which, interpels.

interpellate.c: Interpellate In`ter*pel"late (?), v. t. [See Interpel.] To question imperatively, as a minister, or other executive officer, in explanation of his conduct; -- generally on the part of a legislative body.

interpellation.c: Interpellation In`ter*pel*la"tion (?), n. [L. interpellatio: cf. F. interpellation.]

interpenetrate.c: Interpenetrate In`ter*pen"e*trate (?), v. t. To penetrate between or within; to penetrate mutually.
Interpenetrate In`ter*pen"e*trate, v. i. To penetrate each the other; to penetrate between bodies or their parts.

interpenetration.c: Interpenetration In`ter*pen`e*tra"tion (?), n. The act or process of penetrating between or within other substances; mutual penetration; also, the result of a process of interpenetration. Milman.

interpenetrative.c: Interpenetrative In`ter*pen"e*tra*tive (?), a. Penetrating among or between other substances; penetrating each the other; mutually penetrative.

interpetalary.c: Interpetalary In`ter*pet"al*a*ry (?), a. [Pref. inter- + petal.] (Bot.) Between the petals of a flower.

interpetiolar.c: Interpetiolar In`ter*pet"i*o*lar (?), a. (Bot.) Being between petioles. Cf. Intrapetiolar.

interphalangeal.c: Interphalangeal In`ter*pha*lan"ge*al (?), a. (Anat.) Between phalanges; as, interphalangeal articulations.

interpilaster.c: Interpilaster In`ter*pi*las"ter (?), n. (Arch.) The interval or space between two pilasters. Elmes.

interplace.c: Interplace In`ter*place" (?), v. t. To place between or among; as, to interplace a name. [R.] Daniel.

interplanetary.c: Interplanetary In`ter*plan"et*a*ry (?), a. Between planets; as, interplanetary spaces; interplanetary travel. Boyle.

interplay.c: Interplay In`ter*play` (?), n. Mutual action or influence; interaction; as, the interplay of affection.

interpledge.c: Interpledge In`ter*pledge" (?), v. t. To pledge mutually. [R.]

interpoint.c: Interpoint In`ter*point" (?), v. t. To point; to mark with stops or pauses; to punctuate. [R.]

interpolable.c: Interpolable In*ter"po*la*ble (?), a. That may be interpolated; suitable to be interpolated.

interpolate.c: Interpolate In*ter"po*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interpolated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interpolating.] [L. interpolatus, p. p. of interpolare to form anew, to interpolate, fr. interpolus, interpolis, falsified, vamped up, polished up; inter between + polire to polish. See Polish, v. t.]

interpolated.c: Interpolated In*ter"po*la`ted (?), a. 1. Inserted in, or added to, the original; introduced; foisted in; changed by the insertion of new or spurious matter.

interpolation.c: Interpolation In*ter`po*la"tion (?), n. [L. interpolatio an alteration made here and there: cf. F. interpolation.] 1. The act of introducing or inserting anything, especially that which is spurious or foreign.

interpolator.c: Interpolator In*ter"po*la`tor (?), n. [L., a corrupter: of. F. interpolateur.] One who interpolates; esp., one who inserts foreign or spurious matter in genuine writings.

interpone.c: Interpone In`ter*pone" (?), v. t. [L. interponere; inter between + ponere to place. See Position.] To interpose; to insert or place between. [R.] Cudworth.

interponent.c: Interponent In`ter*po"nent (?), n. One who, or that which, interposes; an interloper, an opponent. [R.] Heywood.

interposal.c: Interposal In`ter*pos"al (?), n. [From Interpose.] The act of interposing; interposition; intervention.

interpose.c: Interpose In`ter*pose" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interposed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Interposing.] [F. interposer. See Inter-, and Pose, v. t.]
Interpose In`ter*pose", v. i. 1. To be or come between.

interposer.c: Interposer In`ter*pos"er (?), n. One who, or that which, interposes or intervenes; an obstacle or interruption; a mediator or agent between parties. Shak.

interposit.c: Interposit In`ter*pos"it (?), n. [From L. interpositus, p. p. of interponere. See Interposition.] An intermediate depot or station between one commercial city or country and another. Mitford.

interposition.c: Interposition In`ter*po*si"tion (?; 277), n. [L. interpositio a putting between, insertion, fr. interponere, interpositum: cf. F. interposition. See Interpone, Position.]

interpret.c: Interpret In*ter"pret (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interpreted; p. pr. & vb. n. Interpreting.] [F. interprêter, L. interpretari, p. p. interpretatus, fr. interpres interpeter, agent, negotiator; inter between + (prob.) the root of pretium price. See Price.]

interpretable.c: Interpretable In*ter"pret*a*ble (?), a. [L. interpretabilis: cf. F. interprêtable.] Admitting of interpretation; capable of being interpreted or explained.

interpretation.c: Interpretation In*ter`pre*ta"tion (ĭn*tẽr`pre*tā"shŭn), n. [L. interpretatio: cf. F. interprétation.]

interpreter.c: Interpreter In*ter"pret*er (?), n. [Cf. OF. entrepreteur, L. interpretator.] One who or that which interprets, explains, or expounds; a translator; especially, a person who translates orally between two parties.

interpubic.c: Interpubic In`ter*pu"bic (?), a. (Anat.) Between the pubic bones or cartilages; as, the interpubic disk.

interpunction.c: Interpunction In`ter*punc"tion (?), n. [L. interpunctio, fr. interpungere, interppunctum, to interpoint. See Inter-, and Point.] The insertion of points between words or sentences; punctuation.

interradial.c: Interradial In`ter*ra"di*al (?), a. Between the radii, or rays; -- in Zoology, said of certain parts of radiate animals; as, the interradial plates of a starfish.

interramal.c: Interramal In`ter*ra"mal (?), a. [Pref. inter- + L. ramus a branch.] (Anat.) Between rami or branches; esp., between the mandibles, or rami of the lower jaw; intermandibular.

interreceive.c: Interreceive In`ter*re*ceive" (?), v. t. To receive between or within.

interregent.c: Interregent In`ter*re"gent (?), n. A person who discharges the royal functions during an interregnum. Holland.

interregnum.c: Interregnum In`ter*reg"num (?), n.; pl. Interregnums (#). [L., fr. inter between + regnum dominion, reign. See Reign, and cf. Interreign.]

interreign.c: Interreign In"ter*reign` (?), n. [Cf. F. interrègne.] An interregnum. [Obs.] Bacon.

interrelated.c: Interrelated In`ter*re*lat"ed (?), a. Having a mutual or reciprocal relation or parallelism; correlative.

interrelation.c: Interrelation In`ter*re*la"tion (?), n. Mutual or reciprocal relation; correlation.

interrenal.c: Interrenal In`ter*re"nal (?), a. (Anat.) Between the kidneys; as, the interrenal body, an organ found in many fishes. -- n. The interrenal body.

interrepellent.c: Interrepellent In`ter*re*pel"lent (?), a. Mutually repellent. De Quincey.

interrex.c: Interrex In"ter*rex` (?), n.; pl. E. Interrexes (#), L. Interreges (#). [L., fr. inter between + rex king.] An interregent, or a regent.

interrogation.c: Interrogation In*ter`ro*ga"tion (?), n. [L. interrogatio: cf. F. interrogation.]

interrogative.c: Interrogative In`ter*rog"a*tive (?), a. [L. interrogativus: cf. F. interrogatif.] Denoting a question; expressed in the form of a question; as, an interrogative sentence; an interrogative pronoun.

interrogatively.c: Interrogatively In`ter*rog"a*tive*ly, adv. In the form of, or by means of, a question; in an interrogative manner.

interrogator.c: Interrogator In*ter"ro*ga`tor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. interrogateur.] One who asks questions; a questioner.

interrogatory.c: Interrogatory In`ter*rog"a*to*ry (?), n.; pl. Interrogatories (#). [Cf. F. interrogatoire.] A formal question or inquiry; esp. (Law), a question or series of questions asked in writing, usually as part of a lawsuit. Macaulay.
Interrogatory In`ter*rog"a*to*ry (?), a. [L. interrogatorius.] Containing, expressing, or implying a question; as, an interrogatory sentence.

interrupt.c: Interrupt In`ter*rupt" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Interrupted; p. pr. & vb. n. Interrupting.] [L. interruptus, p. p. of interrumpere to interrupt; inter between + rumpere to break. See Rupture.]
Interrupt In`ter*rupt", p. a. [L. interruptus, p. p.] Broken; interrupted. [Obs.] Milton.

interrupted.c: Interrupted In`ter*rupt"ed, a. 1. Broken; intermitted; suddenly stopped.
