iridioscope.c: Iridioscope I*rid"i*o*scope (?), n. [See Iris, and -scope.] A kind of ophthalmoscope.

iridious.c: Iridious I*rid"i*ous (i*rĭd"ĭ*ŭs), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to iridium; -- applied specifically to compounds in which iridium has a low valence.

iridium.c: iridium i*rid"i*um (i*rĭd"ĭ*ŭm), n. [NL., fr. L. iris, iridis, the rainbow. So called from the iridescence of some of its solutions. See Iris.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element of atomic number 77, of the same group as platinum, which it much resembles, being silver-white and indifferent to most corrosive agents, but harder, more brittle, and with a higher melting temperature (2410° C, versus platinum 1772° C). With the exception of osmium, it is the heaviest substance known, its specific gravity being 22.4. Symbol Ir. Atomic weight 192.22.

iridize.c: Iridize Ir"i*dize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Iridized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Iridizing (?).]

iridoline.c: Iridoline I*rid"o*line (?), n. [Iridescent + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) A nitrogenous base C10H9N, extracted from coal-tar naphtha, as an oily liquid. It is a member of the quinoline series, and is probably identical with lepidine.

iridosmium.c: Iridosmium Iridosmine { Ir`i*dos"mine (?), Ir`i*dos"mi*um (?), } n. [Iridium + osmium.] (Min.) The native compound of iridium and osmium. It is found in flattened metallic grains of extreme hardness, and is often used for pointing gold pens.

iris.c: Iris I"ris (?), n.; pl. E. Irises (#), L. Irides (#). [L. iris, iridis, the goddess, Gr.?,?, the rainbow, iris of the eye, the plant Iris. Cf. Orris.] 1. (Class. Myth.) The goddess of the rainbow, and swift-footed messenger of the gods. Shak.

Iris diaphragm I"ris di"a*phragm. An adjustable diaphragm, reminiscent of the iris of the eye in its action, by which the diameter of an approximately circular opening may be controlled, as for regulating the aperture of a lens; it consists of a number of movable thin curved plates fastened at regular intervals around the inside of a ring, the positions of which are simultaneously adjusted by a single knob on the outside of the lens. It is used in cameras and microscopes.

irisated.c: Irisated I"ris*a`ted (?), a. [See Iris.] Exhibiting the prismatic colors; irised; iridescent. W. Phillips.

iriscope.c: Iriscope I"ri*scope (?), n. [Iris + -scope.] A philosophical toy for exhibiting the prismatic tints by means of thin films.

irised.c: Irised I"rised (?), a. [See Iris.] Having colors like those of the rainbow; iridescent. Holmes.

irish.c: Irish I"rish (?), a. [AS. īrisc, fr. īras the Irish. Cf. Aryan, Erse.] Of or pertaining to Ireland or to its inhabitants; produced in Ireland.
Irish I*rish", n. sing. & pl. 1. pl. The natives or inhabitants of Ireland, esp. the Celtic natives or their descendants.

irishamerican.c: Irish-American Irish American I"rish A*mer"i*can, I"rish-A*mer"i*can. A native of Ireland who has become an American citizen; also, a child or descendant of such a person.

irishism.c: Irishism I"rish*ism (?), n. A mode of speaking peculiar to the Irish; an Hibernicism.

irishman.c: Irishman I"rish*man (?), n.; pl. Irishmen (?). A man born in Ireland or of the Irish race; an Hibernian.

irishry.c: Irishry I"rish*ry (?), n. The Celtic people of Ireland. “The whole Irishry of rebels.” Milton.

iritis.c: Iritis ‖I*ri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Iris, and -itis.] (Med.) An inflammation of the iris of the eye.

irk.c: Irk Irk (ẽrk), v. t. [OE. irken to tire, become tired; cf. Sw. yrka to urge, enforce, press, or G. ekel disgust, MHG. erklich disgusting; perh. akin to L. urgere to urge, E. urge.] To weary; to give pain; to annoy.

irksome.c: Irksome Irk"some (?), a. 1. Wearisome; tedious; disagreeable or troublesome by reason of long continuance or repetition; as, irksome hours; irksome tasks.

iron.c: Iron I"ron (ī"ŭrn), n. [OE. iren, AS. īren, īsen, īsern; akin to D. ijzer, OS. īsarn, OHG. īsarn, īsan, G. eisen, Icel. īsarn, jārn, Sw. & Dan. jern, and perh. to E. ice; cf. Ir. iarann, W. haiarn, Armor. houarn.]
Iron I"ron (ī"ŭrn), a. [AS. īren, īsen. See Iron, n.]
Iron I"ron, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ironed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ironing.]
Iron works I"ron works`. See under Iron, a.

ironbark.c: Ironbark tree Ironbark I"ron*bark`, I"ron*bark` tree` (?). (Bot.) The Australian Eucalyptus Sideroxylon, used largely by carpenters and shipbuilders; -- called also ironwood. Also applied to other Australian eucalyptuses with a hard, solid bark

ironbound.c: Ironbound I"ron*bound` (?), a. 1. Bound as with iron; rugged; as, an ironbound coast.

ironcased.c: Iron-cased I"ron-cased` (?), a. Cased or covered with iron, as a vessel; ironclad.

ironclad.c: Ironclad I"ron*clad` (?), a. 1. Clad in iron; protected or covered with iron, as a vessel for naval warfare.

Ironclad I"ron*clad`, n. A naval vessel having the parts above water covered and protected by iron or steel usually in large plates closely joined and made sufficiently thick and strong to resist heavy shot. Modern naval vessels are made of steel throughout, and this term is only used in historical contexts.

ironer.c: Ironer I"ron*er (?), n. One who, or that which, irons.

ironfisted.c: iron-fisted ironfisted i"ron*fist`ed, i"ron-fist`ed (?), a. 1. Closefisted; stingy; mean.

irongray.c: Iron-gray I"ron-gray` (?), a. Of a gray color, somewhat resembling that of iron freshly broken. -- n. An iron-gray color; also, a horse of this color.

ironheads.c: Ironheads I"ron*heads` (?), n. (Bot.) A European composite herb (Centaurea nigra); -- so called from the resemblance of its knobbed head to an iron ball fixed on a long handle. Dr. Prior.

ironhearted.c: Iron-hearted I"ron-heart`ed (?), a. Hard-hearted; unfeeling; cruel; as, an iron-hearted master. Cowper.

ironic.c: Ironic I*ron"ic (?), a. Ironical. Sir T. Herbert.

ironical.c: Ironical I*ron"ic*al (?), a. [LL. ironicus, Gr.? dissembling: cf. F. ironique. See Irony.]

ironing.c: Ironing I"ron*ing (?), n. 1. The act or process of smoothing, as clothes, with hot flatirons.

ironish.c: Ironish I"ron*ish, a. Resembling iron, as in taste. Wood.

ironist.c: Ironist I"ron*ist (?), n. One who uses irony.

ironmaster.c: Ironmaster I"ron*mas`ter (?), n. A manufacturer of iron, or large dealer therein. Bp. Hurd.

ironmonger.c: Ironmonger I"ron*mon`ger (?), n. A dealer in iron or hardware.

ironmongery.c: Ironmongery I"ron*mon`ger*y (?), n. Hardware; a general name for all articles made of iron. Gwilt.

ironsick.c: Iron-sick I"ron-sick` (?), a. (Naut.) Having the ironwork loose or corroded; -- said of a ship when her bolts and nails are so eaten with rust that she has become leaky.

ironsided.c: Iron-sided I"ron-sid`ed (?), a. Having iron sides, or very firm sides.

ironsides.c: Ironsides I"ron*sides" (?), n. A cuirassier or cuirassiers; also, hardy veteran soldiers; -- applied specifically to Cromwell's cavalry.

ironsmith.c: Ironsmith I"ron*smith` (?), n. 1. A worker in iron; one who makes and repairs utensils of iron; a blacksmith.

ironstone.c: Ironstone I"ron*stone` (?), 1. n. A hard, earthy ore of iron.

ironware.c: Ironware I"ron*ware` (?), n. Articles made of iron, as household utensils, tools, and the like.

ironweed.c: Ironweed I"ron*weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A tall weed with purplish flowers (Vernonia Noveboracensis). The name is also applied to other plants of the same genus.

ironwood.c: Ironwood I"ron*wood` (?), n. (Bot.) A tree unusually hard, strong, or heavy wood.

ironwork.c: Ironwork I"ron*work` (?), n. Anything made of iron; -- a general name of such parts or pieces of a building, vessel, carriage, etc., as consist of iron.

ironwort.c: Ironwort I"ron*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) An herb of the Mint family (Sideritis), supposed to heal sword cuts; also, a species of Galeopsis.

irony.c: Irony I"ron*y (?), n. [L. ironia, Gr.? dissimulation, fr.? a dissembler in speech, fr.? to speak; perh. akin to E. word: cf. F. ironie.]

iroquois.c: Iroquois Ir`o*quois" (?), n. sing. & pl. [F.] (Ethnol.) A powerful and warlike confederacy of Indian tribes, formerly inhabiting Central New York and constituting most of the Five Nations. Also, any Indian of the Iroquois tribes.

iroquoian.c: Iroquoian Ir`o*quoi"an (ĭr`o*kwoi"ain), a. Of, pertaining to, or designating, one of the principal linguistic stocks of the North American Indians. The territory of the northern Iroquoian tribes, of whom the Five Nations, or Iroquois proper, were the chief, extended from the shores of the St. Lawrence and of Lakes Huron, Ontario, and Erie south, through eastern Pennsylvania, to Maryland; that of the southern tribes, of whom the Cherokees were chief, formed part of Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee, and Kentucky. All of the tribes were agricultural, and they were noted for large, communal houses, palisaded towns, and ability to organize, as well as for skill in war. -- n. An Indian of an Iroquoian tribe.

irous.c: Irous I"rous (?), a. [OF. iros, from ire. See Ire.] Irascible; passionate. [Obs.] Chaucer.

irpe.c: Irpe Irp { Irp, Irpe } (ẽrp), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A fantastic grimace or contortion of the body. [Obs.]

irp.c: irp irp (ẽrp), a. Making irps. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

irradiant.c: irradiant ir*ra"di*ant (ĭr*rā"dĭ*aint), a. [L. irradians, -antis, p. pr. See Irradiate.] Irradiating or illuminating; as, the irradiant moon. Boyse.

irradiate.c: Irradiate Ir*ra"di*ate (ĭr*rā"dĭ*āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Irradiated (ĭr*rā"dĭ*ā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Irradiating (ĭr*rā"dĭ*ā`tĭng).] [L. irradiatus, p. p. of irradiate. See In- in, and Radiate.]
irradiate ir*ra"di*ate, v. i. To emit rays; to shine.
irradiate ir*ra"di*ate (ĭr*rā"dĭ*at), a. [L. irradiatus, p. p.] Illuminated; irradiated. Mason.

irradicate.c: irradicate ir*rad"i*cate (ĭr*răd"ĭ*kāt), v. t. To root deeply. [R.]

irrational.c: irrational ir*ra"tion*al (ĭr*răsh"ŭn*ail), a. [L. irrationalis: cf. F. irrationnel. See In- not, and Rational.]

irrationality.c: irrationality ir*ra`tion*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being irrational; absence of rationality. “Brutish irrationaliity.” South.

irrationally.c: irrationally ir*ra"tion*al*ly (?), adv. In an irrational manner. Boyle.

irrebuttable.c: irrebuttable ir`re*but"ta*ble (?), a. Incapable of being rebutted. Coleridge.

irreceptive.c: irreceptive ir`re*cep"tive (?), a. Not receiving; incapable of receiving.

irreclaimable.c: irreclaimable ir`re*claim"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being reclaimed. Addison. -- ir`re*claim"a*bly, adv.

irrecognition.c: Irrecognition Ir*rec`og*ni"tion (?), n. [Pref. in- not + recognition.] A failure to recognize; absence of recognition. Lamb.

irrecognizable.c: Irrecognizable Ir*rec"og*ni`za*ble (?; 277), a. Not recognizable; unrecognizable. Carlyle.

irreconcilability.c: Irreconcilability Ir*rec`on*ci`la*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being irreconcilable; irreconcilableness.

irreconcilable.c: Irreconcilable Ir*rec"on*ci`la*ble (?; 277), a. [Pref. ir- not + reconcilable: cf. F. irréconciliable.] Not reconcilable; not able to be reconciled or brought into accord; implacable; incompatible; inconsistent; disagreeing; as, irreconcilable enemies, statements. -- Ir*rec"on*ci`la*ble*ness, n. -- Ir*rec"on*ci`la*bly, adv.

irreconcile.c: Irreconcile Ir*rec"on*cile` (?), v. t. To prevent from being reconciled; to alienate or disaffect. [Obs.]

irreconcilement.c: Irreconcilement Ir*rec"on*cile`ment (?), n. The state or quality of being unreconciled; disagreement.

irreconciliation.c: Irreconciliation Ir*rec`on*cil`i*a"tion (?), n. Lack of reconciliation; disagreement.

irrecordable.c: Irrecordable Ir`re*cord"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir-- not + record: cf. L. irrecordabilis not to be remembered.] Not fit or possible to be recorded.

irrecoverable.c: Irrecoverable Ir`re*cov"er*a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being recovered, regained, or remedied; irreparable; as, an irrecoverable loss, debt, or injury.

irrecuperable.c: Irrecuperable Ir`re*cu"per*a*ble (?), a. [L. irrecuperabilis: cf. OF. irrecuperable. See In- not, and Recuperate.] Irrecoverable. -- Ir`re*cu"per*a*bly, adv.

irrecusable.c: Irrecusable Ir`re*cu"sa*ble (?), a. [L. irrecusabilis; pref. ir-- not + recusabilis that should be rejected, fr. recusare to reject: cf. F. irrécusable.] Not liable to exception or rejection. Sir W. Hamilton.

irredeemability.c: Irredeemability Ir`re*deem`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being irredeemable; irredeemableness.

irredeemable.c: Irredeemable Ir`re*deem"a*ble (?), a. Not redeemable; that can not be redeemed; not payable in gold or silver, as a bond; -- used especially of such government notes, issued as currency, as are not convertible into coin at the pleasure of the holder. -- Ir`re*deem"a*ble*ness, adv.

irreducibility.c: Irreducibility Ir`re*du`ci*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being irreducible.

irreducible.c: Irreducible Ir`re*du"ci*ble (?), a. 1. Incapable of being reduced, or brought into a different state; incapable of restoration to its proper or normal condition; as, an irreducible hernia.

irreflective.c: Irreflective Ir`re*flect"ive (?), a. Not reflective. De Quincey.

irreformable.c: Irreformable Ir`re*form"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being reformed; incorrigible. Joseph Cook.

irrefragability.c: Irrefragability Ir*ref`ra*ga*bil"i*ty (ĭr*rĕf"rȧ*gȧ*b'l), n. The quality or state of being irrefragable; incapability of being refuted.

irrefragable.c: Irrefragable Ir*ref"ra*ga*ble (?), a. [F. irréfragable, L. irrefragabilis. See Refragable.] Not refragable; not to be gainsaid or denied; not to be refuted or overthrown; irrefutable; unanswerable; incontestable; undeniable; as, an irrefragable argument; irrefragable evidence. -- Ir*ref"ra*ga*ble*ness, n. -- Ir*ref"ra*ga*bly, adv.

irrefrangibility.c: Irrefrangibility Ir`re*fran`gi*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being irrefrangible; irrefrangibleness.

irrefrangible.c: Irrefrangible Ir`re*fran"gi*ble (?), a. Not refrangible; that can not be refracted in passing from one medium to another. -- Ir`re*fran"gi*ble*ness, n.

irrefutable.c: Irrefutable Ir`re*fut"a*ble (?; 277), a. [L. irrefutabilis: cf. F. irréfutable. See Refute.] Incapable of being refuted or disproved; indisputable. -- Ir`re*fut"a*ble*ness, n. -- Ir`re*fut"a*bly, adv.

irregular.c: Irregular Ir*reg"u*lar (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + regular: cf. F. irrégulier.] Not regular; not conforming to a law, method, or usage recognized as the general rule; not according to common form; not conformable to nature, to the rules of moral rectitude, or to established principles; not normal; unnatural; immethodical; unsymmetrical; erratic; no straight; not uniform; as, an irregular line; an irregular figure; an irregular verse; an irregular physician; an irregular proceeding; irregular motion; irregular conduct, etc. Cf. Regular.
Irregular Ir*reg"u*lar, n. One who is not regular; especially, a soldier not in regular service.

irregularist.c: Irregularist Ir*reg"u*lar*ist, n. One who is irregular. Baxter.

irregularity.c: Irregularity Ir*reg`u*lar"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Irregularities (#). [Cf. F. irrégularité.] The state or quality of being irregular; that which is irregular.

irregularly.c: Irregularly Ir*reg"u*lar*ly, adv. In an irregular manner.

irregulate.c: Irregulate Ir*reg"u*late (?), v. t. To make irregular; to disorder. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

irrejectable.c: Irrejectable Ir`re*ject"a*ble (?), a. That can not be rejected; irresistible. Boyle.

irrelapsable.c: Irrelapsable Ir`re*laps"a*ble (?), a. Not liable to relapse; secure. Dr. H. More.

irrelation.c: Irrelation Ir`re*la"tion (?), n. The quality or state of being irrelative; lack of connection or relation.

irrelative.c: Irrelative Ir*rel"a*tive (?), a. Not relative; without mutual relations; unconnected. -- Ir*rel"a*tive*ly, adv.

irrelavancy.c: Irrelavancy Ir*rel"a*van*cy (?), n. The quality or state of being irrelevant; as, the irrelevancy of an argument.

irrelavant.c: Irrelavant Ir*rel"a*vant (?), a. Not relevant; not applicable or pertinent; not bearing upon or serving to support; foreign; extraneous; as, testimony or arguments irrelevant to a case. -- Ir*rel"a*vant*ly, adv.

irrelievable.c: Irrelievable Ir`re*liev"a*ble (?), a. Not admitting relief; incurable; hopeless.

irreligion.c: Irreligion Ir`re*li"gion (?), n. [L. irreligio: cf. F. irréligion. See In- not, and Religion.] The state of being irreligious; lack of religion; impiety.

irreligionist.c: Irreligionist Ir`re*li"gion*ist, n. One who is irreligious.

irreligious.c: Irreligious Ir`re*li"gious (?), a. [L. irreligiosus: cf. F. irréligieux.]

irreligiously.c: Irreligiously Ir`re*li"gious*ly, adv. In an irreligious manner.

irreligiousness.c: Irreligiousness Ir`re*li"gious*ness, n. The state or quality of being irreligious; ungodliness.

irremeable.c: Irremeable Ir*re"me*a*ble (?), a. [L. irremeabilis; pref. ir- not + remeabilis returning, fr. remeare: cf. F. irréméable. See Remeant.] Admitting no return; as, an irremeable way. [Obs.] Dryden.

irremediable.c: Irremediable Ir`re*me"di*a*ble (?), a. [L. irremediabilis: cf. F. irrémédiable. See In- not, and Remediable.] Not to be remedied, corrected, or redressed; incurable; as, an irremediable disease or evil.

irremediableness.c: Irremediableness Ir`re*me"di*a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being irremediable.

irremediably.c: Irremediably Ir`re*me"di*a*bly, adv. In a manner, or to a degree, that precludes remedy, cure, or correction.

irremissible.c: Irremissible Ir`re*mis"si*ble (?), a. [L. irremissibilis: cf. F. irrémissible. See In- not, and Remissible.] Not remissible; unpardonable; as, irremissible crimes. Burke. -- Ir`re*mis"si*ble, n. -- Ir`re*mis"si*bly, adv.

irremittable.c: Irremittable Ir`re*mit"ta*ble (?), a. Not capable of being remitted; irremissible. Holinshed.

irremovability.c: Irremovability Ir`re*mov`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being irremovable; immovableness.

irremovable.c: Irremovable Ir`re*mov"a*ble (?), a. Not removable; immovable; inflexible. Shak. -- Ir`re*mov"a*bly, adv.

irremunerable.c: Irremunerable Ir`re*mu"ner*a*ble (?), a. [L. irremunerabilis: cf. F. irrémunérable. See Remunerate.] Not remunerable; not capable of remuneration.

irreparability.c: Irreparability Ir*rep`a*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. irréparabilité.] The quality or state of being irreparable; irreparableness. Sterne.

irreparable.c: Irreparable Ir*rep"a*ra*ble (?), a. [L. irreparabilis: cf. F. irréparable. See In- not, and Reparable.] Not reparable; not capable of being repaired, recovered, regained, or remedied; irretrievable; irremediable; as, an irreparable breach; an irreparable loss. Shak.

irreparableness.c: Irreparableness Ir*rep"a*ra*ble*ness, n. Quality of being irreparable.

irreparably.c: Irreparably Ir*rep"a*ra*bly, adv. In an irreparable manner.

irrepealability.c: Irrepealability Ir`re*peal`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being irrepealable.

irrepealable.c: Irrepealable Ir`re*peal"a*ble (?), a. Not repealable; not capable of being repealed or revoked, as a law. -- Ir`re*peal"a*ble*ness, n. -- Ir`re*peal"a*bly, adv.

irrepentance.c: Irrepentance Ir`re*pent"ance (?), n. Lack of repentance; impenitence. Bp. Montagu.

irreplevisable.c: Irreplevisable Irrepleviable { Ir`re*plev"i*a*ble (?), Ir`re*plev"i*sa*ble (?), } a. (Law) Not capable of being replevied.

irreprehensible.c: Irreprehensible Ir*rep`re*hen"si*ble (?), a. [L. irreprehensibilis: cf. F. irrépréhensible. See Reprehensible.] Not reprehensible; blameless; innocent. -- Ir*rep`re*hen"si*ble*ness, n. -- Ir*rep`re*hen"si*bly, adv.

irrepresentable.c: Irrepresentable Ir*rep`re*sent"a*ble (?), a. Not capable of being represented or portrayed.

irrepressible.c: Irrepressible Ir`re*press"i*ble (?), a. Not capable of being repressed, restrained, or controlled; as, irrepressible joy; an irrepressible conflict. W. H. Steward.

irrepressibly.c: Irrepressibly Ir`re*press"i*bly, adv. In a manner or to a degree that can not be repressed.

irreproachable.c: Irreproachable Ir`re*proach"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + reproachable: cf. F. irréprochable.] Not reproachable; above reproach; not deserving reproach; blameless.

irreproachableness.c: Irreproachableness Ir`re*proach"a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being irreproachable; integrity; innocence.

irreproachably.c: Irreproachably Ir`re*proach"a*bly, adv. In an irreproachable manner; blamelessly.

irreprovable.c: Irreprovable Ir`re*prov"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being justly reproved; irreproachable; blameless; upright. -- Ir`re*prov"a*ble*ness, n. -- Ir`re*prov"a*bly, adv.

irreptitious.c: Irreptitious Ir`rep*ti"tious (?), a. [L. irrepere, irreptum, to creep in; pref. ir- in + repere to creep.] Surreptitious; spurious. [Obs.] Dr. Castell (1673).

irresilient.c: Irresilient Ir`re*sil"i*ent (?), a. Not resilient; not recoiling or rebounding; inelastic.

irresistibility.c: Irresistibility Ir`re*sist`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. irrésistibilité.] The quality or state of being irresistible, irresistibleness.

irresistible.c: Irresistible Ir`re*sist"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + resistible: cf. F. irrésistible.] That can not be successfully resisted or opposed; superior to opposition; resistless; overpowering; as, an irresistible attraction.

irresistibleness.c: Irresistibleness Ir`re*sist"i*ble*ness, n. Quality of being irresistible.

irresistibly.c: Irresistibly Ir`re*sist"i*bly, adv. In an irresistible manner.

irresoluble.c: Irresoluble Ir*res"o*lu*ble (?), a. [L. irresolubilis: cf. F. irrésoluble. See Resoluble, and cf. Irresolvable.]

irresolubleness.c: Irresolubleness Ir*res"o*lu*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being irresoluble; insolubility.

irresolute.c: Irresolute Ir*res"o*lute (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + resolute: cf. F. irrésolu, L. irresolutus not loosened.] Not resolute; not decided or determined; wavering; given to doubt or irresolution.

irresolution.c: Irresolution Ir*res`o*lu"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. irrésolution.] Lack of resolution; lack of decision in purpose; a fluctuation of mind, as in doubt, or between hope and fear; irresoluteness; indecision; vacillation.

irresolvability.c: Irresolvability Ir`re*solv`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being irresolvable; irresolvableness.

irresolvable.c: Irresolvable Ir`re*solv"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + resolvable. Cf. Irresoluble.] Incapable of being resolved; not separable into component parts.

irresolvableness.c: Irresolvableness Ir`re*solv"a*ble*ness, n. The quality or state of being irresolvable; irresolvability.

irresolvedly.c: Irresolvedly Ir`re*solv"ed*ly, adv. Without settled determination; in a hesitating manner; doubtfully. [R.]

irrespective.c: Irrespective Ir`re*spec"tive (ĭr`re*spĕk"tĭv), a. 1. Without regard for conditions, circumstances, or consequences; unbiased; independent; impartial; as, an irrespective judgment.

irrespectively.c: Irrespectively Ir`re*spec"tive*ly (ĭr`re*spĕk"tĭv*ly̆), adv. Without regard to conditions; not taking circumstances into consideration.

irrespirable.c: Irrespirable Ir*res"pi*ra*ble (?), a. [L. irrespirabilis: cf. F. irrespirable. See Respirable.] Unfit for respiration; not having the qualities necessary to support animal life; as, irrespirable air.

irresponsibility.c: Irresponsibility Ir`re*spon`si*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. irresponsabilité.] 1. Lack of, or freedom from, responsibility or accountability.

irresponsible.c: Irresponsible Ir`re*spon"si*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + responsible: cf. F. irresponsable.] 1. Not responsible; not liable or able to answer for consequences; innocent.

irresponsibly.c: Irresponsibly Ir`re*spon"si*bly, adv. 1. So as not to be responsible.

irresponsive.c: Irresponsive Ir`re*spon"sive (?), a. Not responsive; not able, ready, or inclined to respond.

irresuscitable.c: Irresuscitable Ir`re*sus"ci*ta*ble (?), a. Incapable of being resuscitated or revived. -- Ir`re*sus"ci*ta*bly, adv.

irretention.c: Irretention Ir`re*ten"tion (?), n. Lack of retaining power; forgetfulness. De Quincey.

irretentive.c: Irretentive Ir`re*ten"tive (?), a. Not retentive; as, an irretentive memory.

irretraceable.c: Irretraceable Ir`re*trace"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being retraced; not retraceable.

irretrievable.c: Irretrievable Ir`re*triev"a*ble (?), a. Not retrievable; irrecoverable; irreparable; as, an irretrievable loss.

irretrievableness.c: Irretrievableness Ir`re*triev"a*ble*ness, n. The state or quality of being irretrievable.

irretrievably.c: Irretrievably Ir`re*triev"a*bly, adv. In an irretrievable manner.

irreturnable.c: Irreturnable Ir`re*turn"a*ble (?), a. Not to be returned.

irrevealable.c: Irrevealable Ir`re*veal"a*ble (?), a. Incapable of being revealed. -- Ir`re*veal"a*bly, adv.

irreverence.c: Irreverence Ir*rev"er*ence (?), n. [L. irreverentia: cf. F. irrévérence.] The state or quality of being irreverent; lack of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a superior.

irreverent.c: Irreverent Ir*rev"er*ent (?), a. [L. irreverens, -entis: cf. F. irrévérent. See In- not, and Reverent.] Not reverent; showing a lack of reverence; expressive of a lack of veneration; as, an irreverent babbler; an irreverent jest.

irreverently.c: Irreverently Ir*rev"er*ent*ly, adv. In an irreverent manner.

irreversibility.c: Irreversibility Ir`re*vers`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. The state or quality of being irreversible; irreversibleness.

irreversible.c: Irreversible Ir`re*vers"i*ble (?), a. 1. Incapable of being reversed or turned about or back; incapable of being made to run backward; as, an irreversible engine; an irreversible process; an irreversible reaction.

Irreversible steering gear Ir`re*vers"i*ble steering gear. (Mach.) A steering gear, esp. for an automobile, not affected by the road wheels, as when they strike an obstacle side ways, but easily controlled by the hand wheel or steering lever.

irreversibleness.c: Irreversibleness Ir`re*vers"i*ble*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being irreversible.

irreversibly.c: Irreversibly Ir`re*vers"i*bly, adv. In an irreversible manner.

irrevocability.c: Irrevocability Ir*rev`o*ca*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. irrévocabilité.] The state or quality of being irrevocable; irrevocableness.

irrevocable.c: Irrevocable Ir*rev"o*ca*ble (?), a. [L. irrevocabilis: cf. F. irrévocable. See In- not, and Revoke, and cf. Irrevocable.] Incapable of being recalled or revoked; unchangeable; irreversible; unalterable; as, an irrevocable promise or decree; irrevocable fate.

irrevokable.c: Irrevokable Ir`re*vok"a*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + revoke.] Irrevocable. [R.]

irrevoluble.c: Irrevoluble Ir*rev"o*lu*ble (?), a. That has no finite period of revolution; not revolving. [R.]

irrigate.c: Irrigate Ir"ri*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Irrigated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Irrigating (?).] [L. irrigatus, p. p. of irrigare to irrigate: ir- in + rigare to water; prob. akin to E. rain. See Rain.]

irrigation.c: Irrigation Ir`ri*ga"tion (?), n. [L. irrigatio: cf. F. irrigation.] The act or process of irrigating, or the state of being irrigated; especially, the operation of causing water to flow over lands, for nourishing plants.

irrisible.c: Irrisible Ir*ris"i*ble (?), a. [Pref. ir- not + risible. See Irrision.] Not risible. [R.]

irrision.c: Irrision Ir*ri"sion (?), n. [L. irrisio, fr. irridere, irrisum, to laugh at; pref. ir- in + ridere to laugh: cf. F. irrision.] The act of laughing at another; derision.

irritability.c: Irritability Ir`ri*ta*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. irritabilitas: cf. F. irritabilité.]

irritable.c: Irritable Ir"ri*ta*ble (?), a. [L. irritabilis: cf. F. irritable. See Irritate.]

irritably.c: Irritably Ir"ri*ta*bly, adv. In an irritable manner.

irritancy.c: Irritancy Ir"ri*tan*cy (?), n. [From 1st Irritant.] (Scots Law) The state or quality of being null and void; invalidity; forfeiture. Burrill.
Irritancy Ir"ri*tan*cy, n. [From 2d Irritant.] The state or quality of being irritant or irritating.

irritant.c: Irritant Ir"ri*tant (?), a. [LL. irritants, -antis, p. pr. of irritare to make null, fr. L. irritus void; pref. ir- not + ratus established.] (Scots Law) Rendering null and void; conditionally invalidating.
Irritant Ir"ri*tant, a. [L. irritans, -antis, p. pr. of irritare: cf. F. irritant. See Irritate to excite.] Irritating; producing irritation or inflammation.

irritate.c: Irritate Ir"ri*tate (?), v. t. [See 1 st Irritant.] To render null and void. [R.] Abp. Bramhall.
Irritate Ir"ri*tate, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Irritated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Irritating (?).] [L. irritatus, p. p. of irritare. Of doubtful origin.]

irritation.c: Irritation Ir`ri*ta"tion (?), n. [L. irritatio: cf. F. irritation.]

irritative.c: Irritative Ir"ri*ta*tive (?), a. 1. Serving to excite or irritate; irritating; as, an irritative agent.

irritatory.c: Irritatory Ir"ri*ta*to*ry (?), a. Exciting; producing irritation; irritating. [R.] Hales.

irrorate.c: Irrorate Ir"ro*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Irrorated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Irrorating.] [L. irroratus, p. p. of irrorare to bedew; pref. ir- in + ros, roris, dew.] To sprinkle or moisten with dew; to bedew. [Obs.]
Irrorate Ir"ro*rate (?), a. (Zool.) Covered with minute grains, appearing like fine sand.

irroration.c: Irroration Ir`ro*ra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. irroration.] The act of bedewing; the state of being moistened with dew. [Obs.] Chambers.

irrotational.c: Irrotational Ir`ro*ta"tion*al (?), a. (Physics) Not rotatory; passing from one point to another by a movement other than rotation; -- said of the movement of parts of a liquid or yielding mass. Sir W. Thomson.

irrubrical.c: Irrubrical Ir*ru"bric*al (?), a. Contrary to the rubric; not rubrical.

irrugate.c: Irrugate Ir"ru*gate (?), v. t. [L. irrugatus, p. p. of irrugare to wrinkle.] To wrinkle. [Obs.]

irrupted.c: Irrupted Ir*rupt"ed (?), a. [L. irruptus, p. p. of irrumpere to break in; pref. ir- in + rumpere to break or burst. See Rupture.] Broken with violence.

irruption.c: Irruption Ir*rup"tion (?), n. [L. irruptio: cf. F. irruption. See Irrupted.]

irruptive.c: Irruptive Ir*rup"tive (?), a. Rushing in or upon.

irvingite.c: Irvingite Ir"ving*ite (?), n. (Eccl.) The common designation of a member of a sect founded by the Rev. Edward Irving (about 1830), who call themselves the Catholic Apostolic Church. They are highly ritualistic in worship, have an elaborate hierarchy of apostles, prophets, etc., and look for the speedy coming of Christ.

is.c: Is Is (?), v. i. [AS. is; akin to G. & Goth. ist, L. est, Gr.?, Skr. asti. √9. Cf. Am, Entity, Essence, Absent.] The third person singular of the substantive verb be, in the indicative mood, present tense; as, he is; he is a man. See Be.

Is- Iso- { I"so- (?), Is- (?). } [Gr. 'i`sos equal.] A prefix or combining form, indicating identity, or equality; the same numerical value; as in isopod, isomorphous, isochromatic. Specif.: (a) (Chem.) Applied to certain compounds having the same composition but different properties; as in isocyanic. (b) (Organic Chem.) Applied to compounds of certain isomeric series in whose structure one carbon atom, at least, is connected with three other carbon atoms; -- contrasted with neo- and normal; as in isoparaffine; isopentane.

isabel.c: Isabel color Isabel { Is"a*bel (?), n., Is"a*bel col"or (?). } [F. isabelle.] See Isabella.

isabella.c: Isabella color Isabella { Is`a*bel"la (?), n., Is`a*bel"la col"or (?) }. [Said to be named from the Spanish princess Isabella, daughter of king Philip II., in allusion to the color assumed by her shift, which she wore without change from 1601 to 1604, in consequence of a vow made by her.] A brownish yellow color.
Isabella grape Is`a*bel"la grape` (?). (Bot.) A favorite sweet American grape of a purple color. See Fox grape, under Fox.

Isabella moth Is`a*bel"la moth` (?; 115). (Zool.) A common American moth (Pyrrharctia isabella), of an isabella color. The larva, called woolly bear and hedgehog caterpillar, is densely covered with hairs, which are black at each end of the body, and red in the middle part.

isabelline.c: Isabelline Is`a*bel"line (?), a. Of an isabel or isabella color.

isagel.c: Isagel Isagelous Is*ag"e*lous (īs*ăg"ĕ*lŭs), a. [Is- + Gr. a`gelos information.] Containing the same information; as, isagelous sentences. “The coded message and the original, though appearing entirely unlike, are completely isagelous.” Bacon “The complementary strands have isagelous sequences.” J. D. Watson. -- Is"a*gel n. One of two or more objects containing the same information.

isagoge.c: Isagoge I"sa*goge (?), n. [L., fr. Fr.?, fr.? to introduce;? into +? to lead.] An introduction. [Obs.] Harris.

isagogical.c: Isagogical Isagogic { I"sa*gog"ic (?), I"sa*gog"ic*al (?), } a. [L. isagogicus, Gr.?.] Introductory; especially, introductory to the study of theology.

isagogics.c: Isagogics I"sa*gog"ics (?), n. (Theol.) That part of theological science directly preliminary to actual exegesis, or interpretation of the Scriptures.

isagon.c: Isagon I"sa*gon (ī"sȧ*gŏn), n. [Gr. 'i`sos equal + gwni`a angle: cf. F. isagone, a.] (Math.) A figure or polygon whose angles are equal.

isapostolic.c: Isapostolic Is*ap`os*tol"ic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Having equal, or almost equal, authority with the apostles of their teachings.

isatinic.c: Isatinic Isatic { I*sat"ic (?), I`sa*tin"ic (?), } a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, isatin; as, isatic acid, which is also called trioxindol.

isatide.c: Isatide I"sa*tide (?), n. (Chem.) A white crystalline substance obtained by the partial reduction of isatin. [Written also isatyde.]

isatin.c: Isatin I"sa*tin (?), n. [See Isatis.] (Chem.) An orange-red crystalline substance, C8H5NO2, obtained by the oxidation of indigo blue. It is also produced from certain derivatives of benzoic acid, and is one important source of artificial indigo. [Written also, less properly, isatine.]

isatis.c: Isatis ‖I"sa*tis (?; 277), n. [L., a kind of plant, Gr.? woad.] (Bot.) A genus of herbs, some species of which, especially the Isatis tinctoria, yield a blue dye similar to indigo; woad.

isatogen.c: Isatogen I*sat"o*gen (?), n. [Isatin + -gen.] (Chem.) A complex nitrogenous radical, C8H4NO2, regarded as the essential residue of a series of compounds, related to isatin, which easily pass by reduction to indigo blue. -- I*sat`o*gen"ic (#), a.

isatropic.c: Isatropic I`sa*trop"ic (?), a. [Is- + atropine.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from atropine, and isomeric with cinnamic acid.

ischiadic.c: Ischiadic Is`chi*ad"ic (ĭs`kĭ*ăd"ĭk), a. [L. ischiadicus, Gr. 'ischiadoko`s, fr. 'ischi`on the hip joint, hip or loin. Cf. Sciatic.] (Anat.) Ischial. [R.]

ischial.c: Ischial Is"chi*al (ĭs"kĭ*ail), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the ischium or hip; ischiac; ischiadic; ischiatic.

ischiocapsular.c: Ischiocapsular Is`chi*o*cap"su*lar (?; 135) a. [Ischium + capsular.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the ischium and the capsule of the hip joint; as, the ischiocapsular ligament.

ischiocerite.c: Ischiocerite Is`chi*o*ce"rite (?), n. [Gr. 'ischi`on the hip + ke`ras a horn.] (Zool.) The third joint or the antennæ of the Crustacea.

ischium.c: Ischium Ischion { ‖Is"chi*on (?), ‖Is"chi*um (?), } n. [L., Gr. 'ischi`on.] 1. (Anat.) The ventral and posterior of the three principal bones composing either half of the pelvis; seat bone; the huckle bone.

ischiopodite.c: Ischiopodite Is`chi*op"o*dite (?), n. [Gr. 'ischi`on the hip joint +?,?, foot.] (Zool.) The third joint of the typical appendages of Crustacea.

ischiorectal.c: Ischiorectal Is`chi*o*rec"tal (?), a. [Ischium + rectal.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the region between the rectum and ishial tuberosity.

ischuretic.c: Ischuretic Is`chu*ret"ic (?), a. Having the quality of relieving ischury. -- n. An ischuretic medicine.

ischury.c: Ischury Is"chu*ry (?), n. [L. ischuria, Gr.?;? to hold, check +? urine: cf. F. ischurie.] (Med.) A retention or suppression of urine.

isentropic.c: Isentropic I`sen*trop"ic (?), a. [Is- + entropy + -ic.] (Physics) Having equal entropy.

isethionic.c: Isethionic I*seth`i*on"ic (?), a. [Is- + ethionic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid, HO.C2H4.SO3H, obtained as an oily or crystalline substance, by the action of sulphur trioxide on alcohol or ether. It is derivative of sulphuric acid.

ish.c: -ish -ish (?). [AS. -isc; akin to G. -isch, OHG. -isc, Goth. & Dan. -isk, Gr.?. Cf. -esque.] A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

-ish -ish. [OE. -issen, fr. F. -is, -iss- (found in the present particle, etc., of certain verbs, as finir to finish, fleurir to flourish), corresponding to L. -escere, an inchoative ending.] A verb ending, originally appearing in certain verbs of French origin; as, abolish, cherish, finish, furnish, garnish, impoverish.

ishmaelite.c: Ishmaelite Ish"ma*el*ite (?), n. 1. A descendant of Ishmael (the son of Abraham and Hagar), of whom it was said, “His hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him.” Gen. xvi. 12.

ishmaelitish.c: Ishmaelitish Ish"ma*el*i`tish (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or resembling, an Ishmaelite or the Ishmaelites.

isiac.c: Isiac I"si*ac (?), a. [L. Isiacus, Gr.?, fr.?.] Pertaining to the goddess Isis; as, Isiac mysteries.

isidorian.c: Isidorian Is`i*do"ri*an (?), a. Pertaining, or ascribed, to Isidore; as, the Isidorian decretals, a spurious collection of decretals published in the ninth century.

isinglass.c: Isinglass I"sin*glass (?), n. [Prob. corrupted fr. D. huizenblas (akin to G. hausenblase), lit., bladder of the huso, or large sturgeon; huizen sturgeon + blas bladder. Cf. Bladder, Blast a gust of wind.]

isis.c: Isis I"sis (?), n. [L., the goddess Isis, fr. Gr.?.]

islam.c: Islam Is"lam (?), prop. n. [Ar. islām obedience to the will of God, submission, humbling one's self, resigning one's self to the divine disposal. Cf. Moslem.]

islamism.c: Islamism Is"lam*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. islamisme.] The faith, doctrines, or religious system of the Muslims; same as Islam, but less commonly used.

islamitic.c: Islamitic Is`lam*it"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to Islam; Islamic; Muslim.

islamize.c: Islamize Is"lam*ize (?), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Islamized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Islamizing (?).] To conform, or cause to conform, to the religion of Islam.

island.c: Island Is"land (?), n. [OE. iland, yland, AS. īgland,?gland,?glond; īg,?g, island + land, lond, land. AS. īg,?g, is akin to AS. eá water, river, OHG.?uwa, G. au meadow, Icel. ey island, Dan. & Sw. ö, Goth. ahwa a stream, water, L. aqua water. The s is due to confusion with isle. Cf. Ait, Eyot, Ewer, Aquatic.]
Island Is"land (?), v. t. 1. To cause to become or to resemble an island; to make an island or islands of; to isle. Shelley.

islander.c: Islander Is"land*er (?), n. An inhabitant of an island.

islandy.c: Islandy Is"land*y (?), a. Of or pertaining to islands; full of islands. Cotgrave.

isle.c: Isle Isle (?), n. [OF. isle, F. île, L. insula; cf. Lith. sala. Cf. Insulate.]
Isle Isle, v. t. To cause to become an island, or like an island; to surround or encompass; to island. [Poetic]

islet.c: Islet Is"let (?), n. [OF. islette (cf. F. îlot), dim. of isle.] A little island.

ism.c: -ism -ism (?). [F. -isme, or L. -ismus, Gr.?.] A suffix indicating an act, a process, the result of an act or a process, a state; also, a characteristic (as a theory, doctrine, idiom, etc.); as, baptism, galvanism, organism, hypnotism, socialism, sensualism, Anglicism.
Ism Ism, n. [See ism, above.] A doctrine or theory; especially, a wild or visionary theory. E. Everett.

ismaelite.c: Ismaelite Ismaelian { Is`ma*e"li*an (?), Is"ma*el*ite (?), } n. (Eccl.) One of a sect of Muslims who followed the practices of the family of Mohammed ben Ismael, of the house of Ali.

isobar.c: Isobar I"so*bar (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? weight.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting or marking places upon the surface of the earth where height of the barometer reduced to sea level is the same either at a given time, or for a certain period (mean height), as for a year; an isopiestic line. [Written also isobare.]

isobaric.c: Isobaric I`so*bar"ic (?), a. (Phys. Geog.) Denoting equal pressure; as, an isobaric line; specifically, of or pertaining to isobars.

isobarism.c: Isobarism I"so*bar*ism (?), n. The quality or state of being equal in weight, especially in atmospheric pressure. Also, the theory, method, or application of isobaric science.

isobarometric.c: Isobarometric I`so*bar`o*met"ric (?), a. [Iso + barometric.] (Phys. Geog.) Indicating equal barometric pressure.

isobathytherm.c: Isobathytherm I`so*bath"y*therm (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? deep +? heat.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting the points on the surface of the earth where a certain temperature is found at the same depth.

isobathythermic.c: Isobathythermic I`so*bath"y*ther"mic (?), a. Of or pertaining to an isobathytherm; possessing or indicating the same temperature at the same depth.

isobront.c: Isobront I"so*bront (ī"so*brŏnt), n. [Iso- + Gr. bronth` thunder.] (Meteor.) An imaginary line, or a line on a chart, marking the simultaneous development of a thunderstorm, as noted by observing the time when the thunder is heard at different places.

isocephalism.c: Isocephalism I`so*ceph"a*lism (?), n. [From Gr.? like-headed. See Iso-, and Cephalon.] (Art) A peculiarity in the design of bas-relief by which the heads of human figures are kept at the same height from the ground, whether the personages are seated, standing, or mounted on horseback; -- called also isokephaleia.

isochasm.c: Isochasm I"so*chasm (?), n. [Iso- + chasm.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting places on the earth's surface at which there is the same mean frequency of auroras.

isochasmic.c: Isochasmic I`so*chas"mic (?), a. Indicating equal auroral display; as, an isochasmic line.

isocheim.c: Isocheim I"so*cheim (ī"so*kīm), n. [Iso- + Gr.?,?, winter.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting places on the earth having the same mean winter temperature. Cf. Isothere.

isochimal.c: Isochimal Isocheimal { I`so*chei"mal, I`so*chi"mal } (?), a. Pertaining to, having the nature of, or making, isocheims; as, an isocheimal line; an isocheimal chart.

isochimenal.c: Isochimenal Isocheimenal { I`so*chei"me*nal (?), I`so*chi"me*nal } a. The same as Isocheimal.

isocheimic.c: Isocheimic I`so*chei"mic (?), a. The same as Isocheimal.

isochimene.c: Isochimene I`so*chi"mene (?), n. The same as Isocheim.

isochor.c: Isochor I"so*chor (ī"so*kôr), n. [Iso- + Gr. xhw`ra space.] (Physics) A line upon a thermodynamic diagram so drawn as to represent the pressures corresponding to changes of temperature when the volume of the gas operated on is constant. -- I`so*chor"ic (#), a.

isochromatic.c: Isochromatic I`so*chro*mat"ic (?), a. [Iso- + chromatic.] (Opt.) Having the same color; connecting parts having the same color, as lines drawn through certain points in experiments on the chromatic effects of polarized light in crystals.

isochronal.c: Isochronal I*soch"ro*nal (?), a. [See Isochronous.] Uniform in time; of equal time; performed in equal times; recurring at regular intervals; as, isochronal vibrations or oscillations.

isochronism.c: Isochronism I*soch"ro*nism (?), n. The state or quality of being isochronous.

isochronize.c: Isochronize I*soch"ro*nize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. -nized; p. pr. & vb. n. -nizing.] [See Isochronous.] To make, or tend to make (the motion of a moving body), uniform in rate of rotation, or in frequency of vibration.

isochronon.c: Isochronon I*soch"ro*non (?), n. [NL. See Isochronous.] A clock that is designed to keep very accurate time.

isochronous.c: Isochronous I*soch"ro*nous (?), a. [Gr.?; 'i`sos equal +? time.] Same as Isochronal.

isochroous.c: Isochroous I*soch"ro*ous (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? color.] Having the same tint or color throughout; uniformly or evenly colored.

isoclinic.c: Isoclinic Isoclinal { I`so*cli"nal (?), I`so*clin"ic (?), } a. [Iso- + Gr.? to incline.] Of or pertaining to, or indicating, equality of inclination or dip; having equal inclination or dip.

isocrymal.c: Isocrymal I`so*cry"mal (?), a. (Phys. Geog.) Pertaining to, having the nature of, or illustrating, an isocryme; as, an isocrymal line; an isocrymal chart.

isocryme.c: Isocryme I"so*cryme (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? cold.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean temperature in the coldest month of the year.

isocyanic.c: Isocyanic I`so*cy*an"ic (?), a. [Iso- + cyanic.] (Chem.) Designating an acid isomeric with cyanic acid.

isocyanuric.c: Isocyanuric I`so*cy`a*nu"ric (?), a. [Iso- + cyanuric.] (Chem.) Designating, or pertaining to, an acid isomeric with cyanuric acid, and called also fulminuric acid. See under Fulminuric.

isodiabatic.c: Isodiabatic I`so*di`a*bat"ic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? to pass through.] (Physics) Pertaining to the reception or the giving out of equal quantities of heat by a substance. Rankine.

isodimorphism.c: Isodimorphism I`so*di*mor"phism (?), n. Isomorphism between the two forms severally of two dimorphous substances.

isodimorphous.c: Isodimorphous I`so*di*mor"phous (?), a. [Iso- + dimorphous.] Having the quality of isodimorphism.

isodrome.c: Isodrome I"so*drome (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? course.] (Nav.) A method of moving a fleet from one formation to another, the direction usually being changed eight points (90°), by means of paths of equal length for each ship. It is prohibited in the United States navy.

isodulcite.c: Isodulcite I`so*dul"cite (?), n. [Iso- + dulcite.] (Chem.) A white, crystalline, sugarlike substance, obtained by the decomposition of certain glucosides, and intermediate in nature between the hexacid alcohols (dulcite, mannite, etc.) and the glucoses.

isodynamic.c: Isodynamic I`so*dy*nam"ic (?), a. [Iso- + dynamic.] Of, pertaining to, having, or denoting, equality of force.

isodynamous.c: Isodynamous I`so*dy"na*mous (?), a. [Gr.?. See Isodynamic.] Of equal force or size.

isogeotherm.c: Isogeotherm I`so*ge"o*therm (?), n. [Iso- + Gr. gh^ the earth + qe`rmh heat.] (Phys. Geog.) A line or curved surface passing beneath the earth's surface through points having the same mean temperature.

isogeothermic.c: Isogeothermic Isogeothermal { I`so*ge`o*ther"mal (?), I`so*ge`o*ther"mic (?), } a. Pertaining to, having the nature of, or marking, isogeotherms; as, an isogeothermal line or surface; as isogeothermal chart. -- n. An isogeotherm.

isogonic.c: Isogonic I`so*gon"ic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. gwni`a angle.] Pertaining to, or noting, equal angles.

isogonism.c: Isogonism I*sog"o*nism (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? offspring, generative parts.] (Zool.) The quality of having similar sexual zooids or gonophores and dissimilar hydrants; -- said of certain hydroids.

isographic.c: Isographic I`so*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to isography.

isography.c: Isography I*sog"ra*phy (?), n. [Iso- + -graphy.] Imitation of another's handwriting.

isohyetose.c: Isohyetose I`so*hy"e*tose` (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. "yeto`s rain.] (Phys. Geog.) Of or pertaining to lines connecting places on the earth's surface which have the same mean annual rainfall. -- n. An isohyetose line; called also isohyet.

isolable.c: Isolable I"so*la*ble (?), a. [See Isolate.] (Chem.) Capable of being isolated, or of being obtained in a pure state; as, gold is isolable.

isolate.c: Isolate I"so*late (ī"so*lāt or īs"o*lāt; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Isolated (ī"so*lā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Isolating (ī"so*lā`tĭng).] [It. isolato, p. p. of isolare to isolate, fr. isola island, L. insula. See 2d Isle, and cf. Insulate.]

isolated.c: Isolated I"so*la`ted (ī"so*lā`tĕd), a. Placed or standing alone; detached; separated from others.

isolatedly.c: Isolatedly I"so*la`ted*ly (?), adv. In an isolated manner.

isolation.c: Isolation I`so*la"tion (ī`so*lā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. isolation.] The act of isolating, or the state of being isolated; insulation; separation; loneliness. Milman.

isolator.c: Isolator I"so*la`tor (ī"so*lā`tẽr or īs"o*lā`tẽr), n. One who, or that which, isolates.

isologous.c: Isologous I*sol"o*gous (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. lo`gos proportion.] (Chem.) Having similar proportions, similar relations, or similar differences of composition; -- said specifically of groups or series which differ by a constant difference; as, ethane, ethylene, and acetylene, or their analogous compounds, form an isologous series.

isomer.c: Isomer I"so*mer (ī"so*mẽr), n. [See Isomeric.] (Chem.) A compound which is isomeric with another body or compound; a compound having the same chemical composition as another compound; a member of an isomeric series.

isomere.c: Isomere I"so*mere (?), n. [Iso- + -mere.] (Zool.) 1. A homologous or corresponding part or segment.

isomerism.c: Isomerism I*som"er*ism (?), n. (Chem.) The state, quality, or relation, of two or more isomeric substances.

isomeromorphism.c: Isomeromorphism I`so*mer`o*mor"phism (?), n. [Isomer + Gr. morfh` form + -ism.] (Crystallog.) Isomorphism between substances that are isomeric.

isometrical.c: Isometrical Isometric { I`so*met"ric (?), I`so*met"ric*al (?), } a. [Iso- + Gr. me`tron measure.] 1. Pertaining to, or characterized by, equality of measure.

isomorph.c: Isomorph I"so*morph (?), n. [See Isomorphous.] 1. A substance which is similar to another in crystalline form and composition.

isomorphism.c: Isomorphism I`so*mor"phism (?), n. [Cf. F. isomorphisme.] 1. (Crystallog.) A similarity of crystalline form between substances of similar composition, as between the sulphates of barium (BaSO4) and strontium (SrSO4). It is sometimes extended to include similarity of form between substances of unlike composition, which is more properly called homœomorphism.

isomorphous.c: Isomorphous I`so*mor"phous (?), a. [Iso- + -morphous.] Having the quality of isomorphism.

isonandra.c: Isonandra I`so*nan"dra (?), prop. n. [Iso- + Gr.?,?, a man, male.] (Bot.) A genus of sapotaceous trees of India. Isonandra Gutta is the principal source of gutta-percha.

isonephelic.c: Isonephelic I`so*ne*phel"ic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? a cloud.] (Phys. Geog.) Having, or indicating, an equal amount of cloudiness for a given period; as, isonephelic regions; an isonephelic line.

isonicotine.c: Isonicotine I`so*nic"o*tine (?), n. [Iso- + nicotine.] (Chem.) A crystalline, nitrogenous base, C10H14N2, isomeric with nicotine.

isonicotinic.c: Isonicotinic I`so*nic`o*tin"ic (?), a. (Chem.) (a) Pertaining to, or derived from, isonicotine. (b) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid isomeric with nicotinic acid.

isonitroso.c: Isonitroso- I`so*ni*tro"so- (?). [Iso- + nitroso-.] (Chem.) A combining form (also used adjectively), signifying: Pertaining to, or designating, the characteristic, nitrogenous radical, NOH, called the isonitroso group.

isonomic.c: Isonomic I`so*nom"ic (?), a. [Gr.?; 'i`sos equal + no`mos law.] The same, or equal, in law or right; one in kind or origin; analogous; similar. Dana.

isonomy.c: Isonomy I*son"o*my (?), n. [Gr.?: cf. F. isonomie. See Isonomic.] Equal law or right; equal distribution of rights and privileges; similarity.

isopathy.c: Isopathy I*sop"a*thy (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? suffering.] (Med.) (a) The system which undertakes to cure a disease by means of the virus of the same disease. (b) The theory of curing a diseased organ by eating the analogous organ of a healthy animal. Mayne. (c) The doctrine that the power of therapeutics is equal to that of the causes of disease.

isopepsin.c: Isopepsin I`so*pep"sin (?), n. [Iso- + pepsin.] (Physiol. Chem.) Pepsin modified by exposure to a temperature of from 40° to 60° C.

isoperimetrical.c: Isoperimetrical I`so*per`i*met"ric*al (?), a. [Gr.?;? equal +? circumference: cf. F. isopérimètre. See Perimeter.] (Geom.) Having equal perimeters of circumferences; as, isoperimetrical figures or bodies.

isoperimetry.c: Isoperimetry I`so*per*im"e*try (?), n. (Geom.) The science of figures having equal perimeters or boundaries.

isopiestic.c: Isopiestic I`so*pi*es"tic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? to press.] (Thermodynamics) Having equal pressure.

isopleura.c: Isopleura ‖I`so*pleu"ra (?), n. pl. [NL. See Iso-, and Pleura.] (Zool.) A subclass of Gastropoda, in which the body is symmetrical, the right and left sides being equal.

isopod.c: Isopod I"so*pod (?), a. (Zool.) Having the legs similar in structure; belonging to the Isopoda. -- n. One of the Isopoda.

isopoda.c: Isopoda ‖I*sop"o*da (?), n. pl. [NL. See Iso-, and -poda.] (Zool.) An order of sessile-eyed Crustacea, usually having seven pairs of legs, which are all similar in structure.

isopodiform.c: Isopodiform I`so*pod"i*form (?), a. [Isopod + -form.] (Zool.) Having the shape of an isopod; -- said of the larvæ of certain insects.

isopogonous.c: Isopogonous I`so*pog"o*nous (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? beard.] (Zool.) Having the two webs equal in breadth; -- said of feathers.

isoprene.c: Isoprene I"so*prene (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Chem.) An oily, volatile unsaturated hydrocarbon (C5H8), obtained by the distillation of caoutchouc or gutta-percha, and used to make synthetic rubber by polymerization. In organic chemistry, it is viewed conceptually as the building block of the terpene series of hydrocarbons.

isopycnic.c: Isopycnic I`so*pyc"nic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. pykno`s dense.] (Physics) Having equal density, as different regions of a medium; passing through points at which the density is equal; as, an isopycnic line or surface.
Isopycnic I`so*pyc"nic, n. (Physics) A line or surface passing through those points in a medium, at which the density is the same.

isorcin.c: Isorcin I*sor"cin (?), n. [Iso- + orcin.] (Chem.) A crystalline hydrocarbon derivative, metameric with orcin, but produced artificially; -- called also cresorcin.

isorropic.c: Isorropic I`sor*rop"ic (?), a. [Gr. 'iso`rropos in equipoise; 'i`sos equal + "roph` downward inclination or momentum.] Of equal value.

isosceles.c: Isosceles I*sos"ce*les (?), a. [L., fr. Gr.?; 'i`sos equal +? leg.] (Geom.) Having two legs or sides that are equal; -- said of a triangle.

isospondyli.c: Isospondyli ‖I`so*spon"dy*li (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'i`sos equal +?,?, a vertebra.] (Zool.) An extensive order of fishes, including the salmons, herrings, and many allied forms.

isospondylous.c: Isospondylous I`so*spon"dy*lous (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Isospondyli; having the anterior vertebræ separate and normal.

isospore.c: Isospore I"so*spore (?), n. (Biol.) (a) One of the spores produced by an isosporous organism. (b) A zygospore.

isosporic.c: Isosporic I`so*spor"ic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. spo`ros fruit.] (Bot.) Producing but one kind of spore, as the ferns and Equiseta. Cf. Heterosporic.

isosporous.c: Isosporous I*sos"po*rous (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. spo`ros fruit.] (Biol.) Producing but one kind of spore, as the ferns.

isostasy.c: Isostasy I*sos"ta*sy (?), n. [See Iso-; Stasis.] The state or quality of being isostatic. Specif. (Geol.), general equilibrium in the earth's crust, supposed to be maintained by the yielding or flow of rock material beneath the surface under gravitative stress. By the theory of isostasy each unit column of the earth, from surface to center, has approximately the same weight, and the continents stand higher than the ocean beds chiefly because the material of the crust has there less density.

isostatic.c: Isostatic I`so*stat"ic (?), a. [Iso- + static.] (Physics & Geol.) Subjected to equal pressure from every side; being in hydrostatic equilibrium, as a body submerged in a liquid at rest; pertaining to, or characterized by, isostasy.

isostemonous.c: Isostemonous I`so*stem"o*nous (?), a. [Iso- + Gr. sth`mwn thread.] (Bot.) Having exactly as many stamens as petals.

isostemony.c: Isostemony I`so*stem"o*ny (?), n. (Bot.) The quality or state of being isostemonous.

isosulphocyanate.c: Isosulphocyanate I`so*sul`pho*cy"a*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of isosulphocyanic acid.

isosulphocyanic.c: Isosulphocyanic I`so*sul`pho*cy*an"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, HNCS, isomeric with sulphocyanic acid.

isotheral.c: Isotheral I*soth"er*al (?), a. Having the nature of an isothere; indicating the distribution of temperature by means of an isothere; as, an isotheral chart or line.

isothere.c: Isothere I"so*there (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? summer,? to heat.] (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean summer temperature.

isotherm.c: Isotherm I"so*therm (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? heat, fr.? hot.] 1. (Phys. Geog.) A line connecting or marking points on the earth's surface having the same temperature. This may be the temperature for a given time of observation, or the mean temperature for a year or other period. Also, a similar line based on the distribution of temperature in the ocean.

isothermal.c: Isothermal I`so*ther"mal (?), a. [Cf. F. isotherme.] (a) Relating to equality of temperature, or an isotherm. (b) (Phys. Geog.) Having reference to the geographical distribution of temperature, as exhibited by means of isotherms; as, an isothermal line; an isothermal chart.

isothermobath.c: Isothermobath I`so*ther"mo*bath (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? hot +? depth.] (Phys. Geog) A line drawn through points of equal temperature in a vertical section of the ocean.

isothermobathic.c: Isothermobathic I`so*ther`mo*bath"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to an isothermobath; possessing or indicating equal temperatures in a vertical section, as of the ocean.

isotherombrose.c: Isotherombrose I*soth`er*om"brose (?), n. [Iso- + Gr. qe`ros summer + 'o`mbros rain.] (Phys. Geog) A line connecting or marking points on the earth's surface, which have the same mean summer rainfall.

isotonic.c: Isotonic I`so*ton"ic (?), a. [Iso- + tonic.] 1. Having or indicating, equal tones, or tension.

isotrimorphism.c: Isotrimorphism I`so*tri*mor"phism (?), n. [Iso- + Gr.? thrice + morfh` form.] Isomorphism between the three forms, severally, of two trimorphous substances.

isotrimorphous.c: Isotrimorphous I`so*tri*mor"phous (?), a. Having the quality of isotrimorphism; isotrimorphic.

isotropic.c: Isotropic I`so*trop"ic (?), a. [Iso- + Gr.? a turning, fr.? to turn.] (Physics) Having the same properties in all directions; specifically, equally elastic in all directions.

isotropy.c: Isotropy I*sot"ro*py (?), n. (Physics) Uniformity of physical properties in all directions in a body; absence of all kinds of polarity; specifically, equal elasticity in all directions.

isouric.c: Isouric I`so*u"ric (?), a. [Iso- + uric.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid, isomeric with uric acid.

israelite.c: Israelite Is"ra*el*ite (?), n. [L. Israëlites, Gr.?, fr.?,?, Israel, Heb. Yisrāēl, i. e., champion of God; sārāh to fight + ēl God.] A descendant of Israel, or Jacob; a Hebrew; a Jew.

israelitish.c: Israelitish Israelitic { Is`ra*el*it"ic (?), Is"ra*el*i`tish (?), } a. Of or pertaining to Israel, or to the Israelites; Jewish; Hebrew.

issuably.c: Issuably Is"su*a*bly (?), adv. In an issuable manner; by way of issue; as, to plead issuably.

issuance.c: Issuance Is"su*ance (ĭsh"u*ains), n. The act of issuing, or giving out; as, the issuance of an order; the issuance of rations, and the like.

issuant.c: Issuant Is"su*ant (ĭsh"u*aint), a. (Her.) Issuing or coming up; -- a term used to express a charge or bearing rising or coming out of another.

issue.c: Issue Is"sue (ĭsh"u), n. [OF. issue, eissue, F. issue, fr. OF. issir, eissir, to go out, L. exire; ex out of, from + ire to go, akin to Gr. 'ie`nai, Skr. i, Goth. iddja went, used as prefect of gaggan to go. Cf. Ambition, Count a nobleman, Commence, Errant, Exit, Eyre, Initial, Yede went.]
Issue Is"sue, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Issued (ĭsh"ud); p. pr. & vb. n. Issuing.]
Issue Is"sue (ĭsh"u), v. t. 1. To send out; to put into circulation; as, to issue notes from a bank.

issueless.c: Issueless Is"sue*less, a. Having no issue or progeny; childless. “The heavens... have left me issueless.” Shak.

issuer.c: Issuer Is"su*er (ĭsh"u*ẽr), n. One who issues, emits, or publishes.

ist.c: -ist -ist (ĭsh"u*ĭst). [Gr.?: cf. F. -iste.] A noun suffix denoting an agent, or doer, one who practices, a believer in; as, theorist, one who theorizes; socialist, one who holds to socialism; sensualist, one given to sensuality.
Is't Is't (?). A contraction of is it.

isthmian.c: Isthmian Isth"mi*an (?), a. [L. Isthmius, Gr.?. See Isthmus.] Of or pertaining to an isthmus, especially to the Isthmus of Corinth, in Greece.

isthmus.c: Isthmus Isth"mus (?; 277), n.; pl. Isthmuses (#). [L. isthmus, Gr. 'isqmo`s a neck, a neck of land between two seas, an isthmus, especially the Isthmus of Corinth; prob. from the root of 'ie`nai to go; cf. Icel. eið isthmus. See Issue.] (Geog.) A neck or narrow slip of land by which two continents are connected, or by which a peninsula is united to the mainland; as, the Isthmus of Panama; the Isthmus of Suez, etc.

isuret.c: Isuret I*su"ret (?), n. [Iso- + urea.] (Chem.) An artificial nitrogenous base, isomeric with urea, and forming a white crystalline substance; -- called also isuretine.

it.c: It It (ĭt), pron. [OE. it, hit, AS. hit; cf. D. het. √181. See He.] The neuter pronoun of the third person, corresponding to the masculine pronoun he and the feminine she, and having the same plural (they, their or theirs, them).

itacism.c: Itacism I"ta*cism (?), n. [Cf. F. itacisme. See Etacism, and cf. Iotacism.] (Greek Gram.) Pronunciation of η (eta) as the modern Greeks pronounce it, that is, like e in the English word be. This was the pronunciation advocated by Reuchlin and his followers, in opposition to the etacism of Erasmus. See Etacism.

itacist.c: Itacist I"ta*cist (?), n. [Cf. F. itaciste.] One who is in favor of itacism.

itacolumite.c: Itacolumite It`a*col"u*mite (?), n. [From Itacolumi, a mountain of Brazil.] (Min.) A laminated, granular, siliceous rocks, often occurring in regions where the diamond is found.

itaconic.c: Itaconic It`a*con"ic (?), a. [From aconitic, by transposition of the letters.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C5H6O4, which is obtained as a white crystalline substance by decomposing aconitic and other organic acids.

itala.c: Itala It"a*la (?), n. [Fem. of L. Italus Italian.] An early Latin version of the Scriptures (the Old Testament was translated from the Septuagint, and was also called the Italic version).

italian.c: Italian I*tal"ian (?), a. [Cf. F. italien, It. italiano. Cf. Italic.] Of or pertaining to Italy, or to its people or language.
Italian I*tal"ian, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of Italy.

italianate.c: Italianate I*tal"ian*ate (?), v. t. [Cf. It. italianare.] To render Italian, or conformable to Italian customs; to Italianize. [R.] Ascham.
Italianate I*tal"ian*ate (?), a. Italianized; Italianated. “Apish, childish, and Italianate.” Marlowe.

italianism.c: Italianism I*tal"ian*ism (?), n. 1. A word, phrase, or idiom, peculiar to the Italians; an Italicism.

italianize.c: Italianize I*tal"ian*ize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Italianized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Italianizing (?).] [Cf. F. italianiser, It. italianizzare.]

italic.c: Italic I*tal"ic (?), a. [L. Italicus: cf. F. italique. Cf. Italian.]

Italic I*tal"ic, n.; pl. Italics (?). (Print.) An Italic letter, character, or type (see Italic, a., 2.); -- often in the plural; as, the Italics are the author's. Italic letters are used to distinguish words for emphasis, importance, antithesis, etc. Also, collectively, Italic letters.

italicism.c: Italicism I*tal"i*cism (?), n. 1. A phrase or idiom peculiar to the Italian language; to Italianism.

italicize.c: Italicize I*tal"i*cize (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Italicized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Italicizing (?).] To print in Italic characters; to underline written letters or words with a single line; as, to Italicize a word; Italicizes too much.

ita.c: Ita palm I"ta palm` (?). (Bot.) A magnificent species of palm (Mauritia flexuosa), growing near the Orinoco. The natives eat its fruit and buds, drink its sap, and make thread and cord from its fiber.

itch.c: Itch Itch (ĭch), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Itched (ĭcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Itching.] [OE. icchen, ȝicchen, AS. giccan; akin to D. jeuken, joken, G. jucken, OHG. jucchen.]

Itch Itch, n. 1. (Med.) An eruption of small, isolated, acuminated vesicles, produced by the entrance of a parasitic mite (the Sarcoptes scabei), and attended with itching. It is transmissible by contact.

itchiness.c: Itchiness Itch"i*ness (?), n. The state of being itchy.

itchy.c: Itchy Itch"y (?), a. 1. Infected with the itch. Cowper.

ite.c: -ite -ite (?). [From Gr.?,?.] 1. A suffix denoting one of a party, a sympathizer with or adherent of, and the like, and frequently used in ridicule; as, a Millerite; a Benthamite.

itelmen.c: Itelmen Itelmen (?), prop. n. 1. (Ethnol.) An aboriginal tribe inhabiting the southern part of the Kamchatka peninsula; called also Kamchadal and Kamtschadal.

item.c: item i"tem (?), adv. [L. See Iterate.] Also; as an additional article.
Item I"tem, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Itemed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Iteming.] To make a note or memorandum of.

itemize.c: Itemize I"tem*ize (?), v. t. To state in items, or by particulars; to list each item in a collection under discussion; as, to itemize the cost of a railroad. [Local, U. S.]

iter.c: Iter ‖I"ter (?), n. [L. See Eyre.] (Anat.) A passage; esp., the passage between the third and fourth ventricles in the brain; the aqueduct of Sylvius.

iterable.c: Iterable It"er*a*ble (?), a. [L. iterabilis. See Iterate.] Capable of being iterated or repeated. [Obs.]

iterant.c: Iterant It"er*ant (?), a. [L. iterans, p. pr. of iterare.] Repeating; iterating; as, an iterant echo. Bacon.

iterate.c: Iterate It"er*ate (ĭt"ẽr*at), a. [L. iteratus, p. p. of iterare to repeat, fr. iterum again, prop. a compar. from the stem of is he, that; cf. L. ita so, item likewise, also, Skr. itara other, iti thus. Cf. Identity, Item.] Uttered or done again; repeated. [Obs.] Bp. Gardiner.
Iterate It"er*ate (ĭt"ẽr*āt), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Iterated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Iterating.] To utter or do a second time or many times; to repeat; as, to iterate advice.
Iterate It"er*ate (?), adv. By way of iteration.

iteration.c: Iteration It`er*a"tion (?), n. [L. iteratio.] 1. Recital or performance a second time; repetition. Bacon.

iterative.c: Iterative It"er*a*tive (?), a. [L. iterativus: cf. F. itératif.] Repeating. Cotgrave. -- It"er*a*tive*ly, adv.

ithyphallic.c: Ithyphallic Ith`y*phal"lic (?), a. [L. ithyphallicus, fr. ithyphallus, Gr.?, membrum virile erectum, or a figure thereof carried in the festivals of Bacchus.] Lustful; lewd; salacious; indecent; obscene.

itineracy.c: Itineracy I*tin"er*a*cy (i*tĭn"ẽr*ȧ*sy̆), n. The act or practice of itinerating; itinerancy.

itinerant.c: Itinerant I*tin"er*ant (i*tĭn"ẽr*aint), a. [LL. itinerans, -antis, p. pr. of itinerare to make a journey, fr. L. iter, itineris, a walk, way, journey. See Errant, Issue.] Passing or traveling about a country; going or preaching on a circuit; wandering; not settled; as, an itinerant preacher; an itinerant peddler.
Itinerant I*tin"er*ant, a. One who travels from place to place, particularly a preacher; one who is unsettled.

itinerantly.c: Itinerantly I*tin"er*ant*ly (i*tĭn"ẽr*aint*ly̆), adv. In an itinerant manner.

itinerary.c: itinerary i*tin"er*a*ry (i*tĭn"ẽr*a*ry̆), a. [L. itinerarius: cf. F. itinéraire. See Itinerant.] Itinerant; traveling; passing from place to place; done on a journey.

Itinerary I*tin"er*a*ry, n.; pl. Itineraries (i*tĭn"ẽr*a*rĭz). [L. itinerarium: cf. F. itinéraire. See Itinerary, a.] 1. An account of travels, or a register of places and distances as a guide to travelers; as, the Itinerary of Antoninus.

itinerate.c: itinerate i*tin"er*ate (i*tĭn"ẽr*āt). v. i. [imp. & p. p. Itinerated (i*tĭn"ẽr*ā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Itinerating (i*tĭn"ẽr*ā`tĭng).] [LL. itineratus, p. p. of itinerari, itinerare. See Itinerant.] To wander without a settled habitation; to travel from place or on a circuit, particularly for the purpose of preaching, lecturing, etc.

itis.c: -itis -i"tis (ī"tĭs), [Gr. 'i`tis, orig, fem. adjective suffix.] A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis, nephritis.

its.c: Its Its (ĭts), poss. pron. Possessive form of the pronoun it. See It.

itself.c: itself it*self" (ĭt*sĕlf"), pron. The neuter reflexive pronoun of It; as, the thing is good in itself; it stands by itself.

itzibu.c: Itzibu It"zi*bu (ĭt"sĭ*bōo), n. [Jap. ichibu.] (Numis.) A silver coin of Japan, worth about thirty-four cents. [Written also itzebu, ichebu, itcheboo, etc.]

iulidan.c: Iulidan I*u"li*dan (?), n. [See Iulus.] (Zool.) One of the Iulidæ, a family of myriapods, of which the genus Iulus is the type. See Iulus.

iulus.c: Iulus ‖I*u"lus (?), n. [L., down, Gr.? down, centipede.] (Zool.) A genus of chilognathous myriapods. The body is long and round, consisting of numerous smooth, equal segments, each of which bears two pairs of short legs. It includes the galleyworms. See Chilognatha.

ivan.c: Ivan Ivanovitch I*van" I*van"o*vitch (?) prop. n. An ideal personification of the typical Russian or of the Russian people; -- used as “John Bull” is used for the typical Englishman.

ive.c: I've I've (?) contrac. Colloquial contraction of I have.
-ive -ive (?) suff. [L. -ivus.] An adjective suffix signifying relating or belonging to, of the nature of, tending to; as, affirmative, active, conclusive, corrective, diminutive.

ivied.c: Ivied I"vied (?), a. [From Ivy.] Overgrown with ivy.

ivoride.c: Ivoride I"vo*ride (?), n. A composition resembling ivory in appearance and used as a substitute for it.

ivory.c: Ivory I"vo*ry (ī"vo*ry̆), n.; pl. Ivories (#). [OE. ivori, F. ivoire, fr. L. eboreus made of ivory, fr. ebur, eboris, ivory, cf. Skr. ibha elephant. Cf. Eburnean.]

ivorybill.c: Ivory-bill ivorybill i"vo*ry*bill`, I"vo*ry-bill` (ī"vo*ry̆*bĭl`), n. (Zool.) A large, handsome, black-and-white North American woodpecker (Campephilus principalis), having a large, sharp, ivory-colored beak. Its general color is glossy black, with white secondaries, and a white dorsal stripe. The male has a large, scarlet crest. It is now rare, and found only in the Gulf States and Cuba.

ivorytype.c: Ivorytype I"vo*ry*type` (?), n. (Photog.) A picture produced by superposing a very light print, rendered translucent by varnish, and tinted upon the back, upon a stronger print, so as to give the effect of a photograph in natural colors; -- called also hellenotype. Knight.

ivy.c: Ivy I"vy (?), n.; pl. Ivies (#). [AS. īfig; akin to OHG. ebawi, ebah, G. epheu.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Hedera (Hedera helix), common in Europe. Its leaves are evergreen, dark, smooth, shining, and mostly five-pointed; the flowers yellowish and small; the berries black or yellow. The stem clings to walls and trees by rootlike fibers.

iwis.c: Iwis I*wis" (?), adv. Indeed; truly. See Ywis. [Written also iwys, iwisse, etc.] [Obs.] Ascham.

ixia.c: Ixia Ix"i*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? birdlime. So called because of the viscid nature of some of the species.] (Bot.) A South African bulbous plant of the Iris family, remarkable for the brilliancy of its flowers.

ixodes.c: Ixodes ‖Ix*o"des (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? like birdlime;? birdlime + e'i^dos form.] (Zool.) A genus of parasitic Acarina, which includes various species of ticks. See Tick, the insect.

ixodian.c: Ixodian Ix*o"di*an (?), n. (Zool.) A tick of the genus Ixodes, or the family Ixodidæ.

ixtli.c: Ixtli Ixtle { Ix"tle, Ix"tli } (ĭx"tle), n. 1. (Bot.) A Mexican name for a variety of Agave rigida, which furnishes a strong coarse fiber; also, the fiber itself, which is called also pita, and Tampico fiber. [Written also istle.]

ixtil.c: Ixtil Ixtle { Ix"tle Ix"til} (?), n. The fine, soft fiber of the bromeliaceous plant Bromelia sylvestris.

izard.c: Izard Iz"ard (?), n. (Zool.) A variety of the chamois found in the Pyrenees.

ize.c: -ize -ize (?) suff. [F. -iser, L. -izare, Gr.?.] A verb suffix signifying to make, to do, to practice; as, apologize, baptize, theorize, tyrannize.

izedi.c: Izedi Iz"e*di (?), n. One of an Oriental religious sect which worships Satan or the Devil.

izedism.c: Izedism Iz"e*dism (?), n. The religion of the Izedis.

izzard.c: Izzard Iz"zard (?), n. [Formerly ezed, prob. fr. F. et zéde and z.] The letter z; -- formerly so called.
